Kyunghoon Han
Categorification of Chemical Reactions
Categorification of Chemical Reactions:
a bottom-up tower from stoichiometry to quantum structure
Prepared for Chemical Reaction Networks in Hawai‘i 2026
Kyunghoon HAN 1,∗
1Department of Physics and Materials Science, University of Luxembourg, Luxembourg
City, Luxembourg
∗Correspondence: kyunghoon.h@gmail.com
Abstract
Chemistry is full of rules with exceptions. The octet rule, Hess’s Law,
detailed balance, and orbital symmetry selection rules all carry disclaimers that
must be memorised separately. These exceptions share a common cause: they
arise when a question belonging to a richer level of mathematical structure is
posed using the vocabulary of a simpler one — a level incompleteness.
This monograph makes the levels explicit. It constructs a canonical tower
of nine categorical levels spanning stoichiometry, thermochemistry, equilibrium,
kinetics, electron-pushing mechanisms, stereochemistry, potential energy sur-
faces, electronic structure, and all-particle quantum mechanics. The tower is
mathematically engineered bottom-up, at each stage by pairs of reactions that
are physically distinct yet indistinguishable at the previous level; the minimal
categorical extension resolving each such ambiguity is provably unique, certified
by a non-trivial cokernel in an automorphism exact sequence, and applied
to reaction networks recovers Feinberg’s deficiency theorems as homological
corollaries.
The exact tower has a perpendicular dimension: every machine-learning
model for chemistry — yield predictors, neural kinetic networks, equivariant
force fields, learned wavefunctions — is a morphism in the parametric Para-
enrichment of one specific tower level, with equivariance and thermodynamic
consistency following as universal properties rather than architectural choices,
and three architectural incompleteness results — Eyring, Wegscheider, and
topological output-type gaps — applying to the current published literature.
The framework descends to running code in the final chapter, which con-
structs an operational functor from a Para-enriched product of the first four
tower levels into the Kleisli category of the probabilistic sub-monad of Haskell
IO, instantiated as a working stochastic simulator of the Briggs–Rauscher
oscillating reaction — the first published Kleisli semantics of the Gillespie
next-reaction method and the first application of the Para construction outside
machine learning.
The passage to all-particle quantum mechanics — realising the Born–
Oppenheimer approximation as the classical limit of a continuous field of
C∗-algebras — remains the deepest open construction, with four candidate
conjectures, including Woolley–Primas, whose obstructions the framework
makes specific.

Acknowledgements
As a mathematician by training, I found chemistry difficult to study: the field is
full of exceptions to its rules, and the exceptions are typically presented as separate
facts to memorise rather than as consequences of any underlying structure. This
manuscript is the record of an effort to learn chemistry well enough that it would
make sense to me during my PhD in the Theoretical Chemical Physics group at the
University of Luxembourg.
The categorical structure developed here was first sketched in the group’s Theo-
retical Minimum sessions for incoming PhD students in 2021. From then to now,
my colleagues, the group leader Prof. Dr. Alexandre Tkatchenko, and my PhD
supervisor Dr. Joshua T. Berryman have shown extraordinary patience in helping
me understand the chemistry and physics of complex molecules. The phrase level in-
completeness, which threads through every chapter of this monograph, was suggested
by Prof. Tkatchenko.
Many colleagues absorbed the cost of my limited chemistry background along the
way. Dr. Ariadni Boziki took the time to walk me through how molecular vibrations
work; Dr. Miguel Gallegos showed me why chemical exceptions are interesting in
their own right; Sergio Suárez Dou gave me much-needed insight into the behaviour
of biomolecules. I thank Dr. Florian Brünig of the same group for his feedback on
the introductory chapter of this work.
Whatever errors and infelicities remain in the chemistry are entirely my own, and
despite the generous teaching of everyone listed above I remain, by professional
chemists’ standards, still learning the field.

§1. Introduction
§1.1. Rules, exceptions, and what they signal
Chemistry is a quantitative subject built on exact rules with long lists of exceptions.
Hess’s Law [1, 2, 3]; detailed balance, in both its physical-chemistry form [4, 5, 6, 7]
and its reaction-network form [8, 9, 10]; the Arrhenius equation [11, 12, 13]; the
Woodward–Hoffmann rules [14, 15, 16] — each is a sharp mathematical statement,
each holds “in most cases,” and the corrections are memorised separately from the
rules themselves. The position of this monograph is that chemistry’s rules sit at
definite mathematical levels; that the levels form a canonical ladder; and that the
principal class of exceptions to those rules is a level incompleteness, the use of tools
from one rung to answer a question that belongs to another.
A hydrogen atom in the reacting bond of an organic molecule replaced by deuterium
— twice the nuclear mass, the same electronic structure — slows the reaction, and the
ratio of the rate for the hydrogen-bearing compound to the rate for its deuterium
analogue is the primary kinetic isotope effect (kH/kD) [17, 18, 19, 20, 21]. Classical
transition-state theory [12, 22, 23, 13] computes this ratio from a Boltzmann factor
whose activation energy is shifted between isotopologues by the harmonic zero-
point-energy difference of the carbon–hydrogen and carbon–deuterium stretching
modes, and for hydrogen transfer at laboratory temperatures the resulting ratio
cannot exceed approximately seven [24, 25, 20]. The double mutant L546A/L754A
of soybean lipoxygenase-1, by contrast, gives kH/kD = 661 ± 27, essentially constant
across six temperatures from 5 to 50 ◦C [26] — nearly two orders of magnitude above
the textbook ceiling.
The factor of one hundred between the two values is not, despite appearances, the
signature of a tower-level mismatch. Both calculations live at the same geometric
level L5 (§8); they differ only in how much of that level’s data is actually used — a
barrier height and harmonic vibrations at the saddle in the textbook formula, versus
the full multidimensional potential surface, semiclassical tunnelling paths along it, and
vibronically nonadiabatic proton-coupled electron transfer in the complete calculation.
The L7 chapter (§10) records this case as a careful caveat: large kinetic isotope
effects do not, by themselves, force a higher tower level, even when they spectacularly
exceed textbook estimates. A different and sharper kind of incompleteness — in
which a question genuinely cannot be answered at one level because the structural
data required for it first appears at a higher one — is what motivates this monograph.
Three textbook examples of that kind, the cleanest available, are recorded next.
Three level incompletenesses, stated plainly
Spontaneity versus rate. Diamond is thermodynamically unstable relative
to graphite at all laboratory temperatures (∆G < 0), so the conversion is
spontaneous. Yet no observable conversion occurs on any human timescale.
“Spontaneous” is a thermodynamic statement about the sign of the free-energy
change; “immeasurably slow” is a kinetic statement about the activation barrier.
The confusion is not chemistry failing; it is two different questions being conflated.
13


## Page 14


Kyunghoon Han
Categorification of Chemical Reactions
Rate law versus mechanism. Under excess nucleophile, the bimolecular
substitution of CH3Br by OH– becomes pseudo-first-order in substrate, and its
rate constant can be tuned to match that of the genuinely first-order solvolysis of
(CH3)3CBr. Kinetically the two reactions are then indistinguishable — yet the
solvolysis yields a racemic mixture at the carbon centre while the bimolecular
substitution inverts configuration. The distinction belongs to mechanism: a
concerted backside displacement against a stepwise unimolecular ionisation, two
electron-pushing pathways that no rate law sees.
Geometry versus electronic structure.
The retinal chromophore in
rhodopsin isomerises from 11-cis to all-trans in approximately 200 fs after pho-
ton absorption — a timescale no model of thermal barrier-crossing on a single
potential-energy surface can reproduce [27, 28, 29]. The reaction passes through
a conical intersection: a seam of nuclear configurations where two electronic
surfaces become degenerate and the Born–Oppenheimer approximation breaks
down. This is a phenomenon of electronic topology, invisible to any description
that works with a single smooth energy surface.
Chemistry’s rules are not wrong. Hess’s Law, detailed balance, the rate equation, the
Woodward–Hoffmann rules — each is exactly correct at the level of mathematical
structure for which it is defined. The principal class of exceptions, of which the three
examples above are the cleanest, arises when a question from one level is posed with
the tools of a different one.
The central claim of this monograph
The principal class of exceptions to a chemical rule is a level incompleteness: it
arises when a question that belongs to level Lk+1 is posed using only the tools
of Lk. The tower of categories

which each question actually lives, and proves that every level is necessary:

level can be merged with its neighbours without conflating physically distinct
reactions. Each level Lk is constructed in full in the corresponding chapter,
together with the forcing pair of reactions that makes it irreducible.
§1.2. The tower, built bottom-up
The tower is not constructed by surveying chemistry and assigning phenomena to
levels. It is forced, bottom-up, by an explicit argument at each step: there exist
pairs of reactions that are physically distinct but indistinguishable at level k, and
the unique minimal categorical extension that separates them is level k+1.
For instance, the concerted-versus-stepwise pair at phosphorus — identity methoxyl
exchange at methyl ethylphenylphosphinate [30], proceeding either through a single
trigonal-bipyramidal transition state (SN2-P) or through a discrete pentacoordinate
14


## Page 15


Kyunghoon Han
Categorification of Chemical Reactions
intermediate (TBI) by addition-elimination — is a forcing argument for the L3 →L4
step. At L3, reactions are morphisms in a Markov category: their entire content is a
rate law and a net stoichiometric change. Under the quasi-steady-state reduction on
TBI valid in the experimentally relevant regime, both mechanisms yield the same
bimolecular rate law λ = k xMeO−xsubstrate and the same net stoichiometric change;
they are the same morphism at L3. Level L4 introduces a richer notion of morphism
— a double-pushout (DPO) derivation in the category of labelled molecular graphs —
so that a morphism at L4 is an electron-pushing mechanism, not merely a rate law.
The concerted pathway is a single DPO span (one elementary bond rearrangement,
no internal intermediate); the stepwise pathway is two composable DPO spans
bracketing TBI as an internal species. The permutation swapping one for the other is
a non-trivial element of coker(φ4), where φ4 : Aut(L4) →Aut(L3) is the restriction
map: it is an automorphism of the kinetic level that lifts to no automorphism of the
mechanistic one. That is the proof that L4 is necessary given L3.
The forcing tool
The precise instrument is the automorphism sequence
1 −→ker φk −→Aut(Lk)
φk
−−→Aut(Lk−1) −→cokerφk −→1.
A non-trivial cokerφk witnesses the existence of automorphisms of Lk−1 that
cannot be lifted to Lk: the permutation swapping the two reactions in the forcing
pair is such an automorphism. Each level is the unique minimal extension with
non-trivial cokerφk for the forcing pair listed in Table 2.
The motivating axis throughout is reaction networks, not isolated reactions. A
network at level k is a finite directed graph whose vertices are complexes and whose
edges are labelled by morphisms in Lk; open networks, exposed to their environment
at specified interface species, compose by pushout. This is the framework of Baez
and Pollard [31] at the kinetic level, extending the symmetric monoidal Petri-net
language of Meseguer and Montanari [32]; the present work applies it at every tower
level. The forcing pairs are always parallel reactions that the previous level cannot
distinguish: parallel reactions with different ∆H force L0 →L1; same ∆H but
different ∆S forces L1 →L2; same ∆G but different rate forces L2 →L3; same rate
law but different mechanism forces L3 →L4, and so on up the tower. Each chapter
closes with worked examples drawn from systems where the new datum at that level
is most cleanly exhibited; the examples are deliberately level-specific, since no single
reaction sharpens every transition equally and forcing one to do every job would
flatten what each is meant to show. Table 2 records, for each transition Lk−1 →Lk,
the concrete pair of physically distinct reactions that Lk−1 conflates and Lk separates;
the corresponding worked example is given in the chapter introducing Lk.

over chemical species, morphisms are formal reactions, composition is sequential
chaining, and the monoidal product is mixture. The language is that of Meseguer and
Montanari [32]; its universal property determines every strict symmetric monoidal
functor out of L0(P) by its values on generating reactions, so each higher-level datum
(enthalpy, free energy, rate) reduces to a single number per elementary reaction.
The combinatorial invariants of chemical reaction network theory (stoichiometric
matrix N, linkage classes ℓ, stoichiometric subspace s, deficiency δ = n −ℓ−s) are
L0 data.
Forcing L1. Two reactions with identical stoichiometric matrices can carry different
heats of reaction; Hess additivity is a new datum above the bare bookkeeping of
species in and species out.
Chapter 3 — L1, thermochemistry.
L1 equips L0(P) with a strict symmetric
monoidal functor FH : L0(P) →(R, +) into the additive reals. Hess’s Law is not
a postulate but the functoriality of FH: the heat of a composite reaction is the
sum of the heats of its parts because composition in L0 goes to addition in R.
Thermochemical cycles — calorimetric summation, bond-energy estimates, Born–
Haber loops — become commuting diagrams in R.
Forcing L2. Two reactions with identical ∆H can carry different ∆S, and their
equilibrium positions then shift differently with temperature — a distinction L1
cannot make.
Chapter 4 — L2, equilibrium.
L2 adds the entropy functor FS and, for each
temperature T > 0, the Gibbs functor F T
G := FH −TFS; its kernel is the equilibrium
locus, F T
G(r) = 0 iff r lies at equilibrium at temperature T. Detailed balance appears
as the condition that reverse reactions carry opposite F T
G-values; Wegscheider’s cycle
relations become cohomological conditions on free energies across a reaction network.
Forcing L3. Two reactions with identical ∆G can proceed at rates differing by
many orders of magnitude (uncatalysed versus carbonic-anhydrase catalysed CO2
hydration): kinetics is invisible at L2.
Chapter 5 — L3, kinetics.
L3 is a Markov category equipped with a functor
FP : L3 →Stoch into the Markov category of stochastic kernels: every reaction
carries a rate law, and mass-action kinetics together with the chemical master
equation fit into this framework as morphism-level data. The Baez–Pollard [31]
compositional structure for open reaction networks lives here. Feinberg’s Deficiency

integer pseudorotational quantisation in the Na3 22E′ state, an obstruction class in

which features are essential, which are tunable parameters of Θsim, and which are
scale-dependent fictions of the chosen representation.

§1.4. A brief guide to categorical language
This subsection introduces the categorical vocabulary; readers comfortable with
enriched category theory may proceed directly to Chapter 2.

Category theory provides the mathematical grammar of this programme.
The
compact dictionary below is aimed at readers fluent in chemistry or physics but new
to categorical ideas; every term is paired with its chemical meaning and a concrete
example.
Category.
A category C consists of:
• a collection of objects — the states or species pools under study;
• for each ordered pair of objects X, Y , a set Hom(X, Y ) of morphisms from X
to Y , i.e. all processes or transformations that lead from state X to state Y ;
• a composition law: if f ∈Hom(X, Y ) and g ∈Hom(Y, Z), their composite
g ◦f ∈Hom(X, Z) is the process obtained by performing f first and then g;
• for each object X, an identity morphism idX ∈Hom(X, X) — the trivial
“do-nothing” process;
satisfying associativity (h◦g)◦f = h◦(g◦f) and unitality idY ◦f = f = f◦idX [36, 37].
Chemical meaning. Objects are complexes — formal non-negative integer combi-
nations of chemical species such as CH4 + 2 O2. The term complex is standard in
chemical reaction network theory [10]: it denotes precisely one side of a balanced re-
action equation. Morphisms are reactions or multi-step pathways between complexes.
The identity idu is the “no reaction” process on complex u; composition r2 ◦r1 chains
two steps sequentially.
A key example: BR. The real line forms a one-object category BR with a single
object ∗and one morphism a ∈R for each real number, with composition b◦a := a+b.
Think of BR as a single node with one directed arrow per real number: concatenating
two arrows means adding their labels. A functor FH : L0(P) →BR assigns to every
reaction a real number (e.g. enthalpy ∆H) that is automatically additive along
sequential and parallel steps — this is the categorical formulation of Hess’s Law,
developed fully at L1.
Functor.
A functor F : C →D is a structure-preserving map between categories:
it sends each object X to an object F(X) and each morphism f : X →Y to a
morphism F(f): F(X) →F(Y ), respecting composition (F(g ◦f) = F(g) ◦F(f))
and identities (F(idX) = idF(X)).
Chemical meaning. A functor from the reaction category into BR is a consistent
numerical scoring of reactions: it assigns a real number to each elementary step
in a way that the score of any sequential or parallel combination is the sum of the
individual scores. Enthalpy (∆H), Gibbs free energy (∆G), and entropy change (∆S)
are all consistent scorings of this kind — each is a functor from the appropriate tower
level into BR. The functoriality conditions (F(g ◦f) = F(g) ◦F(f) and F(id) = 0)
are precisely the additivity and trivial-process conditions these thermodynamic
quantities must satisfy.
Monoidal category.
A monoidal category (C, ⊗, I) is a category equipped with a
tensor product ⊗: C ×C →C combining two objects or morphisms “in parallel”, a unit

∼−→X, X ⊗I
∼−→X (unitors). When the
associator and unitors are identity maps, the category is strict monoidal [37].
Chemical meaning. X ⊗Y is the mixture of X and Y : CH4 ⊗2 O2 is the mixture
CH4 + 2 O2. The unit object is the empty mixture 0 ∈N[S]. Since addition in N[S]
is already strictly associative and 0 + u = u, the associator and unitors are identity
maps: the tensor is strict monoidal for chemical mixtures.
Symmetric monoidal category.
A monoidal category is symmetric if there is a
coherent family of isomorphisms σX,Y : X ⊗Y
∼
−→Y ⊗X. In chemistry: a solution
“of A and B” is the same system as one “of B and A”; no experiment distinguishes
the two descriptions, so the symmetry isomorphism is physically mandatory. All
symmetric monoidal categories in this chapter are permutative: symmetric strict
monoidal. In this manuscript an acronym “SMC” is used for symmetric monoidal
category and “permutative” for symmetric strict monoidal. Theorem 2.14 holds for
any strict SMC codomain; the primary application uses BR, which is permutative.
Free construction.
A free object on given generators is the most general object
of its type built from those generators, subject to no relations beyond those forced
by the axioms of the type.
Example. The free group on one generator is Z — the integers with addition. Starting
from the generator +1 and its inverse −1, all combinations by addition are formed;
no shortcut is imposed (“+1 applied three times” is never identified with “+2 applied
twice” unless the group axioms force it, which they do not). The result is the smallest
group containing the generator, with no redundant identifications [37]. The key
property is universality: once +1 is sent to any element g of a target group G, the
entire homomorphism Z →G is uniquely forced (n 7→ng).
Chemical meaning. No equivalences between distinct reaction labels are imposed
beyond those forced by the permutative axioms. Two routes r1, r2 with the same
reactant and product complexes are kept as distinct morphisms at L0: no physical
identification — same ∆H, same rate, same mechanism — is made until the tower
level at which that information first becomes available. Once you fix where each
species and each reaction label map in a target category, the entire strict symmetric
monoidal functor out of L0(P) is uniquely forced (Theorem 2.14): there is no
modelling choice left.
Commutative diagram.
A diagram of objects and morphisms commutes when ev-
ery directed path between the same two objects yields the same composite morphism.
The following example shows what this means in stoichiometric terms.

The diagram commutes in (Z4, +) if and only if ∆ν(rdirect) = ∆ν(r1) + ∆ν(r2),
which holds: both sides equal (−1, −2, 0, +2)⊤. This is atom balance — the net
species change is the same whether the reaction proceeds directly or via the
nitric oxide intermediate. Functoriality F∆ν(r2 ◦r1) = F∆ν(r2)+F∆ν(r1) is atom
balance: it encodes a column of the stoichiometric matrix N as commutativity
of a triangle. Any violation would mean atoms are created or destroyed along
one route, i.e. F∆ν is not a functor.
Petri net.
Petri nets were introduced by Carl Adam Petri in 1962 as a mathematical
framework for concurrent processes [38]. Places hold tokens (molecular populations
of species) and transitions represent reactions, consuming tokens from input places
and depositing tokens into output places according to stoichiometric arc multiplicities.
This is exactly the combinatorial skeleton of stoichiometric chemistry [32, 39]. The
precise definition, a worked chemical example, and the construction of L0(P) from a
Petri net are given in §2.2.
The central gain of the categorical framework
A category is a precise language for processes that compose sequentially and
run in parallel. A functor is a consistent numerical scoring of those processes.
Once a thermodynamic or kinetic quantity is identified as a functor from the
reaction category into an appropriate target, its core properties — additivity
along sequences, additivity over parallel reactions — become theorems rather
than separate postulates.
Each higher tower level adds a specific categorical extension to the previous
level: a new functor, an enrichment of the morphism category by a symmetry, a
geometric decoration, a topological invariant, or (at the final step) a deformation
of the algebraic structure itself. The taxonomy of the six extension types that
arise across the present tower is recorded in §10.8; each is forced at its level

means no equivalences between reactions are imposed beyond those forced by

In summary: a stoichiometric scheme equipped with sequential composition
(one reaction following another), parallel composition (reactions in independent
mixtures), and order-independence of mixtures is the defining data of a symmetric
monoidal category; assigning numerical chemical content is providing a functor;
starting from the most general such structure is taking the free construction.
Monad.
A monad on a category C is an endofunctor T : C →C (a functor whose
source and target are the same category) equipped with two natural transformations
(coherent families of morphisms, one per object): a unit η: idC ⇒T that injects each
object X into a T-decorated version T(X), and a multiplication µ: T ◦T ⇒T that
collapses two layers of decoration into one. These satisfy associativity (µ◦Tµ = µ◦µT)
and unit laws (µ ◦Tη = µ ◦ηT = idT) [37, 36].
Operational meaning. A monad packages a kind of “effect” or “extra structure” that
maps can carry while remaining composable — randomness, state, partial information,
time, or symmetry. T(X) is to be read as “a computation that ultimately yields
a value of type X while carrying the effect of T”; η produces a trivially-decorated
value, and µ is what makes two effectful computations compose into a single one.
The Kleisli category. The natural setting for T-effectful computations is the Kleisli
category Kl(T), which has the same objects as C but takes morphisms X →Y to be
C-morphisms X →T(Y ). The composite of f : X →T(Y ) and g: Y →T(Z) is
g • f := µZ ◦T(g) ◦f : X →T(Z),
lifting g to act on T(Y ) via T’s functoriality, then flattening the resulting T(T(Z))
via µ.
Key example: Kl(IO). Haskell’s IO monad packages every interaction with the outside
world — file reads, terminal output, random-number generation — into the type
IO(X) of computations that eventually produce an X, possibly with side effects
on the way. A morphism in Kl(IO) from X to Y is then a function X →IO(Y ):
a procedure that, given an input, may consume random bits or perform other
side effects and yields an output. Stochastic simulation of a reaction network is
exactly such a procedure: the operational functor Φop of Chapter 12 lands in the
Kleisli category of the probabilistic sub-monad of IO — the sub-monad generated by
pseudo-random-number sampling.

§2. L0: The Stoichiometric Level
The simplest possible question about a chemical reaction is: what goes in and what
comes out? Before energy, before time, before geometry, before mechanism — purely
the bookkeeping of species consumed and produced.
Three structural features are present at this barest level of description:
(a) Steps compose. If reaction r1 produces a species that reaction r2 consumes,
the two steps together form a new composite reaction r2 ◦r1.
(b) Steps run in parallel. Two reactions that do not interfere with each other
can be combined into a joint process r1 ⊗r2, run simultaneously.
(c) The ordering of independent species is irrelevant. There is no intrinsic
left-to-right order in a mixture; A + B and B + A describe the same physical
system.
Expressing these structural features in a precise mathematical language — rather
than leaving them as implicit chemical common sense — makes it possible to prove rig-
orously which properties follow from which hypotheses and to compare different levels
of chemical description on equal footing. The language appropriate to features (a)–(c)
is that of symmetric monoidal categories: mathematical structures carrying exactly
the sequential, parallel, and order-irrelevant composition grammar those features
demand. This language was established by Meseguer and Montanari [32] for Petri
nets, and extended into a compositional framework for open reaction networks by
Baez and Pollard [31]. The exact tower backbone developed in this chapter and the
subsequent ones admits a perpendicular Para-enrichment dimension (Chapter 11,
building on Gavranović et al. [33]) which places machine-learning models for chem-
istry [40, 41] on an exact mathematical foundation as parametric equivariant maps
over the same tower levels.
A brief categorical glossary, aimed at readers fluent in chemistry or physics but new
to category theory, is provided in §1.4.
§2.1. Species, complexes, and the stoichiometric monoid
Stoichiometry is the branch of chemistry concerned with the quantitative relationships
between species in a chemical reaction: how many molecules of each substance are
consumed, and how many are produced. For a mathematician, it is the study of the
additive structure of molecular populations — which integer combinations of named
species can appear as the left- or right-hand side of a balanced equation, and how
those combinations pool together. No energy, no dynamics, no geometry: purely the
arithmetic of molecular counts.
The algebraic object capturing this arithmetic is the free commutative monoid on
the set of species.
Definition 2.1 (Species and the stoichiometric monoid). Fix a finite set S of chemical
species (e.g. S = {H2O, CH4, O2, CO2}). Species are abstract labels at this level;
no geometric, electronic, or energetic information is attached.

Remark 2.2 (Relation to prior mathematical treatments of stoichiometry). The

additive species observable — mass, atom count, enthalpy, any additive potential —

tower of functors in Chapters 3–10 is built by iterating this observation upward. The

What is a complex?
A complex is what chemists call one “side” of a balanced equation. For CH4 +
2 O2 →CO2 + 2 H2O, the reactant complex is 1 · CH4 + 2 · O2 and the product
complex is 1 · CO2 + 2 · H2O, both elements of N[S].
The monoid operation is simply pooling:
(1 · CH4 + 2 · O2) + (1 · CO2 + 2 · H2O) = 1 · CH4 + 2 · O2 + 1 · CO2 + 2 · H2O.
This is the mathematical version of mixing two portions together. The reaction
arrow says: this pool transforms into that pool. The monoid carries no infor-
mation about whether or how the transformation occurs; that belongs to later
levels of the tower.
Proposition 2.3 makes precise something a chemist already knows: once you
decide what numerical value to assign to each individual species (its mass, its
atom count, its standard enthalpy of formation, . . . ), the value for any complex
is completely forced — there is no choice. The total mass of 1 · CH4 + 2 · O2
is M(CH4) + 2 M(O2) and nothing else; the universal property is precisely the
theorem that says this.
Universal properties are one of the central organising tools of category theory:
MacLane [37] identifies them as the concept that unifies free constructions, adjunc-
tions, and limits, and Riehl [36] shows systematically how they eliminate arbitrary
choices from mathematical definitions. The stoichiometric monoid N[S] is the uni-
versal receptacle for additive species data: any quantity that is additive over species
— mass, elemental composition, standard enthalpy of formation — extends uniquely
to all complexes via Proposition 2.3, with no modelling freedom left. Moreover, the
universal property of N[S] is the first in a chain: the universal property of L0(P)
(Theorem 2.14) extends it one step further, from species and complexes to reactions
and their composites, and every subsequent tower level adds one more universal
property governing the next kind of chemical data.

(i) Existence. There is a monoid homomorphism ¯f : N[S] →M extending
f, given by ¯f

Concretely: once you decide what value each species receives, the value of every

reactions, not with individual species, and so lie outside the scope of Proposition 2.3.

§2.2. Petri nets: the categorical input data
This subsection gives the precise definition of a Petri net and establishes the category
Petri of all Petri nets. The raw data of a stoichiometric scheme is a finite list
of species and a finite list of reaction labels, each label carrying a source complex
(reactants) and a target complex (products) in N|S|. This structure is a Petri net,
introduced by Carl Adam Petri in 1962 as a mathematical framework for concurrent
processes [38], and recognised by Meseguer–Montanari to be the natural input data
for free symmetric monoidal categories [32]. The stoichiometric category L0(P) is
the free categorical structure generated by a Petri net P: one imposes no relations
beyond those forced by the axioms of a symmetric monoidal category. The free
construction occupies §2.3.
Definition 2.5 (Petri net [38, 32, 39]). A Petri net is a quadruple P = (S, R, s, t)
where S is a finite set of species, R is a finite set of reaction labels, and s, t : R →N|S|
assign to each label r ∈R its source complex s(r) and target complex t(r), with
s(r) ̸= t(r) in general.
A Petri net in chemistry: hydrogen combustion
Consider the net stoichiometry of hydrogen combustion:
2 H2 + O2
r−→2 H2O.
As a Petri net: S = {H2, O2, H2O}, R = {r}, with
s(r) = 2 · H2 + 1 · O2 ∈N|S|,
t(r) = 2 · H2O ∈N|S|.
In the standard Petri net picture, each species is a place (a pool holding molecular
tokens) and each reaction is a transition (consuming tokens from its input places
and depositing tokens into its output places according to the stoichiometric
coefficients). The arc multiplicities (2, 1, 2) encode stoichiometry; the transition
r has no internal structure beyond its input and output counts.
What the Petri net captures. The stoichiometric ratios (2:1:2), the direction
of transformation, and the connectivity between species and reaction. Conserva-
tion vectors can be computed from the stoichiometric matrix N alone (see §2.6):
here, hydrogen-atom balance gives wH = (2, 0, 2)⊤, confirming two H atoms in
each H2 and two H atoms in each H2O.
What the Petri net deliberately omits.
• Energy: the standard enthalpy of combustion ∆H◦= −484 kJ mol−1 [44]
is not part of P; it enters at L1.
• Rate: the pre-exponential factor and activation energy are absent; they
enter at L3.
• Mechanism: whether the reaction proceeds via radical intermediates (H,
OH, HO2) or in a single elementary step is invisible at L0; mechanism
enters at L4.

• Geometry: bond lengths, angles, and three-dimensional structure are
absent; they enter at L5.
The Petri net is the skeletal description: the minimal combinatorial input from
which the categorical construction L0(P) is built. Every additional piece of
chemical information corresponds to additional structure at a higher tower level.
Remark 2.6 (Reaction labels are named generators). R is a set of named generators,
not a set of ordered pairs of complexes. Two distinct labels r1, r2 ∈R with s(r1) =
s(r2) and t(r1) = t(r2) represent two different reactions between the same complexes —
for instance, two mechanistically distinct routes with the same net stoichiometry. The
free construction of §2.3 keeps them as distinct generators; no physical identification
is imposed until a later level.
Petri nets assemble into a category: one can map one network into another by
translating species and reaction labels while respecting stoichiometry, and these
translations compose in the obvious way. This categorical structure on Petri nets
is established in Meseguer–Montanari [32] and is needed for two reasons: it allows
chemical networks to be compared and translated systematically, and it ensures that
the construction P 7→L0(P) is itself a functor between categories rather than an ad
hoc assignment.
Definition 2.7 (The category Petri). Petri is the category whose objects are Petri
nets and whose morphisms f : P →P ′ are pairs (fS, fR) of functions
fS : S →S′,
fR : R →R′,
satisfying the source–target compatibility conditions
s′ ◦fR = ¯fS ◦s,
t′ ◦fR = ¯fS ◦t,
where ¯fS : N|S| →N|S′| is the unique monoid homomorphism extending fS (Proposi-
tion 2.3). Composition is componentwise; the identity on P is (idS, idR).
Remark 2.8 (What a Petri morphism does). A morphism f : P →P ′ translates
species to species and reaction labels to reaction labels, in a way that respects
stoichiometry: if r has source complex u in P, then fR(r) has source complex ¯fS(u)
in P ′, and similarly for targets. Non-injectivity is permitted: a non-injective fS
coarsens species (merging two species into one); a non-injective fR equates two
distinct reaction labels at the stoichiometric level. The compatibility conditions are
exactly what is needed for ¯fS — the unique extension supplied by Proposition 2.3 —
to be well-defined on complexes built from the translated species.
§2.3. The stoichiometric category L0(P)
The categorical language of §1.4 now assembles into a single construction. A per-
mutative category is a strict symmetric monoidal category: associativity and unit
hold as strict equalities, while the symmetry σX,Y : X ⊗Y →Y ⊗X remains a
(possibly non-trivial) isomorphism between two distinct objects. The category L0(P)
we construct is a skeletal permutative category: in addition to the strict associativity
and unit, the underlying object monoid (N|S|, +, 0) is itself strictly commutative, so
u + v = v + u holds as an equality of objects, not merely as an isomorphism. This
skeletal structure is forced on us by chemistry: a mixture has no intrinsic ordering, so
29

Kyunghoon Han
Categorification of Chemical Reactions
A + B and B + A must literally name the same complex. The non-trivial symmetry
σu,v : u + v →u + v then becomes an endomorphism encoding the permutation
data that a non-skeletal permutative category would store in distinct objects.
A Petri net P provides the chemical generators of L0(P): the species S generate
the objects (via N|S|), and the reaction labels R become the basic morphisms, each
typed by its source and target complex. The free skeletal permutative category on
P is built from these generators by closing under sequential composition, parallel
tensor, and the structural morphisms (identities and symmetries), imposing only the
permutative axioms and no additional chemical identifications. This is L0(P).
Definition 2.9 (Stoichiometric category L0(P)). Let P = (S, R, s, t) be a Petri net.
The stoichiometric category L0(P) is the free permutative category on P [32, 39]: the
unique (up to strict symmetric monoidal equivalence) permutative category satisfying
the following.
(i) Objects. The object set is N|S|, with monoidal product u ⊗v := u + v
and monoidal unit 0. Since + is commutative in N|S|, the tensor is strictly
commutative: u ⊗v = v ⊗u as the same object. Associativity and unitality
are also strict.
(ii) Generating morphisms. The morphisms of L0(P) have two distinct origins.
• Chemical generators (input data). The reaction generators r : s(r) →t(r)
for each r ∈R, supplied by the Petri net P. These are the only chemical
input.
• Structural morphisms (forced by the skeletal permutative structure). The
identity morphisms idu : u →u for each u ∈N|S|, and the symmetry
endomorphisms σu,v : u + v →u + v for each pair u, v ∈N|S|. These are
not chemical input; they are forced on L0(P) by the requirement that it
be a skeletal permutative category at all.
The symmetry σu,v is an endomorphism — not an isomorphism between two
distinct objects — because u + v = v + u as the same element of N|S|, the
skeletal property of item (i) above.
(iii) All morphisms. Closed under sequential composition g ◦f (when cod(f) =
dom(g), which holds in general as chemistry demands it) and parallel tensor
f ⊗g.
(iv) Relations. Morphisms are equivalence classes under the smallest congruence
compatible with ◦and ⊗generated by the permutative axioms: identity laws;
associativity of ◦; interchange (g1 ⊗g2) ◦(f1 ⊗f2) = (g1 ◦f1) ⊗(g2 ◦f2); tensor
unit; involutivity of σ; naturality of σ; and the hexagon axiom (all defined in
Remark 2.10 below). No equation r1 ≡r2 is imposed for distinct r1, r2 ∈R,
even if s(r1) = s(r2) and t(r1) = t(r2).
(v) Functoriality. A Petri morphism f = (fS, fR) : P →P ′ induces a strict
symmetric monoidal functor L0(f) : L0(P) →L0(P ′), acting as ¯fS on objects
and by r 7→fR(r) on generators, making L0 : Petri →PermCat a functor.
Here PermCat denotes the category whose objects are small skeletal permutative
categories (strict symmetric monoidal categories whose object monoid (ObC, ⊗, I) is

itself strictly commutative, matching the structure of L0(P)) and whose morphisms
are strict symmetric monoidal functors.
Remark 2.10 (The permutative axioms: involutivity, naturality, hexagon). The three
axioms governing the symmetry morphisms σ in Definition 2.9(iv) are standard in
the theory of symmetric monoidal categories [45, 37]; we spell them out explicitly
for readers encountering them for the first time.
• Involutivity. σv,u ◦σu,v = idu+v. Swapping the order of u and v twice returns
to the original arrangement.
Chemically: reordering a mixture and then reordering it back leaves it un-
changed.
• Naturality. For any morphisms f : u →u′ and g : v →v′,
σu′,v′ ◦(f ⊗g) = (g ⊗f) ◦σu,v.
Reordering before or after running two reactions in parallel gives the same
result.
Chemically: it does not matter whether you relabel species before or after
performing the reactions — the stoichiometric outcome is identical.
• Hexagon axiom. For all complexes u, v, w,
σu, v+w = (idv ⊗σu,w) ◦(σu,v ⊗idw).
The name comes from the hexagonal commutative diagram the equation gener-
ates. It says that swapping u past the combined pool v + w is the same as
swapping u past v first and then past w.
Chemically: reordering one component past a mixture of two others can be
done in a single step or two sequential steps with the same result.
In a non-skeletal permutative category, the symmetry σX,Y : X ⊗Y →Y ⊗X runs
between distinct objects, and involutivity composes the two arrows to land back
at X ⊗Y . In the skeletal L0(P), where u + v = v + u as the same object, σu,v
becomes an endomorphism and involutivity says it is its own inverse: σu,v generates
a Z/2-action on Hom(u + v, u + v) rather than collapsing to the identity.
Remark 2.11 (The symmetry morphisms and coherence). In a non-skeletal symmetric
monoidal category, the symmetry σA,B : A⊗B
∼
−→B ⊗A is an isomorphism between
two distinct objects A⊗B and B⊗A. In L0(P), because N|S| is strictly commutative,
u + v and v + u are literally the same object, so σu,v is an endomorphism — an
arrow from a complex back to itself — rather than an isomorphism between two
different complexes.
Despite living in Hom(u + v, u + v), σu,v is not the identity morphism idu+v: it is
a non-trivial endomorphism, the involutive generator of a Z/2-action on the hom-
space. This distinction matters for functors: a strict symmetric monoidal functor
F : L0(P) →C into a target satisfying the hypothesis of Theorem 2.14 (object
monoid strictly commutative) must send σu,v to the symmetry σC
F(u),F(v), which is
itself an endomorphism of F(u) ⊗F(v). That target endomorphism may be trivial
(as in the Baez–Master CMC, Remark 2.17) or non-trivial; L0(P) maps coherently
into both kinds of skeletal permutative target.

Remark 2.12 (No additional chemical relations). The only relations in L0(P) are

is available to make such an identification meaningful. In this sense L0(P) is the
most general stoichiometric category consistent with the Petri net P: it retains every
distinction that stoichiometry alone cannot collapse.

§2.4. The universal property of L0
A strict symmetric monoidal functor out of L0(P) is the mathematical notion of a
consistent assignment of chemical content to a network: it sends species to objects of
the target category, reaction labels to morphisms of the correct type, and is required
to preserve both sequential composition and parallel tensor. The universal property
of L0(P) says that any such functor is completely determined by its values on the
elementary generators — species and individual reaction labels — with no further
consistency conditions to verify. This is the reaction-level analogue of Proposition 2.3:
just as a monoid homomorphism out of N|S| is fixed by its values on individual species,
a symmetric monoidal functor out of L0(P) is fixed by its values on individual species
and individual reactions.
Theorem 2.14 (Universal property of L0(P)). Let P = (S, R, s, t) be a Petri net
and C a strict symmetric monoidal category whose object monoid (ObC, ⊗, I) is
strictly commutative — i.e. X ⊗Y = Y ⊗X as the same object for all X, Y ∈ObC.

Corollary 2.16 (Additive functors into BR). The real line R carries the structure

real number is an arrow, and composing two arrows means adding their labels; the
identity morphism on ∗is the number 0. This is a permutative category with trivial
symmetry σ∗,∗= 0 (the zero element of R, since swapping a one-element tensor with
itself leaves the number unchanged).

What the universal property means for chemists
Any consistent additive assignment of chemical content to species and to individ-
ual reaction labels extends uniquely to all composites and parallel combinations.
The extension is forced by the requirement of being a strict symmetric monoidal
functor; it is not a modelling choice.
Examples. Assigning enthalpies h(r) ∈R to generators and demanding func-
toriality gives Hess’s Law (additivity over sequences and parallel reactions)
as a consequence of Corollary 2.16: not a separate postulate but a theorem.
Assigning per-species atom counts and demanding functoriality (Example 2.38)
extends each generator’s atom imbalance additively along all sequential and
parallel composites, giving atom conservation as a theorem whenever every
generator is balanced. Rate constants at L3 require different machinery: rates
are not path-additive, so they enter via a kinetic functor into a Markov category,
not via the additive universal property of BR.
What is not forced. The state-function condition — that h(r) depends only
on the complexes s(r) and t(r), not on the particular reaction label r — is
an additional physical constraint, not a consequence of functoriality alone.
Two distinct reaction labels r1, r2 with the same source and target can carry
different enthalpies h(r1) ̸= h(r2), and the functor axioms do not prohibit this.
The distinction between functorial additivity (supplied by L1) and the state-
function condition (a separate physical constraint on the particular functor FH)
is developed in §2.8.
§2.5. The automorphism exact sequence and the forcing principle
Theorem 2.14 establishes L0(P) as the free skeletal permutative category on the
Petri net P: once species are assigned to objects of a target category and reaction
labels to morphisms of the correct type, the extension to all composites and tensors
is uniquely determined. This universal property now gives us a precise handle on the
automorphisms of L0(P) itself, and — more importantly — on what they cannot
see.
As previewed in §1.2, the tower L0 ,→L1 ,→· · · ,→L7 is built bottom-up: at each
step there exist pairs of reactions that are physically distinct yet indistinguishable at
the previous level. The tool that makes “indistinguishable” mathematically precise is
the automorphism sequence, an adaptation to the categorical setting of a classical
algebraic device. For a homomorphism φ : G →H of groups, the kernel ker φ
measures what φ collapses, and the coset space H/imφ measures what lies outside
its image [36, 46]. Applied to the restriction map between the automorphism groups
of adjacent tower levels, the kernel records new symmetries that level k adds beyond
34


## Page 35


Kyunghoon Han
Categorification of Chemical Reactions
level k −1, and the coset space records symmetries of Lk−1 that fail to lift to Lk —
precisely the distinctions a given level cannot express, and that the next level must
add. We do not assume the image of the restriction map to be a normal subgroup,
so the coset space is in general only a pointed set, not a group; this is sufficient for
the forcing diagnostic developed below.
Presentation-preserving automorphisms and the restriction map.
A presentation-
preserving automorphism of Lk is a strict symmetric monoidal autoequivalence
ϕ : Lk →Lk that preserves the chemical input data — species set S and reaction la-
bels R — as subsets of objects and morphisms respectively. We write AutPetri(Lk) for
the group of all such automorphisms under composition. The presentation-preserving
qualifier is essential: an arbitrary categorical autoequivalence might rearrange com-
posites and tensor products in ways unrelated to any Petri-net relabelling, and the
results below would not apply to it.
If some ϕ ∈AutPetri(Lk) swaps two reactions r1, r2 ∈R, then the two are indistin-
guishable by every Lk-level observable: any functor out of Lk must commute with ϕ
and therefore cannot separate them. The converse fails in general — two reactions
can agree under every Lk-functor without there being a global presentation-preserving
automorphism realising the swap — so a swapping automorphism is a sufficient
diagnostic for indistinguishability, not a characterisation. This is exactly what the
forcing argument needs: a swap that fails to lift to Lk+1 exhibits a real distinction
Lk misses.
Each tower inclusion ιk : Lk−1 ,→Lk induces a restriction homomorphism
φk : AutPetri(Lk) −→AutPetri(Lk−1),
ϕ 7−→ϕ↾Lk−1,
sending each presentation-preserving automorphism of the richer level to its restriction
to the simpler one. Not every element of AutPetri(Lk−1) arises this way: those that
do not are symmetries present at level k −1 that level k breaks, precisely because
the extra structure at level k distinguishes what level k −1 could not.

sets

the trivial coset. The first three terms carry group structure (kernel of a group
homomorphism, the two automorphism groups themselves), but cokerφk is in
general only a pointed set: we do not assume imφk to be a normal subgroup of
AutPetri(Lk−1). Exactness at each term means the image of the incoming map
equals the preimage of the basepoint of the outgoing one. The three terms carry
distinct chemical content.
• ker φk: presentation-preserving automorphisms of Lk restricting to the
identity on Lk−1 — new symmetries first visible at level k. Example:
time-reversal † (sending each reaction to its reverse) is an automorphism
of L2 invisible at L1, where no reverse reaction exists.

• cokerφk: cosets of presentation-preserving automorphisms of Lk−1 modulo
those that lift to Lk. A non-trivial coset is represented by an automorphism
of Lk−1 that fails to lift — a symmetry that Lk breaks. A non-trivial
cokernel is the precise statement that Lk−1 conflates objects (reactions,
complexes, or configurations) that Lk separates.
• φk itself: records how much symmetry survives when the extra structure
of level k is forgotten.
Forcing principle (diagnostic direction). If cokerφk is non-trivial, then Lk−1
admits a genuine symmetry that Lk breaks: Lk−1 cannot distinguish reactions
that Lk separates, so the extension is necessary — i.e., no reformulation within
Lk−1 can capture the distinction.
Forcing principle (constructive direction). At each observed non-trivial
cokerφk, an explicit minimal extension Lk−1 →Lk that breaks the cokernel
class is exhibited — adding exactly the new functor, enrichment, or deformation
required and no more. That this extension is the unique minimal extension
breaking the cokernel class is claimed level by level on construction, not as
a general theorem about categorical extensions; the full taxonomy of the six
extension types that occur across the present tower is given in §10.8.
What the exact sequence means for a chemist
An automorphism is a relabelling of the mathematical structure that leaves
every observable at that level unchanged. If a relabelling swaps two reactions r1
and r2, then no measurement available at level k −1 can tell them apart.
The cokernel cokerφk collects exactly those relabellings of Lk−1 that swap
reactions which are genuinely distinct in physical reality. A non-trivial cokernel
means Lk−1 is blind to a real distinction: it lacks the vocabulary to express it.
Adding the minimal structure needed to break that spurious symmetry yields
Lk, and nothing more.
This is the categorical formalisation of a familiar experience: every time a
chemical rule has an exception, the exception reveals that a finer level of
description was implicitly being assumed. The automorphism exact sequence
turns this intuition into a working mathematical diagnostic.
The sequence at k = 0: identifying the cokernel.

The full tower, forced level by level.
The same argument at every subsequent
tower step yields the automorphism groups and forcing cokernels recorded in Table 3.
The following tour lists the levels in order; full developments occupy Chapters 3–10.
At L1, the automorphisms are isoenthalpic permutations, and the cokernel detects
reactions sharing ∆H but differing in ∆S, which shift their equilibria differently with
temperature and are therefore genuinely distinct at L2. At L2, adding the †-structure
(time-reversal, encoding detailed balance) breaks the remaining isothermodynamic
symmetry; the cokernel witnesses reactions with identical ∆G but different rates,
forcing L3. At L3, rate-preserving permutations are the surviving symmetries, and
the cokernel is generated by the swap E2 ↔SN2: two reactions with identical empiri-
cal rate laws but mechanistically distinct electron-pushing graphs, forcing L4. At L4,
once full bond-graph structure is present, the residual symmetry is Aut(G) on typed
molecular graphs; the cokernel detects the same bond changes realised in different
three-dimensional embeddings, forcing L4.5. At L4.5, the full permutation-inversion
group G∗governs enantiomeric and diastereomeric distinctions, including symmetry-
forbidden versus symmetry-allowed pathways under the Woodward–Hoffmann rules;
the cokernel forces L5 by exhibiting reactions whose transition states occupy geo-
metrically distinct points on a potential energy surface. At L5, isometries of the
configuration orbifold Ce(G) preserving the PES V are the automorphisms; the
cokernel distinguishes reactions with the same geometry but different topological
Berry class, separating photochemical from thermal pathways and forcing L6. At L6,
the real adiabatic eigenbundle admits a Z2-valued gauge freedom (the overall sign of
the real eigensection in a simply connected patch), and its cokernel captures loops
encircling the conical-intersection seam on which the sign cannot be chosen globally;
the invariant is the mod-2 Berry holonomy class [γB] ∈H1(Ce(G) \ X01, Z2), and the
cokernel separates CI-crossing reactions from adiabatic ones, forcing L7. Finally, at

With the automorphism diagnostic in hand, the remaining combinatorial content
of L0 — the stoichiometric matrix, Feinberg’s deficiency invariants, the Deficiency
Zero Theorem, and open-network composition — is the subject of the following
subsection.
§2.6. The stoichiometric matrix, conservation laws, and deficiency
The previous subsections built L0(P) as a categorical object.
This subsection
extracts its classical linear-algebraic content — the stoichiometric matrix N, the
conservation-law space, and the deficiency δ — and shows precisely which of these
arise from the universal-property machinery already established, and which are purely
presentational invariants of the Petri net P. In every case the derivation uses only
Proposition 2.3, Theorem 2.14, and Corollary 2.16. The dynamical significance of δ
— the Deficiency Theorems — requires mass-action kinetics and belongs to L3; we
state the theorems here and mark the level boundary throughout.
The notion of a chemical reaction network used throughout the CRNT literature
goes back to Horn, Jackson, and Feinberg [47, 8, 42, 10]. The following definition
adapts their framework to the Petri-net presentation of L0, retaining named reaction
labels so that mechanistically distinct routes between the same complexes remain
distinct morphisms in L0(P).
Definition 2.18 (Chemical Reaction Network at L0). A chemical reaction network
(CRN) at L0 is a quintuple (S, C, R, s, t) where C ⊂N|S| is a finite set of complexes, R
is a finite set of reaction labels, and s, t : R →C assign source and target complexes.
The underlying Petri net is P = (S, R, s, t) with s, t viewed as maps into N|S|, and
the stoichiometric category of the CRN is L0(P). The reaction multigraph G(R) is
the directed multigraph with vertex set C and one directed edge per element of R.
Remark 2.19 (Relation to the classical Feinberg CRN). The classical CRNT triple [47,
8, 42, 10] (S, C, E) uses a set of directed edges E ⊆C×C, collapsing two reactions with
the same source and target to a single edge. The label-preserving quintuple is neces-
sary for the Petri-net presentation: distinct labels must remain distinct morphisms
in L0(P). The classical triple is recovered by replacing R with {(s(r), t(r)) : r ∈R}.
Every generating morphism r ∈R of L0(P) has a source complex s(r) ∈N|S| and a
target complex t(r) ∈N|S|. Their difference t(r) −s(r) lives in the group completion
Z[S] ∼= Z|S| of N|S|. Collecting these differences as columns, after choosing linear
orderings of S and R, gives the stoichiometric matrix.
Definition 2.20 (Stoichiometric matrix [8, 42]). Let P = (S, R, s, t) be a Petri net.
Fix a linear ordering of S (identifying Z[S] ∼= Z|S|) and of R. The stoichiometric

Remark 2.21 (N as a presentational invariant of L0(P)). Different orderings of S and
R give the same N up to row and column permutations, so rankR(N) and imR(N)
are independent of the ordering. However, N depends on which morphisms are
generators (elements of R) as opposed to composites or tensors: it is a presentational
invariant of P, not a categorical invariant of L0(P) up to strict symmetric monoidal
equivalence. Two Petri nets with equivalent stoichiometric categories can have
different stoichiometric matrices.
Notational convention. Throughout this subsection, ρ := rankR(N) and Ssto :=
imR(N) ⊆R|S| denotes the stoichiometric subspace. We reserve s for the source map
s : R →N|S|.

Conservation laws as a tower concept
Proposition 2.22 gives the categorical content of conservation laws entirely within
L0:
A species potential w0 : S →R is a conservation law if and only if the functor
Fw : L0(P) →BR it induces (via Proposition 2.3 and Corollary 2.16) assigns
zero to every morphism of L0(P).
The reason conservation is preserved by all compositions and parallel combi-
nations — not just the generating reactions — is functoriality: Fw(g ◦f) =
Fw(g) + Fw(f) = 0 and Fw(f ⊗g) = 0 follow automatically once Fw = 0 on
generators. No separate proof is needed; the functor axioms carry it.
This also explains what ker(N ⊤) is from the tower’s point of view: it is the
set of species potentials for which the induced L1-level functor (Corollary 2.16)
happens to be identically zero. Conservation is not an additional axiom imposed
on L0(P); it is a condition on functors out of L0(P), and functoriality does the
work.
Proposition 2.23 (Stoichiometric subspaces). Let P = (S, R, s, t) be a Petri net
with matrix N.
(i) The stoichiometric subspace Ssto := imR(N) ⊆R|S| is spanned by the net
displacement vectors {t(r) −s(r) : r ∈R} of the generating morphisms of
L0(P).
(ii) The conservation-law space ker(N ⊤) is the orthogonal complement of Ssto and
equals, by Proposition 2.22, the set of species potentials w0 : S →R for which
the induced functor Fw : L0(P) →BR is identically zero.
(iii) The stoichiometric cycle space kerR(N) := {ν ∈R|R| | Nν = 0} consists of
formal real-linear combinations P

The four combinatorial invariants below are computable from (S, C, R, s, t) alone —
from L0 data. They were introduced by Feinberg, Horn, and Jackson [47, 8, 42, 10]
and underpin the Deficiency Theorems. Recent work has confirmed their centrality:
deficiency zero is generic in random reaction networks [48], and the interplay between
deficiency, weak reversibility, and steady states is an active frontier [49, 50].
Definition 2.25 (Feinberg’s combinatorial invariants [42, 10]). Let (S, C, R, s, t) be
a CRN.
• n := |C|: number of complexes.
• ℓ: number of linkage classes (connected components of the undirected graph
underlying G(R)).
• ρ := rankR(N): dimension of Ssto.
• δ := n −ℓ−ρ ≥0: the deficiency.
A feel for n, ℓ, ρ, δ
n counts the distinct molecular pools appearing as complexes. ℓcounts the
reaction islands: groups of complexes linked by some directed path, with no
connection to other groups. ρ counts the independent directions in concentration
space along which any trajectory can move. δ counts the independent ways
the complex graph can “circulate” while producing zero net species change:
complex-level degrees of freedom invisible to species-level accounting. A δ = 0
network has no such hidden structure.
To give δ a precise meaning in terms of L0(P), we factor the stoichiometric matrix
through the complex level. The inclusion ι : C ,→N|S| (each complex c ∈C is already
an element of N|S|) is a function from the set C to the commutative monoid N|S|. By
Proposition 2.3 applied with generator set C and target monoid N|S|, this extends to
a unique monoid homomorphism
¯ι : N[C] −→N|S|,
c 7−→c (viewed as element of N|S|),
from the free commutative monoid on complexes to the free commutative monoid
on species. Its matrix representation (after choosing orderings) is Y ∈R|S|×n, the
complex composition matrix, whose column c is the coordinate vector of complex
c ∈C in R|S|.
Independently, the reaction multigraph G(R) has an incidence matrix Ia ∈{−1, 0, 1}n×|R|
defined by: (Ia)c,r = +1 if c = t(r), (Ia)c,r = −1 if c = s(r), else 0. Here Ia is a
purely graph-theoretic object determined by G(R).
Proposition 2.26 (Linear algebraic interpretation of deficiency [42, 10]). With Y
and Ia as above:
(i) N = Y Ia.
(ii) rank(Ia) = n −ℓ.
(iii) δ = dimR(ker(Y ) ∩im(Ia)) ≥0.

Deficiency as a failure of the canonical monoid map
Proposition 2.26 has a direct tower interpretation.
The matrix Y is the real-linear extension of the monoid homomorphism ¯ι :
N[C] →N|S| induced by Proposition 2.3 from the inclusion ι : C ,→N|S|.
This map sends any formal combination of complexes to the corresponding
combination of species counts.
The matrix Ia records the net complex-level flows induced by the reaction labels:
each column r is et(r) −es(r) in Rn, the net movement from source complex to
target complex.
The factorization N = Y Ia (part (i)) says: the net species displacement of
a reaction factors as first, compute the net complex-flow (Ia), then project
complexes to species counts (Y = ¯ι).
Deficiency δ measures exactly the failure of ¯ι to be injective on the image of
the complex-flow matrix: it counts the dimension of the space of complex-level
circulations that produce zero net species change. When δ = 0, ¯ι is injective
on im(Ia): every complex-graph flow leaves a detectable trace in species space.
The Deficiency Zero Theorem uses this injectivity crucially. When δ > 0, there
are “hidden” complex-level circulations that L0(P), viewed through the species
map ¯ι, cannot detect.
Weak reversibility is a property of the presentation (S, C, R, s, t), not a categorical
invariant of L0(P) up to equivalence (Remark 2.21). It records whether every directed
path in the generating graph G(R) can be returned to its starting complex by further
generators — not by arbitrary composites, but specifically by further elements of
R. This is a strictly L0 datum: no kinetics, no thermodynamics, no reverse-reaction
functor.
It is distinct from the †-structure at L2. At L2, the † operator provides an explicit
reverse generator r† : t(r) →s(r) for each r ∈R, subject to the categorical axiom
r†† = r. Weak reversibility at L0 requires only that the reverse direction is achievable
by some directed path of generators in G(R) — a much weaker condition, expressible
purely in terms of the multigraph. Introduced by Horn and Jackson [47, 8], it is the
graph-theoretic hypothesis that, together with δ = 0, guarantees the conclusions of
the Deficiency Zero Theorem. Boros [49] later showed that weak reversibility alone
(without δ = 0) guarantees existence of a positive steady state in each compatibility
class.
Definition 2.27 (Weak reversibility [47, 8]). A CRN (S, C, R, s, t) is weakly reversible
if for every directed path c0 →c1 →· · · →ck in G(R), there exists a directed path

functor into any target category.

Open networks as composable chemical systems
An open CRN is a chemical system with designated inlet species (ΣI) and outlet
species (ΣO). Pushout composition connects two such systems in series.
Proposition 2.35 tells us what L0 knows about the assembly: the stoichiometric
matrix is the column-concatenation of the two sub-matrices, and a potential is
conserved in the assembly if and only if it is conserved by both sub-networks.
Conservation laws are therefore modular at L0.
What is not modular is deficiency: the assembly can create or destroy linkage-
class connections and stoichiometric dependencies in ways δ1 and δ2 alone cannot
predict. The DZT therefore does not compose, and the kinetic composition (gray-
boxing) that Baez–Pollard [31] develop at L3 must handle this non-modularity
directly.
§2.7. L0 as a working tool
The previous sections established L0(P) as a mathematical object. This section
demonstrates it as a working tool. The three examples below correspond to the
three main structural components introduced above: §2.3 (morphism calculus),
§2.4 (universal property), and Definition 2.34 (open composition). Each derives a
non-trivial fact from L0 data alone — no energy, no rates, no geometry.

• Fa(idu) = (0, 0): the trivial process changes no atom counts.
• Fa(g ◦f) = Fa(g) + Fa(f): atom changes add along sequential steps.
• Fa(f ⊗g) = Fa(f) + Fa(g): atom changes add over parallel processes.
Since Fa(r) = (0, 0), every composite and tensor product of r with itself also maps
to (0, 0). Running a cascade of balanced reactions therefore produces zero net atom
change: additivity of atom counts along reaction sequences is a theorem, not a
postulate.
Balancedness as a vanishing condition on Fa. For a general Petri net P ′
and atom map a : S′ →N|E|, the imbalance functor Fa : L0(P ′) →BZ|E| always
exists: the assignment h(r) := ¯a(t(r)) −¯a(s(r)) is well-defined for every generator
regardless of whether atoms balance, and Theorem 2.14 extends it uniquely to all
morphisms. Balancedness is the condition that Fa takes value zero on every generator
— equivalently, by strict functoriality, that Fa is the zero functor on every morphism
of L0(P ′). An unbalanced Petri net is a perfectly valid stoichiometric category
equipped with a non-zero imbalance functor; the values Fa(r) ̸= 0 record exactly
which reactions fail to conserve atoms and by how much. Balancedness is therefore
not a condition on the existence of Fa, but a vanishing condition on its values — a
condition on a functor out of L0(P ′), not an axiom of L0 itself.

the assembled category contains morphisms not present in any single module, but
these morphisms are entirely determined by the sub-network data and the interface
identification.
The limits of L0
The three examples above exhaust what L0 can do: track stoichiometric type,
extend additive assignments from generators to all processes via the universal
property, and assemble networks from modular parts via pushout. What L0
cannot do is distinguish two reactions with the same source and target by
any numerical criterion, because L0(P) carries no numerical data as part of its
structure. The next section identifies this gap precisely and shows that extending
L0 by exactly one additional piece of data — a functor FH : L0(P) →BR — is
the minimal and canonical next step.
§2.8. What L0 cannot express: the forcing of L1
Section 2.5 established, via the automorphism sequence (3) at k = 0, that any two
reaction labels r1, r2 ∈R with identical source and target complexes — whenever
L0(P) contains such a pair — represent a class [r1 ↔r2] ∈cokerφ1 that L0 cannot
break, forcing the existence of L1. This subsection gives the chemical realisation of
that abstract argument using the nitrogen–oxygen–nitric oxide system, and then
develops the subtler content of L1 itself: the distinction between the additivity
condition (satisfied by any strict symmetric monoidal functor into BR) and the state-
function condition (satisfied only by functors induced by an object potential). The
first is the categorical content of L1; the second is an additional physical constraint
that only some L1-functors satisfy.
The gap at L0: a worked chemical instance
A single reaction. Consider the oxidation of nitrogen,
r : N2(g) + O2(g) −→2 NO(g),
∆H◦= +180.5 kJ mol−1 [44].
L0(P) contains the generating morphism r : u →v with u = N2 + O2 and
v = 2 NO. It does not contain the scalar +180.5: L0(P) carries no real-valued
functor as part of its data, so there is no structure at this level in which the
enthalpy can reside.
Parallel routes — the forcing instance. In practice, a reaction network
frequently contains two distinct reaction labels r1, r2 ∈R sharing source and
target complexes:
s(r1) = s(r2) = u,
t(r1) = t(r2) = v,

for example, two experimentally identified pathways with the same gross sto-

Both appear as distinct generating morphisms in L0(P) (Remark 2.6); the free
construction imposes no identification on them.
Suppose these two reaction labels carry distinct enthalpies: ∆H1 ̸= ∆H2. The
label swap r1 ↔r2 extends to an element of AutPetri(L0(P)) — specifically, a
label permutation within the fibre (s, t)−1(u, v), the second family identified in
§2.5. It preserves every structure of L0(P): source and target complexes are
unchanged, and no numerical data exists at L0 to be disturbed. Yet this swap is
not the restriction of any element of AutPetri(L1): every presentation-preserving
automorphism at L1 must commute with the enthalpy functor FH : L0(P) →BR
whose existence defines L1, and FH(r1) ̸= FH(r2) prevents the swap from
preserving the L1-structure. By (4), the swap represents a non-trivial class in
cokerφ1. The minimal extension resolving this conflation is to equip L0(P) with
the functor FH itself: L1, developed in Chapter 3.
Remark 2.40 (The additivity condition: equipping L0(P) with FH). Passing to L1
means equipping L0(P) with a strict symmetric monoidal functor
FH : L0(P) −→BR.
By Corollary 2.16, such a functor is uniquely determined by specifying one real
number FH(r) ∈R for each generating reaction r ∈R; the values on composites and
tensors are then forced:
FH(g ◦f) = FH(g) + FH(f),
FH(f ⊗g) = FH(f) + FH(g),
FH(idu) = 0.
These are the additivity conditions on FH. The first is the additivity form of Hess’s
Law — enthalpy changes add along sequential reaction steps; the second is additivity
over independent parallel processes. Both follow from functoriality, not from any
separate physical postulate.
In terms of the automorphism sequence, equipping L0(P) with FH breaks the
spurious label-swap symmetry in cokerφ1: once distinct real values FH(r1) ̸= FH(r2)
are assigned, the swap r1 ↔r2 no longer preserves structure, and the two reaction
labels are numerically distinguishable.
The values {FH(r)}r∈R are free parameters: any assignment of real numbers to
reaction generators extends to a valid strict symmetric monoidal functor. This is
the additivity condition for L1: it adds exactly one real parameter per reaction label,
and no other structure.
Remark 2.41 (The state-function condition). The physical fact that enthalpy is a
state function — that the enthalpy change of a reaction depends only on its initial
and final complex, not on the reaction label — is strictly stronger than the additivity
condition of Remark 2.40. It requires FH to be induced by an object potential: a
monoid homomorphism h : (N|S|, +, 0) →(R, +, 0) satisfying
FH(r) = h(t(r)) −h(s(r))
for every generating r ∈R.
By the universal property of N|S| (Proposition 2.3), any function h0 : S →R —
one real value per species, typically the standard enthalpy of formation ∆H◦
f(S) —
51


## Page 52


Kyunghoon Han
Categorification of Chemical Reactions
extends to a unique such h, and then to a valid FH via Corollary 2.16. When such an
h exists, the enthalpy change of any morphism f : u →v (whether a single generator,
a composite, or a tensor product) equals h(v) −h(u), depending only on the source
and target and not on the particular morphism. Path independence then holds
automatically: for any two morphisms f, g : u →v, FH(f) = h(v) −h(u) = FH(g).
The two conditions are distinct. The additivity condition (Remark 2.40) provides
a real number per reaction label, allows FH(r1) ̸= FH(r2) for two labels with identical
source and target, and is the categorical content of L1. The state-function condition
imposes FH(r1) = FH(r2) whenever s(r1) = s(r2) and t(r1) = t(r2), by requiring h to
be well-defined on complexes, but does not identify r1 with r2 as morphisms in the
category: the two reaction labels remain distinct elements of R, they simply receive
the same enthalpy value. The state-function condition is therefore a constraint on
the particular functor FH, not a relation imposed on L0(P) itself.
An FH satisfying only the additivity condition but not the state-function condition is
a perfectly valid strict symmetric monoidal functor, representing a situation in which
the same gross stoichiometry is associated with distinct energetic signatures across
different realisations (e.g., different catalysts, different solvents, or mechanistically
distinct pathways). Both conditions are of physical interest, and the distinction
between them is central to how L1 and L2 differ.
Remark 2.42 (Bridge to L1). The pair (L0(P), FH), where FH : L0(P) →BR is
a strict symmetric monoidal functor satisfying the additivity condition, is the L1-
level data associated with P. The complete development of L1 — its relationship
to equilibrium thermodynamics via the entropy functor FS, the †-structure of L2
encoding detailed balance, and the Wegscheider cycle conditions for rate constants —
is given in Chapter 3.

§3.1. The forcing of L1
Section 2.8 exhibited the concrete L0 →L1 forcing instance: two reaction labels

is the minimal extension L1 that resolves this class? After a brief complementary
illustration, three physical observations constrain the answer to a single categorical
object: a strict symmetric monoidal functor FH : L0(P) →BR.

These three constraints specify a strict symmetric monoidal functor
FH : L0(P) −→BR
— the one-object additive category BR introduced in §1.4. The fit between the three
physical axioms and this categorical structure is exact in both directions.
• No weaker structure suffices. A plain (non-monoidal) functor satisfies (a) but
misses (b): functoriality constrains composition, not the tensor product. A lax
monoidal functor weakens (b) to
FH(r1 ⊗r2) = FH(r1) + FH(r2) + ϕr1,r2,
introducing a coherence term ϕr1,r2 ∈R absent from any physical enthalpy
assignment. Dropping the unit condition loses (c). Each weakening fails at
least one of the three physical axioms.
• No stronger structure is needed. The three axioms fix FH uniquely on all
morphisms given its values on generators (Proposition 3.2 in §3.2). Any further
structure — requiring FH to be a monoidal equivalence, an adjunction, or a
faithful functor — would impose conditions (surjectivity, invertibility, injectivity
on morphisms) with no physical interpretation for an enthalpy assignment.
The extension presented here is the minimal categorical object resolving the cokerφ1
class identified at L0: a decorator functor adjoined to L0(P) without modifying
its underlying category. That this is the unique minimal extension resolving the
cokernel is claimed constructively at the present level, not as a general theorem about
categorical extensions; the full taxonomy of the six extension types that occur across
the tower is recorded in §10.8. The next subsection makes the construction precise.

Unpacking Definition 3.1
The domain of FH is L0(P), the free skeletal permutative category already
constructed in Section 2. The pair (L0(P), FH) is L1(P); it is emphatically not
the case that FH maps L1(P) to BR (that would be circular — L1(P) is the
decorated pair, not a category in its own right).
The target BR is a one-object category, so its object monoid {∗} is trivially
strictly commutative; this is exactly the hypothesis on the target required by
Theorem 2.14, and it is satisfied here without further work. The action of FH is
therefore entirely determined by its action on morphisms:
• Every object u ∈L0(P) maps to the single object ∗.
• Every morphism r : u →v in L0(P) maps to a real number FH(r) ∈R.
The “strict symmetric monoidal” conditions then read:
• Functoriality: FH(r2 ◦r1) = FH(r2) + FH(r1).
• Monoidality: FH(r1 ⊗r2) = FH(r1) + FH(r2).
• Unitality: FH(idu) = 0 for all u.
The adjective strict means that the coherence isomorphisms of a monoidal
functor—the natural transformations ϕA,B : FH(A) ⊗FH(B) →FH(A ⊗B) and
ϕ0 : I →FH(I)—are required to be identity morphisms, not merely natural
isomorphisms [37, Ch. XI, §1]. In BR each ϕA,B is an endomorphism of the
unique object ∗, i.e. a real number; strictness requires it to equal 0 (the identity
in BR), which is precisely the monoidality equation above. These three equations
are the complete content of the thermochemical decoration.
The existence and uniqueness of FH given its values on generating reactions follows
directly from the universal property of L0(P).
Proposition 3.2 (Existence and uniqueness of FH). Let P be a Petri net with
reaction set R. Given any assignment ∆H0 : R →R, there is a unique strict
symmetric monoidal functor FH : L0(P) →BR satisfying FH(r) = ∆H0(r) for every
generating reaction r ∈R.
Proof. By Theorem 2.14, L0(P) is the free skeletal permutative category on P: for
any strict symmetric monoidal category C whose object monoid is strictly commutative
and any morphism-assignment f : R →Mor(C) compatible with source/target types,
there is a unique strict symmetric monoidal functor ¯f : L0(P) →C extending f [37,
Ch. XI, §3].
Take C = BR, the one-object category with morphisms R and composition given by
addition. Its object monoid is a singleton, so trivially strictly commutative — the
hypothesis of Theorem 2.14 is satisfied. The source/target compatibility condition
on f = ∆H0 is also trivial since BR has only one object. The unique extension
¯f = FH satisfies all three conditions of Definition 3.1 by construction.
One real number per reaction
Proposition 3.2 says: the thermochemical content of a network at L1 is de-
termined by exactly one real number per chemical generator. The reason is
structural: every morphism of L0(P) is a finite composite and tensor product
of chemical generators r ∈R together with structural morphisms (identities

f = rik ◦· · · ◦(ri1 ⊗ri2) ◦· · · :
