§3.3. Layer 1: the generic additive functor
The functor FH of Definition 3.1 as stated — one free real parameter per generating
reaction — constitutes Layer 1 of the thermochemical structure. The following
theorem encodes Hess’s Law and its monoidal counterpart as the two defining axioms
of FH. The physical content of Hess’s Law has been understood since 1840 [53]; its
formulation as the functoriality condition of a strict monoidal functor into BR is, to
the authors’ knowledge, original to this work.
Theorem 3.3 (Hess’s Law and parallel additivity — Layer 1). Let FH : L0(P) →BR
be the thermochemical functor (Layer 1 data).
(i) (Sequential additivity / Hess’s Law) For composable reactions r1 : u →v,
r2 : v →w:
FH(r2 ◦r1) = FH(r1) + FH(r2).
(ii) (Parallel additivity) For any reactions r1, r2:
FH(r1 ⊗r2) = FH(r1) + FH(r2).
(iii) (No spurious energy) FH(idu) = 0 for every complex u.
Proof. Parts (i)–(iii) are the functoriality, monoidality, and unitality axioms of FH
respectively. They hold by definition of a strict symmetric monoidal functor; the
content of the theorem is that such an FH exists and is unique given values on
generators, as established in Proposition 3.2.
Remark 3.4 (Two postulates, one equation). Traditional thermochemistry textbooks
state Hess’s Law (part (i)) and parallel additivity (part (ii)) as two separate empirical
postulates [3]. Categorically, both are instances of the single requirement that FH
is a monoidal functor: sequential additivity is functoriality, parallel additivity is
monoidality. The classical textbook presentation reflects the same mathematical
structure, stated in the language of experiments rather than of categories.
Physically, the full path-independence form of Hess’s Law — the enthalpy of a process
depends only on initial and final complexes, regardless of route — is classically derived
from the first law together with the identification of enthalpy as a state function
[54]. Theorem 3.3 captures the additive content of Hess’s Law (along sequential
composites and across parallel processes) directly from functoriality, without invoking
the state-function identification. The path-independence form proper requires the
Layer 2 coboundary condition FH = δ0h developed in §3.4.

§3.4. Layer 2: the state-function condition
Warning 3.5 shows that Layer 1 alone permits thermochemical cycles to accumulate
non-zero enthalpy, in conflict with the first law of thermodynamics. The culprit
is that Layer 1 assigns a real number to each reaction independently; it imposes
no relationship between the enthalpy of a reaction and any intrinsic property of
the complexes it connects. The first law demands more: enthalpy must be a state
function, meaning its value for any process depends only on the initial and final
states, not on the path taken. Mathematically, this means the enthalpy assignment
must be expressible as a difference of potentials defined on the complexes themselves.
Layer 2 is the additional datum that enforces this.
Definition 3.6 (Layer 2: state-function / coboundary condition). A thermochemical
functor FH : L0(P) →BR satisfies the state-function condition (Layer 2) if there
exists a monoid homomorphism
h :

such that, for every generating reaction r : u →v,
FH(r) = h(v) −h(u).
We write this condition as FH = δ0h and call h an object potential (or additive
potential) for FH.
The notation δ0 and the term object potential require some comments. The map h
assigns a real number (a “height” or “potential”) to each complex in N[S], and the
identity FH(r) = h(v) −h(u) says that the enthalpy of a generating reaction is the
difference of the endpoint potentials. This is the discrete analogue of a conservative
field on a graph: individual reactions are directed edges, while sequences of reactions
are directed paths. For an exact edge-labeling, the total enthalpy along a directed
path depends only on its endpoints, and hence vanishes on directed cycles [56, 57].
The symbol δ0 is borrowed from graph cohomology.

Remark 3.8. For arbitrary edge-labelings on a directed graph, vanishing on directed
cycles characterises exactness with respect to an arbitrary vertex-potential. In the
present paper, however, Layer 2 is stronger: the potential must extend additively to
a monoid homomorphism h : N[S] →R. Accordingly, the directed-cycle condition is
a consequence of Layer 2, but not by itself an equivalent replacement for it.
Why the state-function condition is the first law
The condition FH = δ0h encodes the first law of thermodynamics in a single
equation. Saying FH(r) = h(v) −h(u) means enthalpy depends only on the
initial and final complexes, not on which specific reaction or sequence of reactions
connects them. Going around a closed reaction cycle yields zero net enthalpy
because the potential heights h return to their starting values. Layer 1 alone is
the theory of an additive reaction label; Layer 2 additionally demands that this
label derives from an absolute assignment of values to the objects (complexes)
of the network.
Parameter count.
Observation 3.9 (Parameter reduction at Layer 2). The state-function condition
reduces the number of free parameters required to specify a thermochemical network,
exchanging reaction-level freedom for a smaller species-level one.
• Layer 1: |R| free parameters (one real number per generating reaction).
• Layer 2: |S| species values {h(S)}S∈S specify h, hence FH = δ0h; the physically
meaningful content of h is its image under δ0, which has gauge kernel
ker(δ0) ∩HomMon(N[S], R) ∼= ker(N ⊤) ⊆R|S|.
where N ∈Z|S|×|R| is the stoichiometric matrix. Equivalently, two object
potentials h, h′ differ only by an irrelevant gauge iff h −h′ is a conservation
law (Proposition 2.22).
• Net dimension: the reaction-enthalpy parameter space im(δ0) ⊆R|R| has
dimension ρ := rankR(N), the dimension of the stoichiometric subspace (§2.6);
the gauge kernel is |S| −ρ dimensional.
The reduction from |R| to ρ parameters proceeds in two stages, exposing the role
of deficiency. Graph-cycle conditions on the reaction graph alone — equivalent to

Counting calorimetric experiments
A thermochemical network with |R| generating reactions and stoichiometric rank
ρ requires exactly ρ independent calorimetric measurements to fully characterise
all reaction enthalpies; the remaining |R| −ρ values are determined by the
cycle conditions of Proposition 3.7(iv). For deficiency-zero networks, ρ = n −ℓ,
recovering the familiar “n −ℓmeasurements” rule of thumb (where n is the
number of complexes and ℓthe number of linkage classes); non-zero deficiency
requires ρ < n −ℓmeasurements relative to the rule of thumb.
For the Born–Haber cycle of Example 3.15, the cycle constraint relating the
direct formation reaction to the five-step elementary decomposition lets the
lattice enthalpy FH(r5) — which is not accessible to direct calorimetry — be
extracted from the four measurable elementary steps and the net formation
enthalpy.

§3.5. Worked examples
The three examples below are standard exercises from undergraduate thermochemistry
curricula [3, 44]. Every introductory chemistry student learns to add enthalpies along
reaction pathways, to close thermochemical cycles, and to use tabulated formation
enthalpies to predict unmeasurable quantities. The categorical language of L1 reveals
the common mathematical skeleton behind all three: Hess’s Law is functoriality,
cycle closure is the coboundary condition, and a thermochemical data table is an
object potential. Nothing new is computed; what is new is the identification of the
precise categorical structure that makes the computations valid.

compilation, which is internally consistent by construction; cross-source consistency
actively tests whether the four experiments — run in different laboratories with
independent reference states — admit a unified thermochemical description. A
significant non-closure would signal either measurement error or use of inconsistent
reference states, a violation of the Layer 2 coboundary condition detectable without
knowing which individual measurement is wrong. This is the calorimetric analogue
of a Kirchhoff consistency check in an electrical network (Section 3.6).
§3.6. Thermochemical networks and the Wegscheider pre-condition
In 1901, Rudolf Wegscheider showed that in a reversible mass-action reaction network
obeying detailed balance, the rate constants — equivalently the elementary-step equi-
librium constants — cannot be chosen independently; stoichiometric cycle relations
impose multiplicative constraints, now called the Wegscheider conditions [61]. These
conditions are the cornerstone of thermodynamic consistency in chemical kinetics
and underpin everything from enzyme network analysis to the theory of detailed
balance [62, 9].
The constraints enter the tower in two stages. At L2, the full Wegscheider conditions
arise as the coboundary condition for the Gibbs functor F T
G = FH −TFS, restricting
the allowed equilibrium constants via ker F T
G (see Section 4). At the present level
L1, the same mathematical structure appears in a purely enthalpic form: any
thermochemical network with directed cycles must satisfy additive cycle conditions
on the enthalpy assignment. This is the thermochemical pre-condition — the enthalpic-
additive analogue of the full Wegscheider conditions, visible already at L1 before
entropy and free energy enter at L2. Isolating it here makes the tower structure

explicit: the Wegscheider conditions are not a kinetic accident but a consequence of
the coboundary structure that is already forced at the thermochemical level.
The following definition places this classical notion on the categorical footing provided
by L0(P). The underlying idea — that a thermochemical network is a reaction graph
decorated by an enthalpy assignment — goes back to Hess [53] and was made explicit
in the cycle-condition language by Wegscheider [61]; the formulation below is new
in casting it as a pair (P, h) where h is a monoid homomorphism into R and the
enthalpy functor is the induced coboundary FH = δ0h.
Definition 3.17 (State-function thermochemical network). A state-function ther-
mochemical network (a Layer 2 thermochemical network) is a pair (P, h) where P
is a Petri net and h : N[S] →R is a monoid homomorphism (an object potential
in the sense of Definition 3.6). The induced functor FH = δ0h : L0(P) →BR
automatically satisfies both Layer 1 (functoriality) and Layer 2 (the coboundary
condition), and is uniquely determined by h. This is the Layer 2 specialisation of
the generic L1-decoration of Definition 3.1: a generic L1-functor FH is required only
to be strict symmetric monoidal, while a state-function thermochemical network
requires FH to factor through an object potential.
Thermochemical networks in this sense pervade chemistry. The Born–Haber cycles
of ionic compounds (Example 3.15), the Hess cycles for combustion enthalpies
(Examples 3.13, 3.16), and the thermodynamic cycles for ATP hydrolysis coupled to
biosynthetic reactions [63] are all instances: in each case, the physically meaningful
quantity is the object potential h, and the measurable reaction enthalpies are its
coboundary. The parameter count ρ = rankN of Observation 3.9 is the number
of independent calorimetric experiments needed to determine h up to the ker(N ⊤)
gauge (equivalently, up to the choice of reference state); for deficiency-zero networks
this reduces to n −ℓ.

To the author’s knowledge, the connection between this proposition and Kirchhoff’s
Voltage Law has not previously been stated as a theorem in the chemical reaction
network literature, though the analogy between thermochemical cycles and electrical
circuits has been used informally since the early network thermodynamics of Oster,
Perelson, and Katchalsky [64]. The categorical proof makes the connection exact.
Kirchhoff’s Voltage Law in disguise
In an electrical circuit, Kirchhoff’s Voltage Law (KVL) states that the algebraic
sum of voltage drops around any closed loop of circuit branches is zero [65]: in a
conservative (electrostatic) network, voltage drops are differences of an electric
scalar potential, so traversing a directed cycle returns to the starting potential.
Formally: for any directed cycle of circuit branches, the sum of the voltage drops

physical guises. In both cases, a functor (the voltage assignment in circuits;
the enthalpy functor FH in thermochemistry) maps into the one-object additive
category BR and must assign zero to every closed loop. The reason is identical:
both the voltage in a circuit and the enthalpy of a reaction are coboundaries
of a scalar potential (electric potential ϕ in circuits; the object potential h in
thermochemistry). The Born–Haber cycle, Hess’s Law for formation enthalpies,
and the ATP–ADP free energy cycle in cellular metabolism [63] are all chemical
instances of the same categorical fact.

§3.7. What L1 cannot express: forcing of L2
Layer 1 assigns a single real number FH(r) to each generating reaction and propagates
it additively. The physical question it cannot answer is: how does a reaction network
respond to changes in temperature? The temperature dependence of equilibrium is
governed by the Gibbs free energy ∆G = ∆H −T∆S; two reactions with identical
∆H but different ∆S accumulate different free energies at every temperature, yet
are indistinguishable by FH alone. The following makes this gap precise.

the theory. There exists thermodynamic information relevant to binding that is
invisible to L1 but necessary to explain the experimentally observed difference
in affinity. In other words, once one reaches this point, an enthalpy-only level
of the tower is no longer adequate: the tower must be refined by adjoining a
further thermodynamic datum.
Methodological caution. This formulation must be stated at the level of
intrinsic thermodynamic parameters rather than raw observed heats. For protein–
ligand binding, calorimetric enthalpies can be shifted by linked protonation and
buffer effects, so comparison of reaction labels should be made only after such

§4. L2: The Equilibrium Level
§4.1. Forcing the extension: what L1 cannot express
Section 3.7 identified the gap at L1: two reactions with equal enthalpy changes
but different entropy changes respond to temperature in completely opposite ways,
yet are indistinguishable by FH alone. Before making this precise categorically, we
establish the chemical reality that such pairs are not exotic but generic in complex
reaction networks like a biochemical system.
Abstract forcing pair for L2
The mathematical content of the gap at L1 is a pair of generating reactions
r1, r2 : u →v
in some Petri net P, with the same enthalpy but different entropies:
FH(r1) = FH(r2),
FS(r1) ̸= FS(r2).
The label swap σ : r1 ↔r2 preserves the L1-decoration (FH ◦σ = FH on
chemical generators) but does not preserve any decoration recording entropy,
since FS◦σ ̸= FS on {r1, r2}. By the automorphism sequence of §2.5, σ represents
a non-trivial coset in cokerφ2: the forgetful operation U2 (Definition 4.1) is not
injective on decorated triples — the underlying L1-decoration (L0(P), FH) alone
does not determine FS. L1 conflates the two reactions; L2 separates them, since
their Gibbs free energies F T
G(ri) = FH(ri) −T FS(ri) differ at every T > 0.
The chembox below establishes that such pairs are generic in real chemistry —
a feature of biochemical reaction networks under coarse-graining, not a mathe-
matical contrivance.
Binding thermodynamics: ∆H and ∆S need not covary
Isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC) studies of protein–ligand binding show
that the enthalpic and entropic contributions to binding can vary separately
across a ligand series. This is a structural feature of molecular recognition: ∆H
and ∆S report on different physical aspects of binding and there is no general
law forcing them to change together [69].
The binding enthalpy ∆H is often associated with the quality of direct inter-
molecular interactions, such as hydrogen bonding, electrostatics, van der Waals
contacts, and the enthalpic cost of desolvating polar groups. The binding entropy
∆S reflects changes in solvent organisation and molecular freedom, including
favorable release of ordered water and unfavorable losses of ligand and protein
conformational freedom upon complex formation. Because these contributions
arise from different physical mechanisms, modifying one does not in general
determine the other [70, 71, 72].
A useful illustration is provided by Biela et al.’s ITC and crystallographic study
of thrombin inhibitors with systematically varied P3 substituents [73]. These
72

Kyunghoon Han

ligands probe the same hydrophobic S3/4 pocket and therefore belong to the
same stoichiometric reaction class at L0: Inhibitor + Thrombin →Complex.
Across the series, increasing hydrophobic bulk produced an overall affinity
enhancement of about 40-fold that was attributed mainly to a more favorable
entropy term, consistent with stepwise disruption of the pocket water network
[73]. At the same time, the enthalpy changed much less strongly than the
entropy, so the dominant thermodynamic trend in the series was entropy-driven
rather than enthalpy-driven.
For broader context, thermodynamic profiling of marketed HIV-1 protease in-
hibitors shows a wide spread of binding enthalpies. In Freire’s analysis, Indinavir
is enthalpically unfavourable (∆H ≈+7.6 kJ mol−1), whereas Darunavir is
strongly enthalpy-driven (∆H ≈−53.1 kJ mol−1). Across this inhibitor class,
the progression from earlier to later, more potent compounds is accompanied by
increasingly favourable binding enthalpies [70].
What minimal additional structure allows the tower to distinguish the two reactions
of the forcing pair? The same three physical observations that forced FH in Section 3.1
apply to entropy:
(a) Sequential additivity of standard reaction entropy. ∆S(r2 ◦r1) =
∆S(r1) + ∆S(r2): the total entropy change of a sequence of reactions is the
sum of each step’s contribution.
(b) Parallel additivity. ∆S(r1 ⊗r2) = ∆S(r1) + ∆S(r2): independent reactions
contribute independently to the total entropy change.
(c) No spurious entropy. ∆S(idu) = 0 for every complex u: the identity process
produces no entropy change.
These are the same three constraints that characterised FH in Section 3.1, with
enthalpy replaced by entropy. They uniquely identify a strict symmetric monoidal
functor FS : L0(P) →BR. The universal property of L0(P) (Theorem 2.14) guaran-
tees existence and uniqueness of FS given one real number per generating reaction
— the same theorem applied a second time, with ∆S◦
r in place of ∆H◦
r . No new
categorical machinery is required.

Theorem 2.14 is satisfied for both applications.

is trivially strictly commutative, and Theorem 2.14 provides a unique strict symmetric
monoidal functor extending the generator assignment ∆S0.

Proof. Apply Theorem 2.14 twice independently: once with the generator assignment

4.2.1. Reversible Petri nets and the dagger
Physical chemical reactions are, in principle, reversible: thermodynamics does not
forbid the transformation in either direction. For ordinary chemical systems governed
by classical or non-relativistic quantum dynamics, the principle of microscopic re-
versibility is a consequence of the time-reversal symmetry of the underlying equations,
so each elementary reaction step has a corresponding reverse step [77, 78, 79]. The
thermodynamic data (FH, FS) therefore determines not whether the reverse process
exists, but how the equilibrium is biased toward reactants or products [62, 54]. This
has a direct modelling consequence: a faithful Petri net for a system at or near
equilibrium should contain both r and r† for every reaction r it models.
The following definition formalises this and introduces the reversible closure — the
smallest reversible Petri net containing a given one. The term closure is used in its
standard algebraic sense: just as the algebraic closure of a field adjoins all missing
roots and nothing more, the reversible closure of a Petri net freely adjoins, for
each generator r, the reverse generator r† that is missing, and nothing more. The
result is characterised by a universal property: it is the initial reversible Petri net
equipped with an embedding of P. Petri nets as freely generated categorical /
monoidal structures go back to Meseguer–Montanari [32], while open Petri nets and
reaction networks are treated categorically by Baez–Pollard and Baez–Master [31, 43].
Reversibility via adjoining reverse transitions is also standard in the reversible-Petri-
net literature [80, 81]. In the present paper, we call the resulting initial reversible
completion of P its reversible closure.
Definition 4.5 (Reversible Petri net and reversible closure). A Petri net P is
reversible if for every generator r : u →v in R, its reverse r† : v →u is also a
generator in R, with (r†)† = r. The reversible closure ¯P of any Petri net P is the
reversible Petri net obtained by freely adjoining, for each r ∈R, a new generator
r† : v →u subject to (r†)† = r. It is the initial reversible Petri net equipped with a
Petri net embedding ι : P ,→¯P.
Dagger structures and opposite categories
For any category C, the opposite category Cop has the same objects as C but
every morphism f : X →Y in C becomes a morphism f op : Y →X in Cop,
with composition reversed: gop ◦f op = (f ◦g)op [82, 83]. This is a purely formal
construction; it does not equip C with any extra structure, only relates C to a
“mirror” category with the same objects.

chemical generators and then extended contravariantly to composite morphisms,
giving L0( ¯P) the structure of a dagger-symmetric-monoidal category [74]. The
opposite category L0( ¯P)op exists as a formal mirror for any ¯P; what makes L0( ¯P)
a dagger-SMC is the additional datum that the dagger operation is identity on
objects — i.e., a canonical identification of source and target of each reversed
morphism with the original target and source.
Definition 4.6 (Anti-symmetry axioms). For a reversible Petri net, the functor pair
(FH, FS) is required to satisfy, for every generator r ∈R:
FH(r†) = −FH(r),
FS(r†) = −FS(r).
Remark 4.7 (Anti-symmetry is automatic under Layer 2). Definition 4.6 is stated
as a Layer 1 axiom — an additional constraint on the functor pair (FH, FS) beyond
the SMC functor axioms. Under Layer 2 for both functors (Definition 3.6 for FH,
Definition 4.18 below for FS), anti-symmetry is not an additional constraint but a

generator r : u →v,
FH(r†) = hf(u) −hf(v) = −FH(r),
FS(r†) = hS(u) −hS(v) = −FS(r),
by applying Proposition 3.7 separately to each functor. Anti-symmetry is thus
a Layer 1 axiom — required to state detailed balance without invoking Layer 2
structure — that becomes a Layer 2 theorem.
Anti-symmetry: state functions force sign flips
Both conditions are direct consequences of the state-function character of en-
thalpy and entropy — among the most firmly established facts in chemical
thermodynamics [54, 84].
Enthalpy anti-symmetry. Since enthalpy H is a state function, its change
along any path from complex u to complex v depends only on the endpoints:
FH(r) = H(v)−H(u) for r : u →v (Layer 2/coboundary form, Proposition 3.11).
Reversing the reaction gives
FH(r†) = H(u) −H(v) = −FH(r).
This is Hess’s Law applied to a single step: if the forward reaction releases ∆H
kJ/mol, the reverse absorbs exactly |∆H| kJ/mol, and vice versa [53, 54].
Entropy anti-symmetry. Entropy S is likewise a state function (a conse-
quence of the second and third laws [54]). By the same coboundary argument:
FS(r†) = S(u) −S(v) = −FS(r). At the molecular level this reflects microscopic
reversibility [62]: at equilibrium, the forward and reverse fluxes through every

elementary step are equal, so any state-function difference associated with the
step must reverse sign upon reversal of the step. A process that increases the
system’s entropy by |FS(r)| in the forward direction decreases it by the same
amount in the reverse.
What this is, and what it is not. The sign-flip refers to the reaction entropy
change ∆S◦
r — a state-function difference that is positive, negative, or zero
depending on the reaction. It must not be confused with the entropy production
rate σ ≥0, a non-negative quantity in nonequilibrium thermodynamics that
quantifies irreversibility and belongs to the kinetic/open-system level L3, not
to the standard-state L2 decoration. Reaction entropy changes flip sign upon
reversal; entropy production does not.
Both axioms are imposed as constraints on the functor pair (FH, FS), not on
the category L0(P) itself. The underlying category remains the free skeletal
permutative category.
Remark 4.8 (Anti-symmetry halves the parameter count, matching thermochemical
tables). For a reversible Petri net with |R| = 2m generators (forward/reverse pairs),
anti-symmetry reduces the free parameter space of (FH, FS) from 4m to 2m real
numbers: m values of ∆H◦and m values of ∆S◦, one per forward reaction — precisely
the entries of a standard thermochemical table [85, 54].
This matters for two distinct reasons.
First, it is canonical: the reduced parameter count matches exactly the format in
which experimental thermochemical data is tabulated and used. Standard references
[85] list one ∆H◦
f and one S◦per species, not separate entries for forward and reverse
reactions. The anti-symmetry axiom is not an extra mathematical assumption but
the categorical encoding of an empirical convention that is itself forced by energy
conservation and the state-function property.
Second, it is consistency-enforcing: without anti-symmetry, assigning independent
values to r and r† would permit FH(r) + FH(r†) ̸= 0, violating energy conservation
and making the thermodynamic model internally inconsistent. Anti-symmetry is
therefore the minimal algebraic condition that keeps the decorating functors in
agreement with the physical content they are supposed to represent.

It is the same concept as zero set, vanishing locus, or level set at zero, and appears
throughout algebra and geometry [87].

or equilibrium ideal: the algebraic set of concentration vectors x ∈Rn

networks.

4.3.1. Reversal symmetry of the standard Gibbs-zero locus
Detailed balance is a central principle of chemical kinetics and non-equilibrium
thermodynamics. Chemically, it states that at thermodynamic equilibrium, every
elementary reaction step is individually balanced by its reverse: the forward and
reverse fluxes through each step are equal, not merely the net flux around each cycle
[62, 9]. For a single reversible step r : A ⇌B with forward rate constant k+ and
reverse rate constant k−, detailed balance at an equilibrium concentration vector
requires
k+[A]eq = k−[B]eq,
which gives Keq = k+/k−. This is a kinetic flux equality, requiring rate constants
and equilibrium concentrations — data that lives at L3, not L2.
What L2 supplies, and the proposition below makes precise, is the thermodynamic
precondition for detailed balance: when a reaction lies in the standard Gibbs-
zero locus ZG(T) = ker F T
G, so does its reverse, and the standard equilibrium
constants of the two satisfy Kr†(T) = 1/Kr(T). In networks this thermodynamic
precondition extends to a cycle condition — the Wegscheider conditions [61], that
the product of standard equilibrium constants around every directed cycle equals one
(Proposition 4.31). The full kinetic content of detailed balance — equality of forward
and reverse fluxes at given concentrations — is deferred to L3, where it appears as a
consistency condition between the rate constants and the L2 equilibrium constants.

§4.4. Layer 1 and Layer 2 for FS, the third law, and standard chemical
potential
The Layer 1/Layer 2 split introduced for FH in Sections 3.3 and 3.4 applies to FS
with the same categorical structure but one physically decisive difference at Layer 2.
At Layer 1, the structure is identical for both functors: FS is any strict SMC functor
FS : L0(P) →BR, with no constraint beyond the functor axioms (and anti-symmetry
FS(r†) = −FS(r) for reversible nets, Definition 4.6). The Layer 1 parameter space
for FS has |R| free real numbers, reduced to |R|/2 by anti-symmetry for reversible
Petri nets. This is entirely parallel to FH: one real number per generating reaction,
freely chosen, with no further constraint.
At Layer 2, both FH and FS are required to satisfy a state-function condition: each
must arise as the coboundary δ0h of a species-level potential h. The categorical
machinery is identical in both cases: the species-level potential is determined by the
reaction data F = δ0h only up to the gauge ker(N ⊤) ⊂R|S| (Remark 3.12), the space
of conservation laws viewed as species potentials. What differs between FH and FS is
the physical convention used to fix a distinguished representative within this gauge
equivalence class: for FH, a chosen convention (IUPAC: ∆H◦
f(E) = 0 for elemental
references); for FS, an external physical principle (the third law: S(X, 0 K) = 0 for
perfect crystalline ground states). This asymmetry — between conventional and
principled gauge fixing — is the subject of Section 4.4.2 below.

Layer 2 requires FS to satisfy the entropy state-function condition: the entropy
change of a reaction must be expressible as the difference of species-level entropy
values, exactly as the enthalpy change at Layer 2 for FH is the difference of formation
enthalpies.

4.4.2. The third law: an absolute reference for hS
This is the sole asymmetry between FH and FS at Layer 2, and it has no categorical
source: it is a fact about the physical world. The discussion below is needed because
the asymmetry has practical consequences for what thermochemical data can and

the space of conservation laws viewed as species potentials. This gauge applies

§4.5. Thermodynamic theorems at L2
The Gibbs family T 7→F T
G = FH −T · FS suffices to derive, within the categorical
framework of L2, four classical results of chemical thermodynamics as theorems for re-
action networks: the second law criterion for chemical spontaneity (Proposition 4.24),
the van ’t Hoff equation for the temperature dependence of equilibrium constants,
the Gibbs–Helmholtz equation recovering the reaction enthalpy from free-energy
measurements, and Le Chatelier’s principle for temperature perturbations. Each is a
statement about morphisms in L0(P) labelled by the Gibbs family; none requires
data beyond what is already in L2.

at temperature T: the ratio of product to reactant concentrations (or activities)
when the system has reached thermodynamic equilibrium.

The second law of thermodynamics, at constant temperature and pressure, takes the
following form for individual reaction steps.

4.5.3. The van ’t Hoff equation
The van ’t Hoff equation: history and use
The van ’t Hoff equation describes how the equilibrium constant of a reaction
changes with temperature. It was derived by Jacobus Henricus van ’t Hoff in
1884 from the Clausius–Clapeyron equation and Hess’s Law [94, 54], and is one
of the most practically important equations in chemical thermodynamics.
Its primary use is measurement: plotting ln Keq against 1/T (the van ’t Hoff
plot) gives a straight line with slope −FH(r)/R and intercept FS(r)/R when
FH and FS are temperature-independent. This allows FH(r) and FS(r) to be
extracted from equilibrium constant measurements at multiple temperatures,
without calorimetry. The van ’t Hoff plot is the experimental foundation for the
Layer 1 parameter space: it is the direct measurement procedure that assigns
one real number (F T
G, at any chosen reference temperature) to each reaction.

4.5.4. The Gibbs–Helmholtz equation
The Gibbs–Helmholtz equation: physical meaning and practical use
The Gibbs–Helmholtz equation [93, 95, 54] is the relation between the tem-
perature dependence of the Gibbs free energy and the enthalpy of a process.
Physically, it answers the following question: if one measures ∆G◦
r = F T

The answer is yes: FH(r) is the slope of the function F T

route to the Layer 1 parameter FH(r) that does not require measuring heat
directly. This is important in practice whenever calorimetry is difficult (e.g., for
reactions in solution or in biological systems), where ∆G can be measured via
Keq but ∆H is harder to access [54, 70].

4.5.5. Le Chatelier’s principle
Observation 4.29 (Le Chatelier’s principle, under the constant-FH approximation).
Under the temperature-independent-enthalpy approximation inherited from Proposi-
tion 4.26, for any generator r:
• FH(r) > 0 (endothermic): d ln K/dT > 0, so K increases with T. Heating
shifts equilibrium toward products.
• FH(r) < 0 (exothermic): d ln K/dT < 0, so K decreases with T. Heating shifts
equilibrium toward reactants.
• FH(r) = 0 (thermoneutral): K is independent of T.
This is Le Chatelier’s principle [96] for temperature perturbations: a system at
equilibrium responds to heating by shifting in the endothermic direction. At L2 it
is a theorem in the same approximation that supports the van ’t Hoff equation; if
heat-capacity effects change the sign of ∆H◦over the temperature interval considered,
the directional statement must be re-evaluated using the integrated van ’t Hoff form.

Wegscheider conditions in the CRNT literature
The Wegscheider conditions were introduced by Rudolf Wegscheider in 1901 [61]
as necessary constraints on the equilibrium constants of a reversible reaction
network with cycles. For a directed cycle r1, . . . , rk in the reaction graph, the

Their physical content is that thermodynamics forbids perpetual motion: no
network of reactions can have a cycle in which every step is spontaneous, since
that would allow work to be extracted from a system at uniform temperature
and pressure.
In the CRNT literature, the Wegscheider conditions appear as linear constraints
on the vector of ln Keq values. Horn and Jackson [8] showed that they are
equivalent to the existence of a thermodynamic potential (a species- level free
energy function) whose coboundary gives the reaction free energies — precisely
the Layer 2 condition F T
G = δ0hµ◦of Proposition 4.22. Feinberg [9] used the
conditions as a necessary criterion for detailed balance in mass-action systems.
Müller and Regensburger [97] gave a systematic treatment of the conditions in
the context of generalised mass-action kinetics.
What is new in Proposition 4.31 below is not the conditions themselves but
their derivation: they follow directly and necessarily from Layer 2 applied
independently to FH and FS, without invoking kinetics or rate constants. In
the standard CRNT treatment, the conditions on ∆H◦and ∆S◦are stated
separately from the multiplicative condition on Keq values. The proof below
shows they are the same condition at different levels of the tower.
Before stating the proposition, we fix notation for the reaction graph.
Definition 4.30 (Reaction graph G(R) and directed cycle). The reaction graph
G(R) of a Petri net P is the directed graph whose vertices are the complexes u ∈N|S|
and whose directed edges are the generating reactions r : u →v in R. A directed
cycle in G(R) of length k is a sequence of generators r1, . . . , rk ∈R such that the
target of each ri equals the source of ri+1 (indices modulo k):
r1 : u1 →u2,
r2 : u2 →u3,
. . . ,
rk : uk →u1.
Such a cycle determines a composite morphism rk ◦· · · ◦r1 : u1 →u1 in L0(P)
whose source and target coincide. This composite need not equal idu1 — in the free
skeletal permutative category L0(P), distinct sequences of chemical generators can
yield distinct morphisms with the same source and target. The cycle conditions that
follow are the statement that this composite maps to 0 under FH, FS, and FG, despite
not being the identity morphism.
For a Petri net satisfying Layer 2 for FH (equivalently, for any coboundary functor),

For kinetics, the corresponding additive structure lives on Markov-semigroup gener-
ators, not on rate constants themselves. The generator contribution of a reaction
r is the operator FP(r) = Mλr(Rr −I) on observables f : N|S| →R (Defini-

r FP(r), and parallel reactions on disjoint species combine via Kronecker sum

therefore the cone gS of Markov-semigroup generators on NS, viewed as a one-object
strict SMC with sequential composition by addition, monoidal product by Kronecker
sum, and unit the zero generator (Remark 5.3). Every complex u ∈L0(P) maps to
the unique object of this one-object category, interpreted as the global state space
NS.
Markov kernels (probability transition functions) live in the ambient symmetric
monoidal category Stoch [103, 104], but enter the picture only via finite-time
evolution: a generator L ∈gS exponentiates to a one-parameter Markov semigroup
{etL}t≥0 of kernels in EndStoch(NS). This exponentiation expt : L 7→etL is not an
SMC functor (sequential composition fails to commute with addition off the abelian
locus, by Trotter–Kato), and that failure is the precise categorical content of the
L3 →L4 forcing pair (Section 5.9). The shorthand “FP : L0(P) →Stoch” that
appears in some places in this chapter abbreviates the composite expt ◦FP, with FP
landing in gS at the categorical level.
The same physical logic that forced FH and FS at earlier levels forces FP : L0(P) →gS
here, with three axioms whose content is now non-trivial:
(a) Sequential composition. For composable reactions r1 : u →v, r2 : v →w
in L0(P), the composite r2 ◦r1 maps under FP to the additive sum
FP(r2 ◦r1) = FP(r2) + FP(r1)
in gS
(Proposition 5.10). This is the generator of the CTMC in which both reaction
channels r1 and r2 are simultaneously available; it is not an effective single-step
rate law for the coarse-grained reaction u →w obtained by eliminating v. Such
a coarse-graining requires a quasi-steady-state or rapid-equilibrium reduction,
which lies outside the strict L3 functorial assignment and is recovered only as
a derived approximation under additional hypotheses on the rate constants.
(b) Parallel composition. If r1 and r2 act on independent subsystems with
disjoint species sets S1, S2, their combined generator on the joint state space
N|S1| × N|S2| is the Kronecker sum
FP(r1 ⊗r2) = FP(r1) ⊗I + I ⊗FP(r2)
(Proposition 5.11), the infinitesimal of the kernel tensor product in Stoch.
(c) Identity. The “do nothing” morphism idu produces no state change: FP(idu) =
0 ∈gS (Definition 5.5), the zero generator, which exponentiates to the identity
Markov kernel e0 = idNS ∈EndStoch(NS).

§5.2. Definition of L3(P) and the target Stoch
5.2.1. The Markov generator algebra and the ambient Stoch
The stochastic description of a chemical reaction network is classical: given the
countable state space of species-count vectors x ∈N|S| — or a finite closed irreducible
subset of it, when conservation laws bound the total copy numbers — the network
evolves as a continuous-time Markov chain (CTMC) whose generator encodes the
rates at which each reaction fires [107, 10].
This description underlies a large
body of work in the CRNT literature — on stationary distributions [108, 109], on
product-form Poisson distributions and their extensions [110], and on stochastic
approximation of arbitrary distributions [111] — without requiring a categorical
language.
Two categorical objects are needed to make the compositional structure of CTMCs
explicit:
• the symmetric monoidal category Stoch, in which finite-time Markov kernels
K( · | x) compose by Chapman–Kolmogorov integration — the ambient setting
in which the time-evolved chain lives;
• the cone gS of Markov generators on N|S|, viewed as the morphism set of the
one-object strict SMC BgS, with sequential composition by addition, monoidal
product by Kronecker sum, and unit the zero generator — the actual functorial
target of the kinetic functor FP.
Generators and kernels are linked by exponentiation expt : L 7→etL, which sends a
generator L ∈gS to its one-parameter Markov semigroup {etL}t≥0 in EndStoch(N|S|).
This section defines both, and shows that FP targets BgS at the categorical level —
with Stoch entering only as the home of finite-time evolution.
Definition 5.1 (Stoch). The category Stoch has:
• Objects: measurable spaces (X, ΣX).
• Morphisms: Markov kernels K : X →Y , i.e. functions K : X × ΣY →[0, 1]
such that (i) for each x ∈X, K(x, ·) is a probability measure on (Y, ΣY ), and
(ii) for each A ∈ΣY , the map K(·, A) : X →[0, 1] is measurable.
• Composition: for K : X →Y and L : Y →Z, (L ◦K)(· | x) :=
R
Y L(· |
y) K(dy | x) (Chapman–Kolmogorov integration).
• Monoidal product: (X, ΣX)⊗(Y, ΣY ) := (X×Y, ΣX⊗ΣY ), with (K1⊗K2)(· |
x1, x2) := K1(· | x1) ⊗K2(· | x2).
• Monoidal unit: the one-point space I = ({∗}, {∅, {∗}}).
Stoch is a symmetric monoidal category under this structure; it is moreover a
Markov category in the sense of Fritz [103], with a canonical copy/discard structure
that encodes conditional independence [103, 104].

Definition 5.2 (The generator algebra BgS). The Markov-generator algebra gS is
the positive cone of generators of Markov semigroups on N|S|: a (possibly unbounded)
operator L on observables f : N|S| →R with off-diagonal-non-negative matrix entries
and rows summing to zero, closable to a CTMC under standard non-explosion condi-
tions [112]. The one-object category BgS has a single formal object ∗— interpreted
as the global state space N|S|, the carrier on which every complex u ∈L0(P) acts
under FP — and morphism set End(∗) = gS. BgS is a strict symmetric monoidal
category:
• sequential composition: addition, L1 + L2;
• monoidal product: Kronecker sum, L1 ⊗I + I ⊗L2 (the infinitesimal of the
kernel tensor product in Stoch);
• unit: the zero generator on N|S|.
All associativity, unit, and symmetry equations hold as equalities, not merely up to
isomorphism.
BgS versus BR
At L1 and L2 the target was BR: one object, morphisms R, sequential composi-
tion and monoidal product both given by addition. FH and FS were essentially
monoid homomorphisms (Mor(L0(P)), ◦, ⊗) →(R, +, +), labelling each reaction
by a single real number.
At L3 the target BgS is structurally parallel — one object, morphism set
additive, with sequential composition and monoidal product both additive in
their respective senses — but the additive monoid is enriched from R to the
cone gS of Markov-semigroup generators on N|S|. This enrichment has three
direct probabilistic consequences:
• Morphisms encode full stochastic transitions. A generator L ∈gS
encodes, via exponentiation etL, the entire family of finite-time transition
probabilities P(x(t) ∈· | x(0) = x) of the underlying CTMC [107]. At
L1 and L2, a reaction r was labelled by a single real number; at L3 the
label FP(r) ∈gS is an unbounded operator on observables that determines,
after exponentiation, every conditional probability associated with r.
• Sequential composition is operator addition, extending real ad-
dition. For composable reactions, FP(r2 ◦r1) = FP(r2) + FP(r1) in gS
(Proposition 5.10). This sum is the generator of the CTMC in which
both reaction channels are simultaneously available; it is not an effective
single-step rate law for the coarse-grained reaction u →w obtained by
eliminating the intermediate (which would require a quasi-steady-state
reduction outside the strict L3 functorial assignment). The collapse to
scalar addition recovers L1/L2 additivity in the degenerate one-state case.
• Monoidal product is Kronecker sum, extending real addition. For
reactions on independent subsystems with disjoint species sets, FP(r1 ⊗
r2) = FP(r1) ⊗I + I ⊗FP(r2) as generator contributions on the joint state
space (Proposition 5.11). This is the infinitesimal of the kernel tensor
product in Stoch and encodes probabilistic independence [103]: each
subsystem evolves on its own Poisson clock. Again, this collapses to real
101

addition in the degenerate one-state case.
The three axioms of a strict SMC functor FP : L0(P) →BgS have non-trivial
probabilistic content while preserving the structural role of “additive functor”
that FH and FS played at lower levels. The Markov-kernel interpretation of these
data — the finite-time transition probabilities — lives in Stoch and is recovered
from FP(r) by exponentiation et FP(r), which intertwines addition with kernel
composition only on the abelian locus of gS (the Trotter–Kato obstruction; this
non-functoriality of expt is the categorical content of the L3 →L4 forcing pair,
Section 5.9).
Remark 5.3 (Why expt is not an SMC functor). The functor FP : L0(P) →BgS takes
values in generators, not in finite-time Markov kernels. The link to Stoch proper
is the exponential expt : L 7→etL, which sends L ∈gS to its one-parameter Markov
semigroup of kernels in EndStoch(N|S|) under standard non-explosion conditions
[112]. This exponential is not a symmetric monoidal functor: it intertwines addition
with kernel composition only on the abelian locus of gS (the Trotter–Kato / BCH
obstruction). On a sequential composite r2 ◦r1 in L0(P), FP records the additive
generator FP(r2)+FP(r1) ∈gS — the generator of the CTMC in which both reaction
channels are simultaneously available — whose finite-time kernel et (FP(r2)+FP(r1))
differs from et FP(r2) ◦et FP(r1) by Baker–Campbell–Hausdorff commutator terms.
This loss of path-order information at L3 is precisely the categorical content of the
L3 →L4 forcing pair (Section 5.9); recovering bond-level order information requires
the DPO machinery of L4.
5.2.2. The state space is L0 data
In classical CRNT, species counts in N|S| is read off directly from the reaction
network: the species set S is part of the network definition, and a state is simply a
non-negative integer count for each species. No kinetic data — no rate constants,
no activation energies — are needed to write down N|S|. The stoichiometric change
vector nr of a reaction r is likewise determined by the network’s stoichiometry alone
(the left- and right-hand side complexes), as discussed in Chapter 2. In the tower
language, this means N|S| and nr are L0 data: they are visible at the stoichiometric
level before any rate constants are introduced.
Observation 5.4 (State space from L0). The kinetic state space N|S| is determined
entirely by L0 data:
• The species set S is a L0 datum.
• A state is a species-count vector x = (xs)s∈S ∈N|S|.
• The stoichiometric change vector of generator r : u →v is nr := ν(v) −ν(u) ∈
Z|S|, directly read from the L0 morphism r.
The single new datum at L3 is a positive rate constant kr ∈R>0 per generator.
Everything else required to define FP(r) is already present in L0(P).

The first two extensions add functors into BR (real numbers under addition), re-
flecting the additive nature of standard reaction enthalpies and entropies. The third
adds a functor into BgS, whose additive structure (sequential = addition, monoidal
product = Kronecker sum) extends the additivity of R to the genuinely probabilistic
setting of kinetics: this enrichment of the target’s additive monoid — from R to gS
— is the categorical signature of the passage from thermodynamics to dynamics. The
underlying free skeletal permutative category L0(P) remains unchanged throughout.
Proposition 5.7 (Existence and uniqueness of FP). Given any assignment k : R →
R>0 of positive rate constants to chemical generators, there is a unique strict SMC
functor FP : L0(P) →BgS extending k via r 7→Mλr(Rr −I).
Proof. By Theorem 2.14, L0(P) is the free skeletal permutative category generated by
P: given any strict SMC C with strictly commutative object monoid, an assignment
of (i) species in S to objects of C and (ii) chemical generators r ∈R to morphisms
in C with matching sources and targets extends uniquely to a strict SMC functor
L0(P) →C. The target C = BgS (Definition 5.2) is one-object, so its object monoid
is the singleton — trivially strictly commutative — and the species assignment (i) is
forced to map every species to the unique object ∗; only the morphism assignment
(ii) carries information.
The proposed assignment r 7→Mλr(Rr −I) ∈gS is well-typed: λr ≥0 pointwise,
the matrix entries of Mλr(Rr −I) are off-diagonal-non-negative with zero row sums
(the defining structure of a Markov generator), and the assembled P
r FP(r) admits
a closure generating a Markov semigroup under standard non-explosion conditions
[107, 112]. Applying the universal property of L0(P) to this assignment yields
the unique strict SMC functor FP : L0(P) →BgS extending k; the value on each
generator is determined by nr (from L0, fixing Rr) and kr (the new datum at L3).
Proposition 5.7 has the same logical structure as the existence-and-uniqueness
statements for FH (Proposition 3.2) and FS (Proposition 4.2): in all three cases, the
universal property of the free skeletal permutative category L0(P) guarantees that
a single real-valued assignment per chemical generator extends uniquely to a strict
SMC functor on all of L0(P). The only difference is what the real number labels
and where it lands, which is precisely what the insightbox below records.

§5.3. Mass-action kinetics: unpacking FP
The assignment of a rate constant kr ∈R>0 to each generating reaction r is standard
practice in stochastic chemical kinetics: it is the starting point for Gillespie’s stochas-
tic simulation algorithm [113], for the derivation of the chemical master equation
[114, 115], and for the CTMC models of chemical reaction networks that underlie
the CRNT stochastic literature [116, 107]. The role of this section is to make explicit
how kr enters the functor FP and how the resulting propensity function λr(x) relates
to the stoichiometric data already present in L0(P).

5.3.2. Functoriality unpacked
Two reactions r1 and r2 can be arranged in sequence in L0(P): the target complex
of r1 is the source complex of r2, giving a composite morphism r2 ◦r1 in L0(P).
The functor axiom FP(r2 ◦r1) = FP(r2) ◦FP(r1) in the target BgS unpacks — since
sequential composition in BgS is operator addition (Definition 5.2) — as the additivity
of generator contributions:
FP(r2 ◦r1) = FP(r2) + FP(r1)
in gS.
This is a statement about generator-level assembly: the right-hand side is the
generator of the CTMC in which both reaction channels r1 and r2 are simultaneously
available on the joint state space. It is not an effective single-step rate law for the
coarse-grained reaction u →w; eliminating the intermediate complex v requires
a quasi-steady-state or rapid-equilibrium reduction outside the strict L3 functorial
assignment, recovered only as a derived approximation under additional hypotheses
on the rate constants. At the level of stoichiometry, the same composition gives net
shift vector nr2◦r1 = nr1 + nr2, implicit throughout CRNT wherever net reactions
are obtained by adding elementary steps [10].

A note on what this proposition does not say. The shift operators Rr acting on
observables factor multiplicatively along composition, Rr2◦r1 = Rr2 Rr1, while the
generator contributions FP(ri) = Mλri(Rri −I) add. The two live in different algebras
— the shift semigroup of bounded operators on observables and the additive cone gS
of Markov generators — and FP uses each in its proper place: the multiplicative
structure of Rr inside the individual Mλr(Rr −I), and the additive structure of gS
when assembling contributions along a L0 composite. This additive assembly is the
generator of the joint CTMC, not an effective rate law for the coarse-grained one-
step reaction u →w; recovering an effective rate law requires a separate reduction
(quasi-steady state, rapid equilibrium) that is not part of the strict L3 functorial
assignment.
What this proposition means physically, and what it does not
What it says. Sequential reactions compose correctly at the levels of stoi-
chiometry and generator-of-joint-CTMC: if r1 consumes species A and produces
B, and r2 consumes B and produces C, then the net stoichiometric change of
doing both is the shift from the A-count to the C-count, and the generator of
the CTMC with both channels available is FP(r2) + FP(r1). This is the additive
content of Hess’s Law applied to stoichiometry — the overall stoichiometric
balance is independent of how it is decomposed into elementary steps.
What it does not say. The proposition does not claim that the effective rate
at which the coarse-grained reaction A →C proceeds is some simple function
of κr1 and κr2. The actual time evolution of the joint CTMC depends on
both propensities through the Gillespie waiting times [113], and eliminating
the intermediate species B to obtain an effective one-step rate law requires
quasi-steady-state or rapid-equilibrium reduction — a chemical-engineering
approximation valid only when B is short-lived, and not part of the strict L3
assignment. The proposition captures stoichiometric composition and joint-
CTMC assembly; effective coarse-grained rates are a separate, approximation-
dependent question.
5.3.3. Monoidality unpacked
Two reactions r1 and r2 can also be placed in independent parallel subsystems with
disjoint species sets S1 and S2. The monoidal product r1 ⊗r2 is their simultaneous
presence in the joint system, and the functor axiom FP(r1 ⊗r2) = FP(r1) ⊗FP(r2)
demands that the joint generator contribution decomposes correctly. This is the
categorical expression of the familiar CTMC independence result: two reactions on
disjoint species evolve independently, and their joint generator is the sum of the
individual generators, a fact used constantly when constructing modular kinetic
models [116].

Remark 5.12 (Kronecker sum versus tensor product of generators). The Kronecker
sum Ω12 = Ω1 ⊗I + I ⊗Ω2 is the generator of independent parallel evolution:
each subsystem runs on its own Poisson clock, and the two clocks are independent.
The tensor product Ω1 ⊗Ω2 would describe simultaneous firing of both reactions
at every event — a different (and physically unnatural) process. This distinction
is the categorical precision behind the everyday CRNT modelling choice to write
˙c = N1v1 + N2v2 for a combined network rather than any product structure [10].
§5.4. The Chemical Master Equation
The chemical master equation (CME) was introduced by McQuarrie [114] as the mas-
ter equation for stochastic chemical kinetics and was given its definitive probabilistic
foundation by Gillespie [113, 115], who derived it from first principles of molecular
collision theory. Within the tower, the CME is not an independent postulate: it is the
object obtained by assembling all the generator contributions {FP(r)}r∈R assigned
by the kinetic functor. Specifically, FP assigns an operator FP(r) = Mλr(Rr −I)
to each generating reaction r via the universal property of L0(P) (Proposition 5.7).
The CME generator Ωis the sum of all these operators; it is not a single functor
value but a derived object assembled from the full image of FP.
This assembly step — summing over all reactions — is what distinguishes L3 from
L1 and L2: the functors FH(r) ∈R and FS(r) ∈R are direct numerical outputs of
the functor on a single morphism, whereas the CME generator requires summing
FP(r) over all generators in R. The analogue at L1 would be to form P
r FH(r) along
a closed loop — but that sum vanishes identically by the additive content of Hess’s
Law on cycles (§3.3), so it produces no new object; here the sum genuinely produces
a new mathematical entity, the infinitesimal generator of a Markov semigroup.
FP versus Ω: assignment versus assembly
The functor FP assigns an individual generator contribution FP(r) = Mλr(Rr−I)
to each reaction r ∈R via the universal property of L0(P). The CME generator

Reading the CME term by term
Each summand in the CME has two contributions, familiar from any textbook
treatment of CTMCs [116]:
• Gain term: λr(x −nr) p(x −nr, t) — probability flowing into state x
from the predecessor state x −nr via reaction r.
• Loss term: λr(x) p(x, t) — probability flowing out of state x via reaction
r.

§5.5. Layer 1 and 2 for FP: thermodynamic consistency and detailed
balance
Every level of the tower so far has had two sub-layers. Layer 1 is the minimal
structure forced by the universal property of L0(P): given any assignment of the
new datum to generators, a unique functor extension exists. Layer 2 is an additional
coherence condition that locks the new functor to the structure already present at
lower levels of the tower. At L1, Layer 2 was the coboundary condition FH = δ0hf
(Proposition 3.7), which forced FH values around closed loops to sum to zero —
a condition internal to L1. At L2, Layer 2 was the Wegscheider cycle condition
(Proposition 4.31), requiring F T
G to vanish on every closed loop in G(R) — a condition
forced by the †-SMC structure of L2.
At L3, the new functor FP inherits from below: both F T
G (an L2 derived quantity)
and the †-structure on L0(P) (which gives every generator r a reverse r†) are already
present in the tower. The question is: what does it mean for FP to be compatible with
this inherited structure? The answer, derived below, is that FP must be †-compatible:
the Markov chain generated by Ω= P
r FP(r) must satisfy detailed balance with
respect to the thermodynamic equilibrium locus ET from L2. This compatibility
condition is precisely the kinetic Wegscheider condition [61, 9], and it is not an
independent postulate — it is forced by the tower’s †-structure.
5.5.1. Layer 1: any positive rate constants form a valid CME
Layer 1 for FP: any assignment k : R →R>0 defines a valid strict SMC functor
FP : L0(P) →Stoch by Proposition 5.7. For a reversible Petri net with |R| = 2m
generators (forward and reverse pairs), there are 2m free positive-real parameters.
The assembled CME generator Ω= P
r∈R FP(r) (Definition 5.13) is a valid Markov
generator for any such assignment: the columns of Ωsum to zero and off-diagonal
entries are non-negative.
This means FP at Layer 1 is decoupled from the thermodynamics of L2: the rate
constants kr and kr† can be chosen independently, with no reference to FH, FS, or F T
G.
The following insightbox shows what goes wrong categorically when this decoupling
persists.

Layer 2 as †-compatibility across levels
The Layer 2 conditions at each level of the tower share a common categorical
form: they lock the new functor to the structure present one or two levels below.
• Layer 2 at L1: the coboundary condition FH = δ0hf is a condition within
L1, requiring FH values to be consistent around closed loops.
• Layer 2 at L2: the Wegscheider cycle condition Q
i Keq(ri, T) = 1 is a
condition within L2, forced by the †-SMC structure linking FH and FS.
• Layer 2 at L3: the kinetic Wegscheider condition kr/kr† = Keq(r, T) is
the first inter-level coherence condition: it requires the L3 datum FP to
be compatible with the L2 derived quantity F T
G.
The categorical formulation makes the pattern visible: each Layer 2 is a natural
transformation condition, requiring the relevant functor to commute with the
†-structure already present in the tower. At L3 this commutativity is between FP
(the stochastic morphism) and F T
G (the free-energy morphism), and it expresses
thermodynamic consistency: the equilibrium is reached at the same concentration
ratio whether approached via kinetics or thermodynamics.

5.5.3. Cycle form of the kinetic Wegscheider condition
The pairwise condition of Definition 5.21 extends to all closed loops in the reaction

it is a cycle in the directed graph G(R). The cycle form of Layer 2 is then a direct
consequence of applying the functoriality of F T
G to such a cycle, combined with
Definition 5.21.

§5.6. The Deficiency Zero Theorem: level stratification
The Deficiency Zero Theorem (DZT) is the central result of classical CRNT [47, 42].
Within the tower, it has a specific structural role: its hypotheses belong entirely to L0,
while its conclusion is an L3 statement holding uniformly across every choice of FP
over a fixed L0 structure. This section analyses the L0 →L3 transition that makes
such a quantification possible, and relates it to the forgetful map U3 : L3(P) →L0(P).
The DZT hypotheses — weak reversibility and deficiency δ = 0 — were stated
in Definition 2.25 as properties of the Petri net P alone. Within the tower, this
places them squarely at L0: the complex count n, the linkage-class count ℓ, the
stoichiometric rank s, the deficiency δ = n−ℓ−s, and the weak-reversibility condition
on the directed reaction graph G(R) are all invariants of L0(P), computable without
reference to rate constants, enthalpies, or entropies.
The conclusion of the DZT — existence, uniqueness, and asymptotic stability of a
positive steady state — has no analogue at L0: there is no notion of dynamics, let
alone a steady state, without the rate functor FP. The new content at L3 is therefore
entirely on the conclusion side. Specifically, the DZT makes a statement not about
one particular FP, but about the entire fiber of the forgetful map U3 : L3(P) →L0(P)
over a fixed L0 structure:
U −1
3 (L0(P)) ∼= Map(R, R>0),
the space of all positive rate-constant assignments.

FP, but about the entire fiber of the forgetful functor U3 : L3(P) →L0(P) over a
fixed L0 structure.

the L0 →L3 jump for special networks: the L3 structure (any choice of FP) cannot
introduce dynamical complexity that the L0 structure alone forbids.

5.6.2. The stochastic DZT: Anderson–Craciun–Kurtz
Theorem 5.26 and the tower-native fragment of Proposition 5.28 are both statements
about the large-volume limit Φ∞(Ω): they concern the vector field obtained by sending
the stochastic system to its deterministic mean-field RRE. Proposition 5.28(iii)
gave a partial stochastic counterpart under reversibility and Layer 2. A natural
question within the tower is whether the same L0 hypotheses — δ = 0 and weak
reversibility, without a Layer-2 requirement — enforce a canonical form for the
stationary distribution of the full stochastic system on the assembled CME generator
Ωdirectly, before any large-volume limit. The answer is yes: the Anderson–Craciun–
Kurtz theorem [107] establishes that Ωhas a stationary distribution of product-of-
Poissons form, with Poisson parameters given by the complex-balanced equilibrium
c∗(k) of Theorem 5.26(iii). This is the stochastic analogue of the DZT: the same L0
hypotheses, now applied to the full L3 object Ωrather than its large-volume shadow,
and — unlike Proposition 5.28(iii) — without requiring reversibility.

§5.7. Compositional kinetics: gluing open L3 networks
The tower’s L3 assembly is already well-behaved under two operations on reaction
sets: sequential composition of reactions (Proposition 5.10) and disjoint union of
species sets (Proposition 5.11). A mild extension of these properties handles a
third operation that is ubiquitous in real chemistry: gluing two networks at shared
boundary species. Enzymatic modules feeding a metabolic pathway, a receptor
coupled to a downstream signalling cascade, an autocatalytic network buffered by a
reservoir — all are composites of smaller networks joined at interface species. The
compositional framework of Baez and Pollard [31] makes this gluing rigorous and
shows that the tower’s deterministic limit Φ∞(Ω) and its steady states compose
correctly under it.
Informally, an open L3 network is a closed L3(P) together with two distinguished
subsets of S playing the role of inputs and outputs (boundary species where material
may flow in or out of the network), with the remaining species internal. Two open
networks are glued by identifying the output species of the first with the input
species of the second; shared species become internal to the composite, and the rate
constants of both networks are retained. The formal framework uses Fong’s decorated
cospans [119, 31]: cospans of species sets in FinSet decorated by L3 data, with
composition given by pushout of the underlying cospans combined with functorial
composition of decorations.
Theorem 5.30 (Compositional kinetics [31, Thms. 18 and 23]). Gluing of open L3
networks is compatible with both the deterministic dynamics and the steady-state
boundary behaviour. Specifically, for composable open networks L3(P1) and L3(P2)
sharing an interface of boundary species:
(i) (Gray-boxing) The large-volume vector field Φ∞(Ω12) of the composite decom-
poses as the sum of the individual vector fields Φ∞(Ω1) and Φ∞(Ω2), extended
across the shared interface by restriction and summation of reaction velocities.
(ii) (Steady-state composition) The steady-state relation between boundary concen-
trations and boundary flows of the composite is the relational composite of the
individual steady-state relations: if c∗
1 is a steady state of L3(P1) producing
interface flow f, and c∗
2 is a steady state of L3(P2) accepting f at its input, then
together they define a steady state of the composite.

Michaelis–Menten as gray-boxing under quasi-steady-state reduction
The classical enzyme mechanism E + S ⇌ES →E + P is an open L3 network
with input species {S}, output species {P}, and internal species {E, ES}. The
Michaelis–Menten rate law
(product outflow) =

conserved-enzyme constraint [E]tot = cE + cES to eliminate cES. This reduction
is not part of the strict L3 functorial assignment — FP only assembles the
joint CTMC generator of the four reactions, not an effective rate law for the
coarse-grained S →P conversion — but is the standard chemical-engineering
reduction valid when cES is short-lived (cf. the chembox after Proposition 5.10).
Both Vmax and KM depend on individual Layer-1 rate constants k1, k−1, kcat
carried by FP (together with the conserved [E]tot); none is available from L2
data alone.
For a metabolic pathway built from n enzymatic modules, each reduced to its
Michaelis–Menten input–output relation by gray-boxing, Theorem 5.30 says
the pathway’s steady-state boundary behaviour is the relational composite of
the individual module relations under the Baez–Pollard cospan structure. For
monotone cascades — each module’s steady-state map strictly increasing in
its input concentration — the relational composite is itself functional, and the
pathway inherits a single-valued input–output rate law that recovers classical
pipelined Michaelis–Menten analysis. For feedback or multistable subnetworks,
the relation is genuinely multi-valued: a single boundary input may correspond
to several internal steady states, and the relational composition framework is
the natural setting in which to track this — the cospan structure does not
collapse the multi-valuedness, whereas a functional-composition framing silently
would. This compositional treatment is the mathematical foundation of modular
metabolic control analysis.

What L3 cannot express. The propensity λr(x) = kr xCH3Cl · xOH−describes the

The forcing observation for L4 is sharper still: two reactions with the same L3 data
— same complexes, same propensity functional form, same rate constant — can still
differ at the level of bond-level mechanism. The classical L3 →L4 forcing pairs are
the concerted SN2 versus the stepwise ion-pair SN1, and the concerted E2 versus the
irreversible-stepwise E1cb; both are taken up in the L4 chapter (Chapter 6), where
the bond-graph rewriting machinery of double pushout (DPO) provides exactly the
discriminating structure that L3 lacks.
A common misreading should be guarded against: SN2 versus E2 is not an L3 →L4
forcing pair. The bimolecular elimination of, say, 2-chlorobutane with hydroxide
␀C4H9Cl + OH−→C4H8 + H2O + Cl−
is also second-order in concentrations, but
it produces an alkene plus water rather than a substitution product. The two
reactions therefore have different stoichiometric change vectors nr and different
target complexes, so they are already separated at L0 by stoichiometry alone — not
at L4 by bond-level mechanism. Genuine L3 →L4 forcing requires reactions that
agree on every L0, L1, L2, L3 datum and differ only at the bond-graph rewriting layer;
this is strictly subtler than the SN2 versus E2 comparison.
§5.9. What L3 cannot express: forcing of L4
The tower so far — L0, L1, L2, L3 — shares a common underlying category L0(P),
the free skeletal permutative category on P (Theorem 2.14), with each successive
level adding a decorating functor on top of it. Sections 5.1–5.7 have shown what L3
buys us: the CME, the RRE, the Layer-2 coboundary condition, and compositional
kinetics for open networks. This subsection identifies what L3 cannot express, setting
up the forcing pair that Chapter 6 resolves.
Forcing pair for L4: identity substitution at phosphorus
Consider the identity methoxyl exchange at the phosphorus center of methyl
ethylphenylphosphinate [30], with isotopic labelling on the incoming methoxide:
r :
18OMe−+ Et(Ph)P(= O)OMe −→Et(Ph)P(= O)18OMe + OMe−.
Source and target complexes are identical up to the 18O permutation; the only
chemical change is which methoxyl group is bound to phosphorus and which is
free.
This transformation is realised in the laboratory by two distinct mechanisms:
System A (concerted SN2-P): methoxide attacks the phosphorus apically and
displaces the leaving methoxide through a single trigonal-bipyramidal transition

## Page 134


Kyunghoon Han

state.
System B (addition-elimination): methoxide adds first to form a discrete
pentacoordinate trigonal-bipyramidal intermediate (TBI) with five P-bonds; the
leaving methoxide then eliminates from TBI in a second step.
At the bulk-kinetic level of L3, the two mechanisms are indistinguishable. System
A is a single bimolecular generator with propensity λ(x) = k xMeO−xsubstrate.
System B has TBI as an internal species and two elementary steps; under
the quasi-steady-state reduction on TBI (valid when TBI is high-energy and
short-lived, the standard regime for phosphoryl chemistry under laboratory
conditions), elimination of TBI from the rate equations yields a coarse-grained
generator with the same bimolecular form
λ(x) = k xMeO−xsubstrate,
where the effective k aggregates the addition rate constant and the elimination
selectivity at TBI. In this regime — the experimentally relevant one — Systems
A and B share every L3 datum. Outside the quasi-steady-state regime, System
B exhibits a Michaelis–Menten rate law that L3 can distinguish from System
A’s strict bimolecular form; the L3 ambiguity between concerted and stepwise
phosphoryl mechanisms is therefore contingent on the coarse-graining, not
categorical, but the contingent regime is precisely the one in which the laboratory
operates.
Mikolajczyk et al. [30] note explicitly that “the kinetic measurements are often
unable to distinguish” SN2-P from addition-elimination at phosphorus; DFT com-
putation of the full energy profile, together with stereochemical analysis through
Berry pseudorotation, was required to settle the mechanism for the substrate
above (System B applies; the analogous chloride exchange in (EtO)Et(P=S)Cl
goes by System A [30]). The same kinetic blindness pervades enzymatic phos-
phoryl transfer, where the concerted-versus-stepwise question has been a central
mechanistic debate for decades [131].
The two mechanisms correspond to distinct chemical generators
rconcerted, rstepwise ∈R

What minimal new structure resolves the ambiguity? The principled content dis-
tinguishing rconcerted from rstepwise is the mechanism: which bonds break and form,
whether the reaction proceeds through a single transition state or through a discrete
intermediate, and — if an intermediate exists — what species it is. Encoding this
requires replacing the underlying category L0(P) with a richer one in which mor-
phisms carry bond-level data and intermediates are themselves species. This is not
a decoration of L0(P) but a structural extension, and constructing it is the task of
Chapter 6.
This forces L4, which must add two ingredients [132, 133, 134]:
(i) A category LGraph of labelled molecular hypergraphs whose vertices carry
atom type, formal charge, and lone-pair count, and whose edges carry bond
order. Species in S become objects of LGraph.
(ii) Double pushout (DPO) rewriting: a reaction mechanism is a span L ←K →R
in LGraph, specifying which bonds break (L \ K) and which form (R \ K).
Application to a molecular graph is a DPO in LGraph [135]. The underlying
category L4(P) has DPO spans in LGraph as morphism generators, with
composition by sequential rewriting and monoidal product by disjoint union
(Chapter 6).
The two pathways correspond to distinct DPO morphisms on the same input graph
(methyl ethylphenylphosphinate + isotopically labelled methoxide):
• Concerted (SN2-P): a single DPO span L ←K →R in LGraph in which
the P–OMe bond is broken and the P–18OMe bond is formed simultaneously.
The interface K retains the phosphorus and its three non-participating ligands.
• Stepwise (addition-elimination): a composable pair of DPO spans L1 ←
K1 →R1 followed by L2 ←K2 →R2, with the intermediate state graph
encoding the pentacoordinate TBI as an additional species in L4. The first
span forms the P–18OMe bond without breaking any bonds (addition); the
second breaks the P–OMe bond (elimination).
The two DPO morphisms are genuinely different in L4(P) but project to the same
morphism in L3(P) under the forgetful functor U4. The non-trivial element of
coker(φ4) is the swap between these two morphisms while fixing their common L3
image. The extension to L4 is forced by the existence of mechanistically distinct
reactions whose L3 data coincide — a phenomenon documented across substitution
chemistry [30, 131], phosphoryl-transfer biochemistry, and beyond.
Remark 5.34 (On stereochemistry). The stereochemical outcome of substitution at
phosphorus — whether the configuration at the P-stereocenter is inverted (as in
concerted SN2-P) or retained (as can occur in A–E pathways via Berry pseudorotation
at the trigonal-bipyramidal intermediate) — is a further, finer forcing observation.
It is invisible not only at L3 but also at L4 as constructed here, because LGraph
records bond topology but not three-dimensional configuration at stereocenters.

§6. L4: The Mechanistic Level
§6.1. Forcing the extension: a structural break in the tower
The previous chapter identified the gap at L3: two reactions with the same source
complex, target complex, enthalpy, entropy, and mass-action propensity — the latter
agreeing in functional form by stoichiometry and in rate constant under steady-state
on a buried intermediate — can proceed through a single transition state, or stepwise
through a discrete intermediate species, yet L3 records no trace of the distinction.
The cleanest documented case is identity nucleophilic substitution at phosphorus,
where concerted SN2-P and stepwise addition–elimination through a pentacoordinate
intermediate are routinely indistinguishable by bulk kinetics [30, 131]. This section
pinpoints the minimal structural change at L4 required to separate them.
The conflation is in the underlying category
At L0 through L3, the underlying category is always L0(P) = FreeSMC(P):
morphisms are stoichiometric transitions u →v generated by reactions of P,
and the functors FH, FS, FP decorate this category by assigning values to each
morphism.
The Petri net P may contain distinct generators r1, r2 ∈R with identical source
and target complexes — two reactions consuming and producing the same
species in the same quantities, differing only in mechanism. L0(P) is therefore
not thin: it can carry several distinct morphisms between the same pair of
complexes.
For genuinely competing mechanisms with the same source and target, identity
at L3 obtains whenever all four decoration values agree. FH and FS depend only
on source and target by Hess’s law and agree automatically. The mass-action
functional form of FP is fixed by the stoichiometry, hence agrees automatically.
The remaining datum is the rate constant: this agrees when the rate-limiting
step in either mechanism couples the same molecules in the same orders — in
particular, under steady-state on a buried intermediate with matching effective
rate constants [30, 131]. The forcing pair below is an idealisation in which
all four L3 decorations agree exactly; this is the regime in which bulk kinetic
measurements cannot distinguish the mechanisms, and is the regime in which the
categorical indistinguishability witnessed by an element of Aut(L3(P)) holds.
The principled content separating r1 from r2 is the mechanism: which bonds
break and form, whether the reaction proceeds through a single transition state
or through a discrete intermediate, and what that intermediate is. Encoding this
requires replacing L0(P) with a category in which morphisms carry bond-level
data and intermediates are themselves species — a structural extension, not a
decoration.

§6.2. Labelled molecular graphs: the ambient adhesive category
Section 6.1 identified two generators rconcerted, rstepwise ∈R with identical L3 data,
distinguished only by their identity tags in the Petri net. The tower up to L3 accepts
them as distinct only by fiat: no categorical structure on L0(P) = FreeSMC(P)
supplies a principled reason why they are different morphisms.
The resolution
requires a new underlying category whose morphisms carry bond-level information —
atoms, bonds, formal charges, electron counts — so that two generators projecting to
the same stoichiometric transition can nonetheless be distinct morphisms by virtue
of their internal structure. This section constructs that category in three steps: the
label algebra that replaces species names with molecular graphs (§6.2.1), the category
LGraph of such graphs with its monoidal and adhesive structure (§6.2.2–§6.2.3),
and the grounded variant LGraphP that connects molecular graphs back to the
139


## Page 140


Kyunghoon Han
Categorification of Chemical Reactions
species set S of the Petri net P (§6.2.4).
6.2.1. Label algebra and chemical validity
At L0(P) through L3(P), an object is an element of N|S|: a formal sum of species
names Si, recording how many molecules of each type are present but recording
nothing about their internal structure. To distinguish mechanisms with the same
source and target complexes — whether already separated at L3 or not — we need
objects that encode atoms, bonds, formal charges, and electron pairs. The following
label algebra does precisely this.
The label set below is not original: it is a categorical reformulation of the data
encoded in the bond-electron (BE) matrix of Dugundji and Ugi [137], the standard
matrix representation of molecular structure in cheminformatics and computer-aided
synthesis planning since its introduction in 1973, in continuous use [138, 139], and
the basis of some modern machine-learning approaches to reaction prediction that
enforce electron conservation [140]. What is new here is the organisation of that
data into a quintuple (el, iso, q, ρ, ℓ) that serves as a vertex label in a typed graph,
making the connection to the DPO rewriting framework canonical. Chemical graph
transformation with typed molecular graphs is developed in detail in Andersen et al.
[138, 134]; our formulation is tailored to make the validity condition explicit and to
sit naturally inside the adhesive category framework of Section 6.2.3.
Definition 6.2 (Atom label and bond label). Let ΛV denote the set of all atom

• iso ∈Iso(el) ∪{∗}: nuclear-mass label (e.g. 16O, 18O) or the wildcard ∗for

• q ∈Z: formal charge;
• ρ ∈{0, 1, 2}: radical electron count (0 closed-shell, 1 monoradical, 2 diradical);

A bond label is an integer b ∈{1, 2, 3} encoding bond order (single, double, triple).
Absent bonds carry the implicit value b = 0.

pairs (Section 6.1, where the incoming methoxide is tagged 18O). What is postponed
to L7 is not isotope bookkeeping but isotope-dependent quantum phenomena: nuclear
quantum statistics, tunnelling, vibrational zero-point kinetic isotope effects. The
wildcard ∗is the default for atoms whose chemistry is isotope-independent.
