What the label set distinguishes. Each mechanistic distinction below is
expressed as a condition on (el, iso, q, ρ, ℓ) or on the graph topology:
• Concerted vs. stepwise at heteroatom centres (the L3 →L4 forcing pair,
Section 6.1): the stepwise derivation passes through a discrete intermediate
graph whose central vertex carries a coordination number not realised in
any concerted derivation projecting to the same L3 observables (e.g. the
pentacoordinate TBI in identity substitution at phosphorus). Visible via
the vertex degree in the intermediate graph.
• Charged intermediates (already distinguished at L3 for SN1/SN2 and E1/E2,
see Remark 6.1): the stepwise derivation passes through a graph with a
carbocation vertex (q = +1, ℓ(v) = 0); the concerted derivation has q = 0
throughout. Visible via the q label.
• Radical vs. ionic mechanisms: a radical intermediate carries ρ(v) ≥1
on at least one atom (monoradicals at one site, diradicals at one site or
distributed across two sites); an ionic intermediate has ρ(v) = 0 everywhere.
Visible via the ρ label.
• Pericyclic vs. ionic reactions: a pericyclic DPO rule has a reaction centre
with cyclic graph topology (the atoms forming and breaking bonds lie on a
cycle in L); an ionic reaction has acyclic reaction-centre topology. Visible
via the topology of L.
6.2.2. The category LGraph
The label algebra of the preceding section gives data for individual atoms and bonds.
To speak categorically about reactions, we need molecular graphs to be objects and
structure-preserving maps between them to be morphisms. The following definition
assembles these ingredients into a symmetric monoidal category LGraph, which will
serve as the ambient category for the DPO rules that generate L4(P).
Originality and comparison to existing work. The use of typed molecular
graphs in chemical graph transformation goes back to Ehrig et al. [133] and An-
dersen et al. [134]. Those works use a general typing morphism to a type graph,
without committing to a specific label algebra; our specialisation to the quintuple
(el, iso, q, ρ, ℓ) of Definition 6.2 is what makes LGraph a suitable ambient category
for mechanistic organic chemistry. The architectural choice that distinguishes our
development is to keep LGraph as the ambient typed-graph category (adhesive
in the sense of Lack–Sobociński [136], Proposition 6.10), with chemical validity
(Definition 6.4) imposed as a predicate on objects rather than as a defining feature
of category membership. This separation matters because pushouts of chemically
valid graphs in LGraph may produce chemically invalid graphs: adhesivity holds
for the ambient typed-graph category, while validity is enforced as an admissibility
condition on rule patterns and their products (Remark 6.11 below).
Definition 6.6 (Labelled typed graph). A labelled typed graph is a tuple G =

• V is a finite set of vertices (atoms).
• E ⊆

• λE : E →{1, 2, 3} is the bond-order function.
No chemical-validity constraint is imposed on G at the level of object membership;
chemical validity (Definition 6.4) is a predicate on objects of LGraph used as an

A chemically valid graph (Definition 6.4) determines a BE-matrix unambiguously.
The reverse direction is partial: a BE-matrix together with element types and isotope

graphs. To make reactions into morphisms, we now equip the labelled graphs with
the structure of a category.

Proposition 6.8 (LGraph is a well-defined strict symmetric monoidal category).
LGraph with the structure of Definition 6.7 is a strict symmetric monoidal category.
Proof. Category. Composition of label-preserving monomorphisms is again a label-
preserving monomorphism (injectivity and label preservation are both stable under
composition). The identity injection idG is label-preserving by definition, and serves
as the two-sided identity. Associativity of composition is inherited from function
composition.
Strict monoidal. By the strictification convention adopted in Definition 6.7, disjoint
copies are fixed by a chosen tagging, so ⊔is strictly associative ((G1 ⊔G2) ⊔G3 =
G1⊔(G2⊔G3) as objects) and strictly unital (G⊔∅= G). The symmetry isomorphism
G1 ⊔G2 ∼= G2 ⊔G1 is the swap of tagged copies, natural in G1 and G2.

6.2.3. Adhesivity of LGraph
The category LGraph carries more than just a monoidal structure: it is adhesive
in the sense of Lack and Sobociński [136], a property that makes DPO rewriting
internally consistent.
Adhesive categories.
A category C is adhesive [136] if: (i) it has pushouts
along monomorphisms; (ii) monomorphisms are stable under pushout (the pushout
of a monomorphism is again a monomorphism); and (iii) pushout squares along
monomorphisms satisfy the van Kampen condition: they are also pullbacks in a
suitable double-categorical sense. Condition (iii), the van Kampen condition, is
what makes DPO rewriting well-behaved: combined with conditions (i) and (ii), it
guarantees that pushout complements are unique up to isomorphism (so the gluing
context D in a DPO step is well-defined; see Remark 6.12 on why D is not a chemical
intermediate) and that independent rewriting steps can be applied in either order
with the same result (Local Church–Rosser). Without adhesivity, neither of these
properties is guaranteed and DPO rewriting in LGraph would be ill-defined.
Proposition 6.10 (LGraph is adhesive). The category LGraph with label-preserving
monomorphisms is adhesive in the sense of Lack and Sobociński.
Proof. The category Graph of (directed or undirected) graphs can be presented as
a presheaf topos: it is the functor category [G, Set] where G is the graph schema
s, t : E ⇒V (two objects and two parallel morphisms, encoding source and target of
edges). Every presheaf topos is adhesive [136, Corollary 3.6], so Graph is adhesive.
Now identify LGraph with the slice category Graph/TGΛ, where TGΛ is the type
graph: the graph whose vertices are the atom labels ΛV and whose edges carry
all possible bond labels {1, 2, 3} between every pair of label vertices. A labelled
typed graph G in the sense of Definition 6.6 is precisely a graph homomorphism
G →TGΛ (the typing morphism assigns each atom its label and each bond its
order); LGraph ∼= Graph/TGΛ as categories. This identification is standard in
typed graph transformation; see Ehrig et al. [133, Chapter 2].
By Lack–Sobociński [136, Proposition 3.5(ii)], if C is adhesive then so is C/X for
every object X. Since Graph is adhesive and LGraph ∼= Graph/TGΛ, it follows
that LGraph is adhesive.
The three consequences of adhesivity for mechanism-level rewriting deserve explicit
statement. Adhesivity is what makes DPO derivations well-defined: without unique
pushout complements, the gluing context in a DPO step would not be well-defined;
without Local Church–Rosser, the order of independent steps would matter and
sequential composition would be ambiguous. These are not abstract concerns — they
correspond to concrete questions about mechanism: “Is the carbocation produced
by ionisation in SN1 uniquely determined by the rule and the substrate?” (yes, by
uniqueness of gluing contexts and by the fact that the carbocation is a distinct
molecular graph between two derivations); “Does it matter whether we first abstract
144

Kyunghoon Han
Categorification of Chemical Reactions
the proton or first ionise the leaving group in an E1 mechanism?” (Local Church–
Rosser says no, when the steps are independent).
What adhesivity gives for chemistry
Proposition 6.10 guarantees three essential properties for DPO rewriting of
labelled typed graphs:
(i) Unique gluing contexts: if a DPO rule applies to a labelled graph,
the gluing context D (the host with the reaction-centre bonds removed,
prior to gluing of R) is unique up to isomorphism (Lemma 4.5 of [136]).
D is a categorical artefact of a single rule application, not, in general, a
chemically isolable intermediate (Remark 6.12).
(ii) Local Church–Rosser: two independent reaction steps (steps whose
reaction centres share no atoms) applied to the same molecule can be
sequenced in either order, reaching the same product (Theorem 7.7 of
[136]). This is the mechanism-level analogue of the fact that parallel
reactions in distinct parts of a molecule do not interfere.
(iii) Concurrency: a sequence of independent DPO steps can be represented
by a single composite rule (Theorem 7.11 of [136]). This is a semantic
statement about independent steps, not the basis of the free SMC structure
of L4(P), which is by construction (Section 6.4).
Together, these guarantee that mechanism-level rewriting in LGraph is well-
defined and compositional — exactly what is needed for L4(P) to be a category.
Remark 6.11 (Chemical validity is admissibility, not membership). Pushouts of
chemically valid graphs in LGraph may produce chemically invalid graphs: a
pushout that introduces a bond at an atom already saturated produces a graph
whose row-sum law fails at that atom. The full subcollection LGraphch ⊂LGraph
of chemically valid graphs (Definition 6.4) is therefore not closed under pushouts
in LGraph and is not adhesive in its own right. The architectural choice taken in
this chapter is to perform all DPO constructions in the ambient adhesive category
LGraph and to require chemical validity as a separate admissibility condition: a
chemical DPO rule (Section 6.3) is a span L ←K →R in LGraph with L and R
chemically valid, and a chemically admissible match m : L ,→G into a valid host G
requires the resulting product graph H to be chemically valid. The validity check is
local — the row-sum law (or its hypervalent extension) at every atom of the product
— and is the content of Layer 2 at L4 (Section 6.7).
Remark 6.12 (The gluing context D is not a chemical intermediate). The pushout
complement D supplied by adhesivity is the host graph G with the reaction-centre
bonds of L \ l(K) deleted, prior to gluing of R. D is a categorical construction
internal to a single DPO step and is in general not a chemically isolable intermediate.
A chemical intermediate, when present, is a complete molecular graph appearing
as the target of one DPO derivation and the source of the next: the carbocation
in SN1 (Section 6.9), the trigonal-bipyramidal phosphorus intermediate in stepwise
identity substitution (Section 6.8). The categorical role of D is to mediate the two
pushouts of a single rule application; its chemical interpretation, when it has one, is
a transient gluing context, not a species of the network.

6.2.4. The grounded category LGraphP
The category LGraph treats labelled typed graphs as abstract combinatorial objects
with no reference to the Petri net P. But L4(P) must sit in the tower above L0(P):
its host objects must be compatible with the stoichiometric generator set of P, so
that the forgetful functor U4 : L4(P) →L0(P) (Section 6.6) is well-defined. The
grounded category LGraphP enforces this compatibility: it equips every host graph
with an assignment of its connected components to species names in S, binding the
abstract graph structure to the chemical species of the network.
Definition 6.13 (Grounded labelled graph category LGraphP). Given a Petri net
P with species set S, the grounded category LGraphP has:
• Objects: pairs (G, spec) where G ∈LGraph and spec : π0(G) →S assigns
each connected component of G to a species in S.
• Morphisms: label-preserving monomorphisms f : G ,→H compatible with
spec (each component of G maps into the component of H bearing the same
species label).
The monoidal product is grounded disjoint union; the unit is the empty graph with
vacuous spec. The category LGraphP is adhesive; the proof reduces to adhesivity
of LGraph via a comma-category argument analogous to the slice argument for
LGraph itself (Ehrig et al. [133]).
The BE-matrix shadow of a DPO rule
A DPO rule (L ←K →R) in LGraphP admits a BE-matrix shadow: a pair
(B, B′) of BE-matrices [137] related by the reaction matrix RBE = B′ −B
[138, 141]. The reactant graph L supplies B (off-diagonal entries = bond orders,
diagonal entries = 2ℓ(v) + ρ(v)); the product graph R supplies B′; the context
K identifies the rows and columns on which RBE vanishes.
The shadow is faithful for net electron rearrangement but strictly weaker than
the DPO rule. What it does not record: isotope labels (16O and 18O share
the same matrix); atom-tracking under composition (BE matrices add, but the
addition does not say which atom in one matrix corresponds to which atom in
the next — supplied categorically by K and the match m); the species-grounding
spec; and the categorical match data of a derivation. The DPO framework on
LGraphP is therefore strictly richer than the matrix shadow.
With LGraphP in hand, the three ingredients needed for L4(P) are in place: host
graphs are S-typed labelled graphs in LGraphP, the generating morphisms are
admissible chemical DPO rules (chemically valid spans, Section 6.3), and the ambient
adhesive structure of LGraph guarantees that DPO derivations are well-defined.
The free strict SMC structure of L4(P) is supplied by the universal property of the
free SMC on the directed signature of admissible DPO derivations (Section 6.4).
§6.3. DPO rules and derivations in LGraphP
Section 6.2 built the ambient category LGraphP: a strict symmetric monoidal
adhesive category whose objects are S-typed labelled graphs and whose morphisms
are label-preserving monomorphisms. Chemical validity (Definition 6.4) is enforced
146


## Page 147


Kyunghoon Han
Categorification of Chemical Reactions
as an admissibility condition on rule patterns and matches, not as a defining feature
of object membership (Remark 6.11). The morphisms of L4(P) will be sequences
of DPO derivations in LGraphP — the precise way of saying “bonds break and
form according to a specified rule.” A DPO (double pushout) derivation specifies
a reaction by two pushout squares in LGraphP, encoding the following chemical
information:
• L (left graph) — the reactant pattern: the subgraph that must be present in
the host molecule for the rule to fire; contains the reaction-centre atoms with
their pre-reaction labels and the bonds to be broken.
• K (context graph) — the unchanged frame: atoms and bonds that persist
through the reaction, embedded in both L and R by label-preserving monomor-
phisms.
• R (right graph) — the product pattern: the subgraph produced by the reaction;
contains the reaction-centre atoms with their post-reaction labels and the bonds
formed.
• G (host graph) — the substrate molecule: the full molecular graph to which
the rule is applied.
• D (derived context) — the gluing context: G with the atoms and bonds of
m(L \ l(K)) removed; the unique pushout complement guaranteed by the
adhesivity of LGraphP. D is a categorical artefact of a single rule application
and is not, in general, a chemically isolable intermediate (Remark 6.12).
• H (host graph after reaction) — the product molecule: obtained by gluing R
onto D via the second pushout.
Together the two pushouts implement the chemical intuition that a reaction (i)
removes the bonds and relabels the atoms of the reaction centre, and (ii) installs
the new bonds and relabelled atoms, leaving everything outside the reaction centre
unchanged. This is the categorical replacement for the stoichiometric transition
used as a morphism at L0(P): instead of merely recording which species disappear
and appear, a DPO derivation records exactly which bonds break and form, in
what sequence, and on which atoms. The free SMC on such derivations is L4(P),
constructed in Section 6.4.
6.3.1. DPO rules
Definition 6.14 (Chemical DPO rule). A chemical DPO rule for P-species is a pair
p = (s, γ) consisting of:
• a span s = (L

• a generator label γ(p) ∈P identifying which Petri-net reaction of P this rule
realises at the stoichiometric level.
The span graphs carry their usual interpretation:
• K: the context — atoms and bonds unchanged by the reaction.

• L \ l(K): atoms or bonds consumed (broken or label-changed at the reaction
centre).
• R \ r(K): atoms or bonds produced (formed or label-changed at the reaction

A rule is valence-conserving if every atom in K satisfies the same valence constraint
in L and in R, and stoichiometrically consistent if for every species S ∈S, the
number of connected components of R labelled S minus that of L labelled S equals
the stoichiometric change ν(v)S −ν(u)S of the Petri-net generator γ(p) : u →v. We
restrict to valence-conserving, stoichiometrically consistent rules throughout.
Two distinct rules may share the same span but carry different generator labels
(when P has parallel generators with identical stoichiometry); two distinct rules may
also share the same generator label but carry different spans (when a single Petri-net
reaction admits multiple mechanistic realisations). The Petri net P is assumed
rich enough to contain a generator for every named chemical transformation in the
reaction network under study, whether or not that transformation is mechanistically
elementary.
Remark 6.15 (Atoms with changing labels in the DPO span). In our label set
ΛV = {(el, iso, q, ρ, ℓ)} (Definition 6.2), a reaction that changes any component of
an atom’s label cannot place that atom in K: the monomorphisms l and r are
label-preserving, so K can only contain atoms whose labels are identical in L and in
R. An atom v with label λL
v ̸= λR
v must therefore appear in L\l(K) (as a “consumed”
vertex with its pre-reaction label) and separately in R \ r(K) (as a “produced” vertex
with its post-reaction label). Chemically, this means the atom is formally deleted
and recreated; its physical identity is preserved by the match morphism m : L ,→G,
which tracks which vertex in the host graph G corresponds to which vertex in L. This
non-attributed encoding is equivalent to attributed DPO rewriting [133], where vertex
attributes (q, ρ, ℓ) may change on persistent vertices via attribute equations on K;
the non-attributed formulation chosen here keeps LGraphP as a standard adhesive
category without additional attribute-algebra structure. In particular, isotope labels
rarely change (they enter the formalism as classical tracers, Remark 6.3), and for
octet atoms ℓis determined by (q, ρ, β) via the row-sum law (6), so a generator that
specifies changes in (q, ρ, β) also fixes the change in ℓ.
6.3.2. DPO derivations and the dangling condition
A DPO rule is an abstract pattern. A DPO derivation is the application of a rule to
a specific host molecule G: it specifies where the rule fires (the match) and produces
the concrete product molecule H. This is the level at which a mechanism becomes
an actual chemical transformation on a named substrate.
Definition 6.16 (DPO derivation). Let p = (L ←K →R) be a DPO rule and
G ∈LGraphP a host graph. A match is a monomorphism m : L ,→G identifying
where the reactant pattern occurs in G.

where both squares are pushouts in LGraphP. The left pushout computes D (the
pushout complement): G with the atoms and bonds of m(L \ l(K)) deleted. The
right pushout computes H: D with the product pattern R glued in via the shared
context K.
For a DPO derivation to exist, the gluing context D must be well-defined. By the
adhesive structure of LGraphP (Proposition 6.10), the pushout complement exists
and is unique precisely when no atoms outside the reaction centre are left with
“half-broken” bonds — the dangling condition. This is not a restriction on chemistry
but a consistency requirement: any correctly specified mechanism must close off all
bond changes at the reaction centre before the rule fires.
Proposition 6.17 (Gluing / dangling condition). Let p = (L ←K →R) be a DPO
rule and m : L ,→G a match. The pushout complement D in LGraphP exists and
is unique if and only if the dangling condition holds: no atom in G \ m(L) is bonded
to an atom in m(L \ l(K)).
Proof. For injective matches in adhesive categories, the pushout complement D exists
if and only if the dangling condition holds (the gluing condition of [136, Def. 7.2],
which in LGraphP unpacks to the dangling condition [133]); when it exists, it is
unique up to isomorphism by [136, Lem. 4.5].
The dangling condition in chemistry
The dangling condition says: a reaction-centre atom or bond cannot be deleted
if an atom outside the reaction centre is still attached to it. Concretely, consider
an SN2 rule for the substitution CH3Br + OH−→CH3OH + Br−: the rule
deletes the C–Br bond, repurposes a lone pair on OH−as the new bonding pair,
and creates the C–O bond. The rule’s L must include every atom that, in the
host G, is bonded to a reaction-centre atom; for instance, the three hydrogens on
C must be present in L (and hence in K, as unchanged context), since otherwise
the carbon’s relabelling between L and R would leave them with bonds into
a deleted vertex. In practice, reaction mechanisms are formulated so that the
reaction centre L is self-contained: all atoms incident to the reaction-centre
atoms are included in L, making the dangling condition automatically satisfied
for any well-posed rule.

a minimal collection of rules from which every organic reaction mechanism can be

The decomposition of any reaction mechanism into elementary electron-pair or radical
movements is the foundation of the mechanistic approach to organic chemistry and has
been formalised independently by Herges [142] (topological classification), Dugundji
and Ugi [137] (BE-matrix reaction types), and Andersen et al. [138] (algorithmic
rule composition). The six generators below are the categorical counterpart of this
decomposition, expressed as explicit DPO spans in LGraphP. In the tower, they
are the generators of L4(P) in the sense of Proposition 6.25: any assignment of these
six spans to morphisms of a strict SMC C extends uniquely to a functor L4(P) →C.
Definition 6.18 (Elementary DPO generators for organic chemistry). For brevity we
write atom labels in the abbreviated form λv = (elv, qv, ρv) throughout the generators
below. This stands for the full quintuple (elv, ∗, qv, ρv, ℓv) of Definition 6.2 with
isotope iso = ∗(natural abundance) suppressed and lone-pair count ℓv fixed by
the octet row-sum law (6) from (qv, ρv, βv) at every reaction-centre atom. Isotope
labels appear explicitly only in identity-tracer mechanisms (Section 6.1); hypervalent
atoms (where ℓis not octet-determined) appear only in the stepwise mechanisms
of Section 6.8. In each span below, K contains the atoms and bonds whose labels
are unchanged by the reaction; atoms with changing labels appear in L \ l(K) and
R \ r(K) per Remark 6.15.
g1: Heterolytic bond formation (lone pair →bond). A nucleophilic atom Nu
donates a lone pair to form a new single bond to an electrophilic atom E. Since
both atoms change formal charge, neither can sit in K (Remark 6.15); the
physical identity of each atom across the rule is supplied by the match m.
• K: remaining molecular context (atoms and bonds outside the reaction
centre).
• L \ l(K): two isolated vertices {Nu : (elNu, q, 0), E : (elE, q′, 0)}, no edge
between them.
• R \ r(K): two vertices {Nu : (elNu, q + 1, 0), E : (elE, q′ −1, 0)} connected
by a new edge b = 1.
Effect: q(Nu) increases by 1 (Nu loses negative charge), q(E) decreases by 1 (E
gains electron density); the derived lone-pair counts update via Definition 6.4,
giving ∆ℓ(Nu) = −1 (one lone pair used to form the bond) and ∆ℓ(E) = 0.
g2: Heterolytic bond cleavage (bond →lone pair). A bond breaks heterolyti-
cally; both electrons go to the more electronegative atom X.
• K: remaining context.
• L \ l(K): two vertices {C : (elC, q, 0), X : (elX, q′, 0)} connected by edge
b = 1.
• R \ r(K): two isolated vertices {C : (elC, q + 1, 0), X : (elX, q′ −1, 0)},
no edge.
Effect: q(C) increases by 1 (C becomes more positive), q(X) decreases by 1 (X
gains lone pair), ℓ(X) increases by 1. This is the formal inverse of g1 at the
bond-rearrangement level: applying g1 then g2 to the same atom pair returns

g3: Concerted electron-pair shift through a 3-atom subgraph (charge or

{A−B, B =C} (bond orders b1 −1 on AB and b2 + 1 on BC).
Effect: the cation migrates from C to A along the conjugated π-system; the
row-sum law (6) balances the bond-order change against the charge change at
each terminal. Atoms A and C are in L \ l(K) / R \ r(K) because their labels
change; only B resides in K.
g4: Homolytic bond formation (two radicals →bond). Two radical atoms
combine to form a new single bond.
• K: remaining context.
• L \ l(K): two isolated vertices {A : (elA, qA, 1), B : (elB, qB, 1)} (each
monoradical, ρ = 1), no edge.
• R \ r(K): two vertices {A : (elA, qA, 0), B : (elB, qB, 0)} connected by
edge b = 1.
Effect: ρ decreases from 1 to 0 on both atoms (radical electrons pair into the
new bond), ℓis unchanged on each. This is the radical counterpart of g1.
g5: Homolytic bond cleavage (bond →two radicals). A bond breaks homolyti-
cally; each fragment retains one electron.
• K: remaining context.
• L\l(K): two vertices {A : (elA, qA, 0), B : (elB, qB, 0)} connected by edge
b = 1.
• R \ r(K): two isolated vertices {A : (elA, qA, 1), B : (elB, qB, 1)}, no edge.
Effect: ρ increases from 0 to 1 on both atoms; the shared bonding pair
becomes two unpaired electrons, one on each fragment. g5 reverses the bond-
rearrangement of g4: applying g4 then g5 to the same atom pair returns the
molecular graph to its initial state, although the composite is a non-identity
morphism in L4(P).

Remark 6.19 (Status of the generating set). Definition 6.18 proposes six generators
as a working basis for all organic reaction mechanisms.
The claim that these
six generators suffice to generate every organic reaction mechanism by sequential
composition and monoidal product is supported by the following evidence:
• Herges [142] partitions all concerted organic reactions into three topological
types (linear, pericyclic, coarctate); the linear type aligns with the topological
shape of patterns built from g1–g3, while pericyclic and coarctate types require
additional primitive generators (§6.3.4).
• Dugundji and Ugi [137] identify ∼30 reaction-matrix types; ∼10 types cover
∼93% of all single-step transformations, consistent with a small generating set.
• Andersen et al. [138] develop the algorithmic machinery for rule composition
in typed-graph DPO and apply it to ionic organic chemistry, where rules of
the g1–g3 shape suffice. The radical and SET generators g4–g6 are added here
to cover homolytic and single-electron-transfer chemistry, which are needed for
the radical sub-network of the Briggs–Rauscher reaction (Section 6.9) and for
organic photochemistry more broadly.
A formal proof that Definition 6.18 is both minimal and complete is not available
in the published literature. The tower provides a framework for investigating this
question: completeness would follow from showing that the automorphism exact
sequence 1 →ker φ4 →Aut(L4(P))
φ4
−→Aut(L3(P)) →coker(φ4) →1 is exhausted
by the bond-change patterns generated by g1–g6 — i.e., that every element of
coker(φ4) is the image of a composition of these generators. Minimality would
require showing that no proper subset of {g1, . . . , g6} generates L4(P) as a free SMC.
Both statements are conjectured and constitute an original research direction opened
by the categorical framework of this chapter. We proceed with the six generators as
a well-motivated and empirically supported working basis.
6.3.4. Pericyclic rules: cyclic reaction-centre topology
The six generators of Definition 6.18 cover stepwise bond rearrangements: each
generator acts on two atoms (or three, in the case of g3), and larger mechanisms are
built by sequential composition and monoidal product. But a significant class of
organic reactions is concerted across a closed ring of atoms — pericyclic reactions
152


## Page 153


Kyunghoon Han
Categorification of Chemical Reactions
— and cannot be decomposed into a sequential chain of two-atom steps without
introducing intermediate molecular graphs that the mechanism provably lacks. These
reactions require DPO rules of a different shape.
Definition 6.20 (Pericyclic DPO rule). A pericyclic DPO rule is a chemical DPO
rule p = (L ←K →R) in LGraphP for which the reaction centre L\l(K) (together
with its incident atoms in K) forms a cycle in the underlying graph of L, with the
corresponding cycle in R obtained by a simultaneous reassignment of bond orders
around the ring. No vertex labels change; all bond-order changes occur within the
cycle and are applied concurrently as a single rule.
Remark 6.21 (Pericyclic rules are primitives). A pericyclic rule is not a composite of
g1–g6. Attempting to decompose, say, a Diels–Alder step into sequential applications
of g1 and g3 would force the derivation to pass through intermediate molecular graphs
(the host after one g1, before the next g3, etc.) that carry formal charges or unpaired
electrons not present in either the reactant or the product, and that the concerted
mechanism does not produce. A single pericyclic DPO step has the entire ring of
bond-order changes occurring in one rule application, with no intervening discrete
molecular graphs at all. The correct treatment within our framework is to admit
pericyclic rules as additional primitive generators, one for each pattern of cyclic
bond-order reassignment. These primitives are characterised by Herges’ topological
classification [142]: linear (no cycle in the reaction centre), pericyclic (a single cycle),
or coarctate (two cycles sharing an atom). The generator basis for L4(P) is therefore
{g1, . . . , g6} ∪{pericyclic primitives}, with the pericyclic primitives indexed by cycle
length and Herges type. A complete classification of pericyclic primitives — and
the question of whether they can be further reduced to a finite subset — is an open
problem left to future work.
Pericyclic reactions in the DPO framework
The three canonical pericyclic reaction types all have cyclic reaction-centre
topology:
• Diels–Alder cycloaddition [143]: a diene and a dienophile combine through
a six-membered cyclic concerted step; three π-bonds break and one π-bond
plus two new σ-bonds form, all within a single ring of six atoms.
• Electrocyclic ring closure [15]: a terminal π-bond becomes a σ-bond closing
a ring; the reaction centre is the newly formed ring itself.
• [1, j] sigmatropic shift [144]: a σ-bond migrates across a π system; the
reaction centre is the cycle traced by the migrating group and the atoms
it visits.
At L4, all three are handled by pericyclic primitives of Definition 6.20 with the
appropriate cycle length and Herges topology. What L4 cannot do is predict
whether a given pericyclic rule is thermally or photochemically allowed — that is
the content of the Woodward–Hoffmann rules, which depend on orbital symmetry
along the reaction coordinate and are treated at L4.5 in the stereochemistry
chapter.
§6.4. Definition of L4(P)
Definition 6.22 (Mechanistic level L4(P)). Let P be a Petri net with species set S.
The mechanistic level L4(P) is the strict symmetric monoidal category defined as

follows.
• Objects: finite disjoint unions of S-typed molecular graphs in LGraphP.
• Generating morphisms: valence-conserving chemical DPO rules (Defini-
tion 6.14) for P-species.
• Morphisms: composable sequences of DPO derivations in LGraphP, taken
up to the congruence relations of a strict symmetric monoidal category (as-
sociativity and unitality of composition, monoidal axioms, naturality of the
symmetry).
• Monoidal product: disjoint union G1 ⊔G2 of molecular graphs on objects;
parallel juxtaposition of DPO derivations on morphisms.
• Monoidal unit: the empty graph ∅.
That L4(P) as defined is the free strict SMC on the generating DPO rules requires
verification on two fronts: that the concrete construction is well-defined as a strict
SMC (not just a category, since SMC structure includes symmetry and tensor
coherence), and that it satisfies the universal property of the free SMC on the chemical
DPO signature. The three properties of LGraphP established in Section 6.2.3 are
what make the SMC structure hold concretely; the universal property then follows
from the standard construction of free SMCs on a directed signature.
Proposition 6.23 (L4(P) is the free strict SMC on its generating DPO rules). The
category L4(P) of Definition 6.22 is a free strict symmetric monoidal category over
the signature of valence-conserving DPO rules for P-species in LGraphP.
Proof. The construction in Definition 6.22 presents L4(P) concretely: morphisms
are equivalence classes of DPO derivation sequences in LGraphP modulo the SMC
congruence (associativity, unitality, monoidal axioms, naturality of the symmetry).
We verify that this construction is the free strict SMC on the directed signature Σ of
valence-conserving DPO rules for P-species, in two parts: (a) the construction is a
well-defined strict SMC, and (b) it satisfies the universal property of the free SMC
on Σ.
For (a), the three properties of LGraphP from §6.2.3 establish that the SMC
structure holds concretely for derivation classes.
(i) Adhesivity makes derivations well-defined. Each generating rule p = (L ←
K →R) applied at a match m : L ,→G has a unique gluing context D when the
dangling condition holds (Proposition 6.17); for well-posed chemical rules whose
reaction centre is enclosed by L, the dangling condition is automatic (Section 6.3).
The product H is therefore unique up to isomorphism, and sequential composition
of derivations is well-defined and associative on derivation classes.
(ii) Local Church–Rosser realises commutativity of independent steps
concretely. The SMC’s interchange law and the naturality of the symmetry τ
together imply that two independent generators applied to disjoint parts of an
object commute up to SMC congruence. What requires concrete verification is that
this abstract commutativity is faithfully realised on derivation classes. The Local
Church–Rosser property (Theorem 7.7 of [136]) supplies it: two derivations d1, d2
154

at disjoint reaction centres in the same host produce isomorphic products whether
applied in either order.
(iii) Concurrency realises composition concretely. The Concurrency theorem
(Theorem 7.11 of [136]) supplies a single composite rule whose application produces
the same end product as the sequence. The composition of derivation classes is
therefore representable as a single-rule derivation, consistent with the abstract SMC
composition.
For (b), freeness on Σ follows from the standard universal-property construction of
the free strict SMC on a directed signature [37, §XI.2], [145, §1]: the morphisms
of L4(P) are finite formal composites of generators under sequential and monoidal
composition, modulo the SMC congruence, with two composites identified iff forced
equal by the SMC axioms. The DPO interpretation in LGraphP, validated by
(i)–(iii), contributes that each generator can be applied at any chosen match in
any host satisfying the gluing condition, witnessing the formal morphism without
introducing any non-SMC-congruent identifications.
L4(P) as the free SMC: a tower-language derivation
The free SMC structure of L4(P) is automatic from the universal-property
construction of free SMCs on a directed signature [37, §XI.2]: given the signature
Σ of valence-conserving DPO rules, the free SMC has morphisms = equivalence
classes of formal composites under the SMC congruence (associativity, unitality,
monoidal axioms, naturality of the symmetry). What the three properties
of LGraphP from Section 6.2.3 contribute is the faithfulness of the semantic
interpretation of these formal morphisms as concrete DPO derivations.
Adhesivity ⇒semantic well-definedness. At L0(P)–L3(P), a morphism
from complex u to complex v is a stoichiometric transition: a pair (u, v) with no
internal structure. At L4(P), a morphism is a DPO derivation G ⇒p,m H: the
unique gluing context D (guaranteed by adhesivity of LGraphP) is the categori-
cal bridge between L and R, not in general a chemical intermediate (Remark 6.12).
A chemical intermediate, when present (e.g., the trigonal-bipyramidal phospho-
rus intermediate in stepwise identity substitution, Section 6.1), is the molecular
graph H output by one derivation and serving as input to the next, distinct
from any single rule’s gluing context D.
Local Church–Rosser ⇒semantic commutation of independent steps.
The free-SMC symmetry τG1,G2 : G1 ⊔G2 →G2 ⊔G1 is automatic by construc-
tion. What LCR provides is its semantic realisation: two derivations at disjoint
reaction centres commute as DPO operations, instantiating the abstract symme-
try concretely. Without LCR, the abstract symmetry would still hold formally
in L4(P), but the order of derivations could matter in LGraphP, leaving the
abstract SMC symmetry without a faithful LGraphP-realisation.
Concurrency ⇒semantic single-rule composites. The free-SMC composi-
tion is automatic by construction. What the Concurrency theorem provides is a
representation result: any composite of independent derivations can be realised
as a single composite DPO rule whose pushout produces the same end product
(Theorem 7.11 of [136]). The abstract composite morphism in L4(P) thus has a

concrete single-rule realisation in LGraphP.
Summary. Free SMC structure: by construction. Semantic interpretation
in LGraphP: well-defined derivations (adhesivity), independent commutation
(Local Church–Rosser), single-rule composites (Concurrency). The freeness
comes from category theory; the chemistry comes from the semantic faithfulness
via LGraphP. The generating data are the chemical DPO rules of Defini-
tion 6.14; the elementary basis {g1, . . . , g6} together with pericyclic primitives
(Sections 6.3, 6.3.4) is a conjectured minimal subset (Remark 6.19).
Having established that L4(P) is a free strict SMC, one can now state precisely
how it sits in the tower. The forgetful functor U4 : L4(P) →L0(P) (constructed in
Section 6.6) provides the downward connection: it sends each molecular graph to its
species-count vector and each DPO derivation to the corresponding stoichiometric
transition. The decorating functors FH, FS, FP of the lower levels lift to L4(P) via
U4 (Proposition 6.32): no new primitive numerical functor enters at L4 beyond those
lifted from L3 via U4, but the free SMC that carries them is genuinely new. The
universal property of L4(P) (Proposition 6.25 below) is what makes this connection
canonical: any interpretation of the DPO generators in a target SMC — whether a
chemical database, a retrosynthesis planner, or a Para-level ML model — extends
uniquely to a functor from L4(P).
Remark 6.24 (The structural break stated precisely). At every previous level L0(P)
through L3(P), the underlying free SMC was L0(P) = FreeSMC(P), with objects
in NS and morphisms as stoichiometric transitions.
New levels added functors
FH, FS, FP on top of the same underlying category.
At L4(P), the underlying category is genuinely new: objects are molecular graphs, not
species-count vectors; morphisms are DPO derivations, not abstract stoichiometric
transitions. L4(P) is not the free SMC of P with additional decoration. It is a
different free SMC, generated by richer data, connected to the previous levels only
via the forgetful functor U4 of Section 6.6.
Proposition 6.25 (Universal property of L4(P)). Let C be any strict SMC. An
assignment of the valence-conserving DPO rules of P-species to morphisms of C,
compatible with source and target molecular graphs, extends uniquely to a strict SMC
functor F : L4(P) →C.
Proof. By Proposition 6.23, L4(P) is the free strict SMC on the generating DPO
rules. The universal property of a free SMC states precisely that any assignment of
generators to morphisms of any strict SMC C extends to a unique strict SMC functor.
Existence: define F on generators by the given assignment and extend to composites
and monoidal products by the SMC axioms; the SMC congruence in L4(P) ensures
F is well-defined. Uniqueness: every morphism of L4(P) is, by freeness, a unique
composite of generators up to SMC congruence, so the value of F on generators
determines F on all morphisms.

The tower updated: two qualitatively different extension types
The tower L0 ,→L1 ,→L2 ,→L3 ,→L4 now contains two qualitatively different
types of extension:
• Decorator extensions (L0 →L1, L1 →L2, L2 →L3): the same
underlying free SMC L0(P) is retained; each new level adds exactly one
new functor into BR or Stoch (or more precisely, gS). The universal
property of L0(P) does all the work.
• Structural extension (L3 →L4): the underlying free SMC is replaced
by a new one, L4(P), generated by DPO rules rather than stoichiometric
transitions. Previous decorations lift via U4. No new primitive numeri-
cal functor is added beyond those inherited from L3 via pullback along
U4; the new content is in the morphisms themselves (DPO derivations
rather than stoichiometric transitions). The structural break is forced by
the coker(φ4) obstruction of Section 6.1 and cannot be resolved by any
decorator extension.

§6.6. The forgetful functor U4 : L4(P) →L0(P)
The free SMC L4(P) sits above the rest of the tower via a forgetful functor U4 that
strips away all bond-level information and returns the plain stoichiometric data
of L0(P). This functor is the categorical bridge that embeds the new mechanistic
level into the existing tower: the previous decorations FH, FS, FP lift to L4(P) by
precomposing with U4, and the tower structure from L0 through L3 is recovered by
factoring through U4.
6.6.1. Definition and well-definedness
Definition 6.27 (Forgetful functor U4). Recall from Definition 6.13 that every
object of LGraphP is a pair (G, spec) where G is a labelled molecular graph and
spec : π0(G) →S assigns each connected component of G (each individual molecule)
to a species name in S.
The forgetful functor U4 : L4(P) →L0(P) is defined as follows.

target complexes), U4(d) cannot be defined as “the unique morphism from U4(G) to
U4(H)”; there may be several candidates. The explicit label γ(p) in the DPO rule
data (Definition 6.14) resolves the ambiguity: U4(d) is the specific generator γ(p), not
merely any morphism with matching source and target. This matters precisely for
the forcing pair of Section 6.1: when the Petri net P contains two distinct generators
rconcerted, rstepwise ∈R that realise the same identity substitution at phosphorus
through mechanistically distinct routes, the corresponding DPO rules pconcerted and
pstepwise carry distinct labels γ(pconcerted) = rconcerted and γ(pstepwise) = rstepwise. U4
projects them to these two parallel generators in L0(P) — distinct morphisms with
identical source and target complexes — rather than collapsing them to a single
morphism. When P has only one generator per stoichiometry (the generic case), the
label is redundant and can be inferred from (U4(L), U4(R)).

strict symmetric monoidal functor.
Proof. Well-definedness on objects. U4(G) ∈N|S| by construction: the sum
counts components by their species assignment spec.
Well-definedness on morphisms. For each DPO derivation d, the generator label
γ(p) is a fixed datum of the rule p (part of the grounding structure of LGraphP).
Thus U4(d) = γ(p) is a specific, uniquely determined morphism in L0(P), independent
of which host graph G the derivation acts on or what match m was chosen.
Functoriality. For the identity derivation idG, U4(idG) = idU4(G) since idG imple-
ments the trivial (empty) generator. For sequential composition d2 ◦d1: U4(d2 ◦d1) =
U4(d2) ◦U4(d1) by the definition of U4 on composites and the functoriality of compo-
sition in L0(P).
Strict monoidality. U4(G1 ⊔G2) = U4(G1)+U4(G2): the species count of a disjoint
union is the sum of the individual counts (the spec maps are independent on disjoint
components). U4(∅) = 0: the empty graph has no components, hence contributes
zero to every species count. For morphisms, U4(d1 ⊔d2) = U4(d1) ⊗U4(d2): parallel
derivations on disjoint graphs map to the monoidal product of the corresponding
L0(P)-morphisms.
Symmetry. U4 sends the symmetry isomorphism τG1,G2 : G1 ⊔G2
∼−→G2 ⊔G1 in
L4(P) to the symmetry isomorphism τU4(G1),U4(G2) in L0(P), since both simply swap
the two summands.
What U4 forgets and retains
Retained: which Petri-net generator the DPO rule realises (via its label γ),
and therefore which species are consumed and produced (stoichiometry).
Forgotten: the molecular graphs of reactants and products; which bonds formed
or broke; the sequence of elementary DPO steps; the identity of the reaction
centre; the presence or absence of intermediate molecular graphs in stepwise
mechanisms; all stereochemical information.
For the forcing pair of Section 6.1, the concerted-SN2-P DPO rule and the
stepwise A–E DPO rule (realising identity substitution at phosphorus through
distinct mechanisms) carry distinct Petri-net labels rconcerted and rstepwise when
both appear as parallel generators of P. Their U4-images are different but
parallel generators in L0(P): distinct morphisms sharing source and target
complexes. U4 thus preserves the information that the two mechanisms yield
identical reactants and products, while discarding the internal DPO structure
that distinguishes them at L4 and justifies their existence as separate generators
in the first place. The existence of parallel generators in P is unmotivated at
L0–L3 (where it can be postulated only by fiat) and finds its principled structural
basis at L4 (where it reflects genuinely distinct DPO derivations).

Remark 6.33 (No new numerical functor at L4). Proposition 6.32 is the categorical
statement that no new primitive numerical functor enters at L4: every numerical
functor on L4(P) factors through U4 as F (4) = F ◦U4 for some functor F on
L0(P). The extension from L3(P) to L4(P) adds structural information — the
bond-change mechanism — but not a new real-valued or stochastic-valued label
generated independently of the L3 data. This contrasts with L1–L3, where each level
added exactly one new functor into BR or gS.
A chemist might expect the activation energy Ea to enter at L4, since bond breaking
and forming are precisely the mechanism-level events that set the energy barrier.
However, Ea is the minimax of the potential energy surface V : Ce(G) →R along
the intrinsic reaction coordinate — a quantity that requires the full geometric
configuration space Ce(G) = R3n/(SE(3) ⋉Aut(G)) at L5, not merely the bond-
change graph at L4. A DPO rule specifies which bonds break and form, but the
same rule can correspond to different values of Ea depending on the 3-dimensional
arrangement of atoms (e.g. a bulky substituent at the phosphorus centre raises Ea
for an SN2-P step relative to an unhindered analogue, even though both go through
the same DPO rule). Ea is therefore not functorial at L4; it enters the tower at L5
as the minimax of V along the IRC (Section 8).

The Layer 1/Layer 2 split established at L1–L3 recurs at L4, but with a structurally
different character.

6.7.1. Layer 1: valid DPO rules
Layer 1 for L4 admits any chemical DPO rule p = (s, γ(p)) in the sense of
Definition 6.14: a valence-conserving, stoichiometrically consistent span s = (L ←
K →R) in LGraphP together with a generator label γ(p) ∈R, subject to the
dangling condition (Proposition 6.17) for all intended matches. The free parameter
at Layer 1 is the choice of reaction-centre graphs L, K, R — the specific bond-change
pattern — for a given generator label γ(p). For some Petri-net labels there are
multiple Layer 1-valid rules, corresponding to different mechanisms by which a single
reaction can proceed; for other labels, there may be no single-span Layer 1 rule at all,
and the only realisations are as composites of other rules through intermediate species.
The forcing pair of Section 6.1 — rconcerted versus rstepwise for identity substitution at
phosphorus — exhibits exactly this asymmetry: rconcerted is the U4-image of a single
Layer 1 rule pconcerted, while rstepwise admits no single-span realisation and arises at
L4 only as the composite pelim ◦padd through the trigonal-bipyramidal intermediate.
6.7.2. Layer 2: valence coherence
A Layer 1 rule (Definition 6.14) already guarantees stoichiometric consistency between
the span and its generator label, and valence conservation at every context atom in
K. What remains to check is the product side: atoms in R \ r(K) acquire new labels
(el, q′, ρ′) and new incident bonds during the reaction, and these must combine to
give a valid molecular graph. Layer 2 imposes this one remaining condition.
Definition 6.35 (Layer 2 condition at L4). A chemical DPO rule p = (L ←K →
R, γ(p)) (Definition 6.14) satisfies Layer 2 if every vertex of the product graph has a
non-negative integer lone-pair count:
ℓ(v) ∈N
for all v ∈V (R),
where ℓ(v) is the lone-pair component of v’s vertex label — determined by the basic
valence formula of Definition 6.4 at non-hypervalent atoms, and supplied as part of
the label at hypervalent atoms (the pentacoordinate trigonal-bipyramidal phosphorus
of the forcing pair being a representative case).
Layer 2 as inter-level coherence
Where the condition lives. The context atoms in K satisfy the valence
constraint automatically: by definition, K contains atoms whose labels and
bonds are unchanged between L and R (Remark 6.15), so their lone-pair counts
are preserved trivially. The genuine content of Layer 2 is at the reaction-centre
atoms in R \ r(K): their post-reaction labels (el, q′, ρ′) together with their new
bond orders must combine to give ℓ(v) ≥0 as a non-negative integer.

§6.8. The forcing-pair derivations and their distinctness
Section 6.1 identified the L3 →L4 forcing pair: identity nucleophilic substitution
at phosphorus, realisable either by a single concerted SN2-P transition state or
by stepwise addition–elimination through a pentacoordinate trigonal-bipyramidal
intermediate (TBI). Both pathways carry the same source and target complexes in
N|S| and (under steady-state on the TBI) the same L3 propensity; what distinguishes
them is the DPO-derivation structure at L4. This subsection makes that distinction
precise.
Throughout, P denotes the central phosphorus atom of the substrate methyl ethyl-
phenylphosphinate, written Et(Ph)P(= O)OMe.
We write OMe for the leaving
methoxide and 18OMe for the isotopically labelled incoming methoxide. The ethyl
group, phenyl group, and doubly-bonded oxygen retain their labels and their bonds
to phosphorus throughout every rule below, and sit in K together with phosphorus
itself (Remark 6.15). The two methoxides change charge between L and R (neutral
when bonded to P, −1 when free), so each appears outside K at any step where its
bonded/free status changes.
Remark 6.37 (On hypervalent phosphorus). The pentacoordinate phosphorus in the
TBI is hypervalent: its incident bond-order sum is P
e b(e) = 6 (Et, Ph, P=O, plus
two single P–O bonds to the methoxides), giving ℓ(P) = (5 −0 −0 −6)/2 = −1/2

electron counting and does not accommodate the three-centre four-electron bonding
characteristic of hypervalent main-group atoms. A standard remedy is to extend the
formalism so that, at hypervalent vertices, ℓis supplied as part of the vertex label
rather than computed from (vel, q, ρ, P b); the basic formula is then recovered as the
special case where the supplied ℓmatches the octet-derived value.

under the bonded/free charge convention recorded above.

P–OMe bond; 18OMe−as a free isolated component.

{padd, pelim}; the two multisets are disjoint, so the morphisms are distinct.
§6.9. Four mechanisms as distinct morphisms in L4(P)
Section 6.1 established the forcing pair for L4: concerted vs stepwise mechanisms
at a single heteroatom centre (the phosphorus identity-substitution example), the
only kind of pair L3 genuinely conflates. The classical mechanism pairs SN1 vs SN2
and E1 vs E2 are not forcing pairs in this sense — their different propensity forms
(v = k1[RX] vs v = k2[RX][Nu], and analogously for E1/E2) separate them already at
L3. What L4 adds for these familiar pairs is a structural account that complements
the kinetic distinction at L3: each mechanism becomes a specific DPO derivation,
with intermediate molecular graphs that appear (or fail to appear) according to
whether the mechanism is concerted or stepwise. This section constructs explicit DPO
derivations in LGraphP for all four mechanisms and verifies pairwise distinctness in
L4(P).
Throughout, atoms are labelled by (el, q, ρ) and bonds by their order b. The Layer 2
valence check at each step verifies that every atom of the product graph R satisfies
ℓ(v) ∈N (Definition 6.4). For consistency with Remark 6.15, atoms whose label
(el, q, ρ) changes between L and R appear in L \ l(K) and R \ r(K) separately; only
atoms with unchanged labels sit in K.

Both mechanisms realise the same net transformation

and carry the same reactants and products in N|S|. They are distinguished at L3
by their propensity forms (v = k1 [RX] for SN1, v = k2 [RX][Nu] for SN2). The
DPO derivations below show why the propensities differ: the two mechanisms have
different DPO-level structure, with SN1 passing through an intermediate molecular
graph that SN2 does not.

Proof. (i) Substitution pair. The SN2 derivation is a single DPO step whose
intermediate graph D contains neither a carbocation nor any other chemically
distinguished non-substrate vertex. The SN1 derivation is the sequential composite
p2 ◦p1 passing through the intermediate molecular graph G1, which contains a vertex
with label (C, +1, 0) — the carbocation. In L4(P), a morphism is an equivalence
class of DPO derivations under SMC congruence (associativity, unitality, symmetry);
no SMC congruence can collapse a derivation passing through a (C, +1, 0) vertex
to one that never visits such a vertex. Hence the two derivations represent distinct
morphisms.
By Definitions 6.14 and 6.27, U4(SN2) = γ(pSN2) = rSN2 is a single L0 generator, while
U4(SN1) = γ(p2)◦γ(p1) is the 2-step composite of the elementary heterolytic-cleavage
and -capture generators (by functoriality of U4). A single generator and a 2-step
composite of distinct generators are distinct morphisms in the free SMC L0(P), so
U4(SN2) ̸= U4(SN1) even though both share source RX + Nu−and target RNu + X−
in N|S|. The composite U4(SN1) is parallel to the postulated generator rSN1 ∈R but
distinct from it: rSN1 has no single-span L4 realisation.
(ii) Elimination pair. Analogous: the E2 derivation has no intermediate graph,
while the E1 derivation passes through the carbocation vertex (C, +1, 0). The two
are distinct in L4(P); U4(E2) = rE2 is a single generator, while U4(E1) = γ(p2)◦γ(p1)
is a 2-step composite, parallel to the postulated rE1 ∈R but distinct from it.
(iii) Cross-class distinctness. The substitution generators and the elimination
generators have distinct source and target complexes in N|S|: substitution consumes
RX + Nu−and produces RNu + X−, while elimination consumes RX + B−and
produces alkene + BH + X−. In particular, the number of species produced differs.
Thus no substitution morphism coincides with any elimination morphism at L0,
and since U4 is well-defined on L4 morphisms, no substitution morphism coincides
with any elimination morphism at L4 either (else their U4-images would coincide in
L0).
What L4 expresses that L3 cannot
The proposition shows how the four classical mechanism types are pairwise
distinguished as morphisms in L4(P). This is not the forcing argument of
Section 6.1 (which concerns the L3-indistinguishable phosphorus pair); rather, it
demonstrates that the same DPO machinery automatically separates mechanism
types that L3 also distinguishes kinetically. In each case, L3 already distinguishes
the two mechanisms numerically via their different propensity forms, but L3
supplies no structural account. L4 supplies that account: the two mechanisms
correspond to DPO derivations with genuinely different internal structure — one
single-step without intermediate graphs, the other two-step passing through a
carbocation vertex (C, +1, 0).
Substitution. At L3: rSN1 and rSN2 are distinct generators with propensity val-
ues k1xRX and k2xRXxNu respectively. These propensity forms suffice to separate
the two morphisms in L3 but give no structural reason for the difference. At L4:
the propensity difference is explained by the different DPO derivation structures
— SN2 as a single concerted rule, SN1 as a composite through the carbocation

intermediate graph. The structural distinction has familiar downstream con-
sequences (Walden inversion for SN2; partial racemisation for SN1 via planar
carbocation attack from either face), but these stereochemical consequences
require three-dimensional data and enter the tower at L4.5 rather than at L4.
Elimination. At L3: rE1 and rE2 are distinct generators with propensities k1xRX
and k2xRXxB, which separate them numerically but again give no structural
account. At L4: the difference is explained by the DPO derivation structures
— E2 as a single concerted rule with cyclic reaction-centre topology, E1 as
a composite through the same carbocation intermediate graph as SN1. The
stereochemical consequences (E2’s required anti-periplanar geometry, absent in
E1) again live at L4.5.
Summary. L4 explains why the Petri net carries parallel generators that L3
distinguishes only by their propensity values. The explanation is structural:
two DPO derivations with different intermediate graphs. Three-dimensional
consequences of this structure (stereochemistry, orbital-symmetry selection rules)
are the content of L4.5 (Section 7).
6.9.4. L4 in action: the Briggs–Rauscher oscillating reaction
The examples of Section 6.9 involved pairs of mechanisms competing for a single
substrate. The Briggs–Rauscher (BR) oscillating reaction shows a richer phenomenon:
a network in which two categorically different mechanism types compete and switch
roles periodically, producing macroscopic colour oscillations visible to the naked
eye. It illustrates how mechanism-level information — the structural data of L4 —
governs the topology of reaction networks in ways that rate constants alone do not
encode, and provides the first case in this monograph where a global property of
a reaction network (the structural origin of oscillation) is exhibited as an L4-level
predicate.

Observation 6.46 (One BR oscillation period as a composite morphism in L4(P)).
Setup. Let PBR be the Petri net containing all elementary reactions of the BR

MA := morphisms generated exclusively by g1, g2 (heterolytic)

The claim is MA∩MB = {id}: no non-identity morphism belongs to both families. In

of generators, and the multiset of generators appearing in that composite (counted
with multiplicities) is invariant under the SMC congruence. Since the generator sets
{g1, g2} and {g4, g5, g6} are disjoint, no non-identity morphism expressible using only
generators from one set can be SMC-congruent to one using only generators from
the other; hence the two generated sub-SMCs intersect only in the identity.

The Briggs–Rauscher reaction thus illustrates a general principle that the tower
makes precise: the structural origin of oscillation is an L4 predicate: it requires that
the network contain morphisms from at least two distinct mechanism families that
compose into a cyclic trajectory. A kinetic model at L3 can fit the oscillation period
and amplitude to data once the reaction network is supplied, but only L4 provides
the structural account of why the network admits oscillatory dynamics in the first
place.

§6.10. What L4 cannot express: forcing of L4.5
The mechanistic level L4(P) was forced by the concerted versus stepwise pathway at
phosphorus: two reactions sharing source, target, and (under steady-state on the TBI)
L3 propensity, distinguishable only at the level of DPO derivations (Sections 6.1, 6.8).
The same machinery applies to the analogous mechanism pairs of carbon chemistry
— SN1 versus SN2, E1 versus E2, and ionic versus radical pathways in oscillating
networks — though for these L3 already provides kinetic separation; what L4 con-
tributes is the structural account (Section 6.9). It does so by replacing stoichiometric
transitions with DPO derivations: objects are molecular graphs, morphisms encode
the sequence of bond changes, and mechanistically distinct reactions are distinct
morphisms.
Yet L4(P) remains blind to spatial orientation. The label set (el, q, ρ) records element
type, formal charge, and radical count; bond-order labels record connectivity. None of
these encode the three-dimensional arrangement of substituents around a stereocentre.
Two molecules that are mirror images of each other are graph-isomorphic in LGraphP
— identical vertex labels, identical edge labels, identical adjacency structure — and
are therefore identified by L4(P), which sees nothing beyond graph isomorphism.
Any DPO rule that applies to one applies identically to the other. The following
forcing pair makes this concrete.
Forcing pair for L4.5: enantiomers under SN2
Consider the SN2 reaction of 2-bromobutane with hydroxide, which has a
stereocentre at C2 (bonded to H, CH3, CH2CH3, Br — four distinct substituents).
The reaction can proceed from either enantiomer:
(R)-2-bromobutane + OH−−→(S)-2-butanol + Br−,
(S)-2-bromobutane + OH−−→(R)-2-butanol + Br−.
Both reactions use the same DPO rule from Example 6.41: break C–Br, form C–
OH, concerted single step. The molecular graphs of (R)- and (S)-2-bromobutane
are graph-isomorphic in LGraphP: same element types, same formal charges,
same radical counts, same bond orders, same adjacency. No datum in (el, q, ρ)
distinguishes a left-handed from a right-handed arrangement of the four sub-
stituents around C2.
Yet the reactions are physically distinct: their products are different enantiomers,
and a chiral agent (an enzyme, a resolving agent, an asymmetric catalyst) reacts
with one but not the other. The swap (R) ↔(S) is an automorphism of L4(P)
— it preserves all categorical structure at the graph level — but corresponds to
genuinely different physical reactions. It is a non-trivial element of coker(φ4.5)
in the exact sequence
1 →ker φ4.5 →Aut(L4.5(P))
φ4.5
−−−→Aut(L4(P)) →coker(φ4.5) →1,
extending Proposition 6.26 to the next level. The same pattern recurs throughout
stereochemistry: (E)/(Z) alkene isomers, cis/trans cycloalkane diastereomers,
endo/exo cycloadducts.

forcing pair — the conrotatory/disrotatory selectivity of pericyclic ring closures

The type of extension L4 →L4.5.
The extensions L0 →L1 →L2 →L3
were decorator extensions: the underlying free SMC L0(P) was retained and a
new numerical functor was appended at each step. The extension L3 →L4 was a
structural extension: the underlying free SMC was replaced by a new one generated
by DPO rules, with no new numerical functor. The extension L4 →L4.5 is of a
third type: an equivariant extension. The free SMC of DPO derivations is retained;
no new numerical functor is added. Instead, the category is equipped with an
action of a group encoding spatial orientation, and morphisms are required to be
equivariant with respect to that action. Chirality, stereochemical descriptors, and
orbital-symmetry selection rules are then the orbit structure and representation
theory of this equivariant extension. The construction is developed in the following
chapter.

same DPO rule applied to (R)- and (S)-substrates produces different physical prod-
ucts that L4 cannot distinguish. This section develops that forcing rigorously and
introduces a second independent forcing pair — the conrotatory / disrotatory distinc-
tion in pericyclic ring closure — which manifests the same L4 blindness in a different
chemical setting. Both pairs are then resolved by a single discrete algebraic datum:
a chirality label σ: Stereo(G) →{+1, −1} at each stereocentre (see Definition 7.6),
augmenting the molecular graph without introducing 3D coordinates. Throughout,
φ4.5 denotes the restriction map Aut(L4.5) →Aut(L4) in the automorphism exact
sequence of the tower.
Remark 7.1 (Why L4.5: a symmetry layer over L4). The fractional index 4.5 is not
a notational convenience. It encodes the mathematical relationship between this
level and its predecessor: L4.5(P) is L4(P) seen through a symmetry filter. The
objects are augmented molecular graphs — the same combinatorial kind as L4,
decorated with chirality labels — and the morphisms remain DPO derivations; but
now only the G∗-equivariant derivations are admitted. L4.5(P) is a category over
L4(P) via the forgetful functor U4.5 : L4.5(P) →L4(P) that drops the chirality labels:
its morphisms are G∗-equivariant DPO derivations on chirality-labelled graphs, with
the same DPO machinery as L4(P). It is not a sub-SMC of L4(P) in the literal sense
— its objects are augmented graphs (G, σ), not bare graphs — but neither is it a new
category built from scratch: the underlying combinatorics and rewriting machinery
are inherited from L4.
This places L4.5 in contrast with the two surrounding transitions. The extension
L3 →L4 was a structural break: L4 introduced an entirely new class of morphisms
(DPO derivations in LGraphP) that L3 had no access to. The forthcoming extension
L4.5 →L5 will be a geometric break: L5 introduces genuinely continuous and
geometric data — 3D atom positions and the continuous potential energy landscape
they define — a qualitatively new mathematical structure.
By contrast, L4 →L4.5 is a symmetry enrichment: the same DPO framework,
restricted to its G∗-equivariant part.
No new numerical functor is added; the
underlying free SMC is not rebuilt. The fractional index 4.5 records exactly this:
we are still in the L4 world, but looking at the part of it that respects a discrete
symmetry group. Separating L4.5 from L5 honours the bottom-up forcing principle:
each level is the unique minimal extension resolving a specific pair of reactions, and
the two forcing pairs of this section are resolved by the discrete G∗-datum alone.
Two forcing pairs for L4.5
Forcing pair 1: enantiomers under SN2.
Consider the bimolecular substitution of 2-bromobutane (stereocentre at C2,
bonded to four distinct substituents: CH3, C2H5, H, Br) by hydroxide, starting

from each enantiomer:
rR :
(R)-2-bromobutane + OH−→(S)-2-butanol + Br−,
rS :
(S)-2-bromobutane + OH−→(R)-2-butanol + Br−.
Walden’s 1896 observation that nucleophilic substitution at a stereocentre pro-
ceeds with inversion of configuration [148] was mechanistically explained in the
1930s: Hughes and Ingold [149] identified back-side attack as the SN2 mechanism,
and Cowdrey, Hughes, Ingold, Masterman, and Scott [150] established in 1937
that the clean elementary SN2 step at a configurationally stable tetrahedral
stereocentre proceeds with complete inversion; mixed mechanisms involving SN1
contributions, neighbouring-group participation, or ion-pair effects appear in
the tower as compositions of multiple L4.5-morphisms with L3-level rate weights,
not as deviations from the elementary SN2 rule. The question for the tower is
whether this experimental fact is visible as a theorem or only as an empirical
constraint.
In LGraphP, the molecular graphs of (R)- and (S)-2-bromobutane are isomor-
phic: identical element types, formal charges, radical counts, bond orders, and
adjacency. No datum in (el, q, ρ, b) distinguishes left-handed from right-handed
arrangements of substituents around C2. This rests on a modelling convention:
the L0 species set is not pre-refined by stereodescriptors. Inserting (R)- and (S)-
as primitive species labels at L0 would build into the model the very distinction
L4.5 is constructed to derive. Under this convention, both reactions apply the
same DPO rule (Example 6.41) to graph-isomorphic substrates and produce
graph-isomorphic products:
rR = rS
as morphisms in L4(P).
The permutation πχ that exchanges the two graph-isomorphic enantiomer copies
at the L4 level is an automorphism of L4(P) identifying the two reactions —
but the physical reactions are distinct: their products differ in sign of optical
rotation, binding affinity to chiral receptors, and metabolism by enzymes. The
entire field of asymmetric synthesis rests on the distinction being real. Hence
[πχ] is a non-trivial element of coker(φ4.5).

Remark 7.2 (Resolving forcing pair 1: enantiomers). In L4.5(P) the objects are
augmented molecular graphs (G, σ) (Definition 7.12). The two enantiomers (GR, σR)
and (GS, σS) share the same underlying graph but carry opposite chirality labels:
σR(C2) = +1 and σS(C2) = −1. They are distinct objects, sitting in different orbits
of the G∗-action: the natural G∗-orbit of (GR, σR) is the singleton {(GR, σR)} at the
level of unrooted graphs, and likewise for (GS, σS).
The cokernel non-triviality of [πχ] now follows directly. The permutation πχ identifies
(GR, σR) with (GS, σS) as objects of L4(P) (where they are graph-isomorphic). A
lift eπχ ∈Aut(L4.5(P)) would have to identify them as objects of L4.5(P) as well,
mapping (GR, σR) to (GS, σS) on the nose. But these are distinct objects of L4.5(P),
so no such lift exists. Hence [πχ] ∈coker(φ4.5) is non-trivial.
A separate, stronger statement is that the G∗-equivariant lift of the SN2 DPO rule
(Example 6.41) produces only the inverted product — the wrong-handed product is
not in its image. This is the categorical content of Hughes–Ingold complete inversion,
made rigorous in Theorem 7.27. For the present section we need only the weaker
statement above: L4.5 separates the two enantiomers as objects, which suffices to
make [πχ] a non-trivial cokernel class.
Remark 7.3 (Resolving forcing pair 2: conrotatory vs. disrotatory). In L4.5(P) the
two ring-closure products carry distinct chirality labels at the new stereocentres C3
and C4:
(Gcb, σtrans):

σ(C3) · σ(C4) = −1
(opposite orientations).

A G∗-equivariant DPO rule for electrocyclic ring closure must map reactants to
products consistently with the G∗-action: the conrotatory closure produces the
trans product (matching orientations), while the disrotatory closure produces the
cis product (opposed orientations), and these outcomes are controlled by which
symmetry element of the transition state the rule respects (C2 for conrotatory, Cs for
disrotatory). The permutation πec identifying the two products in L4 does not lift to
an equivariant morphism of L4.5, because the two products have different σ-signs at
their stereocentres. Thus [πec] ∈coker(φ4.5) is non-trivial.

The two datums at L4.5
The minimal new structure at L4.5 consists of two datums, both discrete and
algebraic:
• Chirality labels σ: Stereo(G) →{+1, −1} on each stereocentre, aug-
menting the molecular graph. Six decades of asymmetric synthesis encoded
as a sign.
• The chirality-symmetry group G∗= Aut(G) ⋉Zk
2 (Definition 7.5),
acting on chirality-labelled graphs by permuting atoms and flipping σ at
subsets of stereocentres. The Woodward–Hoffmann selection rules are
captured as G∗-equivariance of the DPO rules — no 3D geometry required.
Both datums are discrete and algebraic:
the hallmark of the symmetry-
enrichment character of L4.5. Three-dimensional consequences (specific molecular
geometries, activation barriers, vibrational modes) are deferred to L5.
§7.2. The chirality symmetry group G∗
Section 7.1 showed that both forcing pairs for L4.5 — enantiomer substrates under
SN2 and conrotatory/disrotatory electrocyclic closures — are resolved by equipping
molecular graphs with discrete chirality labels σ: Stereo(G) →{+1, −1} and by
letting a finite group G∗act on these labels. This section defines that group, identifies
its two factors, and verifies that it acts sensibly on chirality-labelled graphs. The
G∗-action on L4.5(P), projected through the forgetful functor U4.5, makes the forcing

enrichment to L4.5 removes.
The group G∗has two factors. The first, Aut(G), is the group of label-preserving
graph automorphisms of G: permutations of the vertex set V that fix the labelling
functions λV , λE and the bond-order function b. These are the physically meaningful
relabellings — permutations of identical-nucleus atoms that also respect the bonding
pattern — and form a graph-theoretic restriction of the permutation part of the
Longuet–Higgins framework [154], namely those nuclear permutations expressible
from the connectivity data L4 has made available.
The second factor encodes
orientation flips at stereocentres. For a molecule with k = |Stereo(G)| stereocentres,
the minimal group that can independently invert the orientation at each centre is
Zk
2. A single global Z2 suffices to relate the two members of an enantiomer pair (via
simultaneous flips at all centres) but cannot relate an enantiomer to a diastereomer
— e.g. no element of a global Z2 takes (R, R)-tartaric acid to meso-tartaric acid, since
the latter requires flipping σ at one stereocentre but not the other. The independent
single-centre flips in Zk
2 are required for that distinction, as the tartaric acid example
below will make explicit.

The stereocentres on which G∗acts are now identified.
Definition 7.6 (Stereocentre: graph-theoretic detection). Let v ∈V (G) be a vertex
with exactly four neighbours w1, w2, w3, w4. For each neighbour wi, the rooted CIP
tree T v
wi is the labelled rooted tree obtained from G \ {v} by depth-first traversal
outward from wi, with any back-edge (an edge that would close a ring within G\{v})
replaced by a phantom leaf labelled by the element type of its target vertex.
The vertex v is a stereocentre in G if:
(i) v has exactly four neighbours in G (tetrahedral valence), and
(ii) the four rooted CIP trees T v
w1, T v
w2, T v
w3, T v
w4 are pairwise non-isomorphic as
labelled rooted trees.
Condition (ii) is the graph-theoretic form of the Cahn–Ingold–Prelog (CIP) distinct-
ness condition [155]: it is the precise criterion that makes a priority ordering of the
four substituents unique and well-defined. For acyclic neighbourhoods, the rooted
CIP trees coincide with the four connected components of G \ {v} rooted at the
respective wi, and the criterion reduces to the standard form. For ring stereocen-
tres (e.g. ring atoms in cyclobutenes, cyclohexanes), the phantom-leaf construction
handles ring closures and recovers the standard CIP priority assignment.
Both conditions are decidable from (λV , λE) alone; no 3D information is needed. The
set of stereocentres of G is denoted Stereo(G).
Remark 7.7 (CIP priorities and the chirality label). The Cahn–Ingold–Prelog rules [155]
assign a total priority order to the four substituents of a stereocentre based on atomic
number and then on graph topology (the “hierarchical digraph” algorithm). This
order is computable from G ∈LGraphP alone: atomic numbers are part of el, and
topology is the graph structure.
Given the CIP priority order, a chirality label σ(v) ∈{+1, −1} determines the
stereodescriptor: σ(v) = +1 corresponds to the (R)-configuration (priority sequence
1 > 2 > 3 > 4 runs clockwise when substituent 4 points away) and σ(v) = −1 to (S).
At L4.5, however, σ(v) is an abstract binary label: it records that a stereocentre has
an orientation and that the two orientations are distinct, without committing to
which spatial arrangement σ = +1 realises. The CIP rules establish that the label is
well-defined and graph-computable; which physical enantiomer it corresponds to is a
statement deferred to L5.

objects. The G∗-element relating them (E∗in part (i), a partial flip in part (ii)) is
not an element of Aut(G) alone, so the relation is not a LGraphG∗
P -isomorphism.
An automorphism of L4.5(P) would have to send each object to an isomorphic object;
the labelling distinction obstructs this, so the identification cannot lift. Under U4.5,
which forgets the chirality labels, the two objects collapse to the same underlying
graph, and the G∗-relation becomes a non-trivial automorphism of L4(P) — the
cokernel class.
Remark 7.10 (Provenance: classical chemistry, new categorical framing). Proposi-
tion 7.9 records the categorical form of a result that is well-established in molecular
symmetry theory. The use of permutation-inversion groups in molecular symme-
try theory goes back to Longuet-Higgins [154], who introduced the spectroscopic
permutation-inversion group as the symmetry group of the full molecular Hamiltonian
under feasible permutations of identical nuclei combined with the parity operation
E∗; Bunker and Jensen [156] develop this framework systematically for spectroscopic
applications. This spectroscopic group is not G∗(G): the Longuet-Higgins construc-
tion has a single global E∗, whereas G∗(G) has k independent flips Zk
2, the refinement
needed to separate diastereomers from enantiomers in molecules with multiple stere-
ocentres. That refinement was developed in the algebraic theory of stereoisomerism
due to Dugundji and Ugi [137] and by Ruch [157], the latter introducing the “chirality
function” σ: Stereo(G) →{+1, −1} used here. The tartaric acid example of the
chembox above is classical, going back to van ’t Hoff’s original demonstration of
stereoisomerism in 1874.

cokernel classes of the automorphism exact sequence φ4.5, and the resulting char-

obstructions [πχ] and [πec] identified in §7.1. The classical group-theoretic machinery
is thus deployed here to serve a specifically categorical purpose: making the forcing
argument of §7.1 rigorous and showing that no smaller group-theoretic datum would
suffice.
Remark 7.11 (Minimality of the two factors). Both factors of G∗(G) = Aut(G) ⋉Zk
2
are necessary. Without Aut(G), the action cannot identify equivalent stereocentres:
for instance, it would treat the two labellings (+, −) and (−, +) of tartaric acid as
distinct objects, introducing spurious stereoisomers. Without Zk
2 in full (replacing
it with a proper quotient such as the single global Z2), the action cannot relate
enantiomers to diastereomers, as the tartaric acid example makes explicit. The
semidirect product Aut(G) ⋉Zk
2 is therefore the smallest group containing both
factors with the required action of Aut(G) on Zk
2 by index permutation, and the
action of Definition 7.5 realises precisely the structure needed to separate the forcing
cokernel classes of §7.1 while identifying chemically equivalent relabellings.
Proposition 7.9 makes precise the sense in which L4.5 is “L4 with a symmetry layer”:
the G∗-action is exactly the additional structure needed to separate the forcing
cokernel classes, and Remark 7.11 records that both factors of G∗are independently
required. The chirality-labelled molecular graphs (G, σ) on which this action operates
are introduced in the next section.

and (G, ∅) is achiral.

Why chirality-compatibility is the right morphism condition
A morphism f : (G, σ) →(H, τ) in LGraphG∗
P
is an LGraphP-monomorphism
that preserves every chirality label it transports. Chemically: a reaction step that
does not mechanistically touch a stereocentre cannot change its configuration.
When f(v) remains a stereocentre in H, the label σG(v) must equal σH(f(v));
this is what chirality-compatibility says. Steps that do touch a stereocentre are
handled by DPO: the reactive vertex passes through the context graph K (where
its reduced neighbour count makes it non-stereogenic by Definition 7.6(i)), so
Stereo(K) omits it, and it re-emerges in R with a new chirality label assigned
by the rule’s chirality lift. The label change is a consequence of the pushout
construction, not of a morphism that flips σ in transit.

fewer than four neighbours in K), so they fail Definition 7.6(i) and Stereo(K0)
