σR agree on vertices that appear in both L0 and R0 unchanged (via K0).
The pair (σL, σR) encodes the stereochemical action of the rule.
Different lifts
correspond to different stereochemical behaviours of the same bond-graph mechanism:
• A lift with σR(v) = −σL(v) at a reactive stereocentre v encodes a back-side
attack (inversion) mechanism.
• A lift with σR(v) = +σL(v) encodes a front-side attack (retention) mechanism,
as in SNi substitution.
The forgetful functor U4.5 collapses all lifts of p0 to the same L4-rule — confirming
that L4 is blind to this stereochemical refinement. This is the precise categorical
sense in which L4.5 refines L4: the same bond-graph mechanism is enriched with
a chirality assignment, and different assignments correspond to physically distinct
stereochemical outcomes.

inverting lift (σR = −σL) and the retaining lift (σR = +σL) are G∗-equivariant

them for a given physical mechanism is supplied by external input: back-side attack

for SNi. The tower-level separation is precise: LGraphG∗
P
provides the ambient data
for chirality lifts; G∗-equivariance ensures that any chosen lift propagates uniformly
across every G∗-orbit of substrates; mechanism-specific input selects which lift to
use. The resulting morphisms of L4.5(P) are the G∗-equivariant DPO rules together
with their chirality lifts.
Equivariance as commutation with the G∗-action
Equivariance (Definition 7.18) is the condition that the DPO rule and the G∗-
action commute as operations on LGraphG∗
P : for every element (π, ϵ) ∈G∗(G)
and every match m, applying the rule then the G∗-action yields the same result
as applying the G∗-action first (with its induced match (π, ϵ) ◦m) and then the
rule. The rule’s stereochemical behaviour is thus required to be uniform across
every element of every G∗-orbit.

7.5.1. Walden inversion
In 1896 Paul Walden observed that malic acid could be converted to chlorosuccinic
acid and back through a sequence of reagents, with the recovered malic acid displaying
flipped optical rotation: the configuration had been inverted somewhere in the cycle
without any obvious cause [148].
The mechanism remained contested for four
decades. Hughes and Ingold’s systematic kinetic work in the 1930s [149] established
that bimolecular nucleophilic substitution (SN2) proceeds by back-side attack: the
nucleophile approaches from the face opposite the leaving group, forcing a “Walden
inversion” of the four substituents around the reactive carbon. Cowdrey, Hughes,
Ingold, Masterman, and Scott provided the definitive stereochemical evidence in
1937 [150]: every SN2 reaction gives complete inversion of configuration, on every
substrate, in every solvent, at every temperature.
This empirical universality demands a structural explanation that is insensitive to the
continuous parameters L4.5 does not know about (solvent, temperature, conformer).
At L4.5, universality is a theorem.

7.5.2. Racemisation via SN1
Remark 7.29 (Racemisation, for mathematicians). A racemic mixture is an equal-
parts mixture of the two enantiomers of a chiral molecule. It has zero net optical
rotation because the contributions of (G, +1) and (G, −1) cancel. Racemisation is
a process that converts an enantiomerically pure starting material into a racemic
mixture; it destroys stereochemical information. In tower language: racemisation is
the passage from a non-E∗-symmetric state (pure enantiomer) to an E∗-symmetric
state (racemic mixture). The SN1 mechanism achieves this by passing through a
planar intermediate in which the reactive carbon is no longer a stereocentre.

7.5.3. Net retention via double inversion: neighbouring group participation
The previous two subsections treated single-step stereochemical events: SN2 preserves
and inverts the chirality label in one rule application (Theorem 7.27); SN1 destroys and
regenerates it across two rules (Theorem 7.30). A third case, due to Winstein [159],
combines two inversion steps to give net retention: the reaction proceeds with
inverted configuration at the intermediate and inverted again at the product, so
the initial and final configurations match. This mechanism is neighbouring group
participation (NGP), also called anchimeric assistance.
Remark 7.33 (Neighbouring group participation, for mathematicians). In NGP, the
substrate carries a nucleophilic heteroatom or π-bond positioned close to the reactive
carbon — for example, a β-acetoxy group on a cyclohexyl tosylate, Winstein’s
classical system. When the leaving group departs, the neighbouring nucleophile
attacks the reactive carbon from the opposite face, forming a bridged intermediate
(in Winstein’s case, a five-membered acyloxonium ring). The reactive carbon remains
four-coordinated throughout: it loses the bond to the leaving group but immediately
forms a bond to the bridging nucleophile, hence is a stereocentre in the bridged
intermediate. An external nucleophile then attacks the bridged intermediate, again
from the opposite face, opening the ring and giving the final product. The classical
experimental observation is that the reaction gives complete retention of configu-
ration at the reactive carbon, despite involving two nucleophilic attack steps [159].
Historically this was puzzling because neither step individually retains: each inverts.
Two inversions give retention.

• r1 has the inverting chirality lift at v (back-side attack by the neighbouring
nucleophile);
• r2 has the inverting chirality lift at v (back-side attack by the external nucleophile
on the bridged intermediate).
Then the composition r2 ◦r1 satisfies
σfinal(v) = σ(v),
i.e. the net stereochemical outcome at v is retention of configuration.

What the theorem says about NGP chemistry
Theorem 7.34 recovers, in two lines, a result that historically required careful
experimental design to establish.
Winstein’s evidence [159] included: rate
acceleration (the neighbouring group assists the ionisation, giving first-order
kinetics despite formal bimolecular reactants), racemisation in the absence
of external nucleophile (the bridged intermediate can open from either face,
analogous to Theorem 7.30(ii)), and complete retention when the external
nucleophile is present in excess (the two sequential back-side attacks dominate
the kinetics).
At L4.5, the argument is structural and does not require the ion-pair analysis that
made Winstein’s original treatment subtle. Two G∗-equivariant back-side-attack
DPO rules compose to a rule that preserves the chirality label at v. The bridged
intermediate is a valid object in L4.5(P) because the reactive carbon remains
four-coordinated throughout — the bond to the leaving group is replaced by
the bond to the bridging nucleophile — so the carbon is still a stereocentre in
the intermediate, with its chirality label inverted by the first step.
The theorem generalises immediately to longer sequences: any sequence of 2n
back-side-attack steps at v gives net retention; any sequence of 2n + 1 gives
net inversion. This is the L4.5-level parity rule for nucleophilic substitution
sequences, recovered from Theorem 7.27 by composition.

nition of enantiomers that the construction makes available is given, and shown to
capture the classical chemical notion.

• Stereo(G) = ∅: trivially (G, ∅) = E∗· (G, ∅) — achiral without stereocentres.

textbook example is meso-tartaric acid (§7.2), where the centre-of-symmetry
exchange of the two stereocentres maps (+1, −1) to (−1, +1).
A molecule is chiral iff it has a distinct enantiomer.

Enantiomers: the tower account
Properties (i)–(v) together reproduce, from the tower construction, the full
chemical concept of a pair of enantiomers.
Property (ii) encodes why enantiomers have identical achiral physical properties:
same boiling point, same melting point, same NMR spectrum in an achiral
solvent, same reaction rates with achiral reagents. All of these are Lk-level data
for k < 4.5, and they are identical for the two enantiomers because U4.5 collapses
the pair to a single object.
Property (iv) encodes the categorical statement that within L4.5, no morphism
flips the chirality label at a bond-graph stereocentre while leaving the under-
lying graph fixed. This captures the chemistry of configurational chirality at
tetrahedral stereocentres — the case where four distinct substituents at sp3
carbon define the chirality datum.
Several real interconversion mechanisms fall outside this framework because they
are not visible at L4.5: amine inversion (umbrella flipping at nitrogen via a planar
transition state), atropisomer interconversion (rotation around a single bond),
and helical inversion in helicenes all interchange “enantiomeric” stereoisomers
without breaking the bond graph. These phenomena require 3D-coordinate data
(transition-state planarity), barrier heights (whether the inversion is thermally
accessible at room temperature), or both — inputs that enter the tower only at
L5 and above. Property (iv) is the L4.5-level shadow of configurational chirality
specifically; the broader physical concept of “stereochemical interconvertibility”
lives at higher levels.

Property (v) encodes the central principle of asymmetric synthesis. A G∗-
equivariant reaction treats both enantiomers uniformly, producing enantiomeric
products in equal amounts. To produce one enantiomer preferentially, a reaction
must break the G∗-symmetry — by using a chiral catalyst or reagent modelled as a
fixed object (C, σC) in the reaction network. When the catalyst appears explicitly
with a fixed chirality label σC, the two combined substrates (G, +1) + (C, σC)
and (G, −1)+(C, σC) have different sources in L4.5(P) and are genuinely distinct
morphisms of the composite system. The G∗-symmetry is broken not by violating
equivariance, but by holding one component of the reaction fixed. This is the
categorical account of enantioselective catalysis at L4.5.
The four theorems of this section — Walden inversion, racemisation, net retention
via double inversion, and the enantiomer properties — together exhibit L4.5’s char-
acteristic contribution to the tower: universal propagation of mechanism-selected
stereochemical outcomes across G∗-orbits of substrates. The next section (§7.6) ap-
plies the same framework to pericyclic reactions, where the Aut(G)-factor of G∗
supplies the combinatorial content of the Woodward–Hoffmann selection rules.
§7.6. Pericyclic stereochemistry at L4.5: a theorem and a Woodward–
Hoffmann conjecture
The stereochemical theorems of §7.5 treated reactions at a single stereocentre. The
present section takes up the second forcing obligation of §7.1 — the electrocyclic
forcing pair [πec] — and asks what L4.5 can say about the pericyclic selection rules
more generally. The answer has two parts: a theorem providing the categorical content
(α-equivariance selects one chirality lift from two), and a conjecture identifying the
equivariant lift with the thermally allowed Woodward–Hoffmann product. The
theorem is established here; the conjecture is accompanied by verification in the
principal case (electrocyclic) and a discussion of its scope and limitations.
7.6.1. Background
A pericyclic reaction is a concerted reaction — bond-making and bond-breaking occur
simultaneously, with no ionic intermediate — whose transition state has a cyclic
arrangement of the participating atoms and bonds, allowing electron reorganisation
around a closed loop [15]. At L4(P), pericyclic reactions are DPO rules whose
reaction centre L \ K together with R \ K traces a cyclic subgraph topology [142].
The three principal families are electrocyclic ring closures/openings, cycloadditions,
and sigmatropic shifts.
Woodward and Hoffmann discovered in 1965 [151, 15] that the stereochemical outcome
of every pericyclic reaction is governed by a single principle: the symmetry of the
molecular orbitals must be conserved along the reaction path. For ground-state
(thermal) reactions, this means the orbitals of the reactant must flow continuously
into those of the product without crossing a symmetry-imposed barrier. Reactions
that satisfy this are thermally allowed; reactions that would require a barrier crossing
are thermally forbidden (but photochemically allowed, since the barrier vanishes
upon electron promotion).

Conrotatory means the two terminal groups rotate in the same direction; disrotatory
means they rotate in opposite directions. Suprafacial (supra) means the new bond
forms on the same face of the π system; antarafacial (antara) means it forms on
the opposite face. The work earned Hoffmann the 1981 Nobel Prize in Chemistry,
shared with Fukui for related frontier-orbital analysis [153, 152]; Woodward had died
in 1979 and the prize could not be awarded posthumously.
Pericyclic reactions are about stereochemistry — which product isomer is produced
and through which transition-state geometry — and this is exactly the content
that lives at L4.5 as chirality labels and nowhere lower in the tower. At L4, the
thermally allowed and thermally forbidden outcomes of a pericyclic reaction share
the same bond-graph DPO rule (L ←K →R); the distinction between them is
purely stereochemical (which face of the π-system the new bond forms on, and the
resulting relative configuration of the new stereocentres) and invisible until L4.5. At
L3, the rate constants of allowed and forbidden processes are different in practice
(forbidden reactions face higher activation barriers), but L3 does not explain why
they differ; the structural reason — α-equivariance or its failure at the chirality lift —
is a L4.5 fact. L4.5 is thus the first tower level where the allowed/forbidden distinction
can be stated structurally, not merely registered as a numerical rate difference.
7.6.2. The categorical theorem
The connection between WH and L4.5 rests on a single graph-theoretic observation.
A pericyclic reaction centre is a cyclic subgraph, and cyclic graphs admit non-trivial
automorphisms — specifically, the reflections that swap pairs of stereogenic terminal
atoms. These automorphisms project from the 3D symmetry elements (C2 axes, σv
planes) of the transition state to the graph level, where they act on the vertex set by
permuting the reaction-centre atoms. Call such an automorphism a reaction-centre
automorphism of the rule.
Theorem 7.37 (α-equivariance distinguishes pericyclic product lifts (ring-closure
direction)). Let p0 be a pericyclic ring-closure DPO rule in LGraphP — a rule
whose reactant side L has the participating atoms in an open-chain π-system (sp2
hybridisation at the termini) and whose product side R has the new σ-bond closing
those termini into a ring (sp3 at the new stereogenic positions). Let α be a reaction-
centre automorphism of p0 — that is, an involutive graph automorphism α ∈Aut(L)∩
Aut(R) that exchanges a pair of stereocentres {v1, v2} ⊂Stereo(R). Then:
(i) p0 admits exactly two chirality lifts ˜p+, ˜p−distinguished by the relative sign of
σR(v1) and σR(v2):
˜p+ : σR(v1) = σR(v2),
˜p−: σR(v1) = −σR(v2).

(ii) Exactly one of the two lifts is α-equivariant: ˜p+ is α-equivariant and ˜p−is not.
Proof. (i). The reaction produces the two stereocentres v1, v2 ∈Stereo(R) from
sp2 atoms in L (hence v1, v2 /∈Stereo(L): at the L-side these vertices have three
neighbours each, failing condition (i) of Definition 7.6). A chirality lift of p0 is
therefore a choice of (σR(v1), σR(v2)) ∈{+1, −1}2 at the product side — four options
in total. Identifying lifts related by the E∗action (σR 7→−σR), which produces
the enantiomeric product and hence the same stereochemical content up to overall
enantiomer choice, the four options collapse into two equivalence classes:
• ˜p+ = {(+, +), (−, −)}: the lifts with σR(v1) = σR(v2).
• ˜p−= {(+, −), (−, +)}: the lifts with σR(v1) = −σR(v2).
(ii). The α-equivariance square (Definition 7.18) for ˜p± with α acting on chirality
functions by σ 7→σ ◦α−1 requires σR ◦α−1 = σR on {v1, v2}. Since α exchanges
v1 ↔v2:
(σR ◦α−1)(v1) = σR(v2),
(σR ◦α−1)(v2) = σR(v1).
α-equivariance thus requires σR(v1) = σR(v2): exactly the condition defining ˜p+.
Hence ˜p+ is α-equivariant; ˜p−, with σR(v1) = −σR(v2), fails the equivariance condi-
tion.
Remark 7.38 (What the theorem says, tower-natively). Theorem 7.37 separates a
pericyclic rule into two chirality-lift classes defined by the relative sign pattern at
the new stereocentres. At L4, both lifts collapse under U4.5 to the same bond-graph
rule: the distinction is L4-invisible. At L4.5, the reaction-centre automorphism α
is a non-trivial element of Aut(G) ≤G∗(G), and α-equivariance singles out exactly
one of the two lifts. The tower contribution is the classification of pericyclic product
lifts by α-parity, not the identification of which class is thermally allowed — that
identification is the content of the conjecture below.
7.6.3. The Woodward–Hoffmann identification conjecture
Theorem 7.37 gives the combinatorial skeleton: for every pericyclic reaction with a
reaction-centre automorphism α, one of two chirality lifts is α-equivariant. The ques-
tion this section poses is whether that combinatorial skeleton tracks the Woodward–
Hoffmann selection rules.
Conjecture 7.39 (Woodward–Hoffmann identification at L4.5, electrocyclic case).
Let p0 be an electrocyclic ring-closure rule with N π-electrons in the reactant π-system,
and let α be its reaction-centre automorphism (the reflection exchanging the two
terminal stereocentres). Let ˜p+, ˜p−be the two chirality lifts of Theorem 7.37. Then
the thermally allowed Woodward–Hoffmann product corresponds to:
• the α-equivariant lift ˜p+ when N ≡0 (mod 4) (i.e., 4n electrons);
• the non-α-equivariant lift ˜p−when N ≡2 (mod 4) (i.e., 4n + 2 electrons).
The photochemically allowed product corresponds to the opposite lift in each case.
Remark 7.40 (What the conjecture claims). Theorem 7.37 is a combinatorial theorem:
it classifies product lifts by α-parity. Conjecture 7.39 adds empirical content: it
identifies which α-parity corresponds to the thermally allowed outcome, with an
alternation governed by N mod 4. The alternation itself — the hallmark of the

Woodward–Hoffmann rules — is the conjecture’s substantive claim. Below L4.5, the
alternation is invisible because chirality labels are absent; at L4.5, it is expressible but
not derivable from categorical axioms alone. The identification between α-parity and
thermal allowedness requires input from the orbital-symmetry analysis of Woodward
and Hoffmann, and this input is not currently derivable from the tower structure
below L6 (where the full electronic Hilbert bundle becomes available).

7.6.6. Further pericyclic reactions
The same α-parity analysis applies to other pericyclic reactions but with two compli-
cations that moderate the scope of Conjecture 7.39.
Hexa-1,3,5-triene →cyclohexa-1,3-diene (6π, 4n + 2). The forcing pair’s
4n electron count is complemented by this 4n + 2 case. Using cyclohexa-1,3-diene
numbering for the product (ring carbons C1=C2−C3=C4−C5−C6, the new σ-bond
closing C5−C6), the new stereocentres are C5 and C6, and the reaction-centre
automorphism α swaps C1 ↔C4, C2 ↔C3, and C5 ↔C6, the graph-level shadow of
the C2 axis through the midpoints of C2−C3 and C5−C6. An analogous chirality-label
computation shows: the cis product (with σR(C5) = −σR(C6)) is non-α-equivariant
(˜p−), while the trans product is α-equivariant (˜p+). Woodward and Hoffmann’s
1965 analysis [151] identifies the cis product (from disrotatory motion) as thermally
allowed for 4n + 2 electrons, i.e. the non-α-equivariant lift: this is the 4n + 2 branch
of Conjecture 7.39. The alternation between 4n (thermal ↔α-equivariant) and
4n + 2 (thermal ↔non-α-equivariant) is the WH hallmark.
Cycloadditions and sigmatropic shifts. The categorical theorem (Theorem 7.37)
extends to cycloadditions and sigmatropic shifts whenever the reaction centre admits
an involutive graph automorphism exchanging new stereocentres. The Diels–Alder
[4+2] cycloaddition, for instance, has reaction centre {C1, . . . , C6} (four from the

the two possible cycloadduct stereochemistries. Substrates without such substitution

follows the same (4n) vs. (4n + 2) alternation as the electrocyclic case; the conjecture
extends accordingly but verification requires case-by-case substrate choice.
7.6.7. Scope and limitations
Remark 7.41 (What L4.5 can and cannot distinguish). Theorem 7.37 and Conjec-
ture 7.39 together express the L4.5-visible content of the Woodward–Hoffmann rules.
Two scope boundaries should be made explicit.
Product-level vs. motion-level distinctions. The reaction-centre automorphism α
is a graph-level object: it permutes vertices without reference to 3D geometry. A
single graph automorphism α can be the shadow of either a C2 rotation axis (as
in conrotatory motion) or a σv mirror plane (as in disrotatory motion); both act
identically on the vertex set. Consequently, L4.5 distinguishes the two products
(trans vs. cis, supra-supra vs. supra-antara) but not the two transition-state motions
(conrotatory vs. disrotatory, axial vs. planar). The motion-level WH content —
which orbital symmetry element is preserved during the continuous reaction path —
requires the 3D geometry introduced at L5, where the Euclidean group E(3) acts
on configurations. At L5, the distinction between C2-preserving and σv-preserving
transition states becomes meaningful, and WH’s orbital-conservation argument can
be stated in full.
The conjecture’s status. The categorical theorem (Theorem 7.37) is established
here. The WH identification conjecture (Conjecture 7.39) has been verified for the
hexa-2,4-diene forcing pair (4n) and hexa-1,3,5- triene (4n + 2); its extension to
cycloadditions and sigmatropic shifts follows the same α-parity pattern but requires
case-by-case substrate choice to ensure the σ-analysis is non-vacuous. The alternation
with electron count — the substantive WH claim — has been checked case-by-case
but is not derivable from L4.5 axioms alone. A derivation would require the tower to
supply the orbital-count dependence intrinsically, which presumably occurs only at
L6 where the electronic Hilbert bundle and its symmetry-adapted basis enter.
7.6.8. Tower reading
What the theorem and conjecture say together
Theorem 7.37 and Conjecture 7.39 together provide the following account of the
Woodward–Hoffmann rules at L4.5.
Theorem content. Every pericyclic rule with a reaction-centre automorphism
α exchanging new stereocentres decomposes into exactly two chirality lifts,
distinguished by whether σR is α-invariant or α-anti-invariant. The α-invariant
lift (˜p+) is α-equivariant; the α-anti-invariant lift (˜p−) is not. Here α is a specific
element of Aut(G) ≤G∗(G), and the relevant equivariance is under the cyclic
211


## Page 212


Kyunghoon Han
Categorification of Chemical Reactions
subgroup ⟨α⟩≤G∗(G) generated by it, not under all of G∗(G) — the latter
would also require E∗-equivariance, which intrinsic-σR pericyclic rules do not
satisfy.
Conjecture content. The Woodward–Hoffmann (WH) rules assert an empirical
identification: the α-equivariant lift is the thermally allowed product for 4n
electrons, and the non-equivariant lift is thermally allowed for 4n + 2 electrons.
The alternation is the WH hallmark.
Tower boundary. The bond-graph transformation underlying the thermally
forbidden disrotatory closure of hexa-2,4-diene is a perfectly valid morphism of
L4(P). Its L4.5 chirality lift to the cis product, however, is not α-equivariant
(Theorem 7.37), hence not G∗-equivariant, hence not a generator of L4.5(P).
The cis product itself is a perfectly valid object of L4.5(P) — it exists as a real
molecule with a well-defined chirality function — but the rule producing it via
thermal closure is inadmissible at L4.5. This is the categorical incarnation of WH
at L4.5: the inadmissibility of the forbidden pericyclic rule, not of its product,
is the failure of the chirality lift to be G∗-equivariant. The orbital-symmetry
conservation argument of Woodward and Hoffmann supplies the 3D geometric
justification for why α-equivariance should correspond to thermal allowedness
— this justification operates at L5 (3D geometry) and fully at L6 (electronic
structure), both beyond the present chapter.
The categorical theorem and the WH identification conjecture together close the
analysis of L4.5-level stereochemistry as responsive to the two forcing cokernel classes
of §7.1: the enantiomer obstruction [πχ] is fully resolved in §7.5 by Walden, racemi-
sation, and the enantiomer properties; the electrocyclic obstruction [πec] is partially
resolved here via the categorical theorem, with the Woodward–Hoffmann identifica-
tion as an outstanding conjecture whose full resolution awaits higher tower levels.
The tower’s passage from L4.5 to L5 — where 3D geometry becomes available and
the motion-level WH content enters the frame — is taken up in §7.7.
§7.7. What L4.5 cannot express: forcing of L5
The forcing pair of §7.1 drove the tower from L4 to L4.5 through a symmetry enrich-
ment: a group action G∗(G) ↷LGraphG∗
P
was added to an existing combinatorial
category. The forcing from L4.5 to L5 is qualitatively different. It does not promote a
qualitative distinction L4.5-invisible to L4.5-visible; instead, it promotes a quantitative
distinction whose source is the 3D geometry of the transition state — a datum that
does not exist anywhere in the tower below L5.
For the first time in the tower, geometric continuous data (3D positions on a
configuration manifold) is unavoidable; lower levels admitted continuous numerical
decorations (free energies at L2, rate constants at L3) but not continuous geometric
structure.

same vertex labels, same G∗-orbit.
System A: CH3Br+OH−→CH3OH+Br−(SN2, water, 298 K). Rate constant
kH ≈4 × 10−3 M−1s−1 [160].
System B: CD3Br + OH−→CD3OH + Br−(same reaction with all three H
at the reactive carbon replaced by D). Rate constant kD ≈3 × 10−3 M−1s−1,
giving the α-secondary kinetic isotope effect kH/kD ≈1.3 at 298 K [161, 24].
The L4.5 collapse, structurally. Both systems use the same G∗-equivariant
DPO rule pSN2 of §7.5. Neither substrate has a stereocentre: Stereo(CH3Br) =
Stereo(CD3Br) = ∅. The categorical data at every tower level up to and including
L4.5 coincide for the two systems: identical L0-stoichiometries, identical L4-DPO
mechanisms, identical L4.5-chirality lifts (both empty). Numerical decorations
attached at lower levels (L1 enthalpies, L2 free energies, L3 rate constants)
differ by small isotope-dependent amounts that the levels themselves record
but do not explain — the ZPE shifts and the corresponding rate-constant ratio
kH/kD ≈1.3 are stored as numerical inputs at L1–L3, with no derivation from
those levels’ structural data.
The forcing, sharpened. What L4.5 cannot do is derive the rate-constant ratio
from its categorical structure. At L4.5, the two systems share every structural
attribute (DPO rule, chirality lift, G∗-orbit); the empirical rate ratio is an
isotope-specific number that the level cannot account for, only record. The
forcing into L5 is therefore explanatory: L5 provides the 3D-geometric machinery
(configuration orbifold Ce(G), Born–Oppenheimer PES, TS geometry, vibrational
ZPE) from which the rate-constant ratio can be derived rather than stipulated.
In tower terms, the forgetful functor U5 : L5 →L4.5 has a non-trivial fibre
over the single L4.5-morphism pSN2: the fibre splits into isotope-distinguished
L5-morphisms that share the L4.5-projection but differ in their TS-vibrational
signature.
The L5 refinement. Experimentally, the two rate constants differ by a factor
of 1.3. At higher L5 resolution, System A and System B become distinct objects:
their nuclear masses enter the transition-state (TS) vibrational partition function,
yielding different activation barriers and hence different rate constants. The
forcing is thus an object refinement: two objects identified at L4.5 split into
distinct objects at L5 once 3D geometry and mass-weighted dynamics become
available.
Physical origin of the KIE. The α-secondary effect kH/kD ≈1.3 arises because
the C−H and C−D bending vibrations change character at the SN2 transition
state.
The reactive carbon passes through a nearly pentacoordinate geometry
(bipyramidal around the central carbon, with the leaving group and nucleophile at
the apical positions and the three remaining substituents on an equatorial plane),
and one bending mode at the reactive carbon softens significantly between the
reactant (tetrahedral, bending frequency ≈1340 cm−1) and the TS (bending frequency

7.7.1. What L5 must add
The forcing pair exposes a chain of dependences that L4.5 cannot express:
3D geometry ⇒TS geometry ⇒activation barrier Ea ⇒rate constant k.
None of the arrows can be reversed from L4.5-level data. L5 closes the chain by
introducing three new objects, together constituting the tower’s first geometric break:
(i) The configuration orbifold Ce(G) = R3n/(SE(3) × Aut(G)): the space of
all molecular shapes — all assignments of 3D coordinates to atoms, modulo
rigid-body motions and permutations of identical atoms. A point R ∈Ce(G)
is a specific shape of the molecule. This is the first genuinely continuous and
geometric object in the tower.
(ii) The Born–Oppenheimer potential energy surface V : Ce(G) →R, where
V (R) is the electronic ground-state energy at geometry R. The landscape of
V encodes stable conformers (local minima), transition states (saddle points),
and reaction paths (steepest-descent curves on V ).
(iii) The activation barrier and Eyring equation: the barrier Ea is the height
of the saddle point above the reactant minimum along the intrinsic reaction co-
ordinate. Within the transition-state-theory approximation [12] (no recrossings,

7.7.2. The 3D realisation of chirality labels
The passage to L5 also completes a deliberate deferral from L4.5. At L4.5, the
enantiomers (G, +1) and (G, −1) were declared distinct objects, but the sign σ ∈
{+1, −1} was abstract: the category recognised the two as different yet could not
say which 3D arrangement corresponded to which sign. The Cahn–Ingold–Prelog
convention for identifying σ with (R)/(S) (Remark 7.7) was an external labelling
convention, not derivable within L4.5.
At L5, the Born–Oppenheimer PES V on Ce(G) for a chiral molecule with a con-
figurational stereocentre at carbon has two distinct minima separated by a high
racemisation barrier (the energy cost of inverting the stereocentre, typically much
larger than kBT for tetrahedral carbon). The configuration orbifold Ce(G) itself
remains connected as a topological space, but its low-energy region — the union of
basins of attraction of the local minima at thermally accessible energy — decomposes
into two disjoint basins, one for each enantiomer. The abstract parity E∗∈G∗(G)
from §7.2 acquires a geometric realisation as the involution exchanging the two basins,
physically effectable only by traversing the racemisation barrier. The chirality label
σ(v) ∈{+1, −1} then admits a canonical geometric interpretation: it is the basin
label on Ce(G), recording which low-energy basin the molecule inhabits.
Remark 7.42 (Multi-stereocentre and meso refinement). For molecules with k >
1 stereocentres, σ takes values in {+1, −1}k and the low-energy region of Ce(G)
generically decomposes into up to 2k basins. When Aut(G) contains an element
identifying σ with another assignment σ′ ̸= σ, the corresponding basins are identified
in the orbifold quotient: meso compounds (§7.5, Definition 7.35) thus have fewer than
2k distinct basins, with the basin count given by the Aut(G)-orbit decomposition
of {+1, −1}k. The basin label is canonical; its value space is determined by the
molecule’s symmetry group.
This completes the geometric picture of stereochemistry. At L4.5, σ was a discrete
sign separating two abstract objects; at L5, it is a basin label on the appropriate
configuration orbifold. The L4.5-theorems of §7.5 translate into L5-geometric state-
ments; below, Ce(Gjoint) denotes the configuration orbifold for the joint set of atoms
participating in the reaction (substrate plus reagents), with bond-graph changes
treated as transitions between PES regions in the standard reactive-PES sense:

• Walden inversion (Theorem 7.27) is a reaction path on Ce(Gjoint) connecting
the substrate basin to a product basin of opposite chirality, with the back-side-

• Racemisation (Theorem 7.30) is a path that visits the planar SN1 carbocation
TS — a saddle point lying equidistant (in barrier height) from both enantiomer
basins — and descends with equal probability into either basin, matching the
racemic outcome at L4.5.
• Net retention via double inversion (Theorem 7.34) is a path that crosses the
inversion saddle twice (substrate →bridged intermediate →product), with the
two basin crossings composing to a path that returns to the starting basin’s
chirality class.
The passage from L4.5 to L5 is thus not only the addition of new content (PES, rates,
barriers); it is also the geometric realisation of content already established at L4.5 as
discrete combinatorial data. Chapter 8 develops this realisation in full.

§8. L5: The Geometric Level
§8.1. Forcing the extension: geometry from the kinetic isotope effect
Section 7.7 closed with the forcing pair: CH3Br and CD3Br undergoing the same SN2
reaction are structurally identical at L4.5(P) (isomorphic graphs, identical DPO rule,
no stereocentre) yet react at different speeds, with kH/kD ≈1.3 recorded empirically
as a L3-decoration. This section develops the forcing argument rigorously, identifies
the minimal new structure the rate difference demands, and explains what this
structure fundamentally represents.
The central claim is simple: the rate difference requires knowing where the transition
state is in 3D space — a geometric datum that does not exist anywhere in the tower
below L5. This forces not just a configuration space, but a full Riemannian geometric
structure on that space, together with a real-valued function (the potential energy
surface) on it.
Forcing pair for L5: same symmetry, different activation barrier
The two systems.

Both at 298 K in water [160]; kD is not independently measured here but derived

breaks and the new C–O bond forms, while the three H/D atoms remain attached
throughout. The distinction between rH and rD therefore cannot come from the
bond-graph mechanism — it cannot be seen at L4 or L4.5.
Structural indistinguishability at L4.5. At every level of the tower con-

FH, FS, FP from L1–L3 records small isotope-dependent numerical differences in

empirical numerical attachment to its reaction generator — but nothing in the
structural data of any tower level below L5 can predict, derive, or even motivate
the value 1.3. The factor-of-1.3 slowdown that accompanies every C–H→C–D
substitution at the reactive carbon, in every solvent, at every temperature in
the harmonic-thermal window, points to a structural feature the tower has not
yet named.
The chemist’s intuition supplies the answer immediately. The deuterium atom is
twice as heavy as the protium it replaces, the C–D bond therefore vibrates more
slowly than C–H, and the lower zero-point energy of C–D shifts the activation
barrier upward by a small amount that accumulates over three substitutions

The fourth type of tower extension
The tower has so far exhibited three types of extension (Remark 7.24): decorator
(L0 →L3), structural (L3 →L4), and symmetry enrichment (L4 →L4.5).
The extension L4.5 →L5 introduces a fourth type: geometric decoration.
The new functor FV assigns to each species not a single real number (as at
L1–L3) but a smooth function on a continuous space: an infinite-dimensional
datum.
This is a genuine structural break in the tower. At L1–L3, specifying a reaction
means giving one or two real numbers per generator (e.g. ∆H and k). At L5,
specifying a reaction means giving the full shape of V along the reaction path —
in principle, a function on all of Ce(G). This data can only be obtained by:
• First-principles computation: solving the electronic Schrödinger equation
at each geometry (quantum chemistry: HF, DFT, CCSD(T), etc.), exact
but expensive;
• Experimental measurement: spectroscopy, crystallography, and kinetics
data constrain V at specific geometries; or
• Machine-learning approximation: a Para-level model F Θ

All three approaches converge towards the exact Born–Oppenheimer surface,
with first-principles computation exact in the complete-basis-set, full-CI limit
and approximate in any practical truncation, while measurement and machine-
learning approaches are intrinsically approximate. The categorical framework
records what datum is needed (FV as a functor into OrbMorse) without specifying
how to obtain it.

Why L5 is genuinely new: a narrative.
The tower from L0 to L4.5 is entirely shape-independent. Stoichiometry, thermo-
dynamics, kinetics, bond-graph mechanisms, and stereochemical outcomes are all
properties of how atoms are connected (and with what orientation) — but not of
where they sit in 3D space. An organic chemist can write every mechanism in this
thesis using only topology and signed graphs, without ever drawing a 3D picture.
L5 is where 3D pictures become indispensable. It is the level of the tower at which
the following phenomena first have a mathematical home:
• Steric effects: the activation barrier of a reaction increases when bulky sub-
stituents crowd the transition state — a purely geometric statement about the
saddle-point height on V .
• Ring strain: three- and four-membered rings have higher energy than five- and
six-membered ones because their bond angles deviate from the tetrahedral
optimum — readable from the local geometry of minima on V .
• Conformational analysis: the preference for axial vs. equatorial substituents
in cyclohexane, the barrier to rotation about a C–C bond, the gauche effect —
all are features of the PES landscape.
• Molecular dynamics: the time evolution of nuclear positions under Newton’s
equations mi ¨Ri = −∇RiV on the Riemannian manifold (Ce(G), g) first exists
at L5.
• Transition-state theory: the Eyring rate expression k = (kBT/h) e−Ea/kBT [12]
is computable from (V, g) in the classical-TST approximation (no recrossing,
no tunnelling, harmonic TS partition function), giving the L3 rate constant
FP as a derived quantity rather than a primitive datum. The exact L3–L5
coherence condition (§8.5) upgrades this to the full TST formula with prefactor
and transmission corrections, all L5-computable.
In categorical terms: the step L4.5 →L5 is the first step in the tower where the
new datum is not determined by any finite assignment to generators. V is a smooth
function on a manifold — infinitely many independent values, constrained only
by global symmetry (invariance under SE(3) × Autµ(G); V is a scalar function, so
invariance is the appropriate notion) and the requirement that it be bounded below.

Riemannian orbifolds equipped with a Morse function — and whose morphisms are

(Vfull, RTS, γ) between distinguished minima of V , with γ the IRC through one index-1
saddle of Vfull; general morphisms are finite compositions thereof (see §8.4 for the
precise construction).

§8.2. The configuration orbifold Ce(G)
Standing assumption: the Born–Oppenheimer framework. Throughout
this section, all geometric and energetic content is understood within the Born–
Oppenheimer (BO) approximation [164]: electronic and nuclear motion decouple
at leading order in the small parameter ε = (me/M)1/2, where me is the electron
mass and M a typical nuclear mass (ε ≈10−2 for light molecules). At this order,
electrons relax adiabatically to the ground state for each fixed nuclear geometry R,
and nuclei move on the resulting ground-state potential energy surface V (R). This
222

Kyunghoon Han
Categorification of Chemical Reactions
separation produces two well-defined objects — the configuration orbifold Ce(G)
defined below, and the PES V : Ce(G) →R defined in §8.3 — which together
(with the mass-weighted metric g) constitute the Morse triple (Ce(G), V, g) that the
categorical functor FV : L4.5(P) →OrbMorse assigns to each molecular graph at the
L5 level.
The BO approximation is accurate for the vast majority of ground-state thermal
chemistry: away from degeneracies, the error introduced by the adiabatic decoupling
is of order ε = (me/M)1/2 [165], and exponentially small in 1/ε whenever the ground
and first excited states are separated by a uniform spectral gap [166]. For typical
molecules (ε ≈10−2) in the regime of ordinary ground-state thermal chemistry, BO
corrections are usually smaller than the dominant electronic-structure and solvation
errors of practical computational methods, so bond lengths, vibrational frequencies,
and reaction barriers computed on the ground-state adiabatic surface are reliable to
within chemical accuracy [164, 167]. BO corrections become non-negligible in high-
resolution spectroscopy, light-atom isotope shifts, precision thermochemistry, and
near non-adiabatic regions; the leading mass-dependent corrections — the diagonal
Born–Oppenheimer corrections (DBOC) — lie outside the scope of the leading L5
analysis and enter as higher-order refinements.
Its limitations arise at conical intersections (CIs): geometries where the ground
and first excited states become degenerate so the spectral gap closes, the adiabatic
decoupling breaks down, and nuclear motion couples the two surfaces [154, 168, 169].
That failure is precisely the phenomenon that forces L6 (§8.7); by construction, the
entire L5 framework operates in the open dense subset of Ce(G) where the spectral
gap is positive.
8.2.1. Construction
Having accepted the BO separation, nuclear configurations R = (r1, . . . , rn) ∈R3n
become the fundamental geometric objects. Two configurations represent the same
molecular shape if they differ only by an overall rigid-body motion (translation or
rotation of the entire molecule) or by a permutation of nuclei that are physically
identical. The natural mathematical object encoding this identification is not a
manifold but an orbifold: the quotient of R3n by the combined group of these
equivalences has non-trivial stabilisers at symmetric configurations, and fixed-point
quotients produce orbifold singularities rather than manifold charts. The definition
records this quotient precisely.

strata, each of codimension at least one. Highly symmetric geometries (tetrahedral
methane, octahedral complexes) sit at deep strata with large isotropy subgroups.
This stratification has been studied in the context of rotation-vibration spectroscopy,
where the strata contribute differently to the density of states and selection rules [170].
What Ce(G) is, for the chemist
An organic chemist working with a ball-and-stick model manipulates exactly
the object that Ce(G) formalises.
• A point [R] ∈Ce(G) is a molecular shape: a specific 3D arrangement
of the nuclei, with overall position and orientation removed (rotating
or translating the model does not give a new point), and with identical
atoms treated as interchangeable (numbering the two hydrogens in water
differently does not give a new point).
• The dimension 3n −6 (or 3n −5 for linear configurations, per Observa-
tion 8.4) is the number of independent internal coordinates: bond lengths,
bond angles, and dihedral angles.
• The Riemannian metric g weights each coordinate direction by the
corresponding nuclear mass. This is why C–H vibrational modes have
higher frequencies than C–D modes: the curvature of V is the same, but
the mass factor in ω =

Removing the 6-dimensional SE(3) action gives a smooth stratum of dimension
3n −6 for non-linear configurations (n ≥3 non-collinear), and 3n −5 for linear
configurations (per Remark 8.3, where the SO(2) stabiliser reduces the effective
SE(3)-quotient dimension by one). For the SN2 transition state (n = 7 atoms,
non-linear): dim = 3(7) −6 = 15 internal coordinates.
Remark 8.5 (Tower coherence: why the dimension count matters). The dimension
of Ce(G) is the first continuous geometric datum in the tower. At all lower levels,
the category Lk(P) deals with discrete data: sets of species, real numbers (∆H, ∆S,
kr), or graph morphisms. The object Ce(G) is a continuous orbifold of dimension
3n −6 (generically), and the functor FV assigns to it an infinite-dimensional datum
(a smooth function on this space).

8.2.2. Point groups as isotropy subgroups
Molecular point groups are one of the most practically useful concepts in chemistry.
Every undergraduate learns to classify a molecule by its symmetry elements (rotation
axes Cn, mirror planes σ, improper rotations Sn, and inversion i), assign it to a
point group (C2v, Td, D6h, etc.), and then read off selection rules for spectroscopy
and orbital interactions from the corresponding character table [171, 172]. This is
almost always presented as a classification procedure: examine the molecule, list its
symmetry operations, identify the group.
What is less often made explicit is that these symmetry operations have a dynamical
origin. A symmetry operation of a molecule at geometry R is precisely a rigid-
body motion (rotation or improper rotation) that, combined with a permutation of
identical nuclei, maps R to itself. This is the definition of the permutation-inversion
group introduced by Longuet-Higgins [173] and developed into a comprehensive
spectroscopic framework by Bunker and Jensen [172]; it is the same G∗group
introduced at L4.5 (Definition 7.5).
The categorical statement below identifies
molecular point groups as the isotropy subgroups of the G∗-action on Ce(G). While
the permutation-inversion framework itself is standard, its expression as G∗-isotropy
within a tower extension—and the consequent derivation of point-group classification
from structure already present at L4.5—appears to be original to this framework.

8.2.3. Realisation of the chirality label
At L4.5, each object of L4.5(P) carries an abstract chirality label σ ∈{+1, −1}k
distinguishing the 2k stereoisomers of a molecule with k stereocentres. That label was
introduced axiomatically: the permutation-inversion group G∗contains the parity
E∗as an abstract operation, and σ records on which side of E∗a given stereoisomer
sits at each stereocentre. The question deferred at L4.5 is: what does this discrete
label correspond to geometrically?
The answer is supplied by the topology of the potential energy surface. The idea
has precursors in the literature on molecular topology: Woolley [174] argued that
molecular structure itself is not a purely quantum-mechanical concept but requires
appeal to the PES, and Amann [175] formalised chirality as a superselection rule
arising from the topology of the molecular state space. The following proposition
makes the relevant topological invariant explicit as the connected-component structure
of the accessible region of Ce(G). The single-stereocentre case is stated below for
clarity, with the general case deferred to a remark.

Remark 8.11 (Pyramidal-inversion energetics). For a tetrahedral carbon stereocentre
bonded to four distinct substituents, Einv is very large: direct pyramidal inversion
requires an essentially planar tetracoordinate carbon—four substituents coplanar
with the central atom, retaining all four bonds—which is geometrically strained and
costs hundreds of kJ/mol. In practice, stereocentre interconversion of such centres
occurs only via bond-breaking pathways (e.g., SN1 through a planar carbocation, or
base-catalysed enolisation), which are not single-surface processes on the starting
substrate’s V . Under normal chemical conditions (T ≈300 K, accessible thermal
energies ≲kBT ≈2.5 kJ/mol above the ground state), the accessible region Ce
acc(G)

invariant of the molecular state.
The contrast with nitrogen stereocentres (e.g., NH3, amines) is instructive: nitrogen
inversion through a planar tricoordinate TS has a barrier of only ∼24 kJ/mol,
well within thermal access, so nitrogen stereocentres are typically not resolvable as
distinct enantiomers under standard conditions. This difference in barrier heights
is itself an L5 datum: the same abstract group-theoretic structure at L4.5 yields
different topological consequences depending on the PES landscape, which only L5
sees.

The chirality bridge between L4.5 and L5
Proposition 8.8 closes the explanatory gap opened at L4.5: the abstract label
σ ∈{+1, −1} was promised a geometric realisation, and here it is.
The key conceptual point is that Ce(G) itself is topologically trivial (path-
connected): the two stereoisomers are not distinguished by any topological
property of configuration space alone. What distinguishes them is the energetic
structure of V —specifically, the existence of a large inversion barrier that
partitions the accessible region into two components. Chirality is therefore not
a topological invariant of the molecular graph (an L4 or L4.5 statement) but a
topological invariant of the accessible PES (an L5 statement). The L4.5 label σ
is the shadow of this PES topology projected back onto the graph level.
§8.3. The potential energy surface (PES), Hilbert bundle, and Born–
Oppenheimer section
The configuration orbifold Ce(G) constructed in §8.2 is the geometric stage on which
the L5 functor FV operates. This section adds four layers of structure to that stage,
each derived from the previous:
(i) The electronic Hilbert bundle π : Hel →Ce(G) (§8.3.1): packages the family of
electronic Hamiltonians { ˆHel(R)}R∈Ce(G) into a single geometric object. The
bundle is trivially trivial as a Hilbert bundle (all fibers are isomorphic), but
the Hamiltonian family ˆHel : Ce(G) →SA(Hel) is non-trivial and carries all
the electronic structure information.
(ii) The BO ground-state section σ0 : Ce(G) →Hel and the PES V = E0 + Vnn :
Ce(G) →R (§8.3.2): the Layer 1 and Layer 2 data that define the L5 functor
FV . The PES is the infinite-dimensional datum that replaces the finitely many
reals (∆H, kr) of lower levels.
(iii) The Morse structure of V (§8.3.3): minima, index-1 saddle points, and the
intrinsic reaction coordinate (IRC) — the chemically observable consequences
of the PES landscape, derived from the metric g and function V already
introduced.
(iv) The Berry connection A0 on the ground-state line bundle L0 ≤Hel (§8.3.4):
the geometric phase structure of σ0.
At L5, on the simply-connected CI-
free open subsets where the framework operates, A0 can be gauged to zero
(Proposition 8.21); its obstruction to global vanishing around loops encircling
conical intersections is the datum that forces L6.

8.3.1. The electronic Hilbert bundle
At each level Lk(P) for k ≤4.5, the objects of the tower are molecular graphs (G, σ)
with various discrete decorations (∆H, kr, DPO mechanisms, chirality labels), but
no information about where atoms sit in 3D space. The BO approximation (§8.2,
standing assumption) assigns to each nuclear geometry R ∈Ce(G) a well-posed
quantum-mechanical eigenvalue problem: find the ground state of the electronic
Hamiltonian ˆHel(R). The electronic Hilbert bundle is the geometric object that
packages this family of eigenvalue problems into a single structure over Ce(G).
This construction has a multi-layered history in the molecular and mathematical-
physics literature. Mead and Truhlar [168] introduced the molecular vector potential
in the BO approximation, recognising that the R-dependence of the electronic
wavefunction produces an effective gauge field entering the nuclear Hamiltonian. The
fiber-bundle interpretation of this geometric phase — with the Berry connection
identified as a U(1) connection on a line bundle over parameter space — was developed
by Simon [176] following Berry [177]. The rigorous adiabatic-theoretic foundation,
justifying the decomposition of Hel into adiabatic sub-bundles and controlling the
errors, was established by Teufel and Panati–Spohn–Teufel [178, 179]. All of this
machinery is what L5 inherits.

8.3.2. The Born–Oppenheimer section and PES
The Hilbert bundle provides the arena; the BO section selects the physically relevant
state in each fiber. At each geometry R, the electronic Hamiltonian ˆHel(R) has an
isolated ground-state eigenvalue E0(R) at the bottom of its spectrum (existence of
bound states for neutral molecules is a consequence of Zhislin’s theorem [181] and is
standard for chemically relevant geometries), with σ0(R) the corresponding unique
(up to phase) normalised eigenstate. Varying R smoothly while tracking this ground
state defines the BO section.
Definition 8.14 (BO section and potential energy surface). The Born–Oppenheimer
(BO) ground-state section is the map
σ0 : Ce(G) −→Hel,
σ0(R) ∈Hel(R),
assigning to each geometry R the normalised ground-state electronic wavefunction:
ˆHel(R) σ0(R) = E0(R) σ0(R),
∥σ0(R)∥= 1,
where E0(R) is the lowest eigenvalue.
The Born–Oppenheimer potential energy surface (PES) is
V : Ce(G) −→R,
V (R) = E0(R) + Vnn(R),
where E0(R) = ⟨σ0(R)| ˆHel(R)|σ0(R)⟩is the ground-state eigenvalue of the electronic
Hamiltonian (matching the notation in the BO section above), and
Vnn(R) =

is the nuclear–nuclear Coulomb repulsion. Both terms are needed: Vnn supplies
the short-range nuclear repulsion that prevents atom coalescence, and without it V
would have wrong asymptotics.
Remark 8.15 (Physical meaning of σ0 and V ). Computationally, V (R) is the quantity
returned by a single quantum-chemistry calculation at geometry R: a Hartree–
Fock, DFT, or coupled-cluster calculation solves for the ground-state electronic
wavefunction σ0(R) with nuclei clamped at R, and returns the total energy E0(R) +
Vnn(R), with the nuclear–nuclear repulsion typically added automatically by the
code [167]. Mapping out V over a grid of geometries is what quantum chemists mean
by “computing the potential energy surface.”
In the tower language: the section σ0 is the first object in the tower that is a section
of a bundle over a continuous space, rather than a map between discrete categories.
The PES functor FV : L4.5(P) →OrbMorse assigns the triple (Ce(G), V, g) to each
molecular graph G, and the entire §8.3.3–§8.3.4 derives from (σ0, V, g).

Layer 1 and Layer 2 for FV at L5
Layer 1: any smooth function V : Ce(G) →R on the configuration orbifold.
There is no “one real per generator” universal property: V requires specifying
its value at every point of the (3n −6)-dimensional orbifold Ce(G), an infinite-
dimensional datum. Layer 1 asserts that such a function must exist and be
smooth on the non-degenerate (CI-free) subset of Ce(G).
Layer 2: two additional conditions tying V to the physics of ˆHel.
(a) BO derivation: V (R) = ⟨σ0(R)| ˆHel(R)|σ0(R)⟩+Vnn(R). The PES is not
an arbitrary smooth function but the sum of the ground-state electronic
eigenvalue and the nuclear–nuclear Coulomb repulsion.
(b) Global existence of σ0: the ground state is non-degenerate on the
relevant open subset of Ce(G), so σ0 is a smooth section of Hel →Ce(G)
over that subset.
Condition (b) is the Born–Oppenheimer approximation proper. It fails at conical
intersections where E0(R) = E1(R) (ground and first excited states become
degenerate): σ0 is undefined at such geometries, and the global section fails to
exist. That failure forces L6 (§8.7).
Using V in the tower. Layer 2(a) makes V computable from first principles.
Layer 2(b) ensures the ground-state line bundle L0 := span{σ0(R)}R is globally
trivial (§8.3.4), which in turn means the Berry connection A0 vanishes identically
(Proposition 8.21). Together, conditions (a)–(b) also underpin the TST coherence
condition (§8.5): the rate constant kr at L3 is derived from the saddle-point
value of V at L5.
8.3.3. Critical points of V and the IRC
With V and g in hand, a central task of computational chemistry becomes precise:
navigate the landscape of V to identify stable geometries, reaction pathways, and
barriers. The mathematical language for this navigation is Morse theory — the study
of smooth functions via their critical points and gradient flows.
In practice:
• Geometry optimisation is gradient descent on (V, g) to find local minima —
the stable molecular structures. Every structure deposited in the Cambridge
Structural Database or the NIST WebBook corresponds to a minimum of V .
• Transition-state (TS) search is finding index-1 saddle points — configurations
where the energy is stationary but has one direction of descent (the reaction
mode) and all other directions of ascent. Methods such as QST2/QST3 and
eigenvector-following locate these points by following the negative Hessian
eigenvector uphill.
• IRC calculation follows the gradient flow from the TS downhill (in the mass-
weighted metric g) to identify the reactant and product connected to that TS.
The IRC in mass-weighted coordinates was formalised by Fukui [162] and given
its modern treatment by Miller, Handy and Adams [163].
In categorical terms, this entire computational toolkit is the exploration of the Morse
structure of FV : the functor FV : L4.5(P) →OrbMorse assigns to each molecular

on (V, g) that identifies the reactant and product basins connected to a given TS,
not a dynamical path. Genuinely dynamical treatments — trajectory ensembles,
instanton tunneling, semiclassical quantisation — enter at L7.
8.3.4. The Berry connection
The BO section σ0(R) is a wavefunction, hence defined only up to an overall complex
phase eiϕ at each geometry. The question of how this phase choice changes as the
nuclei traverse a closed loop γ in Ce(G) is not a gauge artefact: the holonomy of
the phase (the total accumulated phase around γ) is a gauge-invariant observable.
This holonomy is the geometric phase or Berry phase [177, 176], identified in the
molecular context by Mead and Truhlar [168].
The physical significance is direct: a nuclear wavepacket that traverses a loop in Ce(G)
returns to its starting point with a modified electronic phase. If this phase is −1 (a sign
change of the electronic wavefunction), the nuclear wavepacket acquires destructive
interference with itself, producing observable spectroscopic consequences [154]. This
is the molecular Aharonov–Bohm effect. In the tower language:
• At L5 (Layer 2 condition: no conical intersections), the Berry phase is trivial
for all loops (Proposition 8.21 below).
• At L6, conical intersections are the sources of non-trivial Berry holonomy: a
loop encircling exactly one CI acquires phase −1. This non-trivial holonomy is
precisely the datum that L5 cannot encode and L6 must introduce.
The Berry connection is therefore the bridge datum between L5 and L6 in the tower.

suffices.

Remark 8.22 (Simple connectivity of Ce(G) and the L5 vs. L6 boundary). The
real-gauge argument of Proposition 8.21 works locally on any simply-connected open
subset of Ce(G), and extends globally provided Ce(G) itself is simply connected.
When Ce(G) has non-trivial topology — in particular, when conical intersections
form a codimension-2 submanifold XCI ⊂Ce(G) (codimension 2 because CIs of a
real-symmetric Hamiltonian satisfy two real conditions on the 2 × 2 effective block)
— the complement Ce(G) \ XCI has non-trivial π1 (loops encircling XCI cannot be
contracted), and the global real-gauge extension can fail around such loops. The
standard example is the H3 system, where the D3h conical intersection creates a
loop with Z2 holonomy (Berry phase π): the ground-state wavefunction changes
sign under a traversal of this loop [154, 168]. That failure is precisely the L5 →L6
transition: L5 operates on simply-connected, CI-free regions where all holonomies
are trivial; L6 admits CI-induced holonomies in coker(φ6).
The spinless assumption in the proposition is likewise standard in BO theory for
ground-state thermal chemistry. For electrons with spin-orbit coupling, time-reversal
is T 2 = −1 (Kramers) and the analysis changes: additional Z2 structure enters the
Berry connection. These effects become relevant at L6 and beyond and are not
treated here.
Remark 8.23 (What the proposition establishes in the tower). Proposition 8.21 has
three distinct consequences for the tower, each at a different level of abstraction.
Physical consequence. The electronic wavefunction accumulates no geometric
phase as the nuclei traverse any loop in Ce(G). Nuclear dynamics on the ground-
state BO surface is self-consistent: the electronic subsystem does not distinguish
one traversal of a nuclear loop from another, and there is no quantum interference
between paths with different winding histories. This is the regime of adiabatic thermal
chemistry — the regime in which all of organic chemistry, most of thermodynamics,
and most of kinetics operates.
Categorical consequence. On the simply-connected CI-free open subsets where the
L5 framework operates, the functor FV : L4.5(P) →OrbMorse captures the relevant
L5 structure through the PES triple (Ce(G), V, g) alone: the ground-state line bundle
L0 is trivial in a real gauge and the Berry connection vanishes (Proposition 8.21), so
no additional topological data from the electronic Hilbert bundle is needed in this
regime. The non-trivial sign holonomy w1(L0) ∈H1(·, Z/2) that arises around loops

§8.4. Definition of L5(P)
The two preceding sections established the raw materials: the configuration orbifold
Ce(G) (§8.2) and the four-layer structure of (V, g, σ0, A0) (§8.3). This section assem-
bles them into the categorical objects that define L5(P), proves that these objects
form a well-defined category, and situates L5(P) coherently in the tower.
The plan is a two-step construction:
(I) Build the target category OrbMorse (§8.4.1): the symmetric monoidal category
that receives the geometric decoration.
(II) Construct the geometric functor FV : L4.5(P) →OrbMorse (§8.4.2), which
assigns to each molecular graph the Morse triple of its configuration space,
PES, and mass-weighted metric, and to each DPO derivation its intrinsic
reaction coordinate.
Together these yield L5(P) := (L4.5(P), FV ) (§8.4.3), a G∗-equivariant SMC decorated
by a lax monoidal functor to OrbMorse.
The central coherence diagram that animates the section is the following, whose
commutativity (up to the TST coherence condition) is proved in §8.5:

8.4.1. The target category OrbMorse
The geometric decoration at L5 targets a category whose objects are the configuration
orbifolds of molecules equipped with a PES and a metric. This category must be
constructed carefully: its morphism structure must capture the physical notion of a
reaction as a gradient-flow path from a reactant minimum to a product minimum
through a transition state, and its monoidal product must encode the combination
of non-interacting molecular systems.
Classical Morse theory provides the necessary ingredient. Initiated by Morse [182], it
assigns to each smooth function V : M →R a critical-point structure (non-degenerate
critical points with integer indices) from which global topological properties of M
can be recovered. In our setting M = Ce(G) is not a manifold but an orbifold — a
topological space locally modelled on Rk/Γ for finite groups Γ [183]. The relevant
Morse theory for orbifolds, developed for our purposes below, is a direct extension:
one works on the smooth stratum (where Ce(G) is a manifold) and tracks the orbifold
strata as additional structure.
Two key structural features determine the correct morphism definition. First, chemi-
cal reactions are atom-conserving: the total multiset of nuclei is unchanged between
reactants and products (no nuclear transmutation under ordinary chemical condi-
tions). For an elementary reaction from reactant system G to product system H with
the same atom set, the appropriate domain for the intrinsic reaction coordinate is the
joint configuration orbifold Ce(G⊔H) introduced in §8.3.3: the configuration orbifold
of the combined reactive complex, large enough to contain both reactant and product
geometries as local minima and the transition state between them as a saddle point.
Second, the full interacting PES Vfull on this joint orbifold is a single smooth function
— not two separate PESs glued at the TS. An elementary morphism in OrbMorse is
therefore a triple (Vfull, RTS, γ) where the gradient flow γ on Vfull connects a reactant
minimum (encoding the source object) to a product minimum (encoding the target
object) through the distinguished saddle point RTS. General morphisms of OrbMorse,
encoding multi-step mechanisms, are compositions of elementary morphisms in the
free-category sense made precise in Definition 8.24 below.
Definition 8.24 (The category OrbMorse). The symmetric monoidal category
OrbMorse is defined as follows.
Objects. Triples (O, V, g) where:
• O is a smooth Riemannian orbifold (locally modelled on Rk/Γ for finite groups
Γ [183]);
• V : O →R is a smooth function, Morse on the open subset of chemically
accessible, CI-free, non-coalescence geometries (all critical points in that region
are non-degenerate);
• g is the Riemannian metric on O.
A distinguished minimum Rmin(O) ∈O marks the reference geometry (the equilib-
rium structure).
Elementary morphisms (geometric channels). For objects (Ce(G), VG, gG) and
(Ce(H), VH, gH) with G and H sharing an underlying atom multiset, an elementary

The interaction term: the ion-dipole complex in SN2
The interaction term Vint is not a mathematical abstraction but a physical
observable with direct chemical consequences.
The SN2 PES. For the reaction CH3Cl + OH−→CH3OH + Cl−, the non-
interacting Layer 1 approximation gives the PES as the sum of the isolated
reactant PESs: a flat surface with a single minimum at the CH3Cl equilibrium
geometry and no barrier. The Layer 1 PES predicts no reaction pathway, no
TS, and no product formation.
The full Layer 2 PES adds Vint, which includes the long-range ion-dipole Coulomb
attraction between OH−and CH3Cl. This attraction creates:
(i) An ion-dipole complex [CH3Cl · · · OH−]: a shallow well (≈−40 kJ/mol
below separated reactants) appearing at intermediate C· · · O distance
≈3.5 Å. This minimum is entirely due to Vint and is invisible at Layer 1.
(ii) The transition state [HO · · · CH3 · · · Cl]‡ at shorter C· · · O and C· · · Cl
distances: the saddle point of the full Layer 2 surface.
(iii) An analogous product complex [CH3OH · · · Cl−] on the exit channel.
The full Layer 2 PES profile is a characteristic double-well potential with two
intermediate complexes flanking the central TS — a well-established feature of
gas-phase SN2 reactions whose shape is entirely due to Vint [167].

Remark 8.32 (What computational methods provide FV , and their position in
OrbMorse). Unlike FH, FS, and FP, the functor FV cannot be specified by a fi-

it is approximated by one of four progressively coarser methods, each occupying a
well-defined position relative to OrbMorse.
(i) Exact BO PES (full CI): the ground-state PES defined by V (R) = E0(R) +
Vnn(R), where E0 is the lowest eigenvalue of the exact electronic Hamiltonian
and Vnn is the nuclear–nuclear Coulomb repulsion. This is the Layer 2 datum.
For fixed lift choices (electronic-structure theory, conformer, TS, IRC branch)
it is well-defined (Theorem 8.33 below), but computationally inaccessible for
all but the smallest systems. It defines the exact object of OrbMorse that FV
targets.
(ii) Coupled-cluster CCSD(T): an approximation ˜V CC ≈V that truncates the
cluster expansion at doubles with perturbative triples [167]. This is the “gold
standard” of computational chemistry, recovering > 99.9% of the correlation
energy for most closed-shell molecules. Its critical-point structure (minima,
saddle points) agrees with the exact PES to within the triples error.
In
OrbMorse: ˜V CC defines an approximate Morse triple that is a perturbation of
the exact Layer 2 object; the Morse structure (and hence the IRC and Ea) is
preserved up to the truncation error.
(iii) Density functional theory (DFT): ˜V DFT = EKohn-Sham, the energy func-
tional of an auxiliary non-interacting system with an approximate exchange-
correlation functional [167]. DFT is computationally efficient and typically
accurate for equilibrium geometries and moderate barriers; it can fail for
dispersion-dominated interactions (e.g. van der Waals complexes) and for open-
shell transition metals. In OrbMorse: ˜V DFT is an approximate object in which
the Morse structure may differ qualitatively from the exact PES when the
exchange-correlation functional is poor near saddle points.
(iv) Classical force fields (GAFF [184], FF19SB [185], CHARMM [186],
OPLS [187, 188]): an analytic approximation ˜V FF = P

8.4.3. Definition and structure of L5(P)
With OrbMorse established as a strict SMC (Proposition 8.25) and FV defined as
a lax monoidal functor into it (Definition 8.29), the geometric level is now fully
specified. The construction is the pair (L4.5(P), FV ): the G∗-equivariant SMC from
L4.5 together with its geometric decoration. Existence of FV satisfying the Layer 2
conditions is established below, with explicit acknowledgement of the ambiguities
(conformer choice, TS choice, IRC branch, theory level) inherent to the construction.
Theorem 8.33 (Existence of FV satisfying Layer 2). For any Petri net P with species
set S, given consistent choices of (i) a level of electronic-structure theory defining
ˆHel, (ii) a reference conformer at each molecular graph (G, σ), (iii) a transition-state
geometry for each DPO derivation, and (iv) a choice of IRC branch from each TS,
there exists a lax monoidal functor
FV : L4.5(P) −→OrbMorse
satisfying the Layer 2 conditions of Definition 8.14: (a) V (R) = E0(R) + Vnn(R)
(BO derivation plus nuclear–nuclear repulsion), and (b) σ0 is a smooth section of
Hel on the relevant CI-free open subset of Ce(G, σ).
The data are unique up to:
• the global Z2 sign ambiguity in the real gauge of σ0 (Proposition 8.21); this
affects σ0 as a sign but not V , g, or the IRC;
• the chosen IRC branch from each TS (two steepest-descent half-curves);
• reparametrisation of each IRC.
The choices (i)–(iv) are not part of the functorial data; they constitute a lift of
L4.5(P) to L5(P) in the sense of Definition 8.35. Different choices give different
functors FV , each satisfying (a)–(b); the categorical content of L5(P) is the decorated
category (L4.5(P), FV ) for a fixed such lift.
Proof. Existence on objects. Fix (G, σ) ∈L4.5(P) with n atoms and nuclear
charges {Zk}.
The electronic Hamiltonian ˆHel(R) is a well-defined self-adjoint
operator on Hel(R) for each R in the non-coalescence subset of Ce(G, σ) (the
Coulomb singularities are Kato-bounded by the kinetic energy with relative bound
zero, so the Kato–Rellich theorem gives self-adjointness on the common Sobolev-type
domain [180]). The spectrum is bounded below by the Lieb–Thirring inequality
(stability of matter for Coulomb systems) [193], and the existence of bound states —
in particular an isolated ground-state eigenvalue E0(R) at the bottom of the spectrum
— follows from Zhislin’s theorem [181] for neutral molecules (and standard extensions
for molecular ions under the usual hypotheses).

points) is not guaranteed by the BO construction but holds for all chemically relevant
molecular systems at all chemically relevant geometries. Non-Morse critical points
do occur in molecular physics — notably at catastrophe geometries where two critical
points merge (fold catastrophe) or a saddle degenerates (cusp catastrophe), and
at conical intersections themselves — but these are non-generic under parameter
variation and belong to higher tower levels (L6 for CIs, L7 for anharmonic and
tunneling phenomena that probe non-Morse regions). For all critical points on the
accessible region Ce

Reading the diagram: the decorator chain L0 →L3 adds one scalar functor
per step (all strict monoidal). The structural extension L3 →L4 replaces the
underlying category with a free SMC on DPO spans. The symmetry enrichment

L4), symmetry enrichment (L4 →L4.5), and geometric decoration (L4.5 →L5,
lax).
§8.5. Transition-state theory and L3–L5 inter-level coherence
Eyring’s transition-state theory (TST) [12, 22, 194] is the central bridge between
kinetics and molecular geometry. Its modern canonical form [195, 196, 197] expresses
the rate constant of an elementary reaction as a thermal flux through a dividing
surface on the Born–Oppenheimer PES:

Three inter-level coherence conditions in the tower
The tower contains three conditions linking data at non-adjacent levels. Each
condition is a statement that a lower-level datum (at level j) is constrained by
higher-level data (at level k > j), not that the lower datum is “derivable from”
the lower level.

All three conditions reside at L5 or below: the constrained lower-level data are

to ZPE or thermal energy dominate (floppy molecules, low-frequency torsions,

computable corrections for essentially all reactions where the BO approximation
itself holds. A genuine L7 signal — a residual not explained by L5 semiclassics
— is addressed in §8.7.

Remark 8.41 (Tower attribution of tunneling: the L5/L7 boundary is sharper than
textbook pedagogy suggests). Proposition 8.40 establishes the secondary KIE as an
L5 theorem. For primary KIEs — including the anomalously large values observed
in enzymatic hydrogen-transfer reactions — the tower attribution requires care:
textbook treatments identify “quantum tunneling” with “nuclear wavefunctions on
the BO surface” and conclude L7 is needed. This identification is incorrect. The
L5/L7 boundary is drawn by the dimensionality of the nuclear wavefunction required,
not by the mere presence of quantum effects:
The tower criterion. L5 admits quantum information at fixed geometry or along
low-dimensional reaction paths: harmonic ZPEs (Hessian spectra at critical points),
1-D anharmonic proton vibrational states in PES slices (vibrationally adiabatic
potential cuts), semiclassical tunneling actions along instantons or corner-cutting
paths, and ring-polymer imaginary-time quantum statistics.
L7 is reserved for
the multidimensional nuclear wavefunction on the full nuclear configuration space:
states on the full nuclear Hilbert space Hnuc, not restrictions to 1-D slices or frozen
environments.

Semiclassical tunneling is L5. All standard tunneling corrections — Wigner,
Bell, Eckart, small-curvature tunneling (SCT), large-curvature tunneling (LCT),
microcanonical optimised multidimensional tunneling (µOMT) [195, 198] — require
only the PES, Hessians along the MEP, and (for LCT) off-MEP PES data for corner-
cutting paths. No nuclear wavefunction is constructed. Ring-polymer instanton
theory (RPI) [202] computes the dominant tunneling trajectory as an imaginary-time
classical orbit on the inverted PES — a stationary-phase saddle of the path integral
— requiring only the PES. Perturbative corrections to RPI [203] achieve few-percent
agreement with exact nuclear QM on benchmark systems using only PES and its
derivatives.
Enzymatic KIEs of 20–700 are L5. Soybean lipoxygenase wild type shows
kH/kD ≈80 at 25 ◦C [204]; the L546A/L754A double mutant reaches kH/kD ≈540–
700 [205], several orders of magnitude above the 298 K semiclassical ZPE ceiling
of ∼7–9. These values are quantitatively reproduced by vibronically nonadiabatic
proton-coupled electron transfer (PCET) models [206, 207] and by ensemble-averaged
variational TST with µOMT tunneling corrections (EA-VTST/µOMT, [208]). Both
frameworks construct the rate from 1-D proton vibrational wavefunctions in frozen
active-site geometries plus semiclassical WKB actions along reaction-path tunneling
routes. No multidimensional nuclear wavefunction is constructed. By the tower
criterion above these calculations are L5: they use (FV , g) plus low-dimensional
quantum refinements that remain “shadowed” by the PES.
What forces L7. Genuine L7 phenomena are those requiring the multidimensional
nuclear wavefunction on the full nuclear configuration space as a primary object.
These include:
• MCTDH wavepacket propagation for reactive scattering (full nuclear Schrödinger
equation on the BO surface);
• Colbert–Miller DVR for full quantum reaction rates on small systems;
• exact nuclear diagonalisation for tunneling splittings in highly symmetric
systems, below the instanton-validity crossover temperature where perturbative
RPI fails to converge;
• ortho/para nuclear-spin statistics, which requires the full nuclear wavefunction
to enforce Bose/Fermi symmetry under the G∗-action of L4.5 (the symmetry
group exists at L4.5; its consequences for the total nuclear-spin-symmetrised
wavefunction live at L7);
• the superselection-sector structure of molecular identity (see Chapter 10).
In the tower, L7 is forced by phenomena that cannot be reduced to L5 data plus
semiclassical corrections — not merely by the presence of large KIE values or strong
quantum behaviour. The forcing argument for L5 ⇒L7 (§8.7) is grounded in such
phenomena.

The KIE provides a window into the tower structure, but the L5/L7 boundary
lies much deeper than the “kH/kD > 10 implies tunneling implies L7” narrative

What this means for the forcing argument. The forcing pair for L4.5 ⇒L5 is
the mundane secondary KIE kH/kD ≈1.3, which requires only the metric g and

8.5.3. Cross-level consistency: FH and FV
The TST coherence condition links FP (L3) to FV (L5) via (19). An analogous
cross-level consistency links FH (L1) to FV (L5): the standard enthalpy of a reaction,
computed thermochemically from tabulated formation enthalpies at L1, agrees with
the electronic-energy drop computed from the BO PES at L5, up to well-understood
corrections. Two logically distinct statements must be kept separate.
• Hess’s law [53]: the enthalpy functor FH : L1(P) →(R, +) respects reaction
composition, FH(r2 ◦r1) = FH(r2)+FH(r1). This is L1-functoriality, established
in Chapter 3 from the state-function character of enthalpy (H = U + pV ); it is
automatically independent of L5 data (BO, RRHO, geometry) because it lives
four levels below.
• BO/RRHO decomposition of FH: a representation theorem expressing the
single real number FH(r) in terms of L5 data — the PES, its Hessians, and
thermal partition functions. This presupposes the BO approximation and the
rigid-rotor harmonic-oscillator (RRHO) factorisation of the molecular partition
function.

§8.7. What L5 cannot express: forcing of L6
The entire L5 framework rests on Layer 2(b) of §8.3: the ground-state section σ0 is a
smooth section of Hel on the relevant CI-free open subset of Ce(G), equivalently, no
266

Kyunghoon Han
