conical intersection (CI) between V0 and V1 lies in the chemically accessible region
traversed by the IRC and its low-energy basins. Within this restriction L5 completely
describes ground-state thermal chemistry via the Morse triple (Ce(G), V0, g). But
Layer 2(b) is not permanent.
It fails for a large class of chemically important
processes, and the failure is not a matter of approximation quality: it is a topological
obstruction invisible to V0.
The key point is that L5 records only the ground-state PES function V0, not the
electronic bundle that fibres over it. A CI is a geometric feature of Ce(G) where
V0(R) = V1(R). At the CI itself the eigenvalue V0 is continuous but not smooth
(Wigner–von Neumann normal form: a conical singularity with V0 ∼VCI −|x| in
the two-dimensional branching plane). On the complement Ce(G) \ XCI where the
eigenvalues are isolated, V0 is smooth and the L5 datum cannot detect that the CI
exists nearby: only the topology of the complement, encoded in the ground-state line
bundle L0 (or equivalently, in its real sub-bundle LR
0 under time-reversal symmetry),
distinguishes systems with and without the CI.
What changes is the topology of the bundles over the punctured base Ce(G) \ XCI.
Both L0 (the complex ground-state line bundle) and its real sub-bundle LR
0 generated
by the real-gauge section ˜σ0 (Proposition 8.21) are well-defined on this complement,
and both carry topological invariants:
c1(L0) ∈H2(Ce(G) \ XCI, Z),
w1(LR
0 ) ∈H1(Ce(G) \ XCI, Z/2).
Which of these is the informative invariant is set by the codimension of XCI in Ce(G):
• For a real-symmetric ˆHel (spinless non-relativistic electrons with time-reversal-
invariant Coulomb interactions), degeneracies of the 2×2 effective block require
two real conditions to vanish (trace shift and off-diagonal coupling), so XCI
has codimension 2. A small loop S1 encircling XCI is a 1-cycle, and the natural
invariant of the bundle around it lives in H1(·, Z/2). This is w1(LR
0 ), and it
is non-trivial: a sign holonomy of −1 around the loop witnesses the Longuet–
Higgins effect [154, 168, 177]. The Chern class c1(L0) around the same loop is
automatically zero — not because L0 is globally trivial, but because the loop
bounds no canonical 2-chain in the punctured complement, so the H2-pairing
does not detect codimension-2 obstructions.
• For a complex Hermitian
ˆHel without time-reversal symmetry (e.g. in an
external magnetic field or with spin-orbit coupling), degeneracies require three
real conditions and XCI has codimension 3. A small sphere S2 around an
isolated CI point is a 2-cycle, and c1(L0) measured by
R
S2 Ω0/2π ∈Z becomes
the Berry-monopole charge.
For the thermal molecular chemistry of L6 — real-symmetric Hamiltonian, codimension-
2 CI seams — the relevant invariant is therefore w1(LR
0 ), and the molecular Aharonov–
Bohm phenomenon is the Z2 sign holonomy. c1 remains a well-defined invariant of
L0 in its own right; it just measures a different (codimension-3) obstruction that is
not generically present without breaking time-reversal symmetry.
L5 sees σ0 only as a function (the PES); L6 sees it as a section of a bundle with
non-trivial Z2-holonomy. The step from function to bundle section — and from
numerical to topological invariant — is the deepest geometric step in the tower.

those whose region does not (e.g. ground-state SN2 at thermal conditions).

The extension L5 →L6 differs in character from every previous extension in the tower.
All lower extensions add structure on the configuration orbifold — a PES function,
a metric, a Morse structure, DPO rules, G∗-equivariance. The L5 →L6 extension
adds structure over Ce(G): the topology of the Hilbert bundle Hel →Ce(G) whose
fibres carry the electronic wavefunctions.

spin-orbit coupling), c1 becomes informative and the codimension-3 Berry-monopole
regime applies. L6 accommodates both regimes; the molecular Aharonov–Bohm
forcing pair lives in the w1 regime.

§9. L6: The Electronic Structure Level
§9.1. Forcing the extension: half-integer pseudorotation quanta in Na3
The vibrational spectrum of Na3 in its 22E′ excited electronic state, measured by
Delacrétaz, Grant, Whetten, Wöste, and Zwanziger [215], is the canonical molecular
example of fractional pseudorotational quantisation. In the ideal free-pseudorotor
model, an ordinary single-valued scalar nuclear wavefunction on the pseudorotation
circle has integer angular quantum numbers j = 0, ±1, ±2, . . .. The Jahn–Teller
Berry sign changes the boundary condition to ψ(ϕ + 2π) = −ψ(ϕ), so the allowed
quantum numbers become j = ±1/2, ±3/2, ±5/2, . . .. The lowest pseudorotational
level lies at ℏ2/(8Ips) above the trough minimum in this limit, with no j = 0 level in
the topological sector.1
This observation forces the passage from the scalar geometric level L5 to the electronic-
bundle level L6. The L5 projection retains only the lower adiabatic surface V−and
the mass-weighted metric g; if the associated nuclear wavefunction is treated as an
ordinary single-valued function on the pseudorotation circle, this scalar description
predicts the integer sector. The physical Jahn–Teller problem instead carries a real
ground-state eigenline
LR
0 →Ce(G) \ ΣCI
whose first Stiefel–Whitney class
w1(LR
0 ) ∈H1(Ce(G) \ ΣCI, Z/2)
evaluates non-trivially on a meridian loop linking the CI seam [218]. This non-trivial
w1 is the topological datum that imposes the antiperiodic boundary condition and
shifts the allowed quantum numbers by one half. The robust discriminator is not
a list of fitted level positions but the boundary condition itself: periodic versus
antiperiodic, an obstruction class in Z/2 that no scalar correction to V−can supply.
The same mathematical invariant also appears in real Bloch-bundle topology [218]:
in systems with a real structure, w1 is the real-bundle form of a quantised Berry
phase. The molecular and band-theoretic settings have different base spaces and
physical interpretations, but the underlying real-line-bundle obstruction is the same.
All three Na atoms are equivalent in Autµ(G) = S3, so the discrimination involves no
isotope labelling and happens within the bound-state spectrum of a single chemical
species. Section 8.7 established the abstract form of this forcing argument; the
remainder of the chapter develops the L6 structure required to express, prove, and
extend it. Section 9.1.1 develops the Mexican-hat Jahn–Teller structure of Na3.
Section 9.2 constructs the rank-2 adiabatic sub-bundle and proves the codimension-2
structure of the CI seam. Section 9.3 constructs the Berry connection and proves
the holonomy formula exp(i

9.1.1. Na3 and the Mexican-hat Jahn–Teller conical intersection
Sodium trimer Na3 has molecular graph G = (Na1, Na2, Na3) with three equivalent
Z = 11 nuclei (each contributing one 3s valence electron) and configuration orbifold
Ce(G) of dimension 3(3) −6 = 3. Na–Na equilibrium distance is ∼3.2 Å. The
ground state X2B2 is Jahn–Teller distorted from D3h equilateral into an obtuse-
isoceles C2v structure, with three equivalent C2v geometries related by cyclic apex
permutation. Of interest here is the electronically excited 22E′ state, accessed by
near-UV absorption.
D3h degeneracy. At equilateral D3h the 22E′ state belongs to the two-dimensional
E′ irreducible representation: two electronic states are degenerate at every D3h
geometry, so the 22E′ state is a double point. Distortion off equilateral lifts the
degeneracy linearly — the Jahn–Teller effect. The cheapest distortion is along the
doubly-degenerate e′ vibrational mode with components qx (asymmetric stretch) and
qy (in-plane bend). The vibronic Hamiltonian to linear order is

Three qualitative failures of the L5 description. (i) Boundary condition:
L5 enforces periodicity ψ(ϕ + 2π) = ψ(ϕ) by treating ψ as a single-valued
function on the pseudorotation circle; the physical eigenstate is antiperiodic. (ii)
Lowest level: L5 predicts a j = 0 ground state at the trough bottom; the L6
lift and experiment exclude this level, the spectrum starting at j = ±1/2. (iii)
Non-adiabatic coupling: dµ
01 = ⟨σ−|∂µ ˆHel|σ+⟩/(V+ −V−) diverges as R →ΣCI;
single-surface Born–Oppenheimer breaks down at the CI [178, 220, 221, 222].
The rank-2 adiabatic sub-bundle is the natural L6 object.
None of (i)–(iii) is a quantitative correction: each is a topological feature of the
L6 lift that no continuous adjustment of the scalar V−supplies. Antiperiodicity
is a Z2 obstruction class, not a numerical parameter.
The three failures identify the new data L6 carries: the codimension-2 CI seam
ΣCI ⊂Ce(G) (§9.2), the Berry connection A0 on L0 with real-gauge sign holonomy
on LR
0 (§9.3), and the codimension-matched invariants w1(LR
0 ) ∈H1(·, Z/2) (real-

Scattering corroboration in H + HD
The same w1 ̸= 0 bundle structure appears in reactive scattering. H3 shares the
D3h Jahn–Teller E ⊗e structure of Na3, with a codim-2 CI seam at equilateral-
triangle geometries. At collision energies above the CI (Ecoll ≈2.77 eV), crossed-
beam imaging experiments resolve forward-scattering oscillations in (v′, j′)-
resolved differential cross sections of H + HD →H2 + D [223]; the analogous
effect below the CI was reported in [224].
Single-surface L5 scattering on
the ground-state PES [225] predicts smooth angular distributions; including
the Mead–Truhlar vector potential, or imposing w1 = 1 boundary conditions
on loops linking the CI seam, reproduces the oscillations quantitatively [214].
The topological sign comes from the electronic CI of the H3 system; the H/D
substitution makes product channels experimentally distinguishable and changes
the scattering kinematics, but the geometric-phase mechanism itself is the Z2
holonomy associated with loops around the H3 CI. Bound-state spectroscopy of
Na3 and reactive scattering of H + HD are two manifestations of the same w1
holonomy in different observable channels.
§9.2. The full electronic Hilbert bundle and the conical intersection seam
9.2.1. From a scalar surface to an electronic bundle

scalar adiabatic shadow: a potential-energy surface V0 : Ω⊂Ce(G) →R and the
mass-weighted metric g. In the clamped-nuclei Born–Oppenheimer setting,
V0(R) = Eel,0(R) + Vnn(R),
where Eel,0 is the lowest eigenvalue of the electronic Hamiltonian ˆHel(R) and Vnn
is the nuclear–nuclear repulsion.

qualitatively incomplete in the presence of a Jahn–Teller / conical-intersection sign

branches of the same L6 construction; thermal molecular chemistry inhabits the
w1 branch.

or as antiperiodic boundary conditions on loops linking X01 [168]. It is the electronic-
bundle datum that the scalar L5 description forgets, not strictly a non-BO quantity.
What L6 means in practice
The L5/L6 distinction is about what datum the computation targets, not which
method is used.
L5 data. Any electronic-structure method that produces a ground-state PES
V0(R) — DFT, MP2, CCSD(T), or a machine-learned force field fitted to any
of these — supplies the FV data: minima, saddles, IRC, barriers, vibrational
frequencies.
L6 data.
Locating X01 and evaluating ηB on loops in Ω◦is a multi-state
question: one needs at least the first two adiabatic PESs V0, V1 and their
degeneracy locus. Single-reference ground-state methods are generally unreliable
for locating and characterising CI seams, because the relevant states typically
have strong multireference character; multireference or state-averaged methods
such as CASSCF, MRCI, NEVPT2, and MC-PDFT are the standard tools [226].
The forgetful functor U6 is the operation of extracting only the ground-state PES
from a multi-state calculation: it compresses (E(N), A, X01, ηB) down to V0 alone.
If the relevant dynamics remains on a single smooth isolated adiabatic surface
and the real eigenline is topologically trivial on the explored region, the L5 scalar
description may be sufficient. ηB = 0 is not by itself a guarantee that L6 data are
unnecessary: photoisomerisation, internal conversion, photodissociation, spin-
orbit-mediated intersystem crossing, and charge-transfer dynamics all require
L6 data — multiple electronic surfaces, derivative couplings, seam geometry,
and (when relevant) the topological sign — and are not determined by V0 alone.

between the unique physical L6 lift (ηB ̸= 0, half-integer sector) and the L5
scalar quantisation that forgets the eigenline topology and produces the integer
sector.

scalar shadow alone cannot.
(ii) The sign sector is topologically protected. Because ηB takes values in the
discrete group Z/2, its evaluation on a fixed loop γ cannot change under
continuous deformations that keep γ inside the gapped complement Ω◦.
The sign sector can change only if γ crosses a degeneracy, the electronic
gap closes somewhere on γ, or the topology of Ω◦itself changes. Unlike
barrier heights or rate constants, the sign sector does not vary continuously
with molecular parameters.
(iii) Sign-changing transport is an adiabatic L6 channel. In the adiabatic-
channel propagator of Definition 9.17, the restriction to the real ground-
state eigenline gives Uγ ∈O(1) = {±1} with
Uγ = −1

transport component of an adiabatic L6 channel whose path encircles X01.
The sign change in the laboratory
The sign −1 has two standard experimental manifestations.
Quantum interference in reactive scattering. When a nuclear wavepacket
reaches a product channel by two paths — one winding around the CI, one
not — the two amplitudes acquire a relative sign −1. Wherever both paths
contribute coherently to the same product, this yields destructive interference
that redistributes the angular distribution of products relative to a scalar single-
surface calculation on the same ground-state PES that omits the geometric-
phase boundary condition. The effect was predicted by Mead and Truhlar [168],
quantitatively modelled for the H + H2 →H2 + H system by Juanes-Marcos,
Althorpe, and Wrede [214], and observed experimentally for the isotopic analogue
H + HD →H2 + D by Yuan et al. above the CI energy [223] and below
it [224]. Measured differential cross sections agree with geometric-phase-inclusive
scattering calculations on the ground-state PES and disagree with calculations
on the same PES that omit the phase. This is the cleanest laboratory signature
to date of a topological (L6) effect in a simple chemical reaction.

In both cases the observable effect is controlled by the discrete class ηB = w1(LR

A scalar calculation on the ground-state PES that omits the geometric-phase
boundary condition gives the trivial sign sector; the physical L6 lift assigns sign
holonomy −1 to loops linking the CI seam. The topological class itself cannot
change continuously: changing the sign sector requires the relevant loop to pass
through a degeneracy, or the gapped real eigenline description to break down
on the loop.
§9.6. Illustrative L6 dynamics near conical intersections
The preceding sections built the L6 framework and established its empirical anchors.
§9.1 forced L5 →L6 through the Na3 half-integer pseudorotation spectrum. §9.2–
§9.4 constructed the rank-N active bundle, the real Berry-sign class ηB = w1(LR
0 ),
and the L6 category whose morphisms are channels (Γ, UΓ) in adiabatic and non-
adiabatic regimes (Definition 9.17). §9.5 provided the observable bridge: the gauge-
invariant O(1)-holonomy of the real ground-state eigenline, manifest in reactive-
scattering interference patterns and in the antiperiodic boundary condition on Na3
pseudorotation.
This section is illustrative rather than constructive: it does not build a complete
theory of non-adiabatic wavepacket propagation, but explains how the L6 channel
data (Γ, UΓ) are interpreted in the standard adiabatic, non-adiabatic, and Landau–
Zener approximations. The Na3 forcing example is a bound-state manifestation of
w1; H + HD scattering is a continuum manifestation; Landau–Zener is a local scalar
estimator for non-adiabatic transfer. None of these scalar reductions replaces the
underlying L6 lift.

Zener formula [229] provides a semiclassical approximation derived in a diabatic basis
near a transverse two-state crossing. Stating the formula precisely — and locating it
in the tower — clarifies both its utility and its limits.

Validity near a CI. LZ is derived for isolated transverse diabatic crossings with
constant |H12| > 0. At a true CI, |H12| and the adiabatic gap vanish simultaneously
in the branching plane, and the standard two-state LZ formula is no longer exact. It
survives only as a local order-of-magnitude estimator for a chosen one-dimensional
passage through a regularised or locally diabatised two-state model near the branching
region. The path-level matrix-valued propagator Uγ on Hel

by the multi-state channel equation (27); a full wavepacket treatment replaces this
by coupled nuclear–electronic dynamics. Unlike the w1-holonomy, PLZ is not a
topological invariant: it varies continuously with velocity, coupling, and local slopes.
Tower location. PLZ requires local two-state Hamiltonian data: two diabatic
potentials, a diabatic coupling, and the trajectory velocity. Equivalently, it requires
the active rank-2 electronic bundle, the projected Hamiltonian, and a chosen local
diabatisation — all L6-level data not contained in the scalar shadow (Ω, V0, g), which
retains only the ground-state PES. The Landau–Zener formula is therefore an L6-level
scalar estimator of a non-adiabatic channel, accompanying but not replacing the full
channel morphism (Γ, UΓ) of Definition 9.17.

§9.7. What L6 cannot express: forcing of L7
Up to L6, the molecular graph G and the associated nuclear configuration space
are taken as input data: the object (G, σ) comes first, and ˆHel(R), Ce(G), and
the adiabatic bundle Hel
(N) are built over a region of that configuration space.
Nuclear permutations may appear as geometric or orbifold symmetries, but the
nuclei themselves are not yet quantised as identical particles. In particular, L6 does
not impose the exchange symmetry of the nuclear wavefunction, nor does it derive
molecular graph structure from the all-particle Coulomb Hamiltonian.
L7 is forced by two observations L6 cannot accommodate:
(1) Nuclear indistinguishability: identical nuclei carry exchange statistics —
antisymmetry under exchange for half-integer-spin nuclei, symmetry for integer-
spin nuclei. Protons give the cleanest forcing example as spin-1
2 fermions.
(2) Molecular identity: despite this indistinguishability, molecular structure
appears as a stable effective sector or correlation pattern in the quantum
description. The emergence of “this molecule” rather than “a superposition
over graphs” must be derived, not postulated.
Both observations concern particle statistics and identity, not reaction rates. Large
kinetic isotope effects and tunnelling corrections are not, by themselves, clean forcing
examples for L7: many such effects can be modelled semiclassically as corrections on
an L5-level potential-energy or free-energy surface (see Remark 8.41 of §8.5). They
force L7 only when the nuclear wavefunction, nuclear spin symmetry, or identical-
particle exchange structure becomes part of the state description rather than a
294

correction functional on a classical PES.
9.7.1. First forcing pair: nuclear indistinguishability
First forcing pair for L7: identical-nucleus statistics
At every level up to L6, nuclei are treated as distinguishable: each occupies a
position Ri on Ce(G), which is modelled on its regular strata as the quotient
of R3n by SE(3) ⋊Autµ(G), with Autµ(G) relabelling graph vertices while
preserving labels and masses. This treats nuclear permutations as a geometric
symmetry of configuration space; it does not impose antisymmetry on the
nuclear wavefunction. The fully quantum treatment requires the total molecular
wavefunction to transform as the correct sign representation under exchange of
any pair of identical nuclei, giving observably different predictions.
Paradigm: ortho/para H2. For ground-state H2, the electronic and vi-
brational factors are symmetric under proton exchange, and the rotational
wavefunction has parity (−1)J. Since the two protons are identical fermions,
the total wavefunction must be antisymmetric under exchange. Hence the
nuclear-spin singlet I = 0 (antisymmetric) pairs with even J to give para-H2,
while the nuclear-spin triplet I = 1 (symmetric) pairs with odd J to give or-
tho-H2. The two spin isomers have different rotational partition functions and
therefore different low-temperature thermodynamic behaviour, and the intercon-
version is symmetry-forbidden in an isolated molecule. In the absence of efficient
paramagnetic, surface, or impurity-mediated conversion channels, ortho–para
interconversion is slow on laboratory timescales, a metastability that underpins
contemporary hyperpolarisation methods such as PHIP and SABRE [230].
What L6 cannot express. The L6 electronic data
(Hel
(N), A, X01, ηB)
are built over a classical nuclear configuration space. They do not include
the nuclear spin Hilbert space, nor the representation of the identical-proton
permutation group. Hence the distinction between
Hpara
nuc
and
Hortho
nuc
is invisible at L6: the L6 electronic lift of the same scalar/electronic geometry
is insensitive to whether the nuclear spin state lies in the ortho or para sector.
The forgetful projection
U7 : L7(P) −→L6(P)
therefore loses a directly observable distinction: the two nuclear spin-statistical
sectors have different allowed rotational quantum numbers and different low-
temperature partition functions.

9.7.2. Second forcing direction: molecular identity from all-particle quantum mechan-
ics (programme-level)
Programme-level forcing direction for L7:
molecular identity from all-
particle quantum mechanics
Unlike the ortho/para example above, the second example is not a completed
forcing theorem in the present manuscript but a programme-level forcing direc-
tion. It points to a deeper limitation of L6: the molecular graph G is still input
data, whereas in an all-particle quantum treatment molecular structure should
emerge from correlations, symmetry breaking, and sector selection rather than
being postulated.
A species in L5(P) is a pair (G, σ), and the L6 electronic lift presupposes
G: the active bundle Hel
(N) →Ω⊂Ce(G) is built over the configuration
region associated with that graph. Given only the Coulomb Hamiltonian for
a collection of identical nuclei and electrons, why does a definite molecular
structure — such as a triangular D+
3 configuration — emerge from a totally
permutation-symmetric all-particle wavefunction? Exact bound eigenstates of
the all-particle Coulomb Hamiltonian inherit the symmetries of the Hamiltonian,
so molecular shape is not represented as a literal fixed nuclear framework in the
naive eigenfunction picture [174, 231]. It must be recovered from correlations,
sector structure, symmetry breaking, or suitable classical/semiclassical limits.
In the Primas–Amann framework, molecular structure is proposed to emerge as
a superselection sector of the full quantum description in the mass-ratio limit
ε = (me/M)1/2 →0 [232, 175]; a general theorem identifying arbitrary chemical
graphs G with such sectors remains an open problem.
Recent numerical work by Lang, Cezar, Adamowicz, and Pedersen [233] provides
a concrete demonstration of structural emergence for D+
3 : Markov-chain Monte
Carlo sampling of a totally permutation-symmetric pre-BO wavefunction recovers
an unambiguous equilateral-triangular structure. A general theorem for arbitrary
graphs G remains open and is treated in §10.7.
What L6 cannot express. At L6, two molecular graphs correspond to different
input objects and there is no operation internal to the theory that derives
one graph sector from the all-particle Hilbert space.
In the full quantum
description, by contrast, identical nuclei live in a single permutation-symmetric
framework, and graph-like molecular structures must emerge as effective sectors
or correlation patterns. This motivates L7, but the general sector theorem
for arbitrary chemical graphs remains open: the present discussion identifies
the structural task that L7 must eventually solve, namely deriving graph-like
molecular sectors from the all-particle quantum theory rather than assuming G
as input.

metric for electrons; spin-dependent for identical nuclei); the BO approximation

L7 as the strictly quantum tower level
The tower L0 →· · · →L6 built chemistry from combinatorics through topology-
decorated fibre structure over smooth configuration orbifolds, with nuclei classical
throughout. L7 is the strictly quantum cap: nuclei become quantum identical
particles, the BO approximation appears as an asymptotic effective theory in the
ε →0 regime, compatible with the classical fibre of the deformation-quantisation
picture, and molecular identity is to be derived rather than postulated.
The next chapter develops L7 in this spirit, necessarily more speculative than
its predecessors: the four open constructions (continuous field for molecules,
groupoid C*-algebra encoding nuclear statistics, possible K-theoretic or real-
bundle refinements of the Z/2 Berry-sign class, superselection-sector theorem
for arbitrary G) are surveyed with explicit state-of-the-art attributions and
open-problem formulations. The ortho/para H2 forcing example establishes the
physical necessity of adding nuclear quantum statistics; the molecular-identity
discussion motivates the broader L7 programme. The mathematical framework
is the subject of what follows.

§10. L7: The Full Quantum Level
§10.1. Forcing the full quantum level
Section 9.7 identified two reasons the tower must pass beyond L6, of different logical
status. The first is a clean forcing example: ortho- and para-H2, which share the
same L6 electronic shadow but differ by nuclear spin-statistical sector. The second is
a programme-level direction: the recovery of graph-like molecular structure from an
all-particle quantum theory, rather than taking G as primitive input.
(I) Clean forcing example: nuclear spin statistics. Ortho- and para-H2 share the
same scalar and electronic L6 shadow. Their distinction is not electronic; it
is nuclear spin-statistical. The distinction lies in the nuclear spin-statistical
sector, an object L6 does not carry. The two spin isomers have different allowed
rotational quantum numbers and hence different rotational partition functions,
including the 1:3 nuclear-spin degeneracy of the para and ortho sectors, with
correspondingly different low-temperature thermodynamic behaviour. In the
absence of efficient paramagnetic, surface, or impurity-mediated conversion
channels, ortho–para interconversion is slow on laboratory timescales; the
precise rate is strongly condition-dependent [238].
(II) Programme-level direction: molecular identity as an emergent sector. The
molecular graph G ∈LGraphP is given data at every level L4–L6: the
DPO rules, the stereochemical symmetry, the configuration region, the active
electronic bundle, and the Berry-sign data all presuppose a chosen graph. The
Woolley–Primas–Sutcliffe problem [174, 232, 231] asks whether such molecular
structure can be recovered from the all-particle Coulomb Hamiltonian rather
than postulated.
This is not a completed forcing theorem in the present
manuscript; it is the programme-level task that motivates the general L7
construction.
The first example gives the clean forcing obstruction: L6 does not contain nuclear
spin-statistical sectors. The second points to the broader completion problem: G
should ultimately emerge from the all-particle quantum theory rather than remain
primitive input. Both motivate L7, but with different logical status.
At L6, nuclear positions are still treated through a classical configuration space.
Permutations may appear as geometric or orbifold symmetries, but there is no
nuclear Hilbert space and no imposed bosonic or fermionic exchange symmetry
of the nuclear wavefunction. At L7 the nuclei become quantum particles whose
algebra of observables carries exchange-indistinguishability constraints, and from
whose representation theory the graph label G should be derivable as an effective
sector rather than postulated.

where the intended data and forgetful projections can be specified explicitly, L7 is
introduced as a mathematical programme. The level is defined by the conditions its
data must satisfy, while the full construction of morphisms and the operator-algebraic
functorial structure remains open.

The shape of Chapter 10
Section 10.2 develops the new physical content of L7 — the nuclear Schrödinger
equation, the PST ε-expansion, and the demarcation between L5 semiclassi-
cal tunnelling and genuinely L7 phenomena. Sections 10.3 and 10.4 present
the two mathematical programmes closest to delivering C2: strict deforma-
tion quantisation (Rieffel, Landsman) and the Georgescu–Iftimovici N-body
algebra. Section 10.5 formulates L7(P) as a category of L6-objects equipped
with candidate full quantum/operator-algebraic lifts, together with a forgetful
projection
U7 : L7(P) →L6(P).
Section 10.6 states four conjectures (the precise form of C1–C4) as the tower’s
original contribution at this level. Section 10.7 develops the Woolley–Primas
problem as the tower statement of C4. Section 10.8 closes with the complete
tower, the corrected list of forgetful extensions, and the three inter-level coherence
conditions.
§10.2. Quantum nuclear dynamics: the new physical content of L7
The forcing arguments of §10.1 identified two structures absent from L6: a wave-
function for the nuclei (with the indistinguishability it carries) and the programme
of recovering molecular identity as an effective superselection or correlation-sector
label. This section develops the first physical content that L7 delivers: the nuclear
Schrödinger equation on the BO surface, the space-adiabatic ε-expansion that re-
covers the Born–Oppenheimer approximation as a controlled asymptotic, and its
semiclassical tunnelling regime. Section 10.2.3 returns to the forcing content with
the ortho/para example.

Warning 10.3 (What this section does not claim). Anomalous primary kinetic isotope
effects — including values of 55 ± 6 [245] and 661 ± 27 [246] in enzymatic hydrogen
transfer — are frequently cited as evidence for a quantum-mechanical treatment of
nuclei. They are not evidence for L7 specifically. Large KIEs are not, by themselves,
clean forcing examples for L7. Many such effects can be estimated using semiclassical
or path-integral approximations built from L5-level geometric data: a PES, a mass
metric, Hessians, and barrier geometry. These methods can account for many large
KIEs in model-dependent settings, but they do not by themselves force the full
L7 structure. What L7 adds is the nuclear Hilbert-space and operator-algebraic
framework in which such approximations are derived, together with nuclear exchange-
statistical sectors that no scalar semiclassical correction can express.
The Agmon–Helffer–Sjöstrand theorem of §10.2.2 is a rigorous ε →0 asymptotic
of the nuclear Schrödinger equation: it formalises what semiclassical tunnelling
methods approximate. The L7 novelty lies not in the tunnelling estimate itself but
in the Hilbert-space/C∗-algebraic setting in which such estimates become theorems,
together with the exchange-statistical sectors developed in §10.2.3.

10.2.3. Ortho and para-hydrogen: the forcing content of L7
The tunnelling content of §10.2.2 is reproduced by L5 semiclassical methods; it sharp-
ens but does not force L7. Ortho- and para-hydrogen, by contrast, are distinguished
by a structure no level below L7 carries: the symmetry of the nuclear wavefunction
under proton exchange. This is forcing pair (I) of §10.1 in concrete form.
Example 10.9 (Ortho/para-H2). The proton is a spin-1
2 fermion. Pauli antisymmetry
requires the total H2 wavefunction Ψ = ψspatial ⊗χspin to be antisymmetric under
proton exchange π12. Since π12ψJ = (−1)JψJ on rotational states with quantum
number J, nuclear-spin states split into:
• para-H2: singlet spin (I = 0, antisymmetric under π12), paired with even J.
Ground state J = 0.
• ortho-H2: triplet spin (I = 1, symmetric under π12), paired with odd J. Lowest
state J = 1, roughly 14.7 meV above para.

At thermal equilibrium, the 3:1 nuclear-spin degeneracy gives ortho:para = 3 : 1
at high T and pure para as T →0. In the ordinary isolated, spin-independent
approximation, the spatial and nuclear-spin sectors are separately preserved, so
ortho and para subspaces are invariant. Conversion requires weak spin-dependent,
magnetic, surface, impurity-mediated, or other environmental interactions.
In the absence of efficient such channels, ortho–para conversion is slow on labo-
ratory timescales; the precise rate is condition-dependent. The two spin isomers
have different rotational partition functions and therefore different low-temperature
thermodynamic behaviour. The lowest ortho level J=1 lies above the para ground
level J=0 by 2B, where EJ = B J(J + 1); for H2, this is about 14.7 meV, and
ortho-to-para conversion releases approximately this gap per converted molecule
upon liquefaction.

Forcing vs content at L7
Sections 10.2.1–10.2.2 developed content that L7 makes rigorous: the nuclear
Schrödinger equation, its ε-expansion with Berry/geometric corrections, and
the Agmon–Helffer–Sjöstrand tunnelling asymptotic. Many of its leading semi-
classical consequences can be estimated from L5-level data; the L7 claim is

statistical sectors, and the resulting ortho/para superselection decomposition.

Three mathematical inputs converge on the construction of F7 on objects. Strict
deformation quantisation (§10.3.1) specifies what the object-level lift F7(G) must be
as an abstract object and supplies the continuous field on smooth configuration spaces.
Space-adiabatic perturbation theory (§10.3.2) identifies how the Berry connection
and related geometric terms from the chosen L6 electronic lift enter the effective
nuclear Hamiltonian in the semiclassical expansion. The Georgescu N-body algebra
(§10.4) supplies the specific algebra to which the molecular Hamiltonian is affiliated.
None of the three, individually or combined, currently suffices: the orbifold/stratified
singularities of Ce(G) are not addressed, and at conical intersections the single-
band PST input fails. The strict-deformation-quantisation framework must then be
refined by a twisted, multistate, or resolved construction rather than by an ordinary
single-valued scalar field.

Theorem 10.11 (Strict DQ for smooth configuration spaces; Landsman [251]). For
any smooth Riemannian manifold Q, there exists a strict deformation quantisation

Construction sketch. The tangent groupoid T (1)Q interpolates between the pair
groupoid Q × Q at t > 0 and the tangent bundle TQ at t = 0. The associated
C∗-algebras are K(L2(Q)) and C0(T ∗Q) respectively (the latter by fibrewise Fourier
transform on TQ). The full C∗-algebra C∗(T (1)Q) assembles them into a continuous
field; Landsman [251] verifies the Dirac and von Neumann conditions via Weyl
quantisation maps.

10.3.2. PST: connecting the field to L6 data
Theorem 10.11 gives the Layer 1 continuous-field template for F7(G) when the relevant
configuration space is smooth, but leaves its connection to the L6 data (σj, A, ηB)
unspecified. That connection is the substance of space-adiabatic perturbation theory
(PST) [179, 178]: it shows how the Berry connection and related geometric terms from
the chosen L6 electronic lift enter the effective nuclear Hamiltonian in the semiclassical
expansion, as Layer 2(b) requires, and provides the Hilbert-space error estimate that
underlies the C∗-algebraic Born–Oppenheimer statement (Conjecture 10.36).
At the clamped-nuclei electronic level, isotopologues such as H2 and D2 share the same
electronic surface and active electronic data (σj, A, ηB). Their leading dynamical
differences enter through the nuclear masses in the effective Hamiltonian, with the
underlying compact-operator fibre abstractly isomorphic (by Remark 10.12) but
carrying different Hamiltonian elements. In addition, their nuclear spin-statistical
sectors differ at L7: protons are fermions and deuterons are bosons, so the total
wavefunction is antisymmetric under proton exchange and symmetric under deuteron
exchange, with correspondingly different spin-rotational sector decompositions (see
§10.2.3). Nuclear-mass data already belong to L5 (Mathbox 10.2.1).
For clarity, we state the PST result in the simplest single isolated non-degenerate
eigenvalue case; the band-cluster version replaces the eigenvector by the spectral
projector and the Abelian Berry connection by its non-Abelian counterpart on the
active bundle.

10.3.3. Where the single-band F7 fails: the conical intersection seam
When X01 ̸= ∅, the single-band PST input fails near the seam. The Landsman
construction may still apply on the underlying smooth configuration stratum, but does
not by itself encode the electronic band crossing or the required multistate/twisted
structure; the single-band construction of F7 breaks down there.
Proposition 10.16 (Single-band PST breakdown at the CI seam; Lasser–Teufel [220],
Fermanian Kammerer–Lasser [221]). At any conical intersection R0 ∈X01:
(i) The single-band gap condition fails: δ(R0) = 0.
(ii) The single-band Theorem 10.14 does not apply: a single-band almost-invariant
projection associated to either crossing eigenvalue E0 or E1 alone cannot be
constructed on any neighbourhood of R0. A rank-2 active-space projection may
still be meaningful when the two-state cluster remains separated from the rest
of the spectrum.
(iii) Under suitable genericity hypotheses, the best available estimates near X01 are
at the Wigner-measure / surface-hopping level: at leading order, the Wigner
function W ε(t) is approximated by the Lasser–Teufel surface-hopping semi-
group Lt [220], with Fermanian Kammerer–Lasser [221] giving schematic quan-
titative bounds of the form ∥W ε(t) −LtW ε(0)∥= O(εα) in the appropriate
Wigner-measure / weak norm, with α > 0 depending on the precise norm and
crossing hypotheses, and Lt implementing classical transport along surfaces
interleaved with Landau–Zener-type transitions in the local crossing/branching
region.
Remark 10.17 (X01 as the failure locus of single-band F7). The CI seam is L6 data
— the zero locus of the spectral gap function, determined by Hel(R) — so the
failure of the single-band F7 at X01 is an L6 failure imported into L7, not a new L7
phenomenon. The single-band object-level lift is expected to be constructible on
adiabatic regions of Cereg(G) \ X01 where the chosen eigenvalue remains uniformly
isolated and the other regularity hypotheses hold; channels whose support enters the
branching region — photochemical and non-adiabatic processes — require multistate
or resolved constructions. The proposed blowup f
Ce(G) →Ce(G) (Conjecture 10.45) is
one way to resolve the local singular geometry and let the active eigenline/eigenbundle
extend over a resolved space, but does not remove the Berry-sign topology, which
reappears as boundary monodromy or twisted-sector data.

The Georgescu algebra in the tower
(i) What A(X) provides. A specific C∗-algebra on L2(X) to which the nuclear-
effective Hamiltonian Hε = −(ε2/2)∆+ V (R) is affiliated, where V is the BO
eigenvalue selected at L6 (Remark 10.20). The SDQ axioms of Definition 10.10
specify the abstract structure of F7(G); A(X) names a concrete algebra to which
the correct Hamiltonian is affiliated.
(ii) The graded structure tracks particle-cluster asymptotics. R(X)
is graded by a semilattice S of linear subspaces of X describing the relative-
coordinate quotients of the system — equivalently, by particle-cluster partitions.
This lattice is related to, but not identical with, the L0 stoichiometric bookkeeping:
L0 records species and reaction balances, whereas R(X) records asymptotic
cluster decompositions of a fixed N-body Hamiltonian. Chemical dissociation
channels emerge by interpreting certain cluster partitions as molecular fragments.
The HVZ theorem (Theorem 10.23) computes the essential spectrum from this
lattice.
(iii) The compact ideal is the localised spectral regime.

What the Georgescu algebra means for chemistry
An ambient algebra for the nuclear N-body problem. The standard
class of nuclear-effective Hamiltonians Hε = −(ε2/2)∆R +V (R) with admissible
decaying pair interactions is affiliated to A(X) under the Georgescu–Iftimovici
hypotheses. This class includes Coulomb-type pair interactions, which are not in
C0(X/Wij) (they are singular on the collision set) but are admissible unbounded
affiliated potentials (Remark 10.20). A(X) is not a particular approximate
Hamiltonian model; it is a canonical ambient C∗-algebraic framework to which
the relevant Hamiltonians are affiliated, with graded structure capturing the
particle-cluster partition lattice.
The dissociation ladder. For water H2O (labelled atoms {H1, H2, O}) there are
B(3) = 5 set partitions: {H1H2O}, {H1} | {H2O}, {H2} | {H1O}, {O} | {H1, H2},
and {H1} | {H2} | {O}. After identifying the two hydrogen labels, these five
partitions reduce to four symmetry orbits: the undissociated channel and three
dissociation channels — H+OH, O+{H, H}, and H+H+O. Whether the {H, H}
cluster supports a bound H2 state is spectral information of the corresponding
cluster Hamiltonian, not part of the partition lattice itself.
HVZ as the quantum dissociation threshold. The bottom of σess(HH2O)
is the minimum cluster threshold across non-minimal partitions: the quantum-
mechanical dissociation threshold of the chosen Schrödinger Hamiltonian. After
adding zero-point and electronic corrections, this threshold is the spectral
analogue of the dissociation energies organised at L1 by Hess-law bookkeeping —
now derived as an algebraic consequence of the ideal structure of A(X).

Remark 10.24 (HVZ across the tower: L0 →L7). The union in Theorem 10.23 runs
over a particle-cluster partition lattice, related to but distinct from L0 stoichiomet-
ric bookkeeping: L0 records species and reaction balances, whereas A(X) records
asymptotic cluster decompositions of a fixed N-body Hamiltonian. Chemical dissoci-
ation channels are obtained by interpreting certain cluster partitions as molecular
fragments. Algebraic HVZ is therefore a C∗-algebraic computation of a quantum
dissociation threshold whose thermochemical analogue is the Hess-law L1 dissociation
energy, mediated by the appropriate zero-point and electronic corrections: the cluster
lattice, invisible in the electronic structure at L6, reappears at L7 as the ideal lattice
of A(X).

10.4.3. Channels vs species: the gap to Construction C4
What A(X) encodes, and what remains for C4
What is encoded. The graded structure of R(X) tracks asymptotic cluster
behaviour: which atoms separate as |R| →∞, and at which thresholds. HVZ
and Mourre follow from this structure, and every affiliated N-body Hamiltonian
inherits its spectral framework.
What is not encoded. Within K(L2(X)), A(X) does not distinguish which
bound configuration is occupied: bound ground and excited states, and weakly
bound van der Waals states, are all represented in the compact/localised part.
Resonances — non-L2 poles of the resolvent — require separate scattering/res-
onance theory and are not located in K(L2(X)) at all. In tower terms: A(X)
encodes the asymptotic cluster channels but not the molecular identity (the L4
graph G) that must emerge algebraically at L7.
Two steps to close the gap.
(i) G∗-equivariant restriction and descent (L4.5 data). Two related operations
are required: restricting to A(X)G∗(the subalgebra commuting with the
permutation-inversion group G∗), and descending to an algebra on the
quotient/sector Hilbert space associated with Ce(G), compatible with
the Landsman fibre K(L2(Ce(G))) of Theorem 10.11. Ammann–Mougel–
Nistor [254] identify Georgescu’s C∗-algebraic compactification of X with
Vasy’s blowup compactification; this is the geometric scaffold on which
the G∗-action can be implemented equivariantly. The explicit molecular
construction has not been carried out.
(ii) Molecular species identification (Construction C4). Equip the descended
algebra with an observable subalgebra, symmetry, or representation struc-
ture whose sectors are labelled by graph-like molecular structures. The
compact ideal supplies the localised spectral regime, but the graph labels
require additional superselection/observable data, since K(H) is simple as
a C∗-algebra and admits no bare ideal decomposition. This is the content
of Conjecture 10.42(a) and the subject of §10.7; it is logically downstream
of step (i).
§10.5. The full quantum level L7(P): object-level specification
Sections 10.2–10.4 developed the three mathematical strands that make the full
quantum level a candidate for formal definition: the nuclear Schrödinger equation on
the BO surface (C1 at the Hilbert-space level), strict deformation quantisation and
the space-adiabatic ε-expansion (the ingredients of C2), and the Georgescu N-body
algebra (Layer 2(a) ingredients of C2). This section specifies the object-level data
required of an L7-lift over an L6-object, defines the target category C∗Algcont, and
records the conditions that a future functorial construction F7 would have to satisfy.

Remark 10.40 (Real vs. complex Berry structure). The framework above uses real
line bundles and KO-theory because non-relativistic molecular Hamiltonians with
T 2 = +1 yield real eigenstates with Z2-valued holonomies (§9.3). For spin–orbit-
coupled systems (T 2 = −1, outside the monograph’s scope in §10.8.4), the eigenstates
are Kramers pairs, the eigenbundle is complex, and the analogous obstruction lives
in complex K-theory with integer Chern class; Hawkins [244] provides the template
there. Conjecture 10.39 is the real analog of Hawkins’ result, which has not been
worked out for real line bundles over molecular configuration orbifolds.
Chemistry. The sign flip of the real adiabatic eigensection around any loop encircling
a CI seam is directly observable in scattering experiments: Yuan et al. [258] provide
the experimental observation of the geometric-phase effect in the H + HD →H2 + D
reaction associated with the H3 conical-intersection topology, and Kendrick, Hazra,
and Balakrishnan [259] predict large channel- and energy-dependent modifications of
state-resolved rate coefficients in the O + OH →H + O2 reaction through quantum
interference between direct and CI-encircling pathways. Conjecture 10.39 says this
laboratory observation has a KO-theoretic shadow: the same ηB that modifies state-
resolved scattering observables also requires a twisted/local-system quantisation of

ε } rather than an ordinary single-valued scalar realisation. Photochemistry is
mathematically hard partly because the C∗-algebraic object that would ground its

twisted realisation, and additionally, when a CI seam X01 is present, the single-band
gap condition fails at the seam and requires a separate resolution (Conjecture 10.45,
§10.6.4).

§10.7. Molecular identity as superselection sector: the Woolley–Primas
problem in the tower
Construction C4 — the representation-theoretic content layer of the object-level lift
F obj
7
(G) identified in Mathbox 10.5.5 — is the tower’s answer to a question that
quantum chemistry has carried since the 1970s: how does the notion of a definite
molecular species, assumed throughout L0–L6, emerge from the symmetric full-
quantum theory? This section develops that answer in detail, placing the historical
Woolley–Primas problem in tower language, identifying the stabilisation mechanisms
required for Conjecture 10.42 — exact spin-statistical, metastable semiclassical, and
environmental — and recording the evidence that supports each.

10.7.1. The Woolley–Primas problem as a tower statement
Woolley [174] observed that the eigenstates of the full Coulomb Hamiltonian ˆHCoul
for an assembly of electrons and nuclei transform as irreducible representations of the
full symmetry group (spatial rotations, translations, and nuclear permutations); in
isolation they carry no definite nuclear geometry, bond angles, or molecular structure.
Primas [232] elevated the observation into a critique of chemical reductionism:
molecular structure, he argued, is not derivable from quantum mechanics but is
a classical concept imposed from outside. Sutcliffe and Woolley [231] reiterated
that the Born–Oppenheimer approximation itself presupposes an empirically chosen
molecular frame not determined by the theory. The issue remains active: recent work
in Foundations of Chemistry by Scerri [267], a comment by Woolley [268], and a
pedagogical discussion by Agostini and Curchod [269] returns the Born–Oppenheimer
/ molecular-structure debate to the foreground without consensus ([231] remains the
standard position and no rigorous resolution has appeared in the nearly five decades
since Woolley’s 1978 paper).
In the tower, Woolley’s observation is exact. The molecular graph G ∈LGraphP
is given data at every level L4–L6: the DPO rules of L4, the permutation-inversion
group G∗of L4.5, the configuration orbifold Ce(G) of L5, the Hilbert bundle and
Berry connection of L6 — all presuppose that G has been fixed. In the corrected
L7 language, the missing datum is the nuclear exchange-statistical representation
structure: it is invisible to the scalar/electronic L6 description, which works over
the sector-reduced configuration space and does not yet retain the full labelled
spin-statistical representation structure carried by the G∗-action on Qreg
lab(G) and on
the nuclear-spin Hilbert factor.
The tower resolves the problem not by philosophical argument but by identifying the
precise level and mechanism at which G must emerge. The level is L7: the quantum
algebra AG
ε carries the G∗-action from L4.5, and the labelled spin-spatial Hilbert
space HG
lab = L2(Qreg
lab(G))⊗SG decomposes under this action into G∗-isotypic Hilbert
components Vπ ⊗Mπ (Proposition 10.41); the G∗-invariant observable subalgebra
preserves these components. The compact ideal K(HG
lab) itself is simple as a C∗-
algebra and does not, in isolation, decompose into molecular-species sectors. The
mechanism for sector stability has three regimes — exact (spin-statistical invariance
under G∗for identical-particle sectors), kinematic (ε →0 Agmon suppression between
metastable wells), and environmental (Pfeifer–Amann-type bath-induced selection
in the chiral/metastable case) — developed in §10.7.2. For a fixed graph G, the

broader C4 problem is to relate this sector structure, together with localised spectral
data — in the sense of the Georgescu C∗-algebraic compactification of §10.4.3, which
encodes asymptotic dissociation channels and the geometry of nuclear localisation
at spatial infinity — to graph-like molecular identity at L4; this is the content of
Conjecture 10.42.
Chemistry. The practical stakes of Woolley–Primas are concrete. Three familiar
empirical phenomena anchor the C4 question, and the tower assigns each to a different
mechanism of Conjecture 10.42:
• Ortho/para H2. Routinely observed spectroscopically, computed quantum-
mechanically, and stable over laboratory timescales without environmental
intervention. This is the cleanest empirical anchor: an exact identical-particle
sector decomposition that holds at every ε from spin statistics alone (the (a1)
regime).
• Chirality of pharmaceuticals. The two enantiomers of a chiral drug have identical
Coulomb Hamiltonians and identical eigenstates, yet pharmacology treats them
as distinct species over chemically relevant timescales. Thalidomide is the
canonical cautionary example — complicated by in-vivo racemisation, so it
is not a clean exact-superselection case but rather a long-lived metastable
sector, captured by the (a2) regime supplemented by environmental selection
of Pfeifer–Amann type (the (b) regime) in the chiral spin–boson model.
• Isotopic labelling through metabolism. Nuclear isotope identity is conserved
through ordinary chemical reactions, allowing tracer experiments to track
molecular identity through long synthetic and metabolic chains. This is a chem-
ically robust phenomenon but a separate mechanism from G∗-representation
superselection: it relies on the conservation of particle-species labels (proton,
deuteron, . . . ), not on the G∗-isotypic decomposition.
Without Construction C4, these phenomena are facts of chemistry imposed on a
quantum description that does not yet account for them. Conjecture 10.42 gives each
its proper place in the tower, and supplies an architecture in which their differences
in mechanism — exact vs. metastable vs. environmentally selected vs. a conservation
law — are distinguished rather than collapsed.
10.7.2. Amann’s mechanism in the tower
Pfeifer [260] established a model-specific mechanism for the superselection picture in
the chiral case: a two-level system modelling the enantiomeric inversion of a chiral
molecule, coupled to a bosonic bath with ohmic spectral density, becomes effectively
localised in one chiral state in the W ∗-algebraic limit of infinitely many bath modes;
the framework was developed by Amann [175, 263]. The result is model-specific
(a spin–boson model of chirality in a specifically constructed environment), not a
general theorem, but its structure makes the mechanism by which molecular identity
can become effectively localised explicit. Placed in the tower, it separates cleanly
into distinct stabilisation claims.

10.7.4. The tower’s formal resolution
Assembling the pieces: the tower does not postulate molecular identity at L4 and
rediscover it at L7; it conjectures that the identity be recoverable at L7 from the
G∗-representation structure of the labelled spin-spatial Hilbert space HG
lab, together
with the invariant observable algebra and additional localised spectral data, and
outlines the mechanisms by which the recovery is expected to proceed: exact spin-
statistical invariance for identical-particle sectors, kinematic Agmon suppression for
metastable barrier-protected sectors, and Amann-type environmental selection for
the chiral/metastable case.
The Woolley–Primas problem, resolved as far as the tower permits
The molecular graph G assigned at L4 is conjecturally recoverable from the L7
representation-theoretic and localised-spectral structure: the G∗-representation
sectors Vπ ⊗Mπ ⊂HG
lab encode nuclear exchange statistics, while additional
localised spectral data encode graph-like molecular identity. The forgetful chain
U7 ◦U6 ◦U5 ◦U4.5 ◦U4 : L7(P) −→L4(P)
closes the circle by returning the L7 data to graph data; a fixed graph G generally
carries several allowed sectors π ∈c
G∗(e.g. ortho and para of H2), so no single π
“is” the graph.
What is established: ortho/para in H2 at every ε from spin statistics (the (a1)
case of Conjecture 10.42); the mechanism of environment-induced sector selection
for chirality in a specific spin–boson model via Pfeifer–Amann; and numerical
evidence for graph-like structure extraction from a permutation-adapted pre-BO
wavefunction for a system with nontrivial S3 permutation symmetry via Lang
et al.
What the tower conjectures: Conjecture 10.42 for arbitrary G and G∗, with
both sector stability (a) and environmental selection (b). Completing this
requires assembling Renault’s groupoid C∗-algebra theory [264], the Longuet-
Higgins G∗framework [154], and Landsman’s quantisation functor [251] into
the transformation-groupoid algebra C∗(G∗⋉Qreg
lab(G)) for the G∗-action on
labelled configurations, together with its associated-bundle descent over the
quotient Ce
reg(G) (§10.4.3); proving the Agmon stability bound for metastable
barrier-protected sectors; and generalising Amann’s environmental coupling
beyond the spin–boson model.
The Woolley–Primas problem, in this framing, is not a philosophical puzzle
but the concrete mathematical question of whether Construction C4 can be
completed: whether the molecular graph G, assumed at L4, can be recovered
from L7 sector, localisation, and representation data. The tower makes the

10.8.1. The complete tower with forcing pairs
The nine-level tower L0 ,→· · · ,→L7 (the intermediate level L4.5 sits between L4
and L5) is governed by a single principle: at each transition Lk−1 →Lk, the cokernel
coker(φk) of the restriction φk : Aut(Lk) →Aut(Lk−1) is non-trivial. Equivalently,
Lk−1 admits automorphisms that Lk breaks. For each transition, §10.1 (for L6 →L7)
and the corresponding sections of earlier chapters exhibit a concrete reaction pair
distinguishing the two levels. Table 4 records all eight transitions in a single view.
10.8.2. Six extension types: a descriptive taxonomy
The eight transitions of Table 4 group into six qualitatively distinct extension types,
distinguished by the kind of data they add and the algebraic signature of coker(φk).
We present this grouping as a descriptive taxonomy — an empirical observation about
the present tower, not a meta-theorem about categorical extensions of chemistry in
general.
(T1) Decorator (L0 →L1 →L2 →L3). Add a symmetric monoidal functor into
BR or Stoch on the same underlying base category L0(P). The base, its
objects, and its composition are unchanged; a single real- or stochastic-valued
observable is added. Three transitions of the present tower instantiate this
type.
(T2) Structural (L3 →L4). Replace the underlying free SMC with a different
free SMC on richer generators (DPO rules on labelled molecular graphs in
LGraphP). The observable functors are re-evaluated on the new base. One
transition.
(T3) Symmetry enrichment (L4 →L4.5). Restrict morphisms to those equivari-
ant under a group action (G∗on LGraphP); no new numerical functor is
added, but the morphism category is cut down. One transition.
(T4) Geometric decoration (L4.5 →L5). Add a functor into a category of geo-
metric objects (FV : L4.5 →OrbMorse), introducing infinitely many continuous
parameters (the function V : Ce(G) →R). One transition.
(T5) Topological enrichment (L5 →L6). Add a functor into a category whose
morphisms carry discrete topological invariants (F6 : L5 →HilbBund with
Berry-sign class ηB = w1(LR

10.8.4. Scope of the tower
The tower L0–L7 is the canonical categorical framework for a specific regime of
molecular chemistry. The boundary is a precise domain specification.
Within scope: non-relativistic, spin-unresolved, closed-system molecular
quantum chemistry.
• Hamiltonian: non-relativistic Coulomb, ˆH = −1

• Time-reversal symmetry: T 2 = +1 (spin-unresolved or spin-diagonal Hamilto-

• Energy regime: well below mec2 ≈511 keV.
Outside scope.

• Relativistic effects (spin-orbit coupling, mass-velocity, Darwin term): significant
for heavy atoms (Au, Hg, Pb) and lanthanides. Extension: replace the non-
relativistic operator in AG

a re-instantiation of type (T6) with a different base operator. In this regime

the first Chern class c1 (cf. Remark 10.40).

What the L7 chapter contributes
Three contributions distinguish the tower at L7.
Forcing-pair discipline. Table 4 records a concrete reaction pair justifying
each transition Lk−1 →Lk; the tower is built from the bottom upward by this
discipline rather than designed from the top downward. To our knowledge, no
prior categorical treatment of chemistry (Baez–Fong, Baez–Pollard, Coecke)
proceeds by forcing pairs; in those we are aware of, the mathematical structure
is chosen first and chemistry mapped into it. The forcing-pair discipline is a
methodological contribution, not a theorem.
Para enrichment as a separate dimension. Every level Lk carries a Para
shadow LPara

programme.

§11. The Para Enrichment: Machine Learning Models and
Categorical Completeness
The exact tower L0(P) ,→· · · ,→L7(P) built in Chapters 2–10 is the structural
decomposition of chemistry developed in this monograph: species and stoichiometry
at L0, enthalpy additivity at L1, the dagger and detailed balance at L2, the chemical
master equation at L3, bond topology at L4, stereochemistry at L4.5, the Born–
Oppenheimer potential at L5, electronic structure at L6, and nuclear quantisation at
L7. Each morphism in the tower is an exact law. Each extension was forced by a
reaction pair the level below could not distinguish. Nothing in that construction was
statistical; nothing was learned from data.
This chapter turns the tower outward. The models used to compute chemistry in
practice today — MACE [271], NequIP [272], So3krates [273], SO3LR [192], QIM [34],
and the rest of the published molecular machine learning catalogue — are neural
networks, trained force fields, parametric surrogates. The question this chapter asks
is what the tower, as a completed structural object, tells us about these models:
what their architectures already commit to, what they can and cannot represent,
which tower-coherence conditions they silently respect or silently violate.
A direct answer is blocked by a categorical kind mismatch. A tower morphism at
level k is an exact map: one specific, deterministic morphism of Lk(P), delivered
once and for all by the tower construction of Chapters 2–10. A MACE force field is a
parametric family {fθ}θ∈Θ, one map per point in a weight space Θ that the training
procedure selects from. The two sit in different kinds of category: tower morphisms
in hom-sets C(X, Y ), MACE in something like `
Θ C(Θ⊗X, Y ). Asking “which tower
level does MACE occupy?” is a category error in the literal sense; the tower and the
MACE model are different kinds of mathematical object and share no hom-set. To
use the tower as a diagnostic for the ML literature, we need a categorical setting
in which parametric families and exact morphisms both live, with the exact tower
appearing as a distinguished sub-structure of the richer whole.
The construction that does this is the Para 2-category of Gavranović et al. [33].
For a symmetric monoidal category (C, ⊗, I), the 2-category Para(C) has the same
objects as C, but its 1-morphisms X →Y are pairs (Θ, fθ) with Θ ∈C a parameter
space and fθ : Θ ⊗X →Y a morphism of C. 2-morphisms are reparametrisations
r: Θ′ →Θ, encoding weight tying, fine-tuning, and transfer learning. Applied at
each tower level, Para produces a perpendicular enrichment LPara
k
(P): a 2-category
of parametric morphisms standing above the exact morphisms of Lk(P), with a
vertical embedding γk placing each exact law as its trivial-parameter (Θ = I) version.
There is no canonical reverse functor collapsing a parametric morphism back to a
single exact one. Such a reverse would need to canonically select a weight r: I →Θ
for each (Θ, fθ), but the comonoid structure on Θ provides no such section: the
counit !Θ : Θ →I goes the wrong way — it discards the parameter object rather
than naming a point in it — and no canonical I →Θ accompanies it. If such a
canonical section did exist it would name the trained model from the architecture
alone, making training unnecessary. The tower therefore appears in this enriched
setting as the trivial-parameter slice of a richer categorical object populated by the
349


## Page 350


Kyunghoon Han
Categorification of Chemical Reactions
architectures that are actually trained; the structural question an architecture poses
to the tower is the one categorical completeness below formalises — whether the set
of morphisms its weight space can realise lies in Lk(P), and how much of Lk(P) it
covers.
Once the tower and the parametric literature share a categorical home, three struc-
tural questions about any published ML architecture become precisely answerable,
and none of them is answerable by benchmark comparison alone.
Is the architecture’s equivariance a design choice or a theorem?
Each level Lk
carries a canonical symmetry group Gk — species permutations at L0–L3, graph
automorphisms at L4, the permutation-inversion group at L4.5, rigid motions com-
posed with graph automorphisms SE(3) ⋉Aut(G) at L5, gauge transformations on
the electronic bundle at L6, particle exchange at L7. Membership in LPara
k
(P) is
defined by requiring strict Gk-equivariance of the underlying map at every parameter
setting. MACE’s Clebsch–Gordan tensor contractions enforce the L5 symmetry
SE(3) ⋉Aut(G) for all θ, not just the trained one; membership at LPara
5
is therefore
a theorem about the MACE architecture, not a fortunate property of training. An
architecture whose symmetry is merely learned through data augmentation fails the
membership condition and is not, in structural terms, a parametric morphism at
that level.
What can the architecture represent, independent of its training data? An architecture
(Θ, fθ) is categorically complete at level k on a morphism φ of Lk(P) if some parameter
setting r: I →Θ instantiates fθ to φ exactly — equivalently, if φ lies in the
architecture’s function class Func(Θ, fθ) ⊆Lk(P)(X, Y ), the set of instantiations as
r ranges over C(I, Θ) (Remark 11.4). Completeness is a property of the function
class, not of the loss or the training set. An architecture incomplete at level k will
fail on every task requiring a target morphism φ absent from Func(Θ, fθ), regardless
of training-set size, because no choice of weights realises φ.
Which tower-coherence conditions does the architecture enforce? The tower’s forgetful
functors Uk : Lk(P) →Lk−1(P) connect adjacent levels; a model claiming content
at multiple levels must respect the relations Uk imposes on joint content. Three
such conditions are unenforced across the published literature. The Eyring TST
condition couples a learned rate law to the activation barrier of the same model’s
potential energy surface (L3 ↔L5). The categorical Wegscheider condition couples
forward and reverse rate constants through the thermodynamic ∆G◦(L2 ↔L3). The
topological output-type condition demands a Hilbert-bundle-valued output rather
than a scalar energy to carry the Berry-phase invariant [γB] ∈H1(Ce(G) \ X01, Z2)
near conical intersections (L5 →L6). The first two are literature-wide architectural
absences that new designs could close; the third is a theorem about output type
— no reparametrisation of a scalar-energy architecture yields a Berry connection,
regardless of training, body order, or receptive field.
These three questions are the analytical spine of the chapter. They organise what the
tower, read through the Para enrichment, reveals about ML molecular modelling: a
precise structural classification of every major architecture, a completeness diagnostic
that is architectural rather than empirical, and a catalogue of tower-coherence
conditions the current literature does not enforce.

Vocabulary for the computational chemist and physicist
The categorical language below is unfamiliar outside category theory, but each
object has a direct operational reading. The rest of the chapter can be read
with this dictionary alone.
Parametric morphism (Θ, fθ). A neural network. Θ is the parameter space
(the set of possible weight values); fθ is the forward map from input structure
to output prediction. Training selects a point θ∗∈Θ.
Reparametrisation r: Θ′ →Θ. A map relating two parameter spaces. Opera-
tionally: weight tying (one shared weight used in multiple places, realised by
the copy map ∆: Θ →Θ ⊗Θ), fine-tuning, or transfer learning.
Counit !Θ : Θ →I. The unique map from the parameter space to the monoidal
unit, paired with ∆Θ to give Θ its comonoid structure. Operationally, the
categorical bookkeeping that “a parameter object can be formally discarded”
— the counterpart to the comultiplication’s “a parameter can be copied”. It
does not correspond to setting weights to zero or any other ablated value; that
operation, if needed, requires a section zΘ : I →Θ going the other way, which is
extra data the comonoid alone does not provide. The tower’s exact laws enter
the parametric row through the trivial-parameter embedding γk (which uses
Θ = I, the monoidal unit), not through !Θ.
Comultiplication ∆Θ : Θ →Θ ⊗Θ. Weight sharing. In MACE, one learnable
radial MLP Rnl and one shared element embedding hj enter every message-
passing layer; ∆Θ is the categorical record of that sharing.
Symmetry monad Mk. The level-k symmetry group Gk packaged as an
operation on the category Lk(P). A morphism of Mk-algebras is exactly a
Gk-equivariant map.
LPara
k
(P) membership. The architecture’s map is Gk-equivariant by construc-
tion, for every parameter setting, not merely by training regularisation or data
augmentation.
Categorical completeness at level k. The architecture’s function class
contains the target morphism of Lk(P): some parameter setting realises it
exactly. Independent of training data.
With this dictionary the downstream content reads operationally. “MACE lives in
LPara
5
” means Clebsch–Gordan contractions enforce SE(3)⋉Aut(G) equivariance
at every layer, for every θ. “MACE is not complete at L6” means the output
type is scalar energy, which contains no Berry connection no matter how Θ is
parametrised. “Thermodynamic consistency at L2 requires a comultiplication on
Θ coupling forward and reverse rates” means no published kinetic network has
the right weight-sharing structure to guarantee detailed balance.

2-category. Objects, 1-morphisms between objects, and 2-morphisms between
parallel 1-morphisms.
The canonical example is Cat: categories, functors,
natural transformations.

Self-action convention. The Para construction of [33] is defined for an M-
actegory (C, ▷); throughout this chapter we specialise to the self-action case
M = C, ▷= ⊗with (C, ⊗, I) symmetric monoidal. This is sufficient for every

Para(C).
Same objects as C; 1-morphisms X →Y are pairs (Θ, fθ) with
fθ : Θ ⊗X →Y in C; 2-morphisms (Θ, fθ) ⇒(Θ′, fθ′) are reparametrisations
r: Θ′ →Θ satisfying fθ ◦(r ⊗idX) = fθ′. Sequential composition tensors
parameter spaces.
Monad and algebra. A monad (M, η, µ) on C is an endofunctor with unit
η: id ⇒M and multiplication µ: M ◦M ⇒M satisfying standard coherence.
The group-action monad (G×−, η, µ) on Set has M-algebras exactly G-actions
and M-algebra homomorphisms exactly G-equivariant maps. Equivariance, in
this language, is membership in a category of M-algebras.
Lax algebra, and what we use of it. Lax algebras for a 2-monad replace
strict commutativity on the algebra diagrams with explicit 2-cells. We use this
structure in one place only: a lax algebra over Para(T) endows its parame-
ter object Θ with a comonoid structure (counit !Θ : Θ →I, comultiplication
∆Θ : Θ →Θ⊗Θ), realising the parameter-discard and weight-sharing operations
of the chembox above. This result is due to Gavranović et al. [33].
Strict equivariance specialisation. We work throughout with the specialisa-
tion in which the 1-morphism equivariance square commutes strictly (the 2-cell
on that square is the identity); only the parameter-space comonoid structure
remains lax. This matches how current ML molecular architectures enforce
equivariance, and is a proper sub-framework of the full lax-algebra apparatus
of [33] that loses no content we need.
A reader prepared to take the Para 2-category and its parameter-space comonoid as
black boxes can proceed from the chembox translation alone; the formal apparatus
of Section 11.1 is there to make the translations precise, not to add a separate layer
of content.

11.1.1. The Para 2-category
The Para 2-category is a formal device that treats an entire parametric family
{fθ : X →Y }θ∈Θ as a single 1-morphism (Θ, fθ), distinct from any particular trained
instance. This is what lets us speak about what functions an architecture can
represent across its whole weight space, independently of any one training run.
Definition 11.1 (Para(C) [33]). The Para 2-category Para(C) has:
• Objects: the objects of C.
• 1-morphisms X →Y : pairs (Θ, fθ) with Θ an object of C (the parameter
space) and fθ : Θ ⊗X →Y a morphism of C.

Why (Ek) is stated per-parameter. Condition (32) is phrased per-parameter —
one check per r: I →Θ — rather than as a single condition on the pair (Θ, fθ) at
the level of the ambient category Para(C). Two reasons. First, it is directly testable:
given an architecture at a particular trained weight setting r∗, one verifies (32)
by checking that the instantiation at r∗is a morphism of Lk(P), with no further
categorical apparatus required. Second, the per-parameter statement matches the
chemist’s reading of membership from the chapter chembox: an architecture lives
at level k exactly when every weight setting it admits — not just the trained one —
yields a level-k morphism.
Why a comonoid on Θ, and why this particular one. The operations a
parameter space admits — duplicate a weight (for sharing across layers) and discard
a weight (formally forgetting the parameter object) — are exactly those of a comonoid
in a symmetric monoidal category. This is not a structure newly imported from [33]
for the present chapter: Chapter 5 already uses the same (∆, !) data, there as the
copy–delete morphisms on every object of a Markov category, where ∆copies a
random sample and ! discards one. Here the formal content is identical and the
interpretation shifts: ∆routes a single weight into two layers (rather than copying a
sample to two outputs); ! records the parameter object as formally discardable (the
categorical counterpart of the discardable sample, not a weight-zeroing or weight-
ablation operation). We record (Ck) explicitly because weight-sharing discipline is
architectural data: two networks with the same underlying map fθ but different
comonoid structures on Θ are different architectures, and LPara
k
(P) must distinguish
them.

11.1.4. Categorical completeness
Membership in LPara
k
(P) guarantees that every element of Func(Θ, fθ) is a level-k
morphism; it does not say which level-k morphisms appear there. The question
categorical completeness asks is the second one: given a specific target morphism φ
of Lk(P), is φ in the function class?
The targets of applied interest are those produced by the exact tower constructions
of earlier chapters. At L1, the target is the enthalpy the Hess functor FH assigns to
a specific reaction. At L3, it is the Markov kernel FP assigns to a transition. At L5,
it is the Born–Oppenheimer potential FV yields on a specific molecular configuration.
At L6, it is the Hilbert bundle F6 produces on a molecule, including the Berry class
[γB] the bundle carries at a conical intersection. In each case φ is a specific morphism
of the corresponding Lk(P), identifiable in the chapter where the tower construction
was defined.

It is complete on a class S ⊆Lk(P)(X, Y ) if complete on every φ ∈S, and complete
at level k if complete on every morphism of Lk(P)(X, Y ).
Completeness is a property of the architecture — its parameter space, its forward
map, its closure under choice of weights — and is logically independent of any
training procedure. No training recovers a target absent from the function class.
ML molecular architectures are typically complete on physically meaningful subclasses.
At L5, for instance, MACE/NequIP completeness on a dense subclass of smooth
BO potentials is framed conditionally on universal-approximation hypotheses in
Section 11.4. They are not complete on all of L5(P)(X, Y ), and at L6 they are
incomplete in a structurally topological way. Section 11.7 identifies three specific φ —
one at L6 structurally outside the function class of every scalar-energy architecture,
and two at L2/L3 outside the function classes of the published kinetic and joint
kinetic-energetic architectures — that are the tower-coherence gaps the rest of the
chapter analyses.
Completeness is architectural, not empirical
Where does completeness bite? At L6, Proposition 11.19 shows that the Berry
class [γB] ∈H1(Ce(G) \ X01, Z2) carried by the Hilbert bundle F6 at a conical
intersection lies outside Func(Θ, fθ) for every SE(3)-equivariant scalar-energy
force field. The reason is type-theoretic: [γB] is not a pointwise function on Ce(G)
at all but a Z2-valued cohomology class assigning a value to each homology class
of loops in Ce(G) \ X01; a scalar-valued output, which is a function on Ce(G),
cannot represent such a class. No r: I →Θ in a scalar-output architecture
produces a map that carries [γB]. The failure is an output-type obstruction at
the architecture level, revealed by the tower and not addressable by any training
procedure.
§11.2. External categorical frameworks in tower language
The Para enrichment LPara
k
(P) of Section 11.1 unifies, into a single nested hierarchy,
characterisations of the membership condition (Ek) of Definition 11.2 that were
developed independently — before this monograph’s tower — one level at a time. In
detail: (E0) is Meseguer–Montanari’s free-strict-SMC morphism condition [32]; (E3)’s
Markov-kernel core is, on the stochastic-kinetics side, Fritz’s Markov-category mor-
phism condition [275] (positivity, probability conservation), with species-permutation
equivariance the additional tower-specific component; and, on the composable-
networks side, Baez and Pollard’s gray-box functor condition on open reaction
networks [31]; (E4) is de Haan, Cohen, and Welling’s Natural Graph Networks natu-
rality on molecular graphs [274] and Bonchi et al.’s DPO-compatible string-diagram
rewriting of mechanistic graphs [276]; (E5) is Clebsch–Gordan-augmented NGN, as
realised in NequIP [272], MACE [271], and So3krates [273]. Each of these four exter-
nal frameworks characterises one tower level on its own terms and goes no further.
The Cruttwell–Gavranović framework of categorical gradient-based learning [277],
treated separately below, runs perpendicular to this enumeration: it does not pair
with a single tower level but supplies the 2-categorical backdrop for gradient-based
training of any LPara
k
(P) architecture (Section 11.2.3). What the tower adds, via the
forgetful functors Uk : Lk(P) →Lk−1(P) of Section 11.1, is nesting: the hierarchy

The Natural Graph Networks (NGN) framework of de Haan, Cohen, and Welling [274]
gives the categorical language for message-passing neural networks on graphs. Its
central objects are graph feature spaces: functors ρ: Graph →Vec from a groupoid
of graphs (with graph isomorphisms as morphisms) to vector spaces. A natural graph
network layer between two such feature spaces is a natural transformation K : ρ ⇒ρ′,
a family of maps KG : ρ(G) →ρ′(G) commuting with every graph isomorphism.
Naturality is exactly equivariance under graph-level symmetries — that is, under
Aut(G).
Proposition 11.6 (NGN naturality is (E4)). At tower level k = 4, where G4 =
Aut(G) acts on the labelled-graph category LGraphP of Chapter 6:
(i) Graph feature spaces ρ: Graph →Vec restricted to the objects of LGraphP
are exactly the Aut(G)-equivariant feature maps at L4(P).
(ii) The NGN naturality condition of [274] is the membership condition (32) at
k = 4:
fθ(σ · G) = D(σ) fθ(G)
for all σ ∈Aut(G),
where D is the representation of Aut(G) on the output feature channels.
(iii) Local-to-global: an architecture satisfying naturality at every message-passing

11.2.2. Combinatorial tower levels L0, L3, L4: Meseguer–Montanari, Baez–Pollard,
Fritz, Bonchi et al.
Chemically: membership in LPara
0

At the combinatorial tower levels L0, L3, L4 — stoichiometry, kinetics, and bond-
topological mechanisms — the membership conditions (E0), (E3), (E4) each admit
an explicit external characterisation. Four categorical frameworks supply these
characterisations in a form that an architecture can verify or fail, and together they
give the section’s classification criterion for the three lowest non-trivial Para levels.
Stoichiometry at LPara
0
