3
: Meseguer–Montanari and
Baez–Pollard.
The stoichiometric tower category L0(P) is exactly the free strict
SMC on a Petri net P of Meseguer and Montanari [32] (Chapter 2). Baez and
Pollard [31] extend this construction to open reaction networks, producing a gray-box
functor at L3 that reads off the input–output kinetics of a composed network from
its boundary data (Theorem 5.30). A closely related taxonomy of net categories —
commutative monoidal category nets, Σ-nets, and further variants — is developed
by Baez, Genovese, Master, and Shulman [278]; L0(P) of the tower corresponds to
one vertex of that taxonomy (the free strict SMC), with Baez–Master’s CMC [43] a
quotient in which all symmetry morphisms are identified (Remark 2.17).
The Para content of these identifications is direct. A yield or reaction-outcome pre-
dictor (Θ, fθ) lies in LPara
0
(P) iff its function class Func(Θ, fθ) (Remark 11.4) consists
of Sym(S)-equivariant maps with outputs in N|S| (or a real-valued approximation
thereof). A composed reaction-network predictor lies in the open-network analogue of

migration, and their reverses — are the string-diagram generators of the free SMC
that controls bond rearrangements, and DPO rewriting in the labelled-graph category
LGraphP is the operational semantics for their composition.

11.2.3. The Cruttwell–Gavranović framework and the L5–L6 interface
Chemically: bidirectional encoder–decoder–property architectures at the L5–L6 inter-
face, of which QIM [34] is the primary published example (Section 11.6), run in two
directions through a shared latent space: geometry →latent →property prediction,
and geometry →latent →reconstructed geometry. Each constituent forward map
sits at L5-type — strict LPara
5
(P) when the representation is fully equivariant, non-
strict for QIM under its Coulomb-matrix representation (Section 11.6) — and the
architecture as a whole is a triple of such maps trained jointly. The reconstruction
and property errors (RMSD, MAE) are measurable scalar quantities produced by
training, not categorical data attached to the morphisms.
The categorical framework supplied for gradient-trained parametric architectures
by Cruttwell, Gavranović, Ghani, Wilson, and Zanasi [277] differs structurally from
the three preceding bridges.
Markov categories characterise the Markov-kernel
component of (E3); string diagrams characterise the DPO-rewriting component of
(E4); NGN, natively or augmented with SE(3)-equivariant operations, characterises
the equivariance components of (E4) and (E5). Each identifies a specific tower level.
The CGGWZ framework does not. Its subject is the compositional semantics of
gradient-based learning in the 2-category Para(C): a parametric lens is a forward–
backward pair of morphisms, with forward component f : Θ ⊗X →Y in Para(C)
and a backward component propagating changes in outputs to changes in inputs
and parameters, so that sequential composition of lenses realises the chain rule
compositionally. The framework is about how gradient descent composes, not about
what a trained model represents at a particular tower level.
CGGWZ runs perpendicular to the tower. Every LPara
k
(P) 1-morphism trained
by backpropagation admits the CGGWZ lens structure once its gradient data is
made explicit — a kinetic model at LPara
3
just as much as a force field at LPara
5
or a
mechanism predictor at LPara
4

distinguish tower levels, and no forgetful functor Uk : Lk(P) →Lk−1(P) measures
where the framework’s vocabulary runs out, because its vocabulary tracks gradient
flow rather than level-specific structure. The CGGWZ framework is consequently
not a bridge to a single LPara
k
(P) in the sense of the three preceding subsections.

The encoder–decoder triple at the L5–L6 interface, in correct categorical
language. A common informal reading takes QIM’s encoder–decoder structure to be
a parametric lens. The categorical facts do not support this. QIM is three parametric
maps of L5-type through a shared latent Z (Section 11.6; non-strict LPara
5
(P) under
the Coulomb-matrix representation): the structure encoder (Θφ, qφ): Ce(G) →Z, the
structure decoder (Θθ, pθ): Z →Ce(G), and the property encoder (Θψ, pψ): Rd →Z
— the third network added in [34] for inverse design, taking properties to latent, not
latent to properties. pθ is a second forward map, not the backward map of a CGGWZ
lens; the two have different categorical signatures, as the backward component of a
parametric lens must carry a change object (tangent space, in the smooth case) that
pθ’s signature Z →Ce(G) does not. Nor does the encoder–decoder round trip pθ ◦qφ
produce a 2-morphism of Para(C): its deviation from idCe(G) measured on a test set
(the QM7-X RMSD of [34]) is a scalar training residual. A 2-morphism of Para(C) is
a reparametrisation r: Θ′ →Θ satisfying fθ ◦(r ⊗idX) = fθ′ (Definition 11.1), an
equation in C, not a real-valued error. The forward property-prediction path through
the shared latent approximates Π◦σ0 : Ce(G) →Rd (the Born–Oppenheimer ground-
state section followed by observable projection) implicitly, via the joint training
objective rather than a dedicated latent-to-property decoder (Section 11.6); the
approximation is numerical, and its error is not a 2-cell in any 2-category.
The categorical content at the L5–L6 interface is therefore precisely this.

§11.3. Classification of machine learning molecular architectures
Table 7 classifies the major ML molecular architectures by the highest tower level
k for which the function class Func(Θ, fθ) of a parametric 1-morphism (Θ, fθ) is
contained in Lk(P)(X, Y ) — the membership condition (Ek) of Definition 11.2. The
function class, defined in Remark 11.4, is the set of all morphisms the architecture
can represent as r ranges over C(I, Θ); it is independent of any particular training
run. The classification is therefore a statement about what the architecture can
represent, not about where a specific learned weight configuration lands.

DrFP’s map r 7→fp(r) composes SMILES
tokenisation, Morgan-substructure extraction, symmetric set difference R△P, and
hashed bit-folding to a vector in {0, 1}d. Two distinct tower objects fail to lift
through this pipeline. The free commutative monoid N[S] is lost first: hashing
maps distinct substructures to the same bit, bit-folding projects to {0, 1} and erases
counts, so Func(Θ, fp) lands in a multiplicity-forgetting quotient of N[S] strictly
below the free-commutative-monoid structure L0(P) requires. The Hess functor
FH : L1(P) →BR fails consequently: fp(r1 ◦r2) bears no R-additive relation to
fp(r1) ⊕fp(r2), so (E1) cannot even be stated in the codomain fp lives in. The
identity fp(r) = fp(r†) produced by the symmetric difference is not evidence of
L2-membership: it trivialises the dagger by collapsing forward and reverse reactions
to the identity in the codomain, before (·)† has any oriented reaction morphism left
to act on. The ceiling is accordingly the first lossy step in the pipeline: N[S] is
unrecoverable, and every higher structure depending on it — FH, ker(F T
G ), FP, the
DPO span — is unreachable as a matter of type, not training.

signature: labelling SO3LR as a partial L1 inhabitant is therefore a category error.

Level assignment. A model’s level is the highest k for which its function class
Func(Θ, fθ) is contained in Lk(P)(X, Y ) for every θ ∈Θ, not for the specific

attention (So3krates, SO3LR), not by data augmentation.

A ν-fold product captures a centred correlation among atom i and ν of its neighbours,

Body order and the forgetful functor U4
The feature Bi,ν at ACE order ν aggregates contributions from ν neighbours of
atom i through Clebsch–Gordan contraction, producing a (ν+1)-body correlation
indexed by O(3)-irrep labels (l, m) (with ν neighbour indices summed over
internally). The pre-contraction product Qν
k=1 A(1) has a superficial resemblance
to a ν-fold tensor product over bond generators — the combinatorial flavour of
L4(P), where ν-fold bond structures enter through DPO spans on LGraphP.
The resemblance is superficial. In the tower, the forgetful functor U4 : L5(P) →
L4(P) discards the configuration-orbifold data Ce(G) (the metric level of L5)
and retains only the labelled graph G ∈LGraphP, whose edges encode chemical
bonds by combinatorial data (bond order, formal charges, lone pairs). The
neighbour set driving the ACE contraction, by contrast, is metric: N(i) is the set
of atoms inside a sphere of radius rcut, computed directly from the coordinates.
A pair (i, j) can belong to N(i) at one geometry and not at another, without any
bond having formed or broken. The ACE contraction indices run over metric
neighbours (L5 data), not over bonded edges (L4 data), and the body-order
construction — despite its ν-fold appearance — does not factor through U4.
Proposition 11.9 makes this non-factorisation precise.

Remark 11.8 (Comonoid structure on ΘMACE; and what it does not encode).
Clause (ii) of Definition 11.2 requires the parameter space of a Para 1-morphism to
carry a comonoid structure (Θ, ∆, !) in the ambient cartesian category. For MACE
this is realised by the canonical cartesian comonoid: ∆: ΘMACE →ΘMACE⊗ΘMACE is
the diagonal (duplicating a parameter tensor), and !: ΘMACE →I is the unique map
to the terminal object (forgetting parameter dependence, not setting parameters to
any particular value). The terminal map ! carries no architecturally specific content
beyond the cartesian structure; the non-trivial ingredient is ∆.
The architectural role of ∆in MACE is the use of a single learned parameter tensor
in multiple places. The clearest example is element embeddings: a learned vector
hZ is associated with each chemical element Z and fed to every atom of element
Z in the molecule, realised by ∆duplicating the stored tensor into as many copies
as there are atoms of type Z. Within a single message-passing layer, architectural
weight sharing across atom-centred features is likewise implemented by ∆.
This comonoid structure is distinct from the separate expressiveness claim — the
question of which target morphisms the ACE body-order expansion can approximate,
as the ACE order and angular-momentum cutoff grow. The comonoid governs which
parameter reuses the architecture permits; expressiveness bounds what the composed
features can represent. Conflating the two has been a recurring error in informal
discussions of MACE’s tower coordinates.

The conflation in chemical practice
MACE achieves state-of-the-art accuracy for ground-state potential energy
surfaces precisely because LPara
5
(P) is the correct tower level for that task: the
PES is a function on Ce(G), and MACE’s body-ordered expansion produces a
scalar-energy output that is E(3)-invariant in the ambient coordinates R3n, hence
a well-defined function on the quotient Ce(G) = R3n/(SE(3) ⋉Aut(G)). (The
full E(3)-equivariance of the underlying feature map is what enables tensorial
outputs — dipoles, polarizabilities — as sections of the associated equivariant
bundles over Ce(G).) For standard molecular dynamics — propagating Newton’s

The conflation becomes operationally significant in three situations where the L4
content matters by itself. In reactive molecular dynamics, bond formation and
bond cleavage change the L4 labelled graph discontinuously, while MACE’s cutoff
graph registers the same event as a smooth variation in N(i); the architecture
does not mark the categorical transition between distinct objects of LGraphP
that defines a chemical reaction. In retrosynthesis, predicting which bonds cleave
and which form requires separating the L4 topology change from the concomitant
L5 geometry change; MACE cannot perform this separation, because its internal
feature graph is metric-dependent by construction and no functorial U4 lift
extracts the bond-topological component. In mechanism assignment, an SN1
and an SN2 path for the same net transformation pass through configurations
with different intermediate bond graphs G ∈LGraphP: SN1 transits through a
three-coordinate carbocation in one LGraphP-object; SN2 transits through a
pentavalent transition state in another. MACE assigns a scalar energy to each
nuclear configuration along either trajectory, but does not output a bond graph
at each configuration — and so the L4-level labelling that would distinguish
the intermediates (three- versus five-coordinate carbon, distinct DPO spans)
is absent from MACE’s type signature. Reaction-path analysis has to supply
this labelling externally, from data that Proposition 11.9 shows MACE does not
carry.

SO3LR, built on the So3krates backbone, makes a different structural point. It

functional form is known in advance is built into the architecture, leaving the

design factors known physics out of the function class architecturally. Tower-level
membership fixes what a model is blocked from representing; physics-informed range
separation is a separate architectural axis within a single tower level, distinct from
the strategy axis along which MACE and So3krates differ.
The section treats the two models in turn, then synthesises what they demonstrate
jointly.

11.5.2. SO3LR: physics-informed range separation within LPara
5
(P)
Pure neural-network force fields with finite cutoffs — MACE, NequIP, So3krates
in its standard form — predict a PES by learning the full interatomic interaction
from data, inside a receptive field determined by the cutoff radius or the attention
kernel’s support. For isolated small molecules this is adequate: the relevant physics
lives within a few Å of each atom, and the neural component has enough capacity to
represent the resulting short-range interactions. Condensed-phase systems are another
matter. Biomolecules in solvent, liquids, molecular crystals, and extended interfaces
have substantial energy contributions from long-range Coulomb and dispersion
interactions that fall off only polynomially (1/r and 1/r6 respectively) and remain
non-negligible far beyond any practical cutoff. Pure-MPNN architectures address
this either by extending the cutoff (computationally expensive and data-hungry, since
the network must learn 1/r from scratch) or by ignoring the tail (accepting errors
that accumulate over simulations of sufficiently large systems).
386


## Page 387


Kyunghoon Han
Categorification of Chemical Reactions
SO3LR [192] takes a structurally different approach. Its total energy decomposes as
ESO3LR(R) = EZBL(R) + ESo3k(R) + EElec({qi}, R) + EDisp({αi}, R),
where EZBL is the analytic Ziegler–Biersack–Littmark short-range repulsion, ESo3k
is the semilocal neural energy of the So3krates backbone, EElec = P
i<j qiqj/rij is a
pairwise Coulomb term evaluated with learned atomic partial charges qi(R), and
EDisp is a pairwise van der Waals dispersion term with learned atomic polarizabilities
αi(R). The short-range neural component carries the many-body correlations that the
network learns efficiently; the analytic long-range components carry the physics whose
functional form is known in advance and whose pairwise additivity the architecture
imposes as a structural constraint.
Observation 11.13 (SO3LR’s pairwise long-range form is codomain additivity, not
the Hess functor). SO3LR’s primary tower membership is LPara
5
(P): the So3krates
backbone satisfies (E5) architecturally (Proposition 11.10), and the scalar-energy
output places the full model in OrbMorse, subject to the same LPara
6
(P) ceiling as
every other MLFF in this section. What distinguishes SO3LR from a pure LPara
5
architecture is the structural content of its long-range sector. The Coulomb term
EElec = P
i<j qiqj/rij and the dispersion term EDisp are both pairwise additive over
atomic contributions, and this additivity is an architectural constraint, not a training-
emergent approximation: no parameter setting of SO3LR produces long-range terms
that violate it.
The natural temptation is to read this pairwise additivity as alignment with the
Hess functor FH : L0(P) →BR whose existence defines L1.
That reading is a
category error. The Hess functor’s domain is the reaction category L0(P), with
parallel composition of reaction morphisms r1 ⊗r2 and the parallel-composition
axiom FH(r1 ⊗r2) = FH(r1) + FH(r2) stated on those morphisms. SO3LR has no
reaction morphisms in its signature: its input is a nuclear configuration R ∈Ce(G),
its output is a scalar energy in R, and there is no L0(P)-domain on which FH could
be evaluated. The pairwise sum P
i<j V (qi, qj, rij) is additivity in the codomain R,
an algebraic property of how the energy expression is built up over atom pairs at
fixed configuration; it is not functoriality from a reaction category, and labelling
SO3LR’s long-range sector as a partial L1 inhabitant is the same kind of category
error as labelling any pairwise-additive scalar a Hess functor.
The architecturally honest reading of SO3LR’s design contribution is physics-informed
range separation: the functional form of the long-range tails is known analytically
(Coulomb 1/r, dispersion 1/r6), so the architecture supplies these analytically rather
than asking the neural backbone to learn them. The structural gain is independence
from training coverage on the long-range axis. A pure neural model can be made
more accurate on distribution-covered configurations but retains no architectural
guarantee about physics beyond its cutoff; SO3LR has the correct 1/r and 1/r6
behaviour built in, so the long-range functional form is correct even for atomic
configurations the training set never saw. This is a real design commitment, distinct
from MACE’s local Clebsch–Gordan strategy and from So3krates’s global attention,
but it is a design axis within LPara
5
(P), not a second tower-level membership.
The intermediate tower levels L2, L3, and L4 are orthogonal to SO3LR’s architectural
scope rather than violated by it: L2 concerns dagger-SMC detailed balance for
kinetic rate constants; L3 mass-action kinetics; L4 DPO graph rewriting for reaction

What the long-range sector buys SO3LR
For molecules in vacuum at a scale where long-range physics is negligible,
SO3LR and a pure neural force field like So3krates or MACE are structurally
interchangeable: the short-range neural component dominates the total energy
and the analytic tail is numerically small. The distinction emerges in condensed-
phase systems. Consider two subsystems S1, S2 at separation r ≫rcut. A pure
MPNN with a 5 Å cutoff computes E(S1 ∪S2) = E(S1) + E(S2), missing the
Coulomb contribution (∼1/r) and the dispersion contribution (∼1/r6) between
them entirely. SO3LR’s range-separated architecture returns, at that separation,
E(S1)+E(S2)+EElec(S1, S2)+EDisp(S1, S2) — the physically correct long-range
terms, supplied analytically with parameters (qi, αi) the neural backbone has
learned.
The structural gain is that the functional form of the long-range terms does not
depend on training coverage. A pure neural model can be made more accurate
on distribution-covered configurations but retains no architectural guarantee
about physics beyond its cutoff; SO3LR has the Coulomb and dispersion tails
built in, so their form is correct even for atomic configurations the training set
never saw. This is the practical face of the physics-informed range separation
discussed in Observation 11.13: the long-range functional form is a structural
architectural commitment, not an empirical fit, and is independent of training
coverage.
Two axes of architectural design at a single tower level
So3krates and SO3LR together illustrate that tower-level membership is a single
coordinate among several architectural ones. Both are objects of LPara

(P) and
both are categorically blocked from LPara

(P) they differ along two independent axes.
The first axis is the architectural strategy for realising (E5). MACE contracts
through local Clebsch–Gordan tensor products; So3krates couples through SE(3)-
equivariant attention on an SPHC basis. Both produce parametric 1-morphisms
of LPara
5
(P), and the tower does not distinguish them at level 5. This is the

The second axis is whether the architecture incorporates physics-informed struc-

Structure encoder (Θφ, qφ): Ce(G) →Z. Maps a molecular geometry R ∈Ce(G)
to a latent code z ∈Z. The input is presented to the network via the Coulomb-
matrix representation [34], which is SE(3)-invariant by construction (but not Sym(S)-
invariant: atom permutations change the matrix, a representation-inherited limitation
discussed in Observation 11.14 below). The conditional qφ(z | R) is a Gaussian
distribution over Z whose mean and variance depend on R, and z is sampled via the
reparametrisation trick.
Structure decoder (Θθ, pθ): Z →Ce(G). Reverses the encoder. pθ(R | z) is a
conditional distribution over geometries; ˆR = mean(pθ(· | z)) is the reconstructed
structure, recovered from the decoded Coulomb matrix via classical multidimensional
scaling up to a chirality transformation, a residual ambiguity of the Coulomb-matrix
representation documented in [34].
Property encoder (Θψ, pψ): Rd →Z. Maps a target property tuple y ∈Rd to a
latent-code distribution pψ(z | y). This is the third network added in [34] on top
of the standard VAE, enabling inverse design. The naming is deliberate: pψ moves
from properties to latent, not from latent to properties. QIM has no dedicated
latent-to-property map, and the forward structure-to-property path is only implicit
through the shared latent — a point that becomes load-bearing in Observation 11.14.

The shared-latent structure enables three operational modes.
Inverse design, the direction for which QIM is named, applies the property encoder

Forward property prediction follows the opposite path through the shared latent:
apply the structure encoder to obtain z = mean(qφ(· | R)), then recover a property

at training time. No dedicated latent-to-property decoder exists in the architecture;
forward property prediction is an emergent consequence of the joint training (34),
not a primitive operation. The composition approximates Π ◦σ0 : Ce(G) →Rd —
the Born–Oppenheimer ground-state section followed by observable projection —
implicitly, through the shared latent Z.

§11.7. Three incompleteness results
The classification in Section 11.3 identifies three architectural gaps separating current
Para-morphism practice from a hypothetical model that fully inhabits the tower.
The three results differ in both character and severity, and they are presented in
order of increasing severity — with the numbering reversed, so that Gap 1 names
the deepest result and is presented last:
• Gap 3 (structural, presented first): no architecture jointly enforces Eyring
TST coherence between LPara
3
rate-law output and LPara
5
PES output.
• Gap 2 (thermodynamic, presented second): no neural kinetic model with
independently parameterised forward and reverse rate constants enforces the
Wegscheider consistency condition.
• Gap 1 (topological, presented last): architectures with output type OrbMorse
are categorically blocked from LPara
6
(P).
Gaps 3 and 2 are contingent on the state of the published literature: each records
that no current architecture enforces a given tower-coherence condition, but such
an architecture could in principle be constructed without changing output types.
They are therefore stated as literature-survey observations. Gap 1 is intrinsic: a
categorical theorem that LPara
6
(P) membership is unreachable from any architecture
with output type OrbMorse, regardless of training-set size, parameter count, or other
architectural choices within that output constraint. It is stated as a proposition with
proof.

The published literature divides cleanly into two non-communicating communities.
Neural kinetic models — ChemNODE [281], CRNN [282], and their extensions —
predict rate laws (Θk, kθ): L0(P) →Stoch from macroscopic concentration time-
series. CRNN’s Arrhenius parameterisation k = A T b exp(−Ea/RT) encodes an
activation energy Ea as a learned scalar parameter extracted from rate data, not
as a barrier computed from any atomistic PES. Machine-learning force fields —
NequIP [272], MACE [271], So3krates [273] — predict the PES (ΘE, Eθ): L4.5(P) →
OrbMorse from energy and force data. When rate constants are required downstream,
the learned PES feeds into a separate TST, ring-polymer molecular dynamics, or
instanton calculation run as an independent step.
No published architecture contains both (Θk, kθ) and (ΘE, Eθ) as jointly trained
components with condition (TST) enforced: no loss function in the reviewed literature
contains a term penalising the difference between an emergent rate from PES
simulation and a directly learned rate constant. The technical infrastructure for
building such an architecture — end-to-end differentiable molecular dynamics and
rate theory — exists in principle but has not been applied to this problem.
Why the gap matters for reactive simulations
Reactive molecular dynamics with an MLFF simulates trajectories on V0(R) and
reads off an effective rate constant from the observed crossing frequency. Nothing
guarantees that this emergent rate satisfies the Eyring equation relative to the
model’s own barrier, because the model’s energy function was not trained to
produce barrier heights consistent with any experimental rate. In a functorially
coherent architecture, the L3 rate would be derived from the L5 barrier via
condition (TST), with the rate and PES components sharing a single parameter
space as the Para-enriched level LPara

The topological gap is architectural, not empirical
Proposition 11.19 is not a statement about training-set size, model capacity,
or distribution coverage. The Berry-phase class [γB] ∈H1(Ce(G) \ X01, Z2)
assigns a Z2-value to each homology class of loops encircling X01; the analogous

These are not pointwise functions on Ce(G) at all — they are global topological
invariants of the eigenbundle. The Berry connection Aµ
mn is a u(N)-valued 1-
form on Ce(G) with state indices (m, n), again not extractable from a pointwise
scalar. A model with output type OrbMorse produces, at every geometry R,
a real number and a covariant vector: a scalar field on Ce(G), nothing more.

Completeness as an architectural diagnostic.
Classical ML benchmarks
measure accuracy on held-out data at a fixed trained parameter setting.
Defi-
nition 11.5 provides a sharper criterion: a model (Θ, fθ) is complete at level k
on a target morphism φ ∈Lk(P)(X, Y ) if and only if φ lies in the function class
Func(Θ, fθ) ⊆Lk(P)(X, Y ) — equivalently, if some reparametrisation r: I →Θ
instantiates fθ to φ exactly. Completeness is a property of the model’s function class,
independent of training data. A model that cannot express the Berry connection Aµ
mn
as part of its output type will fail at predicting geometric-phase effects in ultracold
reactions, photodissociation branching ratios, and conical-intersection dynamics —
not because it was trained on too little data, but because the relevant structure is not
representable within the function class at all. The diagnostic therefore distinguishes
failure modes that more data can fix from those it cannot.
11.8.2. Three research targets forced by the tower
The tower is not only a classification of what exists. Turned around, it is a design
specification: each level specifies, via its membership condition and forgetful functor
structure, what a model must do architecturally to represent the chemistry at that
level faithfully. The three gaps identified in Section 11.7 define three concrete research
targets — not aspirational goals, but consequences forced by the tower’s structure,
in the same sense that each tower level was forced bottom-up by reaction pairs the
previous level could not distinguish.

§12. The lower tower in executable form: Φop on the Briggs–
Rauscher oscillator
The preceding chapters have constructed a categorical tower that stratifies chemistry
by level of structure: stoichiometry at L0, thermodynamics at L1–L2, kinetics at
L3, mechanism at L4, with L4.5 stereochemistry and higher levels above.
The
tower’s content is not mere vocabulary: at every level it delivers theorems. At L3,
Feinberg’s Deficiency Zero Theorem forces weakly-reversible mass-action networks
with deficiency δ = 0 to admit a unique positive stationary measure per stoichiometric
class — which is precisely why oscillating networks like the Briggs–Rauscher reaction
must have δ > 0. At L4, the parameter projection π4 (§12.8) constrains exactly
which mechanism data can survive into the L3 rate constants, making the gap
between mechanism-resolved and rate-resolved descriptions explicit rather than
tacit. These are not modelling choices that could have gone differently; they are
categorical consequences of the tower’s construction. If the tower is to be more than
a formal scaffold, those consequences have to survive contact with an executable
implementation evaluated against a specific chemistry.
This chapter closes the tower at the bottom by constructing a functor

§12.1. The Briggs–Rauscher reaction as a forcing ladder
12.1.1. The empirical problem
The Briggs–Rauscher (BR) reaction [146] is the clock reaction in which an acidic batch
of iodate, hydrogen peroxide, malonic acid, and a manganese(II) catalyst oscillates
visibly between colourless, amber, and dark blue before settling into equilibrium. Its
net stoichiometry,
IO−
3 + 2 H2O2 + CH2(COOH)2 + H+ −→ICH(COOH)2 + 2 O2 + 3 H2O,
(38)

contains no information about the oscillation: it is L0 data, identical to that of a
hypothetical non-oscillating reaction with the same input and output complexes.
Two parallel skeleton mechanisms were proposed in 1982 by Noyes and Furrow [147]
and independently by De Kepper and Epstein [35] in the same volume of JACS.
Both decompose the dynamics into two pathways for hypoiodous-acid production:
Process A (ionic, dominant at high [I−]), through sequential heterolytic O–I bond
formations via HIO2 and I2 intermediates; and Process B (radical, dominant at low
[I−]), through homolytic IO−
3 + HIO2 →2 IO•
2 with Mn(II)/Mn(III) cycling supplying
single-electron transfer. Process A consumes I−; the iodination of malonic acid by
I2 regenerates it. The system switches between A and B across a threshold in [I−],
and that switching is the mechanical content of the oscillation. The implementation
in BR.Mechanism (§12.3) follows the De Kepper–Epstein variant with two explicit
reverse channels (R3-rev and R4-rev), giving twelve reactions in total.
A and B are indistinguishable below L4: they share the L0 net stoichiometry of (38),
and their bulk net HOI-production rates share the form ˙cHOI = keff [IO−
3 ] [H2O2] with
only keff differing. Their distinction — heterolytic versus homolytic bond character —
is recorded in the DPO graph of each elementary step and is L4 data. The simulation
in §12.7 is provably blind to the A/B distinction; the main tower’s L4 chapter
(Observation 6.46) develops this blindness as a categorical theorem.

§12.2. Target category: Hask and BorelStoch
A categorical interpretation of the simulation must fix a category for total Haskell —
the operational layer in which the program runs — and a target category for the
stochastic content of L3 — the denotational layer in which distributions live — and
a functor sending the first to the second. The payoff is concrete: every claim about
the simulator’s accuracy will attach to a specific morphism in one of these categories
and to a specific user-controllable parameter (§12.5 onwards). This section fixes the
two categories; §12.7 builds the functor.
12.2.1. Why not naive Hask
The naive category with Haskell types as objects and all Haskell functions as
morphisms fails the identity law: Bauer [315] observes that seq ⊥() differs from
seq (⊥. id) (), so id is not a categorical identity under composition. Danielsson,
Hughes, Jansson, and Gibbons [316] prove that the total fragment of a partial lan-
guage forms a bicartesian closed category in which equational reasoning is sound.
By Hask in the rest of this chapter we mean that total fragment.
Assumption 12.1 (Totality and purity of the simulation core). Every function in
the simulation core — the L0 invariants atomConservation, chargeConservation;
the constructors mkReaction, mkNetwork; the L3 realisations BR.ODE.simulate
with stepAdaptive, and BR.SSA.simulate with step — is total and pure on its
domain. Stochasticity in BR.SSA is supplied entirely by the vendored BR.PRNG (a
state-threaded SplitMix64), so the IO monad never appears in the call graph: no
System.Random, no unsafePerformIO, no FFI, no exceptions. File I/O is confined
to BR.Output, which acts only at the simulation boundary and is not invoked by any
function below it.
Remark 12.2 (Why no Kl(IO)). With BR.PRNG pure and explicit, both the ODE and
SSA realisations of L3 live in Hask, not in a Kleisli category of a probability monad
in the sense of monadic semantics for computational effects [317]. Introducing Kl(IO),
the Kleisli category of the Haskell IO monad, would therefore add no structure here:
the simulator would use only the pure Kleisli arrows
A
f−→B
return
−−−→IO B,
i.e. the wide subcategory
{return ◦f : f ∈Hask(A, B)} ⊆Kl(IO)(A, B).
We therefore target Hask directly.

12.2.2. Two-layer semantics: operational and denotational
The stochastic content of L3 requires a Markov category.
Definition 12.3 (Markov category; BorelStoch [312]). A Markov category is
a semicartesian symmetric monoidal category (C, ⊗, I) in which every object X
carries a natural commutative comonoid (copyX, delX) and every morphism f is
counital, delY ◦f = delX. Equivalently, it is a category in which the algebra of
probability — sampling, copying, discarding, composing — is expressible as pure
morphism manipulation, without making measure-theoretic integrals part of the
primary syntax. BorelStoch is the Markov category whose objects are standard
Borel spaces (measurable spaces arising from a Polish topology, i.e. a complete
separable metric — countable sets, Rn, and finite products thereof) and whose
morphisms are measurable Markov kernels. It is a Borel restriction of the Kleisli
category Kl(G) of the Giry monad G [318], the probability-measure monad sending
each measurable space to its space of probability measures.
Hask is Cartesian and deterministic: any morphism in Hask between standard Borel
spaces embeds into BorelStoch as a Dirac kernel — the degenerate Markov kernel
placing all mass on a single point, i.e. the embedding of a deterministic function
as a distribution concentrated at f(a). All Haskell types appearing in this chapter
(Word64, Double, Map Species Int, lists thereof) are countable or Polish, so this
restriction is automatic. Two categories are necessary because the stochastic content
lives in BorelStoch (where one states theorems and accuracy bounds), but the
simulator runs in Hask (where one debugs, profiles, and extends). The functor F
below keeps the two pictures in sync: the seed-marginal of any executable Haskell
program is the Markov kernel it samples from.
Proposition 12.4 (Seed-marginalisation functor). F formalises the operation “run
the simulator with random seeds, infinitely many times, and read off the distribution of
outputs” as a functor. Concretely, let W = Word64 with the uniform distribution µW,

12.2.3. One genuine laxity: γ
In an IO-based formulation of this story (a System.Random-style codebase), Φop
would carry three lax cells: a unit α, an IO-sequencing β, and a truncation/numerical
γ. Two of the three collapse for BR. In pure Hask, Cartesian product is strictly
associative and commutative on the nose, so the parallel composition of two seed-
parameterised morphisms is invariant under sequencing: β is strict, not lax. The
unit cell α becomes the parameter-tensor unit isomorphism of the Para bicategory
Para(Hask), treated as canonical coherence data (§12.6) rather than as a laxity of
Φop. The only cell that remains is γ:
The γ-cell: truncation
γ is the gap between what the simulator returns and the exact stochastic
dynamics it approximates.
The two branches behave differently: SSA’s γ-
component reduces to PRNG- and floating-point-level numerical artifacts (no
separate user knob); ODE’s γ-component is a deterministic step-size error driven
to zero by a user-specified tolerance.

at termination agrees with the exact CTMC state at τ in distribution under all

Neither qualification is a user knob in the ordinary sense; the SSA branch of γ

ODE branch (state-space metric). The implicit-midpoint integrator in
BR.ODE produces a deterministic trajectory; its discrepancy from the true mass-
action trajectory is measured in state-space sup norm rather than TV. The local
truncation error is O(h3) per step, controlled adaptively by step doubling to a
user-specified tolerance — the user knob is the integration tolerance. Embedded
as Dirac kernels in BorelStoch, the discrepancy is invisible to the TV metric
(which collapses to 0 or 1 between distinct Diracs); the relevant metric on the
ODE side of γ is therefore Wasserstein-1 (or directly state-space) rather than
TV.
The two branches differ in both the form of γ (effectively zero in distribution
on SSA, deterministic step-size error on ODE) and the metric in which it is
measured (TV on SSA, state-space on ODE). The asymmetry is structural:
SSA’s exactness modulo numerical artifacts is intrinsic to the Gibson–Bruck
NRM (§12.5), whereas the ODE branch carries a genuine numerical laxity
controllable by odeRTol and odeATol.
Remark 12.6 (Para is base-portable). The Para construction applies over any symmet-
ric monoidal base category; varying the base gives different applications (Smooth
for backpropagation in machine learning, Hask here for executable simulation,
BorelStoch for fully probabilistic kernels). Capucci and Myers [320] show that all
these incarnations are instances of a single two-categorical pattern, so transferring
techniques between them is structural rather than ad hoc. The seed-marginalisation
functor F above realises this bridge from the Hask incarnation to a Markov-category
target for our specific choice of uniform seed distribution on W; other distributions
would yield other functors with the same shape.
§12.3. L0 in Haskell: Multiset Species as free commutative monoid
Level L0 is the tower’s stoichiometric foundation. Its objects are elements of the free
commutative monoid N[S] on the finite species set S (Equation (1)); its morphisms
are stoichiometric changes (reaction vectors in ZS); its functorial invariants are the
combinatorial data (n, ℓ, s) — the number of distinct complexes, the number of
linkage classes (connected components of the reaction graph), and the rank of the
stoichiometric matrix — and the deficiency δ = n−ℓ−s. Two L0 structural integrity
tests — atom and charge conservation — attach to every reaction and must pass
before any L3 dynamics are simulated. This section shows how the BR codebase
410


## Page 411


Kyunghoon Han
Categorification of Chemical Reactions
realises each of these pieces concretely.
12.3.1. The free commutative monoid in Haskell
The set N[S] of Equation (1) carries a commutative monoid structure under pointwise
addition with the universal property that any function φ : S →M to a commu-
tative monoid M extends uniquely to a homomorphism ¯φ : N[S] →M. The BR
implementation realises both in a single newtype.
Proposition 12.7 (L0 implementation). The newtype Multiset Species of
BR.Multiset exactly implements N[S] as an object of L0:
(i) (Bijection.) The invariant that the underlying Map Species Int has no entries
with value ≤0, maintained by every smart constructor, puts Multiset Species
in bijection with N[S].
(ii) (Monoid.) munion is pointwise addition; empty is the identity.
(iii) (Universal property.) For any Haskell commutative monoid M and any φ :
Species →M, the unique extending homomorphism ¯φ : Multiset Species →
M is given by
¯φ = foldMap (\(s, n) -> stimes n (phi s)) .
toList.
Each item is settled directly by the code in BR.Multiset:
BR/Multiset.hs — the function bodies that realise Proposition 12.7
-- Invariant: the underlying Map has no entries with value ≤0.
newtype Multiset a = Multiset { _runMultiset :: Map a Int }
-- Smart constructor preserving the invariant: realises (i).
fromListWith :: Ord a ⇒(Int →Int →Int) →[(a, Int)] →Multiset a
fromListWith f xs = Multiset
(M.filter (> 0) (M.fromListWith f [(k, n) | (k, n) ←xs, n ̸= 0]))
-- The monoid operation: realises (ii).
munion :: Ord a ⇒Multiset a →Multiset a →Multiset a
munion (Multiset a) (Multiset b) = Multiset (M.unionWith (+) a b)
-- The N-action n . s of N[S].
scale :: Int →Multiset a →Multiset a
scale k (Multiset m)
| k ≤0
= Multiset M.empty
| otherwise = Multiset (fmap (* k) m)
Proof. (i) Every smart constructor preserves the invariant — either by an outer
M.filter (> 0) (fromListWith, difference, subtractM) or by structural argu-
ment (munion’s pointwise sum of positives is positive; scale and singleton guard
their non-positive inputs). The positive-coefficient entries of the map are then in
bijection with the nonzero terms of an element of N[S].
(ii) munion unfolds to M.unionWith (+), which is pointwise sum on each key;
commutativity and associativity descend from those of (+) on Int, and empty is the

12.3.2. L0 structural integrity: atom and charge conservation
A multiset r ∈N[S] has only multiplicity data. Attaching it to a reaction rsrc →rtgt
as a L0 morphism, two linear conditions on the reaction vector rtgt −rsrc ∈ZS
must hold for the reaction to represent a physically meaningful elementary step:
conservation of each chemical element, and conservation of total formal charge.
Definition 12.8 (Atom and charge conservation at L0). For each element a ∈
{H, C, O, I, Mn}, let φa : S →N be the function
s 7→M.findWithDefault 0 a (formula s)

canonical monoid-homomorphism extensions to N[S] (Proposition 12.7(iii)) are
denoted ¯φa : N[S] →N and ¯q : N[S] →Z.
A reaction rsrc →rtgt is atom-balanced if ¯φa(rtgt) −¯φa(rsrc) = 0 for every element a,
and charge-balanced if ¯q(rtgt) −¯q(rsrc) = 0. A network is L0-integral if every reaction
in it is both.

12.3.3. Deficiency and the L0 →L3 structure of DZT
The deficiency δ = n −ℓ−s is entirely an L0 invariant: it is computed from the
stoichiometric matrix ν ∈ZS×R — the matrix of L0-morphism data — without
reference to rate constants, thermodynamics, or mechanism. Theorem 2.29 states
the L0 consequence of δ = 0; Theorem 5.26 strengthens this to assertions about the
mass-action vector field once a rate functor FP is supplied at L3.
Remark 12.9 (Cross-level structure of DZT). The hypotheses of Theorem 2.29 (weak
reversibility, δ = 0) are pure L0 data; the conclusions become assertions about the
mass-action flow only once a rate functor FP is chosen, at which point the statement
strengthens to Theorem 5.26. This is the tower’s reading of the Feinberg programme:
DZT and DOT are L0 →L3 theorems whose content straddles the combinatorial and
kinetic levels. A fully categorical proof would make the straddling functorial.
L0 data of the Briggs–Rauscher network
The De Kepper–Epstein implementation (BR.Mechanism.briggsRauscherDE,
§12.1) has |S| = 15 species and twelve reactions (the ten elementary steps
R1–R10 plus explicit reverses R3-rev, R4-rev). Hand enumeration of distinct
source/target multisets gives n = 20 complexes distributed over ℓ= 10 linkage
classes (each elementary forward/reverse pair occupies its own class, since no two
elementary steps share a source or target complex); the rank s of the stoichio-
metric matrix is computable by Gaussian elimination but plays no role below.
Running the L0 checks gives atomConservation briggsRauscherDE == True
(each of H, C, O, I, Mn balanced in every reaction) and chargeConservation
briggsRauscherDE == True (net charge zero in every reaction), so the network
is L0-integral in the sense of Definition 12.8.
Why the deficiency theorems are silent on BR. Of the twelve reactions,
only the two pairs R3/R3-rev and R4/R4-rev carry explicit reverses; the re-
maining eight elementary steps (R1, R2, R5–R10) are unidirectional in the
implementation. The network is therefore not weakly reversible, and the hy-
potheses of both Theorem 2.29 and the Deficiency One Theorem fail regardless
of the value of δ. L0 alone cannot predict the BR steady-state structure —
and indeed, no steady state exists during the oscillatory phase: the system
is held far from equilibrium by the buffered substrate pool (IO−
3 , H2O2, MA,
Mn2+) and cycles between Process A and Process B without converging. This
is the chapter’s first concrete demonstration that L0 data alone is insufficient:
the dynamical content lives strictly at L3 and requires the simulator built in
subsequent sections.
§12.4. L1–L2: detailed-balance constraints on rate constants
Levels L1 (enthalpies) and L2 (free-energy and reversibility) extend L0 by a monoidal
functor FH : L1 →(R, +), an entropy extension giving F T
G = FH −T FS at L2, and a †-
structure identifying each reaction with its reverse. In the BR implementation these
data are not stored: BR.Reaction carries only L0 stoichiometry (rxnReactants,
rxnProducts) and L3 kinetics (rxnRate, rxnRateActive, rxnSaturation), plus
metadata (rxnName, rxnProvenance, rxnCitation). The full record:

FH(r2 ◦r1) = FH(r1) + FH(r2)

FH(id) = 0.
FH is not a field of BR.Reaction; the implementation stores no per-reaction enthalpies,

at one temperature determines ∆G◦(T), not the splitting ∆G◦= ∆H◦−T∆S◦. Hess’s

i FH(ri) = 0 on closed cycles is a non-trivial constraint only when the reaction
graph contains a cycle of length ≥3 (for example, a triangle A ↔B ↔C ↔A); on
a trivial 2-cycle r ◦r−1 it reduces to FH(r) + FH(r−1) = 0, which is already enforced
by the †-structure (below). In BR’s implemented network the only cycles are the
two trivial reverse-pair cycles R3 ◦R3-rev and R4 ◦R4-rev, so Hess’s Law adds no
information beyond the dagger structure. The substantive L1/L2 content of the
network enters at L2 via the free-energy/rate-constant connection treated next.

Level L2 adds an entropy FS(r) and the temperature-dependent free-energy functor
F T
G (r) = FH(r) −TFS(r), together with a †-structure: each reaction has a reverse
r† satisfying FH(r†) = −FH(r), FS(r†) = −FS(r), and hence F T
G (r†) = −F T
G (r). The
equilibrium locus is ker F T
G = {r : F T

In the BR codebase the †-structure is realised explicitly only for two of the ten
elementary steps, by including their reverses as separate mkReaction calls with
reactant and product multisets swapped:
• R3 / R3-rev: iodine hydrolysis HOI + I−+ H+ ⇌I2 + H2O with kR3 =
3.1 × 1012 M−2 s−1 and kR3-rev = 0.73 s−1 (the latter first-order in I2 after [H2O]

The remaining eight elementary reactions (R1, R2, R5–R10) are unidirectional in
the implementation: no reverse Reaction value is paired with them. The †-structure
is therefore incomplete on the implemented network — consistent with BR being not
weakly reversible (§12.3 chembox). The implementation reads each missing reverse
as “physically present but kinetically negligible on the simulation timescale,” an
approximation we revisit empirically in §12.9.

published treatment [147, 35] and is exactly what makes BR not weakly reversible

is therefore confined to the two detailed-balance identities of (40).

§12.5. L3 in Hask: exact SSA and adaptive ODE as parallel operational
realisations
The stochastic content of L3 is carried by a functor FP that sends each reaction
network N with rate constants to the τ-indexed family of time-τ transition ker-
nels of its continuous-time Markov chain (CTMC) on population states. We write
FP(N)τ ∈BorelStoch for the kernel at horizon τ; it is this family that the op-
erational arrows below realise. The BR codebase implements two simulators in
Hask: BR.SSA.simulate samples FP(N)τ exactly (for τ set as ssaTimeMax), and
BR.ODE.simulate integrates the deterministic large-volume shadow of FP.
• BR.SSA.simulate: an exact Gibson–Bruck next-reaction method (NRM) that
samples the CTMC at the molecule-count level. Its denotational image, after
marginalising over the PRNG seed, is FP(N)τ exactly — modulo SplitMix
PRNG quality and floating-point precision; there is no step-budget or τ-leap
truncation.
• BR.ODE.simulate: an adaptive implicit-midpoint Newton integrator that pro-
duces the deterministic large-volume mass-action flow, the V →∞Kurtz limit
of the CTMC [106], with a local truncation error controlled by step-doubling.
Both arrows share their L0 + L3 input — a Network record (§12.4) plus an initial
counts or concentrations map — and both are purely functional: no IO, no global
mutable state, no impurity at the type level. The SSA threads its SplitMix64 PRNG
through the ssaPRNG field of SSAState; the ODE is deterministic and uses no PRNG.
The γ-cell of Φop (§12.2) specialises here to zero in distribution for SSA and to the
implicit-midpoint local truncation error for ODE.

remains the correct product of Exp(aµ) distributions. The step iteration terminates
only when (a) all putative times are infinite (no firable reaction), or (b) the next
firing time exceeds τ. Both are correct stopping rules for the time-τ kernel: in
case (a) the chain has reached an absorbing state and remains there through τ; in
case (b) no further event occurs in [t, τ]. Hence ssaCounts of the last Just-state
equals the CTMC state at time τ in both cases. No truncation is introduced. The
qualifications (i) and (ii) above are the only departures from exactness: SplitMix64
passes BigCrush [319], and exponential (in BR.PRNG) clamps the input to the
inverse-CDF −log(u′)/a at u′ = 2−53 whenever a draw underflows to u = 0; this
replaces only a probability-2−53 tail event with the maximum draw log(253)/a ≈37/a,
leaving the exponential distribution unchanged elsewhere.
Remark 12.13 (The γ-cell of Φop, made concrete). The lax cell γ of Φop (§12.2) is the
TV-metric laxity for the stochastic arrow and the state-space local truncation error
for the deterministic arrow. Theorem 12.12 states that for SSA the TV component of
γ vanishes (up to qualifications (i)–(ii)): BR.SSA has no τ-leap, no step-budget, and
no fixed-step-size approximation. The remaining content of γ lives entirely on the
ODE arrow: the implicit-midpoint scheme with step-doubling control bounds the per-
component local truncation error in species s by odeATol + odeRTol · |cs| (BR.ODE
uses a weighted max-norm of these component errors as its step-control criterion),
accumulated over the trajectory; this is what Remark 12.15 below compares against
the SSA’s exact samples.
Remark 12.14 (Pure-functional rather than Kleisli semantics). Most categorical-CRN
expositions treat the rate-equation ODE only (e.g. Baez–Pollard’s open dynamical
systems [31]); a Haskell-side stochastic treatment of the CME would naturally
reach for a Kleisli category of IO or a similar effect-type framework. The BR.SSA
implementation chooses neither: the PRNG state is a pure value in SSAState, and
step and simulate are total functions in Hask with no Kleisli or monadic structure
visible at the type level. The stochastic semantics enters only via the para-monoidal
lift of §12.2, where the PRNG seed becomes the parameter object W = {0, 1}64 and
seed-marginalisation produces the Markov kernel. This is operationally minimal: no
IO taint propagates, replay is trivial (just store the seed), and the type SSAState

type (Double for concentrations vs. Int for counts). Kurtz’s limit theorem predicts
agreement between CTMC and ODE on macroscopic observables at high molecule
counts; fluctuation corrections of order 1/√V NA (the chemical Langevin / van
Kampen Ω-expansion scale) surface most strongly on low-population radical species
(IO•
2, HO•
2).
12.5.5. The two L3 arrows as parallel operational realisations
Remark 12.15 (SSA and ODE as parallel operational realisations of L3). BR.SSA.simulate
and BR.ODE.simulate are two Haskell functions running side-by-side over the same
L0+L3 input data — a Network record plus an initial counts or concentrations
map — though their precise source and target types differ (see the haskellbox signa-
tures above; the SSA takes one SSAState, the ODE takes a curried ODEConfig →
ODEState →Double). The SSA delivers a sampled trajectory of molecule counts,
the ODE delivers a deterministic trajectory of concentrations. Their denotational
images differ: the SSA’s (under the para-monoidal lift of §12.2) is FP(N)τ itself,
by Theorem 12.12; the ODE evaluates the deterministic large-volume shadow of
FP, realised via the Kurtz limit X/(V NA) ⇝c. Both functions nonetheless read
the rate constants, saturation data, and stoichiometry from a single Network value
without translation, and agree on observables well-defined in the V →∞limit while
disagreeing on finite-population fluctuations.

L3 on the BR network
The implementation briggsRauscherDE (§12.3) is driven at canonical BR con-

3 ]0, [H2O2]0, [MA]0, [Mn2+]0 in the published ranges ∼10−2–1 M

• No step-budget truncation. BR.SSA.step terminates only on (a) all puta-
tive times being infinite (no firable reaction) or (b) the next firing time
exceeding ssaTimeMax. Both are exact stopping rules for the time-τ kernel,
so the TV component of γ (Theorem 12.12) is zero in distribution. The
qualifications are PRNG quality (SplitMix64) and floating-point precision
in exponential.
• Volume choice. ssaVolumeL = 1e-15 (one femtolitre) is the default, chosen
to keep molecule counts tractable: at this volume, a millimolar species
has ∼6 × 105 molecules and a 10 µM species ∼6 × 103. Higher volumes
amplify event rates linearly in V ; the iodine-equilibration channel R3/R3-
rev (rate constants 3.1×1012 M−2 s−1 and 0.73 s−1; §12.4) is typically the
dominant event channel and the principal constraint on the largest tractable
simulation volume.
• Stiffness for the ODE. Numerical rate constants in briggsRauscherDE
span roughly ten orders of magnitude (R3 forward at 3.1×1012 down to R9
at 12.5 and R10 at 37, with R3-rev at 0.73 in different units). This forces
BR.ODE to use an implicit scheme: explicit Runge–Kutta would require
step sizes too small to integrate even one BR oscillation in reasonable
wall-clock time. The adaptive implicit-midpoint Newton method with
step-doubling is the source of the ODE component of γ (Remark 12.13).
• Where SSA and ODE should differ. At the simulator’s tractable volumes
(∼1 fL by default), the SSA is expected to show fluctuations on whichever
species are held at low occupancy by the dynamics — typically radical
intermediates such as IO•
2 — which the ODE smooths to its mean-field
shadow. The rate constants in briggsRauscherDE (shared by both arrows
via the Network record) have been tuned to reproduce the experimental
BR oscillation period under the deterministic ODE (typically reported
in the ∼10–50 s range, depending on initial conditions and temperature
[147, 35]); whether the SSA at the simulator’s small volume also reproduces
this period, or shows drift from finite-population effects, is the empirical
question addressed in §12.9.
§12.6. The Para construction in Hask
The Para construction [277] formalises a morphism parameterised by an external
object. For BR, the parameter is the SplitMix64 seed ssaSeed ∈W = {0, 1}64 that
fixes the SSA’s random trajectory, threaded purely through ssaPRNG (§12.5); for
the ODE, the parameter is empty. Para gives the categorical home for “a Haskell
function plus its stored parameter,” decoupling the parameter algebra (how seeds
compose) from the underlying-morphism algebra (how SSA and ODE trajectories
compose). We give the abstract definition, instantiate it over Hask, and verify the
coherence laws — which here separate cleanly into a strict underlying layer (function
composition in Hask is on the nose) and a bicategorical parameter-tensor layer
426


## Page 427


Kyunghoon Han
Categorification of Chemical Reactions
(tuple-isomorphism coherence).
12.6.1. Abstract Para
Definition 12.16 (Para construction [277, Def. 3.1]). Let (C, ⊗, I) be a symmetric
monoidal category with a right actegory action M ↷C. The bicategory Para(C)
has:
• Objects: those of C.
• 1-morphisms A →B: pairs (P, f) with P ∈M a parameter object and
f : P ⊗A →B a morphism of C.
• Composition: (Q, g) ◦(P, f) = (P ⊗Q, g ◦(idQ ⊗f)); parameter objects
compose by tensor.
• 2-morphisms (P, f) ⇒(Q, g): reparameterisations r : P →Q in M such that
g ◦(r ⊗idA) = f.
• Identity: (I, ηA) with ηA : I ⊗A →A the left unitor of the actegory.
The bicategorical coherence data (associator, left/right unitors for composition) are
inherited from (M, ⊗, I) and the actegory action.
For BR’s pure-functional simulation, we take both C and M to be Hask (the total
fragment, following Assumption 12.1 in §12.2), with Cartesian product as tensor and
the actegory action P ⊗A = (P, A) (tuple type). A 1-morphism (P, f) : A →B then
corresponds, by currying, to a pair (a stored parameter value of type P, a pure Haskell
function of type P →A →B). The distinction from the operationally-effectful
target one might naturally reach for in a Haskell-side stochastic treatment (Para
over Kl(IO)) is exactly the distinction articulated in Remark 12.14: BR.SSA carries
its PRNG state as pure data, not as an IO effect.
12.6.2. The Para wrapper at the type level
The Para shape is a wrapper around any pure Haskell function plus its stored
parameter. The BR codebase does not introduce a named ParaMorphism type —
BR.SSA.simulate and BR.ODE.simulate are written as plain Haskell functions —
but each fits the Para shape once we identify the parameter explicitly. For pedagogical
clarity we display the wrapper that makes the Para structure explicit:
The Para shape over Hask (categorical view; not a BR module)

{ pmParams :: !p
, pmApply

(Q, g) o (P, f) = (P x Q, (p, q) a →g q (f p a)).

Remark 12.18 (Why no monad laws appear). The corresponding result for Para(Kl(T))
over a Kleisli category invokes the monad’s left-/right-unit and associativity laws
to verify the underlying-morphism equalities. In Para(Hask) no monad is present:
composition is plain function composition, and the underlying-morphism equalities
are strict identities of Haskell terms. The bicategorical coherence remains at the
parameter-tensor layer. This is the Para counterpart of the “pure-functional rather
than Kleisli” choice articulated in Remark 12.14.
Remark 12.19 (Structural unity, continued). Capucci–Myers [320] (discussed in §12.2,
Remark 12.6) place Para(C) and Kl(T) as instances of a single abstract construction.
This shared structural placement is the reason a functor Φop : Para(L3) →Hask
(§12.7) can be expected to exist naturally rather than as an ad-hoc construction; we
invoke this structural background implicitly but do not develop it further here.

of an L3 arrow and the exact dynamics it approximates; it is not part of

12.7.3. Corollary: Para applied to a chemical reaction simulation
Corollary 12.25 (Para applied to chemical reaction simulation). The construction
above exhibits the Para construction (Definition 12.16) applied to a chemical reaction

L3 sit as Para 1-morphisms at n = 1 and n = 0 in ParaW(Hask) respectively,
and seed-marginalisation by F produces Markov kernels in BorelStoch. Previously
published applications of the Para construction include machine learning [277, 322],
compositional game theory [313], and active inference [314]; to our knowledge no
prior treatment applies it to chemical reaction simulation.
§12.8. L4 →L3 projection: rate constants as scalar coarse-grainings and
model variants as comparable reductions
The most conceptually delicate aspect of the simulation functor of §12.7 is that L4
mechanism data appears inside the L3 parameter space. At first sight this violates
the tower’s level stratification — L4 bond-level information is supposed to be invisible
at L3. This section shows that the appearance is a parameter projection: the BR
simulation retains only the part of L4 data that survives as scalar rate constants
and, for channels with rate-limiting intermediates, the saturation form of the rate
law. The chapter’s several BR network variants are correspondingly different L3
reductions of the same underlying mechanism, comparable in BorelStoch via the
construction of §12.2.
12.8.1. The L4 content of BR’s rate constants
Level L4 is the category of open reaction networks with full bond-level mechanism
data: a morphism at L4 specifies the elementary-step mechanism (which bonds form
and break), the transition-state geometry, and the parameters determining kinetic
isotope effects, temperature dependence, and solvent dependence [158].
The BR mechanism in BR.Mechanism encodes the De Kepper–Epstein skeleton [35]
as briggsRauscherDE (10 elementary steps plus two explicit reverses; 12 channels).
Each channel is recorded as a Reaction value (§12.4) carrying three pieces of data
relevant to the L4 →L3 projection:
• rxnRate ::
Double — the scalar rate constant used by both BR.SSA and
BR.ODE.
• rxnSaturation ::
[(Species, Double)] — an optional rational denomina-
tor 1+P
i Ci[Si] in the rate law, non-empty only on channels with a rate-limiting
intermediate (e.g., R9 of [35], where I2 saturation supplies the negative feedback
that closes the limit cycle).
• rxnProvenance ::
RateProvenance — metadata tagging each rate as ei-
ther Measured (with a citation key to an independent kinetic study) or
FitToOscillate (the “judicious assignment” of [147]).

Proof. BR.SSA.simulate and BR.ODE.simulate compute propensities using the rate-
law fields rxnRateActive, rxnRate, and rxnSaturation, and update state using
the stoichiometric multisets rxnReactants and rxnProducts. No other reaction
data is consulted: rxnName is a label, and rxnProvenance is metadata visible to
the framework but not read by the rate or update logic. Full L4 mechanism data
(transition states, KIE-sensitivity, etc.) is not represented in the Reaction record
at all. Two L4 mechanisms for the same network whose π4-images agree — i.e.,
produce identical (rxnRate, rxnSaturation) per channel — therefore yield identical
propensities and identical ODE right-hand sides, hence identical simulator outputs
modulo PRNG and IEEE-754 qualifications.
Remark 12.29 (Provenance as a discriminator of L4-strength). The rxnProvenance
tag is L4-strength metadata: not used by the rate formula but visible to the frame-
work. A network all of whose rate constants are tagged Measured (independent
kinetic citations) is L4-strong: the simulation’s qualitative behaviour is not tuned by
free parameters. The 12 channels of briggsRauscherDE are currently all Measured,
making BR an L4-strong test bed within the chapter’s framework; oscillating reac-
tions requiring FitToOscillate constants would sit at a correspondingly weaker L4
strength.

Embedding into a common state space (union of dynamical species sets) is by
extension via Dirac mass on each variant’s pooled coordinates.
L3 reductions: predicted invariance and drift
The categorical framework predicts which BR observables should be invariant
under which L3 reductions:
• Onset preservation. Oscillation onset (the Hopf bifurcation) depends on
both the network’s L2 stoichiometric topology and the sign-pattern of
L3 Jacobian eigenvalues at the fixed point. Reductions that preserve the
autocatalytic feedback channels of the De Kepper–Epstein skeleton (in
particular broCODE5VarNetwork, designed for Hopf bifurcation analysis)
preserve the capacity for oscillation, even if the quantitative bifurcation
point shifts.
• Quantitative drift. Oscillation period and amplitude are L3-quantitative:
they depend on the rate constants retained by π4 together with which
species are dynamical. Variants whose netPoolSpecies removes feedback-
relevant species should show measurable drift in these observables.
• Falsification handle.

Remark 12.31 (What π4 cannot see, for BR). By construction π4 retains only the
scalar rate constant, saturation list, and provenance tag per channel. It drops:
(i) the full elementary-step mechanism (which bonds form and break in each
channel; concerted versus stepwise pathways; radical versus closed-shell inter-
mediates);
(ii) kinetic isotope effects — the rate change under H →D substitution at the
methylene hydrogens of malonic acid (predicted by transition-state theory but
invisible to a scalar rxnRate);
(iii) solvent and ionic-strength dependence beyond the reference conditions absorbed
into rxnRate;
(iv) pressure dependence and any temperature dependence not captured by rxnRate
at the reference temperature.
Any two BR mechanisms agreeing on the dynamical pair (rxnRate, rxnSaturation)
per channel are indistinguishable in the simulation, whether or not their provenance
tags agree (Proposition 12.28; rxnProvenance is metadata, not consulted by the
rate or update logic). This is the L3 →L4 forcing pair of the main tower applied to
inorganic oscillating chemistry — an honest categorical consequence of π4’s range,
not an implementation deficit. Recovery of the dropped data requires either a
higher-detail simulator operating at L4 (mechanism-resolved) or experimental inputs
(KIE measurement, pressure-jump kinetics) whose results would re-parameterise the
L3 scalar at the new reference conditions.
This closes the theoretical development of the chapter. The operational functor
Φop (§12.7) is parameterised by (46), with π4 projecting all L4 information through
a three-component coarse representation; BR’s network variants are different L3
realisations comparable as Markov kernels via (47). The simulation results of §12.9
test these constructions against the briggsRauscherDE network running under the
conditions of [35].

The empirical question is not whether the framework runs — by construction Φop

(P1) The oscillator emerges. Both simulators — the SSA sampling FBR and the

metric predicted in §12.2 and §12.5.

the framework supplies the reason: the ODE realises the V →∞Kurtz limit,
and at V = 10−15 L this limit represents quiescent populations of low-copy

individual realisation.

The third bullet is the most pedagogically informative observation in the section.
The ODE quiescent floors are not numerical artifacts: they are the analytical solution
of the rate equations in the time-asymptotic limit between spikes, and they are
correct as Kurtz-limit ensemble means. At V = 10−15 L, however, an ensemble
mean of 6 × 10−5 MnOH2+ molecules represents a distribution in which essentially
every individual realisation has zero molecules during quiescence, with rare single-
molecule visits. The SSA shows this directly: most realisations have zero MnOH2+
molecules during the quiescent phase, with occasional single-molecule excursions.

12.9.5. Closing
The simulation results do not validate the framework in any absolute sense: a
framework with no empirical content can pass unfalsified by any data. What the
figures establish instead is that the framework’s predictions for BR are structurally
distinguishable from the generic statement “the simulator produces some output”. The
kernel FBR := F(Φop(briggsRauscherDE)) ∈BorelStoch is a specific mathematical
object computed via the construction of §§12.2–12.8; its SSA samples and its ODE
Kurtz limit are two operational evaluations of this object (the SSA samples FBR
directly; the ODE realises its species-mean Kurtz limit), and their visible structural
difference at the chosen volume is the chapter’s γ-cell decomposition in concrete
form.
The framework earns its keep here in three concrete ways:
(1) It predicts. The SSA samples and ODE Kurtz limit must differ in low-copy
regions of state space, with the form of the difference determined by which
semantic layer (exact CTMC vs. V →∞Kurtz limit) is being evaluated. The
figures confirm this. The prediction could have failed in several ways — the
two simulators could have agreed in the quiescent phase, the ODE could have
failed to oscillate while the SSA succeeded (or vice versa), the peak amplitudes
could have differed by orders of magnitude — and none did.
(2) It supplies vocabulary.
Every numerical claim in this section is locatable
in the chapter’s framework decomposition: V is a user-chosen simulation
parameter (separate from Θsim); Θsim contains the parameterisation and network
variant; the simulator type selects between the SSA and ODE morphisms in
ParaW(Hask); the kernel FBR is the derived BorelStoch-object; γODE is the
Kurtz-limit deviation; the discrete quiescent-phase chatter is L3-stochastic
truth that the framework’s L3-deterministic representation cannot capture
at finite V . This decomposition is tacit in standard simulation practice; the
framework makes it explicit.

(3) It equips. Proposition 12.30 embeds every BR variant into BorelStoch via

The variant comparisons, KIE prediction, and volume sweep listed above are
the natural next steps; the machinery to perform them is in place.
The classical chemical phenomena of the Briggs–Rauscher oscillator — period,
amplitude, autocatalytic feedback, the distinction between the spike and quiescent
phases — emerge through this framework. What the framework adds is the discipline
of distinguishing three categories.
Essential features — such as the oscillation
onset itself — are tied to the L2 stoichiometric feedback topology and the L3
Jacobian sign-pattern; they survive across both simulators and would survive across
network variants retaining the autocatalytic skeleton.
Tunable features — the
oscillation period (∼103 s at the chosen parameterisation) and spike amplitudes —
are physical functionals of the L3 rate constants and the π4-coarse L4 data of §12.8;
re-parameterising to classical batch BR conditions would shift them continuously to
the experimental 30–60 s regime. Scale-dependent representational artifacts — the
smooth ODE quiescent floors at ∼10−13 M for MnOH2+, and the ∼15% SSA-vs-ODE
period shift — are not chemistry but artifacts of evaluating an essentially-discrete
process through its continuous Kurtz limit. The floor values are valid ensemble
means at all V but acquire physical referents (as occupied discrete states) only at
sufficiently large V ; at V = 10−15 L they correspond to sub-unity counts that no
individual realisation can occupy. The 15% drift, distinct in V-dependence, is a γODE
residual that vanishes as V →∞by the Kurtz theorem [106]. Both manifest at
V = 10−15 L because the volume is too small for the continuous limit to be faithful
to individual discrete trajectories.
This tripartite separation is tacit in standard simulation practice; the framework
makes it explicit. Simulator outputs then become inputs to inference about chemistry
— the essential-versus-tunable boundary is what falsification tests should target; the
scale-dependent representational artifacts are what should be disregarded — rather
than illustrations of dynamics in which all three categories are silently conflated.

§13.1. The tower in retrospect
This monograph constructed a canonical tower

of categorical levels for chemical reactions, each step forced from the one below by a
non-trivial cokernel in the automorphism exact sequence

but the lower-level forgetful functor Uk collapses (Proposition 6.26 at k = 1, . . . , 4;
§7.1, §8.7, §9.7, §10.1 at the remaining levels). A perpendicular Para dimension
(Chapter 11) classifies machine-learning architectures for chemistry as parametric

Three rules from undergraduate chemistry became provable theorems within the tower.
Hess’s Law is the functoriality of FH : L0(P) →(R, +): the equality FH(r2 ◦r1) =
FH(r2) + FH(r1) is the monoidal-functor condition, not an empirical observation
(Chapter 3). Walden inversion is the statement that the permutation πχ ∈Aut(L4(P))
exchanging the (R)- and (S)-enantiomers has no preimage in Aut(L4.5(P)) under
φ4.5: the chirality-flipping generator E∗∈G∗(G) = Aut(G) ⋊Zk
2 separates the
enantiomers as objects of L4.5 (Theorem 7.27). The Longuet–Higgins sign change is
the non-vanishing of the first Stiefel–Whitney class w1(LR0) ∈H1(Ce(G)\ΣCI, Z/2) of
the real ground-state eigenline on loops linking the codimension-2 conical-intersection
seam (§9.3); the complex Chern class c1(L0) ∈H2 is the codimension-matched
companion.
The forcing argument is structural. At each level, the unique minimal categorical
extension with non-trivial coker(φk) for the relevant reaction pair produces, as a
theorem, what was previously only a rule. The rules did not become theorems
because the mathematics was sharpened. They became theorems because the level
was made explicit.
§13.2. A taxonomy of extension types
The nine constructions L0, L1, . . . , L7 are not nine independent acts of imagination.
With the full tower in view, they fall into seven types, distinguished by the kind of
categorical operation each performs; this classification could not be stated before all
levels were available.
The seven extension types
I (Free construction). L0 is the free symmetric monoidal category on the
Petri net of a reaction system (Meseguer–Montanari). Every subsequent level is
an extension of this base.

§13.3. Open constructions
Five constructions raised in the body remain open; each has a precise statement,
identified ingredients, and known obstructions.
C1: The continuous field for molecules. Construct {Aε}ε∈[0,1] with A0 =
C0(Ce(G)) and Aε the full molecular C∗-algebra, satisfying the Rieffel conditions [234].
The Panati–Spohn–Teufel space-adiabatic perturbation theory [179], the Hagedorn–
Joye asymptotic theory [165], the Landsman tangent groupoid construction [240],
and the Georgescu–Iftimovici N-body framework [323] are all in place; no paper has
assembled them into a single C∗-algebraic framework for molecules.

Proximity to resolution
O1 and O2 are within reach with currently available tools: ingredients in place,
construction pending. C2 needs a single synthesis step. C3 requires a new
technical ingredient — the seam blow-up — but the surrounding framework is
clear. C1 is the deepest: it requires C2, C3, and a resolution of the Coulomb
singularity problem, and is the correct formulation of what it would mean to
complete the L6 99K L7 step.
§13.4. Outlook
The tower has implications for three communities not previously in close contact.
For chemical reaction network theory. The Feinberg deficiency theory and
the Craciun–Yu and Anderson–Shiu multistationarity results sit entirely within L0
(combinatorial hypotheses) and L3 (dynamical conclusions). The tower makes this
level gap explicit for the first time and suggests, via O1, a homological proof of the
Deficiency Zero Theorem that would place these landmark results inside a categorical
framework rather than leaving them as isolated facts. The open mechanistic network
construction O2 extends Baez–Pollard grey-boxing from L3 to L4, giving an algebraic
foundation for compositional analysis of reaction mechanisms.
For machine learning in chemistry. The Para dimension answers a question that
becomes urgent as ML models for chemistry scale: what does it mean for a model
to be physically correct at a given level? The answer is architectural: a model is
physically correct at Lk if and only if the level-k exact functor factors through it. The
equivariance groups grow monotonically through the tower: Sym(S) at L0, Aut(G) at
L4, G∗(G) at L4.5, SE(3)⋊Autµ(G) at L5, and the U(N) structure of the active Hilbert
bundle at L6. A model whose architecture respects only the L5 group cannot represent
L6 phenomena: there is no slot for the line-bundle holonomy that distinguishes
adiabatic from non-adiabatic dynamics — this is the architectural barrier currently
separating photocatalysis and conical-intersection chemistry from the mainstream
ML-for-chemistry stack.
Chapter 12 supplies one concrete executable instance:
the simulation functor Φop : Para(L0 ⊗L1 ⊗L2 ⊗L3) →Kl(IO) composed with
the denotational realisation F into the Markov category BorelStoch (Fritz [103]),
applied to the Briggs–Rauscher oscillator with the φ-cell distinction between exact
CTMC and Kurtz-limit ODE made operational (§12.9).
For mathematical chemistry and mathematical physics. The constructions
C1–C3 would collectively provide the first rigorous categorical treatment of the
Born–Oppenheimer approximation as a limit rather than an ansatz. The Landsman–
Rieffel–Georgescu–Hagedorn–PST literature has reached a point where all ingredients
are available; the obstacle is synthesis rather than any single missing result. O1,

conversely, would connect classical CRNT to homological algebra in a way that has
been suspected since Feinberg’s earliest papers but never made precise.
§13.5. Coda
A hydrogen atom transfers from carbon to oxygen in an enzyme active site. Whether
that transfer is governed by classical barrier-crossing or by quantum tunnelling
depends on which level of the tower the question is posed at. The enzyme does not
know which level the chemist is using. It operates at all of them simultaneously.
The tower does not add new chemistry. Hess’s Law was not more true after FH was
defined. Walden inversion was not more real after the cokernel argument identified it
as a non-trivial automorphism class. The retinal photoisomerisation was not faster
because the Stiefel–Whitney class was computed around the conical-intersection
seam. What the tower adds is precision: each chemical fact is now located at the
unique level where it can be expressed, and the tools available at that level are
exactly those needed to prove it.
Chemistry’s rules are not wrong.
Their exceptions are not failures.
They are
coordinates. The tower is the coordinate system.
The central result of this monograph is negative in form but positive in content.
Negative: no single category suffices to express all of chemistry. Positive: the minimal
number of categories needed, their order, and the unique forcing pair that makes
each one necessary — this is determined, not chosen.
The map is forced.
